News.title: Reform UK promises £80bn cuts to public spending
News.content:
Jenrick is due to give a major speech to the conference on Saturday but speaking at a fringe event with journalist Allister Heath, he sought to reassure voters that Reform's policies would be affordable.

He said it was important to "learn the lessons of [former Prime Minister] Liz Truss" who he said "basically went into a sweetie shop, took everything off the shelves and stuck it into a budget".

"Quite rightly the markets reacted very negatively to that."

Jenrick was a health minister in 2022 when Truss's plan to deliver large energy bill subsidies and Â£45bn shook market confidence in the UK's financial credibility.

Reform has previously said it wanted to cut inheritance tax but Jenrick suggested that would not be a priority, arguing relatively few people were affected by it.

"It's a bold chancellor that would say I'd rather privilege 36,000 families than 40 million [income] taxpayers," he said.

He said his party would retain the triple lock - the mechanism which ensures pensions rise by either 2.5%, the rate of inflation or the rate of average earnings, whichever is highest.

The triple lock is estimated to cost Â£15.5bn per year by 2030 but Jenrick said he could not look pensioners "in the eye" and cut their income "while there is so much waste in the public sector".

He said it would be "fundamentally unfair going to pensions before we have made hard choices elsewhere".

Jenrick has written to investors who hold government debt to set up meetings in London and New York to discuss what fiscal rules he would set with the aim of reducing the cost of borrowing.

The past few days have seen global borrowing costs rise, with the UK's costs increasing to a 28-year high.

Also speaking at the conference, the party's business spokesman Richard Tice set out a number of proposals aimed at increasing house building on brownfield sites - land that has previously been built on.

He said the party would consult on measures including scrapping stamp duty, capital gains tax and tax on rental income for a decade for homes built on brownfield sites.

Under the proposals, affordable housing requirements would be removed for brownfield developments outside major cities.

The party's policy document says its plans would reduce tax receipts but argued that additional homes built as a result would boost the economy.

Tice has also suggested cutting business rates for high street shops, offsetting the cost by increasing the tax for online retailers.

Reform's conference at the Birmingham NEC comes at the end of a turbulent summer which saw its leader Nigel Farage resign and then re-run in his Clacton constituency in a bid to end questions about a Â£5m gift he received before becoming an MP.

There is also a police investigation into donations made to the party.

The main business of the conference is expected to take place on Friday and Saturday, with speeches from Farage and other senior figures, as well as an address by the leader of the French far right National Rally party, Jordan Bardella.

News.title: Badenoch accuses Burnham of kicking defence spending into the long grass
News.content:
Badenoch repeated existing Conservative plans to fund an increase in defence spending, including by reimposing the two-child benefit cap.

The cap, which was scrapped by Labour in April, meant parents could only claim universal credit or tax credits for their first two children.

She said the final part of her party's plans to reach the 3% spending figure on defence had now been completed.

The Tories said this would include saving at least Â£4bn through reforms to housing benefit and removing the VAT exemption for Motability vehicles, saving Â£1bn.

"Alongside savings from the disastrous Chagos deal and re-purposing money from the British Business Bank into defence, we will be able to hit that 3% target," Badenoch said.

Housing benefit made up about 12% of the government's welfare bill this year, with Â£37.3bn forecast to be spent.

The Motability scheme, operated by a private company overseen by a charity, has historically given disabled people in receipt of eligible welfare benefits a 20% VAT discount on cars.

Last year, Rachel Reeves made the first changes to the Motability scheme in 50 years, removing about 50,000 premium cars like BMWs and Mercedes from the scheme and reinstating 20% VAT for most new cars, along with higher mileage charges.

Challenged over whether she was increasing child poverty to fund defence by reimposing the two-child benefit cap, Badenoch denied this.

"It is not going to increase child poverty. What increases child poverty is children's parents not having work or being paid low wages. We want to grow our economy," she told the BBC.

"Right now there are some people making choices not to have children because they can't afford it and paying for other people to have more children. That is not fair."

Responding to Badenoch's speech, a Labour Party spokesperson said: "These unserious plans are hardly surprising from the same Tory Party that hollowed out our Armed Forces, shrinking the British Army to its smallest size since the Napoleonic era.

"Andy Burnham has made it clear that his Labour government is determined to give our Armed Forces the investment needed to keep us safe.

"In just two years, Labour has delivered the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War, with funding already higher than at any point during 14 years of Conservative government."

It comes after Badenoch pressed Burnham over the issue during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, when she urged him to cut welfare spending and invest the money in defence.

Burnham also came under friendly fire from Labour MP Tan Dhesi at PMQs, who called on the prime minister to urgently commit to setting out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

"Defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just isn't going to be enough," he said.

Burnham has insisted his government is committed to fully funding its defence plans, saying it will set out a pathway to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 in the spring.

News.title: Watch: Gloria Steinem dedicated her life to fight for women's equality
News.content:
Gloria Steinem spent more than 60 years as one of the most prominent voices in the fight for women's rights.

She launched herself into the mainstream in the 1960s with an expose of New York City's Playboy Club, documenting the harsh conditions she faced working undercover as a Playboy Bunny.

A powerful and outspoken campaigner at a time of routine discrimination, Steinem faced sexist criticism and harassment from men throughout her long career.

Her lifelong battle saw many victories, including the US Supreme Court's 1973 Roe v Wade decision that guaranteed a woman's right to an abortion.

It also saw setbacks, like that same decision being overturned in 2022.

The feminist icon died on Wednesday at the age of 92, her foundation said in a statement. She never retired.

More on this story here.

News.title: Fifa accuses Uefa of 'smear campaign' against Infantino
News.content:
Fifa has accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" over president Gianni Infantino's scrapped plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Last week European football's governing body filed legal papers in the US requesting disclosure of evidence and documents from Fifa as part of potential criminal claims in Switzerland.

In a dramatic escalation of the controversy, Uefa accused Infantino of "criminal mismanagement" and "a fraudulently off-market price promoted by [him] for his own benefit" over the now-shelved Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme.

However, world governing body Fifa has now responded with court filings lodged in the US - and seen by the BBC - requesting that a court "oppose" the application by the end of the month.

Fifa claims Uefa's argument "suffers from a fundamental defect" and "legal deficiencies".

It said it had "made clear" that the creation of FFE was "only a proposal", adding that it could have only proceeded on the condition that the majority of member associations supported it and "the relevant approvals of the Fifa Council".

"Rather than participate in that democratic process, Uefa issued a press release - the beginning of a weeks-long smear campaign against Fifa and its leadership," it wrote in the court filing.

It also claimed that Uefa's "economic motivation" was to prevent smaller countries from having the "financial strength to compete with the European elite".

"If soccer is strengthened in the developing world, global competition increases, which ultimately reduces Uefa's market power and provides more competition for its flagship tournaments," Fifa said.

"By raising funds to allow some of Fifa's smaller member associations to better develop soccer, FFE would lead to more players from those nations choosing to represent their countries of origin and playing in their home leagues rather than playing abroad."

Uefa has been approached for comment. It has led the rebellion against the Fifa president, who is facing calls to stand down from three confederations.

Uefa has also asked a court in New York to approve a legal document ordering testimony and documents from venture capitalist Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, who was set to be the lead investor in FFE, and his company Thrive Eternal.

Thrive had held talks with Infantino about heading up a $4.2bn (Â£3.1bn) investment in 20% of a new Fifa commercial subsidiary, before the idea was abandoned days after it was revealed in July amid a huge backlash.

At the time, Fifa claimed FFE would have increased the funding distributed to each national association for the 2027-2030 cycle from Â£5.9m to Â£14.7m.

On Sunday, Kushner expressed regret over FFE, saying: "While we stand behind the motivations of FFE, we failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football, and the lengths some would go toâ¦ had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved."

Uefa has also asked for the disclosure of documents from American financier Greg Maffei, who was a key adviser on the deal.

While Uefa says neither Kushner nor Maffei are anticipated defendants in any legal proceedings, it claims the pair first discussed the FFE concept in July 2025 and that Infantino had "been discussing the underlying concept with Kushner for nearly a year before the terms sheet was ultimately signed".

Its lawyers also argue the World Cup was deliberately undervalued at about Â£15bn, which it says is "a figure that was neither the product of an open, competitive auction, nor tested by any independent valuer". Uefa claims Infantino failed to consult Fifa's hierarchy over the plan.

News.title: Trump hints US would not back UK over Falkland Islands due to lack of Iran war support
News.content:
Donald Trump has hinted he would not come to the UK's aid in a potential future conflict with Argentina over the Falkland Islands.

In an interview with GB News, the US president said that Britain had "not been there to help me" with his country's war with Iran, despite later saying his military did not need any support.

Trump's latest remarks come after he previously said the US could revise its neutral position on the islands' sovereignty if the UK failed to increase defence spending.

Argentinian President Javier Milei is due to make a televised statement on Thursday night about what he describes as his nation's "historic" claim to the islands.

The Falklands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina, more than 40 years on from an armed conflict over the territory.

When asked if he would "come to the UK's aid" during a potential territorial dispute, Trump told GB News: "Well look, I was there when they had the first war.

"That was a long time ago and I watched it so carefully, and you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly, but it's a long way away."

Turning his attention to the US' current conflict with Iran, he added: "So, your country's not doing well. Don't forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren't there to help me.

"Your country was not there to help me. We didn't need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, 'why didn't you send a couple of ships?'

Trump said the-then prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer, told him no vessels were available, which "was pretty sad", he added.

He also said: "Nato was not there, even though they get â most of those countries get â a big portion of their oil from there. So we're doing that by ourselves".

Argentina and the UK waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.

Seventy-four days of fighting led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.

Trump's comments come after he was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the islands.

The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."

The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".

A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."

In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

News.title: US billionaire Leon Black defies summons and sues Epstein panel
News.content:
Billionaire investor Leon Black has failed to appear before a US congressional committee investigating the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein - instead filing a lawsuit challenging the committee's efforts to summon him.

The lawsuit calls the subpoenas issued by the House Oversight Committee "invalid" and says they hold "no legitimate connection" to the committee's legislative aim.

Black walked out of the committee in June while giving voluntary testimony after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time.

Black has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein.

The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June.

His lawsuit opposing these summonses, which was filed in federal court in Washington on Thursday, argued that revealing the NDAs might "expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it".

NDAs are contracts where both parties agree to keep information confidential, often as part of a settlement or employment agreement.

"This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr Black," Susan Estrich, an attorney for Black, said in a press release on Thursday.

"We were left with no choice but to file this lawsuit in response to an abuse of Congressional power."

News.title: Households warned gas price spike could pile fresh pressure on energy bills
News.content:
Households across the UK are being warned to brace for higher energy bills this winter as European countries scramble to replenish their natural gas stores before the weather dips.

Wholesale natural gas prices are already at three-year highs, which could lead to increased energy bills for businesses and consumers.

Europe, which delayed its summer stockpiling due to high wholesale costs sparked by the Iran war, had been gambling the conflict would end before winter and prices would in turn fall.

Storage levels are significantly lower than usual for this time of year, with countries facing the prospect of rushing to buy gas now or paying potentially higher prices when the winter comes.

The European benchmark natural gas price topped â¬75/MWh on Wednesday, its highest level since late 2022, the tail end of a spike caused by Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Natural gas prices in the UK this week topped 185p per therm, also the highest since late 2022.

The price has jumped in the past week amid a return to hostilities between the US and Iran, with analysts fearing the renewed fighting will keep the key Strait of Hormuz closed even longer. Typically, around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) is transported through the waterway.

Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said he did not expect the waterway to begin reopening until early 2027.

Even then, there will be a lag before energy is flowing freely through the strait and pressure on energy prices are eased.

"The risks to gas prices are definitely tilted towards the upside," Hussain told the BBC, warning that the gas price would top â¬80 by the end of this year.

Hussain recalled interviews with gas storage operators at the outbreak of the US-Israeli war in Iran saying they would wait three to four months for the crisis to ease before stocking up.

"We are about six months into the strait being effectively closed and that obviously has not happened," he added.

Higher wholesale gas prices feed through to household energy bills by helping determine regulator Ofgem's price cap.

The energy price cap rose in July, and will increase by 4% in October, leaving a typical household paying Â£1,723. But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices could rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households during the coldest months.

Dr Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, told the BBC on Thursday a fresh increase in wholesale prices would "increase pressure on our January price cap forecast".

However, he cautioned that there was "plenty of time to go" and a fall in wholesale prices could ease the pressure.

News.title: Pupil who stabbed teacher in head given four-year detention order
News.content:
A pupil who stabbed a teacher in the head with a kitchen knife after asking her to check his homework has been sentenced to four-and-a-half years in youth detention.

The 16-year-old boy followed Vicki Williams into her empty classroom at Milford Haven Comprehensive School, Pembrokeshire, after asking for help with his work on 5 February.

The teenager pulled a knife from his bag and lunged at her, Swansea Crown Court previously heard, with Williams saying she feared she would die.

After the trial in July, he was found not guilty of attempted murder but guilty of wounding with intent.

On Thursday, Judge Thomas told the court there was a "significant degree of planning" and that "time stood still" for Williams.

During the trial, Williams said the attack "came out of nowhere" after the boy - who cannot be named due to a court order - asked her for help with his work at the end of the school day.

He closed the classroom door behind him and Williams noticed him looking through his bag as he asked her if his work "was correct".

She said he suddenly pulled a large kitchen knife from the bag, and stabbed her in her head.

Williams grabbed the knife, pushed the boy back with her legs, and screamed.

She had injuries to her head, back and hands and said the boy looked at her with "pure hatred".

News.title: Zack Polanski says he'll run for former PM Starmer's seat in by-election
News.content:
Green Party leader Zack Polanski has confirmed he wants to stand in the by-election brought about by Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as an MP.

Polanski, who is currently a London Assembly member but not a member of Parliament, said he was "so excited by the prospect" of being the first Green MP for Holborn and St Pancras.

The Greens are targeting the seat, until now a Labour stronghold, after coming second to Labour in the area in local elections earlier this year.

Sir Keir announced on Tuesday that he was quitting as MP for the London constituency, two months after he stood down as prime minister, setting up a challenging by-election for his successor Andy Burnham.

In comments to the Camden New Journal, external on Thursday morning, Polanski said: "I have lived and worked in this community over many years, I know it well and I love it."

"It's a clear fight between Labour and the Green Party," he added.

Polanski has already been out campaigning in the constituency despite there being no decision on who the Green candidate will be until next week.

In an interview with the BBC, he said: "We had a huge surge here in [local elections] in May. This is somewhere we can win."

He said he wanted to be the Greens' sixth MP so he could "challenge Burnham constructively".

In order to officially be the Green candidate for the seat, Polanski needs to be selected by local party members - something his comments suggest will happen.

But there have been reports in recent days of splits among local Green activists, some of whom are said to favour a Palestinian candidate or a pro-Gaza independent.

Andrew Feinstein, the independent runner-up to Sir Keir in the constituency at the 2024 general election, has appeared to back Polanski's candidacy as he ruled out running himself.

Writing on X, Feinstein said: "Unfortunately I am not in a position to stand this time round."

He said the Camden People's Alliance will meet next week to formally decide its position, adding: "This is a crucial time for progressives in Camden and across the country to be united."

A date has not yet been set for the by-election.

The stakes were already high for Labour at this by-election, because it offers an early test of Burnham's ability to stave off the Green threat in inner-city constituencies.

With Polanski's candidacy, the stakes are even higher for the Greens, to see whether they make good on their leader's oft-stated ambition to replace Labour.

Polanski said a Green victory would be a "clear message that we won't sit by as we get poorer and extreme wealth is concentrated at the very top".

The London Assembly, on which Polanski currently sits, is an elected body of 25 representatives who scrutinise the policies of the mayor of London.

News.title: Bid to withhold MI5 information from synagogue attack inquests
News.content:
The Government has applied to block some MI5 information relating to the fatal Manchester synagogue attack from being heard in public, a court has heard.

A pre-inquest hearing at Manchester Coroner's Court was told the Home Office wanted the information to be withheld when the inquests into the deaths of Adrian Daulby, 53, and Melvin Cravitz, 66, are held next year.

Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, a Syrian-born British citizen, drove into the gates of the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in Manchester on 2 October last year.

He then began attacking with a knife, while wearing a fake suicide belt.

Cravitz died from multiple knife wounds while Daulby was killed by a bullet fired by armed police scrambled to the scene. He was hit as he blocked the synagogue doors to stop Al-Shamie getting in.

The hearing earlier was told by Neil Sheldon KC, representing the Home Office, that making public the information held by MI5 would put national security at risk.

He said: "The Secretary of State asserts that disclosure would harm national security."

But lawyers for the families of the victims said the Government's attempt to withhold the information, through a Public Interest Immunity application, was in "contradiction" to statements made after the attack.

The family lawyers cited statements made by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood and counter-terror police bosses that terrorist Al-Shamie was not on their radar and unknown to them.

Victoria Ailes, representing the Cravitz family, told Judge Alexia Durran, Chief Coroner of England and Wales: "We would respectfully suggest the interest in open justice is heightened."

Anna Morris KC, representing the Daulby family, said there had been a "demonstrable lack of candour" by the security services in "other proceedings".

She said the Daulby family were also concerned that this application and information might contradict statements made publicly that the terrorist was not known to counter terror policing or the security services.

The Daulby family expected a "rigorous investigation" into his death and the family had concerns about any delay in proceedings and "procedural rights", she added.

News.title: Thieves steal 70,000 pints of Guinness in two lorries
News.content:
Thieves have stolen more than 800 barrels of Guinness by driving off from a depot with two HGV trailers.

About 70,000 pints worth of the stout, estimated to be worth Â£115,000, were taken from Whitehouse Industrial Estate on Aston Lane in Runcorn on Monday, Cheshire Police said.

One wagon-load was taken at about 19:45 BST and a second one was stolen at about 21:30.

The stolen barrels - which each would hold about 88 pints - had been destined for pubs, the force added.

Det Sgt McClatchy said: "It is famously said that 'Guinness is good for you', but that is only the case when it has been bought and paid for."

News.title: Fans praise Catherine Zeta-Jones for using her Welsh accent in new series
News.content:
Catherine Zeta-Jones has been praised by fans as she uses her natural Welsh accent in an upcoming thriller series.

The 56-year-old Hollywood actor returned to her hometown of Swansea, where some of the filming took place for Amazon's Kill Jackie.

A trailer released on social media gives viewers their first glimpse of the show, as well as a snippet of Zeta-Jones using her Swansea accent.

The Oscar-winning star plays Jackie Price, an extravagant jet-setter who is trying to stay anonymous after escaping a "dangerous past as an international cocaine dealer," according to Amazon Prime.

One fan said they loved hearing the "queen of Wales sounding Welsh".

News.title: Helicopters to be put on standby when wildfire risk is high
News.content:
The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) will be able to put helicopters on standby when there is a heightened risk of wildfires, the justice secretary has said.

Neil Gray said aerial water bombing was a key part of the effort to deal with a major blaze in the Cairngorms this summer, but helicopters were not available until about 36 hours after the fire broke out.

He said SFRS would be able to use a current contractual framework to prepare commercial helicopters to be mobilised when they might be needed.

Gray also called for England, Wales and Northern Ireland to work with Scotland to deal with an "increased risk" of wildfires caused by climate change.

News.title: 'Naive' police staff who leaked information jailed
News.content:
Prosecuting, Helen Rodger said each had a sexual relationship with men involved in crime, and should have known that these were "disclosable associations".

The first time Doherty accessed information about an incident and passed it on to Robbie Braddock, with whom she was said to be in a relationship, was in December 2023, roughly two months after she completed her control room training.

Doherty shared details about the incident, a fight in which another male had smashed a window, with Braddock.

Rodger said a second incident involving Doherty on 6 March 2024, saw her access details about a search warrant being executed and pass on details about it to the same man as before.

Doherty viewed the details of the incident several times before also checking who was in custody at Ripley custody suite.

Fitzhugh, who was also said to be in a relationship with a man with a criminal record, looked up incidents in spring 2024, out of what the judge called "idle curiosity".

The two women, who met while both working at McDonald's before starting with the force, sat apart in the dock and were accompanied in court by their families.

Spencer speculated that maybe their "friendship has not survived this case" and said "I have little doubt that it will haunt you for the rest of your days".

He said: "It's impossible to recognise the young women who I read about, with such positive qualities, in the women who committed these offences."

Defending Fitzhugh, Elizabeth Power said she had a "lack of awareness" about the "severity of the breaches that she made".

Lowri Butterworth, for Doherty, told the court that she was "acutely aware" and had been using her time since to "give back" to her community.

Both women were charged in April following an investigation led by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) after conduct referrals.

Emily Barry, from the IOPC, said Doherty admitted supplying information to a man with known links to crime within a few months of her joining the force.

"Call handlers are privy to sensitive information and have access to confidential data on police systems," she added.

"It's incumbent on them not to inappropriately disclose information and to only access material for policing purposes."

Barry said the pair were likely to be barred from working in policing again following respective misconduct hearings.

News.title: Are you relying on Social Security more or less than the average American?
News.content:
Social Security payments are the largest income source for retirees, according to a new analysis from Boston College.

Payments account for 30 percent of income for the average American aged 65 years or older, the analysis noted.

“The findings show that Social Security is a really important program for older Americans,” wrote Alicia H. Munnell, a senior retirement research advisor at Boston College. “It is doing its job.”

The lowest-income households rely on Social Security most, with payments making up a staggering 83 percent of their income.

The payments have a much smaller role for the recipients with the highest income - 12 percent.

Social Security payments started in 1942. Workers and employers pay into the system through taxes, and then the system uses that money to make monthly benefit payments to retirees ( AFP/Getty )

The data reveals that the country’s Social Security system is a lifeline for hundreds of thousands of older Americans. And that lifeline is on tenuous footing, according to experts.

Social Security payments started in 1942. Workers and employers pay into the system through taxes, and then the system uses that money to make monthly benefit payments to retirees.

In 1960, there were five workers for every retiree, according to think-tank Bipartisan Policy Center. That ratio meant there was plenty of money flowing into the Social Security Administration’s coffers.

But today, that ratio has dropped to 2.9 workers for every one retiree, the center said. By the 2070s, that ratio will fall to 2.2-to-1.

The Social Security system has had to draw more and more cash from its reserves to make payments meaning one source - the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance fund - is projected to run out by 2032.

That means significant cuts in how much the Social Security Administration pays the nation’s retirees, Bipartisan Policy Center points out.

“Unless Congress acts, current and future beneficiaries alike will see their benefits cut by 22%,” it wrote in a June analysis.

Lawmakers have floated solutions for the pending crisis but none have materialized. One focus is on the current limit on who pays Social Security taxes. Workers stop paying the taxes for any income above $184,500, according to the Internal Revenue Service.

Independent Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed legislation that would raise that limit to $250,000, offering a new source of funding that would help buoy the system’s financial state.

Part of the senator’s legislation also includes a $200 monthly payment boost for most Social Security recipients - the increase has been dubbed the “Bernie bump.”

But like other proposals, Sanders’ legislation has yet to pass votes in the House and Senate. Until then, think tanks and Americans are growing restless as Social Security’s 2032 doomsday gets closer.

“The longer Congress waits to act, the harder the fix becomes, and the greater the burden on retirees and taxpayers,” the Bipartisan Policy Center wrote.

News.content:

U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked his newly appointed CDC director to remove a reference to two Pennsylvania fatalities from the agency’s online measles tracker after questioning whether the virus contributed to the deaths, according to a new report.

Kennedy’s request came after staff at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had already accepted the state’s classification of the deaths as linked to measles, a Pennsylvania official stated.

Despite this, Erica Schwartz, the recently named director of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, agreed to Kennedy’s instruction and implemented it without raising objections, three anonymous sources familiar with the situation told Reuters.

The decision followed a contentious exchange on social media between Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist appointed by President Donald Trump, and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, a Democrat. Both officials blamed each other for politicizing the outbreak in Pennsylvania, the latest state to face a resurgence of measles since the Trump administration took office.

Figures from the CDC and individual state agencies indicate that vaccination rates have been falling, with several medical bodies citing growing vaccine hesitancy as a major factor. In Pennsylvania alone, the state health department has recorded 540 measles cases this year.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has made vaccine guidance a focal point of his second term ( AFP via Getty Images )

Georges Benjamin, chief executive of the American Public Health Association and former secretary of health in Maryland, said it is "unheard of" for the CDC to publicly express doubt over the determinations of state and local health departments, even if the agency wants further details.

"The secretary had no business interfering in the normal process," Benjamin said. "He has an anti-vaccine agenda and he's using this to play out his anti-vaccine agenda."

Grace Davis Jamison, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services which oversees the CDC, said the public health agency "requested details necessary to determine whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths." She pointed to conflicting reports between county and state health officials over what occurred. Jamison did not comment on the involvement of Kennedy or Schwartz in excluding the deaths. Schwartz did not respond to a request for comment.

For years, Kennedy has promoted the claim that vaccines are more dangerous than the diseases they prevent, despite decades of scientific evidence demonstrating that they save lives. The combined measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine routinely administered to children in the U.S. has been shown to offer 97% protection against infection.

As health secretary, Kennedy has sought to downplay the impact of growing U.S. measles cases, which are now at their highest level in over three decades. He has repeatedly cast doubt on whether the virus was directly linked to the several fatalities reported so far.

RFK Jr and Josh Shapiro’s heated exchange

The Pennsylvania health department informed the CDC of two measles-associated deaths on the morning of August 25 before publishing the update on its website, according to the Pennsylvania official, who is close to Shapiro.

Pennsylvania did not provide details regarding the circumstances of the fatalities other than stating that the two individuals were unvaccinated. The CDC raised no concerns regarding the information it received and "signified its ongoing support for the (state health) department’s efforts," the official noted.

open image in gallery Shapiro (pictured) and RFK Jr. have accused each other of politicizing the outbreak in Pennsylvania, the latest state to grapple with a resurgence of measles since the Trump administration took office ( AFP via Getty Images )

Kennedy phoned Shapiro later that day to offer federal assistance to help manage the state’s outbreak, the governor stated at a press conference. Shapiro said he thanked Kennedy and noted that the state had initiated a strong response, including existing help from CDC and HHS personnel, but added he would contact the secretary if further assistance was required.

Shapiro also noted he told Kennedy that the health secretary’s previous statements fueled conspiracy theories and misinformation regarding vaccine safety, "having a negative impact on communities across America."

Kennedy responded on X the following day, August 26, accusing Shapiro of failing to share details with the CDC and questioning whether the deaths were "altogether fabricated by one of the Governor’s hopeful staffers."

That same day, officials from the Pennsylvania health department discussed aspects of the two cases with the CDC, the official close to Shapiro said. The CDC requested medical records containing personally identifiable information about the deceased, which state law prohibits officials from sharing, the official explained. The state offered to supply additional anonymized data, but the federal agency has not completed the necessary paperwork, the official added.

A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania health department stated that the state has "provided all required epidemiological data to the CDC."

On Friday, the CDC delayed its regular weekly update to its measles data webpage. When the page was updated on Sunday, it omitted the Pennsylvania deaths and added an asterisk to its mortality table with the following note: "At this time, available information does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the (Pennsylvania) deaths or whether the individuals died from other causes while infected with measles."

The CDC has not detailed what information it will rely on to determine whether the Pennsylvania deaths were caused by measles, given that it is not collaborating with the state health department in its investigation.

A group of Good Samaritans in Pennsylvania rushed to free a woman trapped beneath a classic Volkswagen Beetle after her e-bike collided with the car, with the dramatic rescue captured on video.

The 44-year-old woman crashed into the Beetle Monday morning as it was turning right onto 11th Street from Lincoln Avenue in Prospect Park, ABC 6 reports. She became trapped beneath the vehicle, and her screams for help prompted nearby worker Christine Vollmer to rush to her aid.

"All I saw were the lady's legs from underneath the car," Vollmer told the outlet. She said she initially tried to lift the vehicle herself before calling 911 as others rushed over to help.

"Once I heard her scream, 'Help,' I just ran outside and tried to lift up the car by myself, and then other neighbors came out," Amelia Cannon of Nolet Home Care Agency, who also helped, told ABC 6.

As more people arrived, Vollmer realized they needed someone stronger to help lift the car.

open image in gallery A group of about half a dozen people rushed to lift a Volkswagen Beetle off an e-bike rider in Prospect Park, Pennsylvania, on Monday, as seen in newly released video footage ( ABC 6 )

"When I saw my delivery driver, I was like, 'Alright, he has muscles,'" she said.

FedEx driver Karl Wise was among those who joined the rescue effort.

"Picked up the Volkswagen Beetle on its side and drug the woman out and I told her, 'Don't move,'" Wise said.

Surveillance video and police body-camera footage released Thursday show about half a dozen people working together to lift the Beetle and free the woman.

The woman was taken to a nearby hospital with chest injuries, Prospect Park Chief Dave Madonna told ABC 7 Chicago. She is expected to be OK and was in stable condition Thursday.

open image in gallery The 44-year-old woman crashed into the Beetle as it was turning right onto 11th Street from Lincoln Avenue in Prospect Park ( ABC 6 )

Madonna credited the group's quick response with helping save the woman's life.

"No special equipment, no training, they just come over and use brute force to lift the vehicle off of the victim," Madonna told ABC 6. The police chief also pointed to the crash as an example of what he considers the dangers of e-bikes. Pennsylvania does not require e-bike riders to have a license or wear a helmet/

"How many more tragedies do we have to see before some type of action is taken?" Madonna said, calling for additional regulations.

Madonna later returned to the scene to thank those who helped.

"You stepped in and did what you had to do, so thank you," he told Cannon.

open image in gallery The e-biker remained in the hospital Thursday in stable condition, and is expected to be OK ( ABC 6 )

Despite the praise, Cannon said she only considers herself a normal person.

"I wouldn't say [I’m a] hero, I just helped someone in need," she said.

The Independent has contacted the Prospect Park Police Department for comment.

Ministers are putting the interests of Big Tech ahead of the public by spending billions on AI and not being transparent about its use, MPs and rights groups have warned.

The UK public sector has awarded more than 2,000 contracts for AI-related projects since 2018, totalling around £5bn of potential spending, according to analysis by consultancy Tussell.

While the cutting-edge tech has the ability to bring huge advantages in areas such as health, campaigners and MPs have warned that the government’s adoption of AI is opaque and unaccountable.

Jim Killock, executive director of the Open Rights Group, said that reports of efficiencies gained by using AI remain largely unproven, with the public “kept in the dark about how systems affect them”.

The Independent has reported on the problems with using AI facial age estimation technology on migrants, something the Home Office is spending hundreds of thousands of pounds to introduce at the UK border.

The UK government is also already using AI to make decisions about policing, housing and Universal Credit and asylum claims. For example, the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has been using machine learning to flag benefit claims as potentially fraudulent, however older claimants and non-UK nationals were being over referred for review, the National Audit Office said.

Elsewhere in the public sector, NHS England has come under scrutiny for a £330m contract with US-firm Palantir to link-up patient data across different locations.

The mayor of London Sadiq Khan blocked a £50m deal between the Met Police and Palantir in June this year, after questions were raised about how the US firm won the contract.

In a new paper published on Thursday, the Open Rights Group argue that government partnerships with private companies risk abuses of power.

The Home Office is using AI in asylum decision making and also using AI facial estimation techn to judge the age of asylum seekers ( AFP/Getty )

Liberal Democrat MP, Victoria Collins, who has written a foreword for the report, said the “burden of identifying and challenging harmful AI systems must not fall to individual members of the public”, adding: “That responsibility belongs to the government and to the industry with which it partners”.

Dr Allison Gardner, Labour MP for Stoke-on-Trent South, said: “AI has the potential to benefit society and bring huge advances in areas such as health, but also to automate inequality and discrimination and harms.

“Clear regulation is vital so that the public can trust these technologies, particularly when used by the state in ways that affect their lives.”

The report calls on ministers to ensure that impact assessments are done of the AI system’s used before they are rolled out, as well as proposing regular audits by experts on AI algorithms in use.

Mr Killock added: “The government is putting the interests of Big Tech ahead of the British public in spending billions on AI systems, which it claims will create efficiencies.

“There are no effective and coherent and mandatory rules to ensure these systems respect human rights. The public is being kept in the dark about how systems affect them. We urgently need AI regulation that puts transparency, accountability and the public interest first, protecting human rights and ensuring AI works for all of us.”

A government spokesperson said: “We are actively shaping the UK AI market using grants, investments and contracts to support British capability and competition.

"Through our new £100 million Sovereign AI R&D Procurement Scheme, we are helping British AI companies tackle some of the country’s biggest challenges, improve public services and compete globally.

"We publish information explaining how and why algorithmic tools are used and have developed clear frameworks to ensure AI is used safely and responsibly across government, with people remaining in control of final decisions.”

Nigel Farage’s party has received another £4m from a British crypto billionaire pardoned by Donald Trump.

The donation brings the total given by Ben Delo, who previously announced he was moving back to Britain to help "build a war chest" for Reform to fight the next election, to £8m.

The businessman was convicted in the US four years ago over failings in an anti-money laundering programme in his business, before being pardoned by the US president.

open image in gallery Ben Delo has donated £8m in total to Reform UK ( Anne Schwarz Photography/CC BY-SA 4.0 )

Reform believes Mr Delo, who was formerly based in Hong Kong, will not be caught by the new overseas donor cap.

According to new figures on donations released by the Electoral Commission, the party did not get any money in the second quarter of the year from the Thailand-based crypto investor Christopher Harborne, who has given £15m to the party since the general election, as well as a £5m “gift” to Mr Farage before that.

That £5m is now at the centre of a probe by parliament’s standards watchdog, which is investigating whether it should have been declared.

Mr Farage insists he did not need to declare it. He triggered a by-election last month in a bid to, as he put it, let the voters in his constituency decide the issue. However, if the findings go against him, he could still face another by-election and potentially be rejected from Parliament.

Reform’s total of £5.3m in donations swamps other parties. Labour received £3.5m, the Conservatives £2.8m and the Liberal Democrats £1.3m.

open image in gallery Nigel Farage’s party has received another £4m from a British crypto billionaire pardoned by Donald Trump ( Getty/The Independent )

Labour received £650,000 from Autoglass founder Gary Lubner and supermarket tycoon Lord Sainsbury, while the entrepreneur Ali Mosawi donated £550,000.

The donor cap, applied since March, states that donors must be on the UK domestic electoral register for at least 12 months, or else they cannot give more than £100,000 a year.

In April, in a piece for The Telegraph, Mr Delo said England was his home and “the biggest obstacle to national recovery is the entrenched self-deception of our elites”.

“Their regime of nonsense now poses such a grave threat to the UK that, for the first time in my life, I’ve become politically active,” he added. “Since the start of this year, I have donated £4m to help Nigel Farage to build Reform UK into a genuine alternative party of government... For the first time, I feel that serious people are looking honestly at what it might take to fix Britain.”

He said that, as an autistic person, he did not like that “the official culture of government now forces everyone to be chronically dishonest”.

News.content:

A couple has been accused of abusing four children in their care and holding them in the cab of a tractor-trailer, described by prosecutors as a “rolling prison,” for six years

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced charges against Keysha Monique Epps, a 51-year-old woman from Atlanta, and Tamra Marshon Stewart, a 37-year-old man from Jacksonville, Tuesday.

Epps, a truck driver, and Stewart hauled the two boys and two girls in the sleeper cab of her tractor-trailer as she ran routes from Atlanta to Miami from January 2020 until last April, according to prosecutors. Epps is the children's grandmother, who now range in age from 11 to 15, and Stewart is her fiancé, according to The New York Times.

The children were forced to share a single bunk and were denied the food, hygiene, education and medical care they needed, prosecutors allege.

open image in gallery Keysha Monique Epps, a 51-year-old woman from Atlanta, and her fiancé have been accused of denying her four grandchildren adequate food and medical care and holding them in a tractor-trailer for six years ( Jacksonville Sheriff's Office )

“These children were trapped in a rolling prison and abused by the adults who were supposed to protect them,” Uthmeier said in a statement. “Florida has zero tolerance for anyone who preys on children. We will seek the maximum punishment under the law.”

Uthmeier’s office said two of the children had untreated burns that left them badly scarred.

One of them had burned her hand on hot noodles and was not taken to the hospital, an arrest warrant obtained by the Times said. The children were also burned as a form of discipline, Jae Williams, a spokesman for Uthmeier’s office, told the publication.

The two girls told authorities that they suffered years of sexual abuse by Stewart. The two boys said they witnessed the abuse and were beaten when they confronted Stewart and told Epps.

open image in gallery Tamra Marshon Stewart, Epps' 37-year-old fiancé from Jacksonville, allegedly sexually abused two of the children ( Jacksonville Sheriff's Office )

Authorities alleged Epps knew of the abuse and did not stop it or report it. One of the children was diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection, according to Uthmeier’s office.

Prosecutors said Stewart admitted to three sexual batteries against one of the girls when interviewed by authorities.

Epps told authorities that she asked the girls if Stewart had touched them and they said no, the Times reported. She also reportedly said she limited the children’s food when they were in trouble but still provided three meals a day, according to the warrant.

Stewart and Epps were each charged with two counts of sexual battery by a person in familial or custodial authority and two counts of child neglect causing permanent disfigurement, among other charges.

John Pickles, who created the famous Jive Bunny music mixes, has died at the age of 84, the Mastermix company he founded has confirmed.

Pickles established the novelty pop group Jive Bunny And The Mastermixers in Rotherham in 1989.

The act went on to achieve three UK number ones with Swing The Mood, That’s What I Like and Let’s Party.

In a tribute, a statement from Mastermix described him as "a true pioneer in the music industry".

The lineup of Jive Bunny And The Mastermixers consisted of Pickles, his son Andrew, who served as a director for Mastermix, alongside Doncaster DJ and producer Les Hemstock.

Their tracks regularly featured synthesisers and sampling to merge contemporary pop music with songs from the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s.

The DJing company’s statement read: “It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of John Pickles, founder and creator of The Music Factory Entertainment Group, Mastermix and Jive Bunny.

“John was a leader, an entrepreneur, a businessman, and an incredibly talented songwriter. He was a true pioneer in the music industry, whose creativity, vision and passion for music touched the lives and careers of so many people around the world, and for the most fortunate of us, he was dad.”

The group also had a UK top 10 album in Jive Bunny The Album and scored five UK top 10 hits including their number ones.

Their album covers and music videos featured a cartoon rabbit, with costumed actors also making promotional appearances as the character.

In December 2024, Mastermix released a new Jive Bunny production called 3, 6, 9, which it said was “celebrating the origins of Jive Bunny while adding a modern twist”.

A pair of U.S. service members have been sent back to the USS Abraham Lincoln after a drunken fight in Thailand, where the aircraft carrier is currently at port following a record 286 days at sea, according to a new report.

The service members, who have not been identified, will now be confined to the ship for the remainder of the five-day stint in Pattaya, a sea-side resort town known as the country’s “Sin City.”

On Thursday morning, a Thai citizen placed an emergency call reporting that two U.S. service members had gotten into a physical altercation near a town bar at 1:30 a.m., MS NOW reported, citing local police. After Thai police responded, the Americans were brought to a U.S.-Thailand joint operations center situated in the town’s Hard Rock Cafe before being transferred back to the aircraft carrier.

Speaking to the outlet, a Thai official described the ordeal as “minor.” He added that the service members were drunk and that the emergency caller was worried the altercation might intensify.

The Independent has contacted the Navy for comment.

open image in gallery Two sailors were sent back to the USS Abraham Lincoln after a drunken brawl in Thailand, according to a new report ( AP )

The USS Abraham Lincoln, a Nimitz-class carrier, made port in Pattaya on Wednesday, following a nearly nine-month period at sea, during which it supported the ongoing Iran war. The deployment, which began in November, had initially been expected to end in May.

The massive vessel became the subject of national headlines after reports emerged of supply shortages and mental health struggles among the 5,000 sailors and Marines on board. Several service members even attempted to jump overboard, family members told The Military Times.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described reports of poor conditions “completely misrepresented” last month.

“I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody,” he told reporters. “What they do in those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls - it's incredible.”

News.title: Bank of England must raise interest rates, says chief economist
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Government borrowing costs edged lower on Thursday as Andy Burnham continues to face scrutiny over the public finances.

The yield on 10-year US treasury bonds – considered a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money – declined slightly to 4.78pc on Thursday after a drop in oil prices.

Pre-market trading of bonds in Britain, France and Germany suggested the market was poised to rally after a brutal first half of the week.

However, Mr Burnham and Chancellor John Healey remain under intense pressure, with analysts estimating that as much as half of the country’s fiscal headroom has been wiped out by the jump in bond yields.

Borrowing costs surged after a jump in oil prices caused by fresh strikes between the US and Iran.

The yield on 10-year gilts, as UK bonds are known, hit levels not seen since the global financial crisis in 2007, while longer-term debt costs hit their highest point since 1998.

It means the Chancellor will have less room for manoeuvre in the Budget next month, with some economists predicting the rise in borrowing costs has wiped out up to £14bn of breathing room.

The rise in bond yields across major economies had deepened concerns about deteriorating financial conditions.

Central banks in the US and Europe are increasingly expected to raise interest rates this month to combat inflation caused by the Iran war, although the Bank of England is expected to hold rates steady for now.

Gavin Friend, an analyst at NAB, said: “If this war ‌were to be ‌put to bed, then that ⁠would certainly be something very positive to bring yields back down again across the board.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

What happened overnight

Oil prices slipped, helping boost stocks and bonds.

Renewed fighting between the US and Iran pushed oil prices sharply higher earlier in the week.

However, Brent crude was trading near $94 a barrel after Donald Trump said he does not expect the US bombing campaign to last “much longer”.

Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 advanced 0.2pc to 64,455.83. Among major gainers, OpenAI investor SoftBank Group rose 2.9pc, memory chipmaker Kioxia rose 0.6pc, and chip equipment manufacturer Tokyo Electron gained 0.8pc.

South Korea’s Kospi rose 1.4pc to 6,656.81. Samsung was 1.3pc higher, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix was up 1.4pc.

In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng edged 0.1pc higher, to 25,344.80. The Shanghai Composite index climbed 0.4pc to 3,958.79.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.5pc to 9,025.10.

The Taiex in Taiwan rose 0.6pc, while India’s Sensex climbed 0.3pc.

It comes after Wall Street bounced back after its sharp sell-off at the start of September, as investors snapped up shares that had fallen in recent days.

The S&P 500 rose, with almost 350 companies ending higher. Dell was among the biggest winners, jumping 14pc after giving an upbeat outlook, while investors were also looking ahead to results from chipmaker Broadcom.

The recovery came despite continued concerns over inflation, with oil prices remaining high as fighting between the US and Iran escalated. Brent crude briefly climbed close to $97 a barrel before easing back after Donald Trump said he did not expect the renewed bombing campaign to last “too long”.

US government bond yields were little changed after surging to their highest levels in several years earlier in the week.

Investors also got a mixed picture from the Federal Reserve’s latest assessment of the US economy. Economic activity increased modestly over the past two months, helped by strong demand from data centres, while companies added jobs at a slower pace in August.

The figures come ahead of Friday’s closely watched US jobs report, which could influence expectations for the next move in interest rates.

News.title: Weapons and mercenaries from foreign states fuelling Sudan’s war, UN report finds
News.content:
The war in Sudan is being fuelled by weapons and mercenaries from external states including the United Arab Emirates, Colombia and Turkey, a United Nations report has found.

An investigation by a UN fact-finding mission published on Thursday found that the supply of drones in particular to both sides in the civil war was extending the fighting’s reach and contributing to war crimes.

“Increasingly sophisticated drone capabilities [has] enabled both parties to strike far beyond immediate front lines”, says the report.

“The [UN] mission calls on States to enforce the Darfur arms embargo and suspend transfers of weapons, drones, components, or military assistance where there is a substantial risk of their use in serious violations”.

Sudan’s civil war erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the head of the military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) as part of a planned transition to civilian rule. Hundreds of thousands have died and some 14 million people have been displaced in what has become the world’s deadliest conflict.

In a previous report in February, following the capture of El Fasher in which at least 60,000 people were killed, the UN said the RSF’s mass killings of Black African ethnic groups, including Zaghawa and Fur, bore the “hallmarks of genocide”.

The latest report said “individuals and entities” in the UAE were part of a transnational network supplying weapons, logistics, training and foreign personnel to the RSF – including NORINCO AH-4 howitzers, FK-20000 air defence systems and Chinese-made CH-95 strike drones.

The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), meanwhile, separately obtained Turkish-manufactured drones, including Bayraktar Akıncı combat drones and Yiha III loitering munitions.

The Turkish embassy in London has been contacted for comment.

News.title: The Ukrainian children struggling to survive alone in Europe
News.content:
Every day begins and ends in the same way for Arsenii, 17: calling his mum back home in Kyiv. A year ago he moved from Ukraine to a school boarding house in Slovakia. One night he fell asleep before phoning. When he woke, his mobile was flooded with messages from the few adults his mum knew in the country: the dorm security guard and agent she paid to become his temporary legal guardian. “She woke up everybody,” he says, still with a sense of guilt. She had been trying, agonisingly, to account for her son from over 1,000km away.

Russia’s unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 triggered Europe’s largest displacement of children since World War II. More than 1.8 million crossed into neighbouring countries in the first month – 90 per cent of them with their mothers or other female relatives. But as bombardments battered the country in the following four years, children continued to leave – only without their relatives.

A year-long investigation by the Telegraph has discovered thousands of Ukrainian children are living in Europe alone in the hope of a better life. Some have adapted to independent living, studying and learning the local language. Others have fallen into illegal work, experienced insecurity and discrimination. A few attempts end in tragedy.

The exact number of Ukrainian children who are now living alone in Europe is unclear. Data collected by EU statistical database Eurostat suggests the total cases since 2022 could be almost 23,500. It shows that 19,580 unaccompanied Ukrainian minors in European Union (EU) countries received EU Temporary Protection Status (TPS) between March 2022 and July 2026.

Non-EU countries offer parallel protection schemes. Eurostat data revealed that in the same time-frame, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland granted their protection status to an additional 3,905 unaccompanied Ukrainian minors.

However, the data is incomplete. Only 20 out of 27 EU members declared their numbers. Among those missing are key Ukrainian refugee destination countries, such as Germany and Poland. Poland alone issued 42,332 temporary guardian orders to Ukrainian minors between 2022 and 2025, according to Polish Ministry of Justice data requested by The Telegraph.

In theory, any child granted TPS protection should have a locally appointed legal guardian to sign their papers. However, our investigation revealed loopholes in the system, leaving this category of children vulnerable to abandonment or poor guardianship arrangements.

Arsenii is among at least 1,024 Ukrainian children aged 14 to 16 who have evacuated to Slovak school boarding houses, according to a snapshot 2025 survey by the Slovak Children’s Commissioner. The real figure is likely to be thousands higher, as this research covered just over half of secondary schools in five of the country’s eight regions. It concluded some 5,000 Ukrainian minors in Slovakia have no responsible adult “close to them”, of whom around 1,000 have no legal representative at all.

News.title: Zika virus mosquitoes breed in Britain for first time
News.content:
The UK has historically been too cold for the tropical mosquitoes to survive, but they have been slowly making their way up through Europe.

As temperatures warm, it is predicted that the mosquitoes could become widespread, potentially bringing with them diseases associated with Africa and the tropics.

“The timing of this detection is particularly interesting because the UK has just experienced its provisionally hottest summer on record,” Dr César López-Camacho, a researcher at the University of Oxford, said.



“Warmer conditions can accelerate mosquito development, extend the period in which mosquitoes remain active and, critically, increase the rate at which viruses such as dengue or chikungunya replicate within a competent mosquito,” Dr López-Camacho added.

Previous government modelling suggested that the mosquitoes would be unlikely to get a foothold in Britain until 2040, but the new discovery of the colony in London suggests it may happen sooner.

It means diseases such as dengue fever – which causes high fevers and severe joint pain, and can be fatal, particularly in the elderly and young children – could become common in southern England.

News.title: Burnham risks Truss moment, warn bond traders
News.content:
Andy Burnham risks a Liz Truss-style market meltdown unless he presents a credible plan to pay for his agenda, bond traders have warned.

Investors said the Prime Minister faces further spikes in borrowing costs unless he outlines tax rises or spending cuts to fund his major policies.

UK borrowing costs have surged to multi-decade highs this week amid a global bond market sell-off. However, investors are particularly concerned about Mr Burnham’s fiscal agenda before his first Budget next month.

Al Cattermole, a portfolio manager at Swiss private bank Mirabaud, said investors were “unclear” about the Prime Minister’s plans and how he would pay for them.

He said: “If you have a lack of credibility about your spending plan and how that will be funded, then you would get spikes in yields similar to [what] we saw during the Liz Truss episode.

“That was about unfunded fiscal spending. And if you get that again, then there is concern about that.”

Mr Burnham refused to rule out increasing borrowing during his first Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday despite recent market turmoil.

Jim Athey, a portfolio manager at Marlborough Investment, said: “Spending cuts are the thing the market wants to hear.

“It would go a long way if this Government were to recognise that it is a challenge that needs addressing – that the path we are on in terms of welfare spending is completely unsustainable.”

He added: “The market knows that, and the market wants to hear that the Government understands that.”

Lord Jim O’Neill said earlier that the Prime Minister must “get real” and cut public spending in order to ease pressure in the bond market.

The cost of long-term government borrowing hit its highest level since 1998 on Wednesday, increasing the strain on the public finances as John Healey, the new Chancellor, prepares for the Budget.

The 10-year gilt yield – a benchmark for what the Treasury pays to borrow money – has risen to its highest point since 2007.

News.title: H5N1 hits US mink farms, sparking calls for an urgent cull
News.content:
H5N1 has been detected on a US mink farm for the first time, igniting fears the infected animals could present a human pandemic risk.

The bird flu virus, which has “jumped” from birds to numerous mammal species and infected hundreds of people in recent years, was detected in at least six mink on a farm in Utah in mid-August, according to a notification from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) released over the weekend.

Mink in captivity have previously been described as pandemic “time bombs”. The size and density of the farms gives invading viruses a perfect environment in which to mutate. Mink also have strikingly similar respiratory systems to humans, which greatly increases the human risk.

The animals are farmed for their fur, which is then typically exported to fashion manufacturers in China, Hong Kong, and Russia and used in items like coats and scarves.

Scientists have long warned that if H5N1 acquires the ability to spread efficiently between people, it could trigger a human pandemic.

“Avian influenza viruses tend to replicate pretty poorly in humans and don’t really have the right sort of properties that allow them to transmit from person to person.

“If H5N1 were to cause a pandemic, it would need to make quite a lot of changes, and there’s a real concern that mink, particularly farmed mink, have a lot of the features that could drive the evolution of H5N1,” Dr Tom Peacock, a virologist at The Pirbright Institute, told The Telegraph.

News.title: Collapsing child vaccination in South Africa ‘a public health emergency’
News.content:
Plummeting child immunisation rates are now a public health emergency in South Africa and risk causing outbreaks of preventable but potentially deadly childhood diseases, the government has said.

The proportion of children under one who have received no vaccinations has trebled in the past decade to nearly a third of infants in South Africa.

Mistrust of vaccines and growing ignorance about the benefits of childhood immunisations risk undoing years of progress made by one of the continent’s most effective health systems.

Outbreaks of measles, diphtheria and whooping cough this year have all been linked to poor immunisation rates and are evidence that herd immunity is breaking down, officials warned.

An alert from the department for health said the proportion of unvaccinated infants had hit 36.3 per cent in the first four months of 2026, up from 12.1 per cent in 2017.

The department warned the jump was “effectively tripling the number of completely unvaccinated children and leaving hundreds of thousands of infants at risk of life-threatening illnesses”.

Coverage of the six-in-one hexavalent infant vaccine that protects against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, polio, meningitis, and hepatitis B declined from 87 per cent to 60.5 per cent over the same period.

Officials said the shortfall was caused by a lack of people coming forward to bring their children for jabs and was not due to any shortage of vaccines.

Dr Nonhlanhla Ndlovu, deputy director general of South Africa’s health department, told the state broadcaster that parents had a poor understanding of the public health benefits of childhood jabs.

She said: “The second one that comes out is the issue of public trust, in terms of the safety of the vaccines, but also the trust in terms of our systems.”

“Theses vaccines are very safe and we have seen the gains that we have had in our years before and now that is changing.

“The benefit of vaccines far outweigh anything we can talk about in public health. We need them to come back and bring the children for immunisation.”

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta handed DOUBLE Arsenal injury blow as key pair miss training ahead of Chelsea clash
Sports.content:
MIKEL ARTETA has been handed a blow ahead of Arsenal’s London derby against Chelsea on Sunday.

Bruno Guimaraes and Cristhian Mosquera were both absent from training on Thursday as preparations begin for the Emirates clash.



Arsenal held an open training session at their London Colney training base and there was no sign of either Guimaraes or Mosquera in the squad.

Guimaraes, who joined from Newcastle in a £75m move this summer, has been managing a groin issue over the past few weeks.



The Brazilian missed Arsenal’s Premier League opener against Coventry with the injury, but returned to play 19 minutes off the bench against Aston Villa on Monday.

Arteta has been managing Guimaraes’ workload since his arrival from the Magpies this summer and the club are taking precaution over his fitness given their wealth of options in midfield.



Mosquera, meanwhile, was forced off with injury during Monday night’s 1-0 victory over Villa.

The Spanish defender was replaced by Ezri Konsa in the 79th minute, but boss Arteta hinted that the substitution was purely precautionary.

Speaking after the game, Arteta said: “He’s fine, but he was feeling like he was about to have something, and that’s why we have the bench that we have, and that’s what we have to bring in Ezri.”

Mosquera’s absence from training suggests that the injury could be worse than first feared.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

If the 22-year-old is unavailable on Sunday it could mean Konsa, who arrived in a £51m deal from Villa last month, is handed his home debut against Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea.

Arteta is already without William Saliba, who remains sidelined for an extended period with a back injury that was exacerbated at the World Cup.

Meanwhile Jurrien Timber remains a doubt for this weekend’s London derby.

Both Arsenal and Chelsea have started the season with two league wins from two and will be hoping to lay down a marker when they face off against each other on Sunday.

Sports.title: Man Utd squad CONFIRMED for season as club drop hint over problem position left unsolved during transfer window
Sports.content:
MANCHESTER UNITED have hinted Patrick Dorgu will be used at left-back after releasing their 25-man squad for the Premier League season.

The Red Devils used the transfer window to rebuild their midfield, with Carlos Baleba becoming the final senior arrival when he sealed a £70million move from Brighton.



And, despite Lewis Hall wanting to join from Newcastle throughout the summer, United failed to bring in a fresh option at left-back before Tuesday’s deadline.

It means Luke Shaw is set to remain Old Trafford chief Michael Carrick’s first-choice selection.



But United appear to have made a controversial call in a bid to solve the problem position.

The Red Devils have listed Dorgu, 21, as a defender when announcing their 25-man squad for the Premier League campaign.



The Dane featured in an advanced position when United got their season underway with a woeful defeat to newly-promoted Hull City.

And Dorgu was also used on the left flank when he replaced Marcus Rashford in last weekend’s comeback win over Ipswich Town.

But Carrick, 45, might now be planning to take advantage of the former Lecce man’s versatility after failing to land fresh competition for Shaw.

The decision not to strengthen at left-back left United supporters baffled when Champions League qualification means there will be even more showdowns this term.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Old Trafford recruitment chiefs left it too late to tempt Newcastle into selling top target Hall.

The Magpies had already flogged Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon for big money when United came calling.

Baleba’s fellow summer arrivals Karl Darlow, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans bagged places in the 25-man squad.

Rashford also made the cut after Barcelona chose not to trigger an option to sign him permanently at the end of his loan spell.

Sports.title: Richarlison AXED by Tottenham after bombshell statement and failed return to Everton leaving striker in transfer limbo
Sports.content:
RICHARLISON has been left out of Tottenham’s Premier League squad as they prepare to sell the Brazilian.

The striker, wanted by Trabzonspor, is not part of the North Londoners’ plans this season, despite being the club’s top-scorer last term with 11 Premier League goals.



According to Spurs sources, he was informed of the club’s decision in advance of Tuesday’s Prem transfer deadline so that he could have the option to leave once the club received a suitable offer.

Spurs had agreed a £35million fee with Richarlison’s former club Everton, but personal terms could not be agreed.



The ex-Watford forward then took to social media to hit out at Spurs where he vowed to “NEVER AGAIN” have anyone decide his future for him.

Within that emotional message, he revealed he wanted to move back to his “beloved” Everton but that due to negotiations happening “only in the way certain people wanted”, the switch was off.



And that “despite this turmoil, I am under contract at Spurs and will remain at the club’s disposal”.

Richarlison is subject of interest from Turkey, with Mo Salah’s new club Trabzonspor particularly keen.

Turkey’s transfer window shuts on Friday, while the Saudi Pro League – where clubs have held a long-term interest in Richarlison – can still bring in players until October 12.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Richarlison started the first game of the season at Brentford, where Spurs were crushed 3-0, but was left out of the squad for Saturday’s 2-0 defeat to Newcastle.



Boss Roberto De Zerbi revealed after the game that Richarlison had said that “too many times he wants to leave”.

The 29-year-old has a year left on his deal with Spurs, having arrived from Everton in 2022 for £60million.

Meanwhile, long-term injury absentees Dejan Kulusevski and Xavi Simons have been included in Tottenham’s Premier League squad.

Sports.title: Gabriel Martinelli’s £60m Arsenal transfer exit FINALLY confirmed after Ian Wright slammed treatment of misfit winger
Sports.content:
ARSENAL have officially confirmed the departure of Gabriel Martinelli.

The forward has left the Premier League champions to join Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal.



The north Londoners have pocketed a cool £60million for the Brazil international, who is now the club’s RECORD sale.

Martinelli’s departure comes as no surprise, as he fell behind the recently departed Leandro Trossard in the pecking order last season.



The summer arrival of Christos Tszolis further confirmed that the writing was on the wall for the 25-year-old.

Martinelli issued a heartfelt goodbye message to the Emirates faithful after the confirmation of his exit, which he alluded to after the Gunners ended their 22-year-long wait to return to the summit of English football.

He wrote on Instagram: The day has come, and honestly, I still don’t feel ready to write a goodbye, but I’ll try.

“When I arrived here, seven years ago, I was just a boy who had only recently turned 18. In my heart, I thought I would stay forever.

“But life is constantly changing, and sometimes our paths take us in directions different from the ones we had planned.

“Will we ever become champions? Will I adapt to a new club, a new country, a new culture? Will I ever score in the Champions League?

“Will I score important goals? Will I have the opportunity to play in the Olympics? World Cup? And imagine, scoring at a World Cup?

“Those were all the thoughts going through 18 year old Gabriel’s mind. And yes, we did it.

“We became FA Cup champions, Community Shield and finally achieved the one we had waited so long for, becoming Premier League champions.

“With Brasil, I won an Olympic gold medal, played in two World Cups, and scored a very special goal. And here, with Arsenal, I reached 98 goal contributions.



“I’ve spent seven years at this club. I feel like an adopted Hale End boy, you could say.

“I found a family that took care of me and watched me grow throughout all these years.

“I can only thank the staff and my teammates. Thank you to the chefs, kit staff, doctors, doormen, security staff, media team, cleaning staff, physios, and every single teammate who has been part of my story from 2019 until today.

“Thank you to everyone who helped me grow during this journey.

“Most of all, I want to thank my family and my wife, who have been by my side throughout this entire journey, giving me all the emotional support I needed to overcome the challenges that only we truly know.

Ahead of his Emirates departure, Gunners boss Mikel Arteta brutally left the winger out of the matchday squads for his side’s clashes against Coventry City and Aston Villa.

His exile wasn’t well received by club legend Ian Wright, who said ahead of his old side’s season opener: “In respect to Martinelli and the way Martinelli has been treated at the moment, it really makes me feel uncomfortable.
