Sports.title: Chelsea Confidential: Xabi Alonso's brutal crackdown on leaks and how it's giving Blues an edge, Behdad Eghbali's French connections and truth about Gini Wijnaldum links
Sports.content:
Chelsea fans want to know if Moises Caicedo is fit, but Xabi Alonso does not want you to know, because if you know, then Mikel Arteta and Arsenal know.

Alonso, much like Arteta, is particularly protective of team news and against doing the opposition any favours by giving an early indication as to who is and isn’t available.

Sources suggest they have noticed an increase in secrecy compared to previous managers, with Chelsea rocked by a mole who was leaking their line-ups last season under Liam Rosenior.

It coincides with heightened security measures having been implemented at Cobham, since Confidential revealed last week how Alonso’s colleague Willie Isa was unhappy when two unknowns managed to walk past what was supposed to be a closed training session.

At least once this season, Alonso has only named his starting XI on the day of the game, and this desire to protect information may have been influenced by his time as manager of Real Madrid, where leaks were a problem. He tried, and often failed, to instil confidentiality into that club.

It is said before Real’s first Club World Cup game against Saudi side Al-Hilal in June 2025, Alonso revealed his XI in advance to the team. It was a test, and they failed, because it was soon reported in the Spanish media that then 21-year-old academy graduate Gonzalo Garcia was surprisingly starting.

Xabi Alonso has been much more evasive than some of his predecessors at Chelsea, wanting to keep a lid on any leaks of his team news

He is unlikely to offer any revealing updates on Moises Caicedo this week after the Ecuadorian came off injured against Brighton - although Caicedo has beenin at Cobham every day

Alonso was candid during Chelsea’s pre-season tour of Australia and Asia. However, now that the games are competitive, he has been much more evasive compared to other loose-lipped managers.

When asked who his primary penalty-taker is, Alonso declined to answer, saying: ‘Nope, sorry.’

When asked who his first-choice goalkeeper is, he declined to answer, saying: ‘Don't ask.’

When asked if Enzo Fernandez was still training while missing out on the match-day squads versus Luton and Brighton, he declined to answer. Now that he has been sold to Manchester City, we believe we can say Fernandez was excused from team training as well as those matches.

Gone are the days when Chelsea used to upload an article to their website listing all of their weekly injuries and doubts, who was ‘in partial team training’ and who was ‘undergoing rehabilitation programme’. That was under Mauricio Pochettino. While helpful for us reporters, it gave their opponents a handy heads up, and we should not expect a return of those weekly round-ups.

As for Caicedo, who has been a daily attendee at Cobham this week, Alonso will be asked about his fitness at his Friday afternoon press conference. It will then be up to him how charitable he is feeling, and whether he wants to make Arteta and the Arsenal analysts’ jobs easier.

EGHBALI IN MONACO… BEFORE THEY ANGERED THE BLUES

BlueCo had no clubs involved in last week’s European draws in Monaco, with neither Chelsea nor Strasbourg having qualified for the Champions League, Europa League or Conference League.

However, Chelsea co-owner Behdad Eghbali was on the French Riviera.

Eghbali flew in for networking purposes, per sources. Alongside the sporting director team, he has been hands-on in a window which should still be seen as a winning one for Chelsea despite how it ended.

Chelsea co-owner Behdad Eghbali was in France for the Champions League draw, despite the Blues not featuring in it

It was late on deadline day when Chelsea thought they had secured a midfield signing in Lamine Camara from Monaco, whose sporting director is Thiago Scuro and who was also present at their Conference League draw.

It was Scuro who decided to pull the plug on Camara’s £47million move to Stamford Bridge minutes before Tuesday’s 11pm deadline. That infuriated the Blues, with sources describing it as a deeply unprofessional way for another club to conduct business.

WHY CHELSEA LEFT IT LATE IN MIDFIELD CHASE

Supporters are within their rights to ask why Chelsea did not get ahead of the Fernandez sale and sign a replacement sooner. However, in their who-blinks-first battle with City as we approached September 1, that would have told their Premier League rivals they were ready to sell them their top target.

Chelsea, up to and including deadline day, had been insisting they would be happy to keep hold of Fernandez if need be. They wound up getting a fixed fee worth £125m out of City, who initially offered £104m before add-ons, but no replacement after how the Camara deal died thanks to Monaco.

Instead, Chelsea will now proceed with midfield options in Caicedo, Romeo Lavia, Valentin Barco, Jordan Henderson and Reece James, their captain who sources suggest is seen as a midfielder under Alonso. Malo Gusto is another candidate if required.

Chelsea say it is not true that they have contacted Georginio Wijnaldum, the 35-year-old free agent.

There is no truth in rumours that Chelsea have made a move for former Liverpool man Georginio Wijnaldum

REECE AS A MIDFIELDER

Regarding James as a midfielder, it will be intriguing to see how he handles those responsibilities, though he has a good record in that position. Just look at last season.

When Chelsea defeated Paris Saint-Germain 3-0 to win the Club World Cup, James was in midfield. When they beat Barcelona 3-0 in the Champions League, James was in midfield. When they thrashed Aston Villa 4-1 in the Premier League, James was in midfield. When they held Arsenal to a 1-1 draw despite Caicedo being red carded after 38 minutes, James was in midfield.

In 2025-26, James managed 2,668 minutes in all competitions. Per Opta, 52 per cent of that was as a right back, 42 per cent as a midfielder, and the remaining six per cent as a right-sided centre back.

YOU-KNOW-WHO WON'T NAME YOU-KNOW WHO

There is much amusement at how Enzo Maresca is seemingly hellbent on not letting the word ‘Chelsea’ slip out of his mouth. A few times now, City’s manager has only referred to them as ‘my former club’ or the ‘club where I was’ or that ‘different club’. It is delightfully petty.

But then, in a way, Maresca is only getting his own back.

When Chelsea announced that they had reached a compensation settlement with both City (£17m) and Maresca (undisclosed), their statement did not name him once.

Rather, Chelsea made a point of purely referring to Maresca as ‘our former head coach’ three times. They ended their swipe by describing Alonso as a ‘manager who has an exceptional football mind and is a professional of the highest integrity’.

Man City's new manager and midfield star, Enzo Maresca and Enzo Fernandez, both seem unable to refer to Chelsea by name

After signing for City, Fernandez copied Maresca in referring to ‘my previous club’ in his first interview.

We can expect an animalistic atmosphere at Stamford Bridge for the return of the two Enzos when these two clubs meet in the Premier League in late April 2027.

OH SNAP!

Before each season starts, journalists are reminded that we cannot take pictures or videos inside the stadium if players are on the pitch, as per Premier League rules.

That goes for before, during and after fixtures.

But we will give Gary Cahill a free pass because he was such a good servant for the club.

Cahill, sitting in the press box, could not help taking a snap as Cole Palmer and Co emerged for their first home game. Like many inside Stamford Bridge, the former defender who now acts as an ambassador for Chelsea was excited to be back. We all were.

Danny Welbeck has been a positive presence at Chelsea's training ground since joining from Brighton

DANNY AND THE BOYS

I have a friend whose son is in Chelsea’s academy, and he was waxing lyrical about Danny Welbeck last week.

A bunch of the Blues’ kids aged around 10 were giddy when they spied Welbeck on their side of the training ground.

The 35-year-old striker, who joined from Brighton this summer, was more than generous with his time when they went running up to meet him.

Sports.title: Dominik Szoboszlai is the only solution to Liverpool's glaring right-back problem. He won't like it, but here's the proof - and why it will also fix Andoni Iraola's midfield, writes LEWIS STEELE
Sports.content:
Not even two games into his new era at Liverpool, Andoni Iraola was left scratching his head and pondering a problem position that had long plagued Arne Slot: right back. Last season, Iraola’s predecessor used seven different players on that side of defence: Jeremie Frimpong, Conor Bradley, Joe Gomez, Calvin Ramsay, Dominik Szoboszlai, Wataru Endo and Curtis Jones. None of them felt like the long-term solution but the one Slot continually returned to was to shove midfielder Szoboszlai out there. With Frimpong struggling as Liverpool chased the game against Nottingham Forest last Saturday, Iraola played the ‘Szoboszlai at right-back’ card and, for the second match in a row, his team fought back to achieve a 2-2 draw with the Basque's in-game changes coming up trumps. The tactic has its pros and cons – Szoboszlai, for one, never seems too happy with it – but club legend Jamie Carragher believes it should be a permanent switch. ‘I've never believed Szoboszlai is a central midfield player,' Carragher said on the Stick to Football podcast. 'Now, he's signed a new contract and I can only imagine in those talks, they were desperate for him to stay, he's almost said "I want to play midfield". He's moved around a bit and he started the season in central midfield. I don't see him as that. ‘For me, in midfield, he's like a Jordan Henderson. Runner, energy, with more of a goal threat. But Liverpool don't play that way and he's not really a No 10. His best role could actually be at right back. He'd get plenty of the ball, he can run and play that Trent (Alexander-Arnold) role. 'But there's no way he's going to want to play there, because he's just signed a new contract for £350,000 a week. He's the vice-captain. 'That's a conversation Iraola is going to have to have going forward, because the midfield is not right and he's part of that midfield not being right.' Dominik Szoboszlai is the perfect solution to Andoni Iraola's right-back problem - but he will take a hell of a lot of convincing that it is his best position Jeremie Frimpong has struggled ever since joining Liverpool last summer from Bayer Leverkusen So is Carragher right? Putting the Hungarian out wide does solve several problems. Chief among them is the balance in midfield. A blatantly obvious issue against Newcastle on the opening weekend, Liverpool were exposed given the midfield trio of Szoboszlai, Ryan Gravenberch and Florian Wirtz are all attack-minded and were caught out on the counter. Anthony Elanga and Joe Willock’s goals at St James’ Park both came from Gravenberch losing possession on the edge of the opposition penalty area, with no one behind him to cover and thwart the counter-attack. Putting Szoboszlai on the right flank allows Iraola to play something more resembling a double-pivot system, where he can drift into midfield alongside Gravenberch in attack and cover for him when Liverpool lose the ball. One concern is that the usual midfield two of Gravenberch and Alexis Mac Allister were often outthought, outmuscled and outrun last season. But instead of Szoboszlai, 19-year-old Trey Nyoni is certainly pushing for a first league start after an impressive cameo off the bench against Forest. Nyoni could be the solution to many midfield issues and is a big reason why the club did not move for a new No6 this summer. Szoboszlai playing deeper also means he does not stand on the toes of No10 Florian Wirtz, who should be the team’s most creative outlet. The German has had a tricky first year on Merseyside but the 2-2 draw against Forest was one of his finest performances in a Liverpool shirt. Szoboszlai is also much better than Frimpong at the hybrid role, which is the whole reason this debate is even taking place. Dutch full back Frimpong has had a tough first 12 months on Merseyside, just like his best pal Wirtz who followed him from Bayer Leverkusen to Liverpool. In his last two seasons in Germany, he managed 19 goals and assisted 24 more – now he can barely beat the first man with a cross. He has also made several individual errors defensively. There is a belief Frimpong – and Milos Kerkez on the other side – are merely suffering from confidence issues but the pair are a huge worry right now.

Your browser does not support iframes.

Kerkez had a bright pre-season and should improve under Iraola, who at Bournemouth turned him into exactly the sort of dynamic left back that Liverpool paid £40million for. But so far he and Frimpong have not cut it and look a seismic downgrade on Alexander-Arnold and Andy Robertson. Szoboszlai certainly has an eye for a pass like Alexander-Arnold. But all the merits to him playing at right back are countered quite easily with one simple statement: he is Liverpool’s best player. Last year's runaway player of the season wants to emulate Steven Gerrard and wears the famous No8 shirt at Liverpool, with a tattoo of his idol to boot. Would a prime Gerrard be shoved out to right back? Absolutely not – the manager would build a team around him. By having Szoboszlai start in defence, Iraola loses out on the sort of individual brilliance that won many points for Liverpool over the last year, though he can still take the inch-perfect free-kicks and penalties that he has become famous for. ‘I haven’t found any situations where players have told me they don’t want to play (certain positions),’ said Iraola on Thursday. ‘I pretty much know the perfect position of everyone. But everyone is ready to help. If we have to play him (Szoboszlai) as a right winger, right back or left back, he is ready to do it. 'He wants to help the team first. It is good to have players who can cover different positions. Especially now that we have injuries, it is very valuable to have players like Dom.’ At left back, Milos Kerkez had a bright pre-season and should improve under Iraola, who at Bournemouth turned him into exactly the all-action defender that Liverpool paid £40m for Szoboszlai, last year's runaway player of the season, wants to emulate Steven Gerrard and wears the famous No8 shirt at Liverpool, with a tattoo of his idol to boot Iraola is right. Pundit Gary Neville said it was ‘clear’ that neither Frimpong nor Kerkez were good enough and that he is ‘stunned’ Liverpool did not sign any new full backs. That is not Iraola’s way of working. Schooled at Athletic Club in Bilbao where only players with Basque heritage can be signed, Iraola’s way of thinking is to find solutions via coaching rather than a chequebook. Improving Frimpong and his former Bournemouth colleague Kerkez must be near the top of his to-do list. But in the meantime, Szoboszlai kills two birds with one stone: the midfield is more balanced and he fixes a glaring weakness at right back.

Sports.title: Refs chiefs cast doubt over Mike Dean's claims over 'minigames' of deliberately not blowing his whistle for 25 minutes or refusing to leave the centre circle during Premier League matches - as furious fans call for probe
Sports.content:
Refereeing chiefs have cast doubt on claims by former official Mike Dean that he used to play ‘minigames’ which taking charge of Premier League matches.

Dean, 58, retired from refereeing in 2023 after over 20 years of officiating at the highest level in English football.

Now that the dust has settled on his professional career in the game, Dean has admitted to playing a game where he would see how long he could go without blowing his whistle during Premier League matches.

The ex-official also revealed that he would try and stay in the centre circle for as long as he could during some games.

‘There used to be games we would have for a laugh,’ Dean said on Jamie Vardy’s Having a Party podcast.

‘It would kick-off, right; see how long we could go without blowing a whistle. I done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR, obviously. Went 20, 25 minutes without blowing the whistle.’

Mike Dean has admitted to sometimes trying to see how long he could go without blowing his whistle when refereeing Premier League matches

Dean was a professional referee in English football for over 20 years before retiring in 2023

Dean continued: ‘I used to do another one in the Premier League, I used to stand in the centre circle and see how long I could stay in the centre circle before I had to leave. That was just me joking about. Got about 15 minutes once, in one game.’

But Daily Mail Sport understands his comments have raised eyebrows within the refereeing community, with senior figures questioning the plausibility of his claim given the lack of detail.

According to senior officials, Dean provided no indication of when these alleged ‘minigames’ took place. He also claimed they occurred before VAR was introduced for the 2019-20 season, meaning any such incidents would have taken place under previous refereeing chiefs - and current bosses are insistent that 'integrity and impartiality' are at the heart of referees' decision-making.

Nevertheless, Dean's revelations sparked outrage within the football community and former Aston Villa striker Gabriel Agbonlahor, reacting on talkSPORT, was angered by Dean’s appearance.

'He’s trying to be funny but it’s not funny. You’re not funny, Mike Dean, that sums you up,' he said.

'He’s throwing himself under the bus. This is the Premier League. Are you a child?

'It doesn’t sit right with me at all. I was thinking "Mike Dean managed a lot of games I played in". One word to describe him, I’d say, is a prat.'

And many fans took to social media to voice their displeasure, with one X user even claimed that Dean should be investigated.

They wrote: 'Why the f***‘s he admitting to this? “Oooh look at me I ruined the integrity of top level football matches while getting paid a f***ing fortune for a laugh”. And people wonder why we all think refs are ****.'

Dean admitted, somewhat dismissively, that sometimes there was an element of wanting to be the ‘centre of attention’ when he was on the field.

‘It’s about wanting to be more a part of the game than what I should have been,’ Dean said. 'If you play an advantage and it works off, you do celebrate it; if you get a decision right you kind of want to celebrate.

‘I’d celebrate with the lads in my ear pieces and stuff. If you play an advantage and somebody scores, I think it’s great. Love it.’

But despite his prior explanations to Vardy, whom he officiated several times while the striker played for Leicester, fans found his declaration ‘baffling’.

Well-known X account, @HLTCO, wrote: ‘Yeah, not like your job was to officiate games properly. Mike Dean has said stuff like this before, Clattenburg has openly talked about letting teams self-destruct too. They seem to think it makes them sound like lads. Baffling mentality.’

Dean revealed his 'minigames' when speaking on Jamie Vardy's podcast, and his quotes have caused outrage

Another person added: '“Professional” referee by the way. This is something you would expect from a Sunday league keeper who’s earning pittance to get abused.

‘What an absolute f***ing ****. Always behaved like he was more important than the game being played around him.’

A different account wrote: ‘How about, and I might be going out on a limb here, concentrating on officiating the matches properly rather than playing silly little games with yourself. Mike Dean thinking this makes him sound like a right lad is baffling to me.’

One football fan believed there should be further furore about what they deem ‘corruption’, despite the already high number of disapproving takes.

'I’m sorry but how is this guy not being taken to the cleaners for brazenly admitting this s*** in public???

‘The first part about seeing how long he could go without blowing whistle is actually corruption, bc that’s tacitly admitting to altering outcomes…’

Sports.title: Inside Crystal Palace's transfer window: How Eagles held on to star duo, why they were happy to let Daniel Munoz go, how Brennan Johnson failure hurt business and what Dario Osorio and Quinten Timber bring to the table
Sports.content:
What was all the panic about? Crystal Palace may have left significant transfer business until after the window had officially closed but they can be content with their summer’s work.

Losing Daniel Munoz and Maxence Lacroix appeared a tricky inheritance for Pierre Sage, who already had the daunting task of succeeding Oliver Glasner, yet Palace – with recruitment led by Matt Hobbs, Iain Moody and chairman Steve Parish – eventually bolstered their squad after a late rush to Tuesday’s 11pm deadline.

Most importantly, Palace have kept Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr, much to the latter’s dismay. The talismanic pair – who scored 37 goals between them last term – both wanted to leave.

Sarr sulked while his agent kicked up a fuss. That was unsurprising, given one source told Daily Mail Sport over breakfast in June that his agent was keen to move him on. Palace remained resolute, though, refusing to sell the attacker with three years remaining on his contract.

Once the window closed, Sarr’s agent had his say, criticising the club for not executing the ‘will of the player’ – a strange comment given Sarr signed a five-year contract without a release clause just two years ago. The club had no obligation to sell him, particularly as he did not submit a transfer request.

But the question remains: how will he return? If Sarr wants to leave in January or next summer, the best way to make that happen is to apply himself and demonstrate why he deserves an upward move rather than continuing to sulk. After all, Palace have Europa League football and fancy their chances of a deep run in the competition.

Crystal Palace have managed to hang onto Ismaila Sarr (right) and Jean-Philippe Mateta

Pierre Sage has the daunting task of succeeding Oliver Glasner as Palace boss

There are no concerns about Mateta’s response. He will do what he did when his move to AC Milan collapsed in January: knuckle down and let the football do the talking once he has recovered from injury.

Holding on to attackers of their class is a triumph and Palace consolidated by adding depth, too. Dario Osorio, signed from Danish club Midtjylland, has plenty of upside as a winger who drifts inside, making him well suited to Sage’s 3-4-2-1 formation. The 22-year-old offers end product, talented ball delivery and averaged a goal or assist every 180 minutes last term.

Dwight McNeil is a curious addition, given he arrived in a straight swap for Brennan Johnson, whom Palace paid £30million for in January. Decision-makers accepted that they had got the Johnson transfer wrong, something a club with Palace's financial constraints cannot afford to do.

The swap did at least remove substantial money from the wage bill. But the Johnson overspend in January limited what Palace could do this summer, with the club finishing the window with a positive net spend as they sought to recoup some of the capital lost on their former record signing.

Evann Guessand has returned on loan following his stint at the club during the second half of last season. Before injury, he was a menace starting from the left and provided adequate back-up to Yeremy Pino.

Zavier Gozo was also signed in attack from Real Salt Lake, with the teenager viewed as one for the future. He came on against Manchester City last week and showed some exuberance. That is the type of business Palace should be doing: signing replacements for players years before their departure, providing them with the chance to learn from established players and adapt to the league before they are asked to fill in for them full time.

Last season, Palace ended the summer window with just four No 10s and wingers, with midfielders Daichi Kamada and Justin Devenny often required to fill in. This term, they have eight players to call upon for those spots. There is competition, alternatives and potential.

Replacing Lacroix with Axel Disasi is, admittedly, a downgrade. Lacroix started for France at the World Cup and is now Chelsea’s first-choice centre back. Disasi, meanwhile, is a Chelsea cast-off and nowhere near the France squad.

Decision-makers at Palace accept they had got the Brennan Johnson transfer wrong and he has been moved on to Everton

Axel Disasi has been brought in to beef up the Palace defence and adds experience

Lacroix held the Palace backline together with his recovery pace and immense physicality, qualities Palace will inevitably miss this season. Most importantly, though, he made Jaydee Canvot and Chris Richards better, guiding them through games.

Disasi may not have the same pace but he is experienced and a solid defender, though he can have his blips in possession. His arrival on loan at West Ham in January markedly improved their defence, helping them keep six clean sheets in 14 games.

Centre back remains the most concerning area. Canvot and Honest Ahanor, a deadline-day arrival from Atalanta, are promising but lack know-how. Ahanor is impressively imposing for his age, although it is a shame Palace are developing a player who will join Chelsea next summer – even if they have procured a skilled defender.

Richards is proven at right centre back but if Disasi becomes unavailable, he would have to move into the middle, where he has looked suspect. Oscar Mingueza, Takehiro Tomiyasu and Jefferson Lerma, who can all play in multiple positions, are viewed as understudies. Not adding another central centre back could be a costly omission as the backline appears fragile without Disasi.

Number-wise, though, it is an improvement. At one point last season, Palace had only four centre backs for three positions. They may lack a sprinkling of quality at the back but they have brought in enough depth to compete in Europe and domestically.

Losing Munoz to Glasner’s Nottingham Forest was emotionally tough for Palace, given the rivalry between the clubs and his role in winning three trophies in two years. But, from a business perspective, it was the right move.

Munoz, now 30, has reached his peak transfer value, leaving for £22m, and the data suggests he will start to decline. In two years, Palace have made a £16m profit and replaced him with Anan Khalaili, whom they believe is a younger version with a higher ceiling. On his debut against Manchester City, the similarities were striking, with the Israeli wing-back relentless from start to finish. Those two transfers were net zero, too.

Quinten Timber, an athletic ball-winner, adds a desperately required profile to Palace’s midfield options, replacing bit-part player Devenny, who moved to Stoke City on a permanent deal.

Losing Daniel Munoz to Nottingham Forest was emotionally tough for Palace. But, from a business perspective, it was the right move

Quinten Timber, an athletic ball-winner, adds a desperately required profile to Palace’s midfield

Adam Wharton and Kamada is a strong pairing but against superior opposition, the two-man midfield has lacked athleticism and bite at times. Timber gives Sage a plan B.

Some sources have suggested Timber’s physical profile should suit the Premier League, given his brother Jurrien’s success at Arsenal. His arrival also helps solve the problem of losing Kamada to the Asia Cup in the new year.

Ben Chilwell – if he can stay fit – is an upgrade on Borna Sosa, who failed to make an impact last season. Chilwell, signed for free from Strasbourg, was at the club on loan from Chelsea when Palace won the FA Cup. He is a leader, homegrown and offensively talented.

His injury record is alarming but he did manage 34 games at Strasbourg last season. Sosa, who has joined Cologne on loan, played a third of the minutes Chilwell did last season because he was not at the level required.

What Palace have successfully done this window is build a complete squad, with multiple options in every position. That was the bugbear last season.

They have a 28-man group, six of whom will need to be cut from the European squad, giving Sage the ability to rotate with at least two players for every position.

Of course, the window could have been improved if moves for Joel Ordonez and Malick Fofana had gone through. But Ordonez’s medical showed his broken metatarsal injury was more serious than initially expected, meaning he would not have been an option until later in the season.

It could be a deal Palace revisit in January. The highly-rated centre back should be available by then and has long been admired by the club.

Ben Chilwell (left) signed for free from Strasbourg and was at Palace on loan from Chelsea when they won the FA Cup

Fofana’s move from Lyon was ultimately hijacked by Sunderland after Palace thought they had beaten the North East club to his signature. Palace sources were frustrated on Tuesday afternoon, as Sunderland offered the player’s family money they could not match. Sage desperately wanted to sign him after working together at Lyon.

There has been significant player turnover at Palace and it will take time for the squad to gel – 11 players have arrived with six first-teamers making way.

On the whole, they are in a stronger position than last year, with a proficient starting XI and solid back-up in every position. That gives them plenty of reason to be optimistic. The proof will be on the pitch but the signs are promising.

Sports.title: Company linked to Chelsea owner Todd Boehly donates £75,000 to Nigel Farage's Reform party
Sports.content:
Reform UK received a £75,000 donation from a company linked to Chelsea co-owner Todd Boehly, it has been revealed.

American businessman Boehly, 52, led the consortium that took over the Blues in 2022 and he currently serves as the club's chairman.

Boehly has been hands-on in his role at Stamford Bridge and also has a number of business interests, including Eldridge Industries, a holding company based in Miami where he is CEO, co-founder, chairman and controlling member.

And, in the latest data published by the Electoral Commission - the independent body which oversees elections and regulates political finance in the UK - Eldridge Capital Management Services (UK) made a £75,000 donation to Nigel Farage's party.

Eldridge Capital Management is the primary division of Eldridge, an asset management and insurance company owned by Eldridge Industries.

According to the Financial Times, Boehly is the ultimate owner of Eldridge Capital Management Services, while he is also listed as a former director.

A company linked to Chelsea co-owner Todd Boehly donated £75,000 to Reform UK

Nigel Farage's party have received several donations from donors across recent months

Among the current directors at the company are Tony Minella, Boehly's co-founder of Eldridge.

Boehly, who has an estimated net wealth of $9.3billion (£6.9bn), has historically provided donations in politics.

Like with Reform, these have tended to support right-wing politicians and parties.

This has included Donald Trump and Republican candidates who are aligned with the US President.

Meanwhile, the Electoral Commission also confirmed that in the three-month period up until June, Reform received the most political donations.

Farage's party were given £5.3million by donors.

For context, Labour received £3.6m, while the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats were handed £2.8m and £1.4m respectively.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
