World.title: MoF Launches 2027 – 2031 MTRS
World.content:
Secretary to Treasury Felix Nkulukusa has said strengthening domestic revenue mobilisation is critical to preventing a return to debt distress while creating fiscal space to finance public services and national development.

Mr Nkulukusa was speaking today, at the launch of public consultations on the 2027–2031 Medium-Term Revenue Strategy (MTRS), under the theme: Mobilising Domestic Resources for Sustainable Growth and National Development.

He noted that the 2027–2031 MTRS, is not a tax-increase exercise, but an effort to create a broader, fairer and more predictable revenue system to support Zambia’s development.

He explained that the government wants to improve tax compliance, address tax avoidance and evasion, simplify the tax system and ensure that all sectors contribute their fair share.

Mr Nkulukusa disclosed that, government has over the years provided tax incentives and relief to priority sectors, with tax expenditure in 2023 and 2024 amounting to between 1.5 and 2 percent of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

The Secretary to Treasury, however, expressed concern over low tax compliance, smuggling and tax avoidance, saying these challenges have contributed to Zambia’s sluggish Revenue-to-GDP ratio.

He said increased compliance could create room for the government to consider reducing some tax rates while still increasing overall revenue collection.

“Zambia can no longer rely on excessive borrowing to finance development, particularly following the country’s debt restructuring, which requires strong and predictable domestic resource mobilisation,” he added.

He also said the success of the MTRS, will depend on building greater trust between government, taxpayers, businesses and citizens.

Mr Nkulukusa has since called on the private sector, professional bodies, civil society and other stakeholders to submit evidence-based and actionable proposals to help shape the strategy.

Speaking at the same event, the Ministry of Finance and National Planning Permanent Secretary for Budget and Economic Affairs, Mwaka Mukubesa said Zambia’s improved economic stability must now be matched with stronger domestic resource mobilisation to support sustainable economic growth and national development.

Ms Mukubesa noted that Zambia has made significant progress in stabilising the economy.

She cited progress in debt restructuring, fiscal consolidation, foreign exchange reserves and inflation.

“The external debt restructuring process is now more than 94 percent complete, while the fiscal deficit had declined to 3.4 percent by October 2025, from about nine percent in 2021,” she added.

And the Budget Office Director under the said Ministry, Willies Chipango, charged that the government has set a target of increasing domestic revenue collection by between two and four percentage points of GDP over the next five years, under the 2027 – 2031 MTRS.

Mr Chipango said the target is aimed at narrowing the gap between government expenditure and revenue, while strengthening Zambia’s fiscal position.

“Zambia collected about 22.2 percent of GDP in revenue in 2025, against expenditure of about 26 percent of GDP, hence, the government therefore wants to narrow the gap between revenue and expenditure to less than two percent of GDP between 2027 and 2029,” said Mr Chipango.

Meanwhile, Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) Commissioner General, Dingani Banda has identified low tax compliance, as the biggest challenge undermining domestic resource mobilisation, with significant gaps recorded across major tax categories.

Mr Banda pointed out that improving compliance could help Zambia raise additional revenue without necessarily increasing tax rates.

“ZRA’s data shows an overall tax return filing compliance rate of about 52 percent between January and July 2026, up from 49 percent recorded in 2025. Compliance remains low across taxpayer categories, with SMEs at about 49 percent, the specialised tax office covering the mining sector at 62 percent and large taxpayers at 68 percent,” said Mr Banda.

He disclosed that if compliance improves to about 74.8 percent, annual revenue could reach approximately K186.6 billion, exceeding the projected target of K169.6 billion, adding that further improvement to about 81.6 percent could push collections to more than K203 billion.

The Commissioner General also said ZRA is therefore implementing Compliance Risk Management, using data to identify taxpayer risk profiles and tailor interventions accordingly.

World.title: Zambia Pushes Back on UN Characterisation of “Political Detainees”
World.content:
Zambia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation has rejected a news release from the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Rights to Freedom of Peaceful Assembly and of Association. The release, issued on 2 September 2026, addressed the aftermath of Zambia’s general election. The Ministry says it contains a factual error, prejudicial language and claims that fall outside the Rapporteur’s mandate.

The core dispute concerns treason. The Special Rapporteur’s release described treason under Zambian law as a “capital offence.” The Ministry says this is false. Zambia abolished the death penalty under the Penal Code in December 2022. It removed the penalty from military law through the Defence (Amendment) Act in December 2023. Parliament then approved accession to the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Zambia deposited the instrument of accession with the UN Secretary-General on 19 December 2024. The Protocol entered into force for Zambia on 19 March 2025. No offence in Zambia today carries the death penalty.

The Ministry also disputes the release’s language on individuals facing criminal charges. It rejects the terms “political detainees” and “post-election crackdown,” arguing these present contested claims as fact and prejudge matters before the courts. The statement contrasts the Special Rapporteur’s approach with that of the UN Secretary-General’s Special Envoy. The Envoy was present in Zambia during the events in question. He facilitated the handover of two opposition figures, first to the Church and then to security agencies.

The Ministry cites the Code of Conduct for Special Procedures Mandate-holders. It argues the release falls short of required standards on objectivity, verification and restraint. It calls on the Special Rapporteur and the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights to issue a public correction with equal prominence to the original release. The Ministry reaffirms Zambia’s commitment to constitutional democracy, the rule of law and continued engagement with UN human rights mechanisms

The full statement, issued by the Ministry, is reproduced below.

GOVERNMENT CORRECTS FACTUAL ERRORS AND PREJUDICIAL CHARACTERISATIONS IN NEWS RELEASE BY THE SPECIAL RAPPORTEUR ON FREEDOM OF PEACEFUL ASSEMBLY AND OF ASSOCIATION

LUSAKA, 3 September 2026. The Government of the Republic of Zambia has noted the news release issued on 2 September 2026 by the Special Rapporteur on the Rights to Freedom of Peaceful Assembly and of Association concerning developments surrounding Zambia’s general election.

In the said press release, the Special Rapporteur is quoted as having stated among other things that:

“Authorities must release all political detainees, respect fundamental freedoms, and restore democratic accountability.”

Zambia values the contribution of the United Nations Special Procedures to the promotion and protection of human rights and remains committed to constructive engagement with all human rights mechanisms. That engagement must, however, rest on accuracy, objectivity, due regard for information supplied by the State, and respect for the specific mandate entrusted to each mandate holder.

The position taken by the Special Rapporteur stands, moreover, in sharp contrast to that of the Special Envoy of the United Nations Secretary-General, who was present in Zambia during the events in question and personally facilitated the handover of the two leaders, first into the care of the Church and subsequently to the security agencies, on the basis of assurances made by the Government of the Republic of Zambia that the fundamental rights of the suspects would be respected at every stage of the due process.

The United Nations Special Envoy engaged directly on the ground and chose constructive facilitation. The Special Rapporteur, from a distance and without such engagement, chose condemnation by news release. The contrast speaks for itself.

The press release contains a fundamental and readily verifiable error of law, presents contested allegations as established fact, adopts language that prejudges matters currently before the courts, and pronounces on questions well beyond the Special Rapporteur’s mandate.

First, the news release is wrong on the law. It describes treason in Zambia as a “capital offence.” It is not. Zambia abolished the death penalty under the Penal Code in December 2022 and removed it from military law through the Defence (Amendment) Act signed in December 2023. Parliament thereafter approved accession to the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty. Zambia deposited its instrument of accession with the United Nations Secretary-General on 19 December 2024, without reservation, and the Protocol entered into force for Zambia on 19 March 2025.

No offence in Zambian law today carries the death penalty. No person charged with treason faces execution. This is not a matter of interpretation but of public record, verifiable in the statute book, in the proceedings of the National Assembly, and in the depositary records of the United Nations itself.

That a United Nations mandate holder should overlook one of Zambia’s most significant and internationally commended human rights reforms raises immediate questions about the rigour of the exercise as a whole.

Second the characterisation of events is unsubstantiated and prejudicial. Describing recent developments as a “post-election crackdown,” and persons facing criminal proceedings as “political detainees,” asserts a conclusion rather than reports a fact. Membership of an opposition party does not place a person beyond the reach of the law, nor does it convert a criminal suspect into a political detainee. Zambia has constitutional responsibilities to protect public safety, national security and the democratic order. Where there is reasonable suspicion that an offence has been committed, the competent authorities are entitled, indeed obliged, to investigate and to institute proceedings in accordance with the law.

This diminishes nothing owed to the accused. Every affected person is entitled to the presumption of innocence, legal representation, humane treatment, a fair and public hearing before a competent court, and access to judicial remedies for any procedural or other shortcoming. The Government is committed to ensuring these protections are respected in every case, and Zambia’s courts are open to test them.

The assertion that senior opposition figures face “concocted charges of treason” goes further still. It pronounces on the merits of live criminal proceedings. Whether the evidence establishes an offence is for Zambia’s independent courts to determine through due process, not for an international mandate holder to settle by news release. To describe charges as “concocted” before any judicial examination risks prejudicing those proceedings and departs from the objectivity, moderation and discretion expected of the Special Procedures.

Third , the release ranges well beyond its mandate. It makes sweeping assertions concerning alleged electoral flaws, intimidation, assaults, abductions, deaths and Zambia’s democratic and human rights environment as a whole. These are serious matters, and they demand careful, independent and comprehensive verification. Several of them do not fall within a mandate on freedom of peaceful assembly and association unless a clear and substantiated connection to those rights is established. No such nexus is demonstrated.

The Government is further concerned that allegations attributed to unspecified sources have been reproduced as authoritative conclusions, with insufficient acknowledgment that they remain contested, are under investigation, or fall for determination by competent national institutions.

Fourth, the cumulative effect of this language raises serious concerns under the Code of Conduct for Special Procedures Mandate-holders. “Crackdown,” “political detainees” and “concocted charges” are not neutral descriptions of reported allegations. They are conclusions about the motives of State institutions and about the legitimacy of judicial proceedings.

Under the Code of Conduct adopted by the Human Rights Council, mandate holders are required to establish facts on the basis of objective and reliable information from credible sources; to cross-check that information to the fullest extent possible; to take comprehensive account of information supplied by the State concerned; to assess matters against the standards relevant to their particular mandate; and to exercise restraint, moderation and discretion in their public statements. Measured against each of these standards, the release falls short.

Zambia welcomes scrutiny and claims no immunity from criticism. But scrutiny must itself meet the standards of fairness, accuracy and impartiality that the Human Rights Council has set.

Independence does not dispense with verification. An allegation does not become a fact by being repeated in a United Nations news release.

The Government therefore calls upon the Special Rapporteur and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights to correct publicly the erroneous description of treason as a capital offence, promptly and with the same prominence as the original statement. It further calls upon them to distinguish clearly between allegation and verified fact, and to reflect Zambia’s responses and legal reforms accurately in any further public communication.

Zambia remains committed to constitutional democracy, political pluralism, freedom of peaceful assembly and association, the rule of law, and constructive cooperation with the United Nations Human Rights System, conducted on those same standards.

ENDS

Issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation,

Government of the Republic of Zambia.

World.title: 22 year old gold miner dies- Chadiza
World.content:
A 22-year-old man of Chadiza District has died after gravel collapsed on him while mining for gold.

Eastern Province Police Commanding Officer Robertson Mweemba confirmed the incident to the media.

Mr Mweemba said the incident occurred yesterday, September 1, 2026 at around 11:00 hours along Tivilili stream.

He said the deceased has been identified as Elias Soko, 22, of Isaac village, in Zingalume chiefdom.

“Brief facts are that yesterday, Tuesday, at around 07:00 hours, Soko went to Tivilili stream to conduct gold mining activities in the company of his sister-in-law, identified as Nelia Zulu, 35 and seven other family members,” Mr Mweemba narrated.

He said upon arrival, they started digging mud along the stream.

“Later, the other six family members left, leaving Elias Soko, Nelia Zulu and his mother Florence Phiri, when the gravel collapsed on Elias Soko who died on the spot,” Mr Mweemba said.

The Eastern Police Commanding Officer said the matter was reported to the police and officers rushed to the scene in the company of officers from the Fire Brigade department.

He said the deceased was trapped under the mud and sustained a deep cut on the right side of the head, a broken right hand, a depressed forehead and a broken jaw.

Mr Mweemba said police do not suspect any foul play.

“Relatives have been advised to proceed with burial while marking the grave,” he said..

World.title: Govt. implements digital civil registration
World.content:
The Department of National Registration, Passport and Citizenship (DNRPC) in Lavushimanda district of Muchinga Province is implementing digital civil registration, a government exercise that commenced in 2022.

Lavushimanda District National Registration Officer Kasapo Musonda urged members of the public to fully participate in the registration exercise.

Mr Musonda explained that the department has registered over 3,000 children under the age of five in the last four months.

He encouraged the public to register their children, obtain digital identification for adults and secure death certificates, noting that the exercise is continuous.

“We want to urge the general public in Lavushimanda to take advantage of this very important national exercise,” he said.

Mr Musonda further explained that the exercise is being implemented through the Integrated National Registration Information System (INRIS).

He said INRIS was deployed to 26 District National Registration Offices across the country in March 2022 to ensure that all districts are connected.

Mr Musonda, however, said that to ensure the public is adequately informed about the exercise, the department is working with the Ministry of Health in the district to engage local communities through Environmental Health Departments (EHDs).

World.title: Agric stakeholders hail HH diversification agenda
World.content:
Stakeholders in the agricultural sector have welcomed President Hakainde Hichilema’s call to scale up production and diversify the agricultural sector through increased investment in technology, science and infrastructure.

The stakeholders say the President’s call provides an opportunity for the country to move beyond stability towards sustainable growth and increased agricultural productivity.

And reacting to the President’s inaugural address, the Agricultural Institute of Zambia Chief Executive Officer Mathews Ngosa has called on stakeholders to work together to achieve the country’s production targets for maize, soya beans, wheat, sugar and beef.

Mr Ngosa noted that the targets set for the commodities are ambitious but achievable with proper planning, good investment and implementation.

He, however, noted that there is a need to address issues of climate change through the promotion of climate smart agriculture, water conservation, soil health and sustainable land management as they are important for the protection of agricultural production for future generations.

He has since called all players in the Agricultural sector to take the pronouncements seriously and take action to yield measurable results.

And the National Association for Small scale Farmers (NASFA) Executive Director says the nation’s economic growth is tied to the Agricultural Sector.

He stressed that out of the eight national focus points, five of them were agricultural related which he said translated that over 50 percent of the National development focus will be on Agriculture.

He said his organisation will continue to work with the government to ensure that all the set goals and the reaching of 10 million metric tonnes of maize production by the year 2031 is achieved.

He since commended the government for responding quickly whenever matters affecting farmers arise calling it a good sign of things yet to come.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 3, 2026
World.content:
Guinea-Bissau Voters Back Expanded Presidential Powers

Voters in Guinea-Bissau have approved a new constitution that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections scheduled for December. Provisional results showed that 70% of voters backed the changes. Under the new constitution, the president will be able to appoint and sack the prime minister and cabinet, create or abolish ministries, and dissolve parliament in a serious political crisis. The reforms also reduced the number of parliamentary seats and electoral constituencies, but retained the five-year presidential term and two-term limit. The military leaders who seized power after a disputed vote in November 2025 say the changes are needed to put an end to repeated political bickering and instability. But the country's main opposition party strongly opposed the referendum and boycotted the vote. It warned that the changes would concentrate too much power in the presidency and undermine democracy. Critics have also questioned the legitimacy of the process and called on the regional bloc Ecowas to intervene. The December elections will be a key test of whether the military authorities fulfil their promise to restore civilian rule and how the expanded powers of the presidency reshape Guinea-Bissau's fragile political system.

Uber Exits Nigeria and Uganda

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Global ride-hailing company Uber has announced the immediate closure of its operations in Nigeria and Uganda after reviewing its business in the two markets. Uber began operating in Nigeria in 2014 and Uganda two years later. It has faced increasingly difficult conditions, including rising fuel costs, pressure from rival ride-hailing platforms and complaints from drivers over low fares and high commission charges. The company's departure from Nigeria and Uganda follows its recent exits from Ivory Coast and Tanzania, further reducing its presence on the continent. Uber said the decision was limited to the two countries and would not affect its remaining operations in sub-Saharan Africa, where it says it continues to see growth opportunities. The company will support affected employees and drivers. Its help centres in Nigeria and Uganda will remain open until later this month to address outstanding issues. Other ride-hailing companies, including Bolt, inDrive and local operators, are expected to compete for customers and fill the gap left by Uber's departure.

Madagascar Ex-Senate Chief Jailed for Protest Crackdown

Madagascar's former Senate president Richard Ravalomanana has been sentenced to 10 years of hard labour over his alleged role in the violent crackdown on youth-led protests that helped bring down the previous government. Ravalomanana, a retired general and close ally of former President Andry Rajoelina, was found guilty of complicity in murder. Prosecutors accused him of directing security forces to use violence against demonstrators during protests in September and October 2025. The protests initially erupted over persistent power and water shortages before developing into a wider movement against Rajoelina's government. At least 22 people were killed and more than 100 others injured during the unrest, according to the UN. Ravalomanana has denied the allegations. He argued that there was no evidence directly linking him to orders given to security forces, and his defence team plans to appeal the ruling. He is among several senior figures associated with the former government who have faced legal proceedings since the change of power.

World Set to Overshoot 1.5°C Climate Target

The world is on course to exceed the 1.5°C global warming threshold within the next few years, with even the most optimistic scenario projecting temperatures to peak at around 1.8°C, according to a new UN Environment Programme report. UNEP warned that remaining above the threshold would expose countries and communities to worsening extreme weather, ecosystem losses, food and water insecurity, and potentially irreversible changes to major climate systems. The organisation is calling for an "overshoot, peak and decline" strategy aimed at keeping the period above 1.5°C as short as possible before bringing temperatures back down. This would require immediate and sustained cuts in greenhouse gas emissions, including methane, a rapid transition away from fossil fuels and, eventually, carefully governed carbon dioxide removal to supplement emissions reductions. UNEP stressed that carbon removal cannot replace deep cuts in emissions and warned that every additional fraction of a degree of warming will increase the risk of irreversible climate tipping points and devastating impacts on vulnerable communities.

Close 

Sudanese Refugees Walk for Aid in Chad

Dozens of Sudanese refugees have walked about 20 kilometres from Marra refugee camp in eastern Chad to the town of Amliouna to demand humanitarian assistance after going about four months without food or cash support. The refugees, who arrived at the camp between five and eight months ago, say they are seeking help from authorities responsible for refugee reception and are calling for regular delivery of food or financial assistance. Their protest comes as heavy rain and strong winds have caused further hardship for refugees in eastern Chad. At Mile refugee camp near Guéréda, storms damaged numerous shelters and injured several people, leaving many refugees, including children and elderly people, without adequate protection. Refugees are now appealing to humanitarian organisations for urgent assistance, including food, clean water, medicines, medical supplies, tents and materials to repair damaged shelters.

World.title: Kenya: Kenya's Cotton Leftovers Are Finding New Value
World.content:
Kenyan businesses and community groups are turning discarded cotton stalks, gin waste and textile offcuts into briquettes, household textiles and mattress filling. The emerging industry could create new income for farmers and women-led enterprises.

For years, Peterson Mwadau regarded the stalks and other plant residue left after his cotton harvest as little more than a disposal problem.

Mwadau grows cotton on 18 acres in Kilifi County on Kenya’s coast. Once the crop has been picked, a considerable amount of plant material remains in his fields. Now, instead of burning or discarding all of it, he sells some of the residue to local businesses.

“I plant cotton on 18 acres, so a lot of waste is produced after harvest,” Mwadau said. “Selling it to small local companies brings immediate extra income into my household.”

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Collectors buy the residue and supply enterprises that convert agricultural biomass into charcoal briquettes. The briquettes are then sold to hotels, schools and other institutions for cooking.

Mwadau’s experience points to an emerging economic opportunity across Kenya’s cotton-growing counties. Cotton stalks, gin trash and factory offcuts - materials that were frequently burned, dumped or sent into municipal waste streams - are beginning to supply small community enterprises and established manufacturers.

These materials should not, however, be treated as a single form of “cotton waste”. Cotton stalks and other crop residue remain on farms after harvesting. Gin trash and short fibres are produced when cotton is cleaned and separated at ginneries. Yarn sweepings and fabric offcuts come from spinning, weaving and clothing factories.

Each material requires a different collection and processing system and produces different end products.

Turning stalks into fuel

In cotton-growing areas such as Kilifi, Kitui, Makueni and Lamu counties, much of the residue left after harvesting has traditionally been burned or abandoned.

“We usually set this waste ablaze or dump it. We see no economic value in it,” said John Katuve, a small-scale cotton farmer.

Burning crop residue can contribute to air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions, while repeated burning may affect soil health. The environmental case for finding alternative uses for cotton waste is therefore significant.

“When a farmer burns cotton stalks to clear the field for the next planting season, they are literally burning potential revenue,” said Jeremiah Njuguna, a well known agronomist who specializes in value addition.

The Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation, or KALRO, has been training farmers in agricultural value addition through the National Agricultural Value Chain Development Project.

According to Dr Patrick Ketiem, cotton stalks can be shredded, carbonised and compressed to produce briquettes.

“Farmers can choose either to sell them, expand their businesses or use them within their homesteads,” Ketiem said.

The KALRO training program educates farmers on value addition. They further train them on the stages of value addition from scratch to finish.

The briquettes can also be sold to hotels, restaurants and schools as an alternative to conventional wood charcoal.

Women-led self-help groups in Wote, Makueni County, are among the community enterprises experimenting with this model.

“We carbonise the raw biomass in kilns, using the cotton stalks and gin trash that we collect,” said Itetani Women group member Mwikali Katuku.

The carbonised material is mixed with organic binders and compressed into dense briquettes. Katuku said the briquettes burn for longer than wood charcoal and produce less smoke.

Mary Mutua, chairperson of the 28-member women’s cooperative in Makueni, said the business had reduced members’ dependence on income from rain-fed farming.

“Before we started collecting and carbonising cotton stalks, we depended entirely on rain-fed crop yields,” Mutua said. “Now waste collection gives us a year-round source of income.”

She said members use the money to pay school fees, obtain health insurance and contribute to savings groups. The cooperative has also introduced a bank account, collection schedules and quality-control standards as it moves from an informal association towards a community enterprise.

Recovering fibre from factories and ginneries

A separate value chain is developing around short cotton fibres, yarn sweepings and textile offcuts.

Manufacturers can clean, sort and card these materials before converting them into mattress and cushion filling, cleaning cloths, floor mops, rugs, blankets and, in some cases, regenerated yarn.

Milan Shah, managing director of Bobmil Ltd in Nairobi, said lower-grade cotton waste they buy and carded fibre could be used as filling for mattresses, cushions, vehicle seats and pillows.

Africa Collect , a Nairobi-based circular-economy enterprise, is also processing different types of discarded material into consumer products.

“We make high-quality products such as blankets, mops and kitchen-cleaning towels,” said Alex Musembi, its general manager and one of its founders.

In cities including Nairobi, Mombasa, Eldoret and Kisumu, textile offcuts and broken threads can be collected from cutting rooms and factories before being sorted and reprocessed.

Without organised collection, some of this material enters municipal waste streams or is dumped. David Ongare who is the Director of Compliance at the National Environmental Management Author (NEMA) confirms.

“Well documented collection points that are well planned are vital in saving our wetlands. Compliance is a challenge”, he said on telephone.

A regional supply chain

Despite Kenya’s emerging waste-processing enterprises, local manufacturers still rely on imported cotton waste and yarn sweepings.

At the Namanga border post between Kenya and Tanzania, trucks transport baled materials into Kenya under East African Community trade arrangements. Some consignments have already been sorted or carded in Tanzania, while others enter as raw fibre waste for processing in Kenyan factories.

The material is transported to manufacturing centres such as Nairobi’s Industrial Area, Ruiru and Thika.

According to the Observatory of Economic Complexity trade data, Kenya imported between US$600,000 and US$1 million worth of cotton waste and related material in 2024, with Tanzania reportedly accounting for about 60% of the supply.

Tanzania’s supply has an advantage because the material can arrive in large, pregraded bales with relatively consistent fibre quality and pricing. Kenya’s domestic supply is more fragmented: small quantities are spread across farms, ginneries and workshops, making collection and transport expensive

This is according to different reports from Kenya National Cotton Textile and Apparel (CTA) and Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis (KIPPRA).

The missing link is an aggregation system that can collect, sort and compress material close to where it is produced. Regional centres equipped with hydraulic balers could reduce transport costs and give manufacturers a more predictable domestic supply.

Close 

From scattered projects to an industry

Kenyan Cabinet Secretary for Agriculture and Livestock Development Mutahi Kagwe has identified value addition as an alternative to exporting unprocessed agricultural commodities.

“Value addition is the best alternative for the country,” Kagwe said. “It is environmentally safe and also creates jobs and reliable income.”

He said that the government will work together with banks to ease the approval of loans

Kenya also offers a range of investment incentives for qualifying businesses. Some of these incentives are tax deductions, tax holidays, and VAT exemptions on green technology imports.

Commercial banks including Equity Bank, Co-operative Bank of Kenya, Absa and KCB provide agricultural and small-business financing, but the draft does not yet establish whether they have facilities designed specifically for cotton-waste enterprises.

“The door is wide open for anyone with a good idea,” Equity Group chief executive James Mwangi said. “We have been giving loans for agricultural value addition, including cotton.”

The opportunity is visible. Kenya has farmers willing to sell residue, community groups producing briquettes and companies finding new uses for discarded fibre. Now it needs to grow it coordinated system connecting these suppliers to reliable buyers.

For Mwadau, the emerging industry already means earning something from material that once had little perceived value. He hopes to expand his business one day and begin to be an exporter.

According to the Observatory of Economic Complexity trade data, Kenya imported between US$600,000 and US$1 million worth of cotton waste and related material in 2024, with Tanzania reportedly accounting for about 60% of the supply.

World.title: Cameroon: Garoua Textile Centre Takes Early Steps To Empower Young Women
World.content:
A new training centre in Garoua is teaching young women to turn locally grown cotton thread into finished fabric. Still operating on a modest scale, Gaaraadji is creating incomes, developing scarce textile skills and showing how Cameroon could process more of one of its most important crops at home.

Twenty-year-old Solantine Maifrigi counts the threads one by one. She lifts her feet in a steady rhythm, passes a wooden shuttle from hand to hand and concentrates on preventing the threads from breaking as she weaves a 30-metre length of cotton fabric.

After the grandmother she had been caring for died, Maifrigi returned to her parents without a business or an income. She initially hoped to become a seamstress and paid FCFA 5,000 (US$8.90) a month for training. But when her younger sister, whom she had encouraged to learn a craft, became interested in weaving, Maifrigi decided to try it too.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Before joining the Gaaraadji Training Centre in Garoua’s Poumpoumré neighbourhood in northern Cameroon, she had never encountered textile weaving.

“During my free one-year training at the centre, I learned how to weave, dye and embroider clothing. I was asked to stay after completing the course,” she says.

Her monthly stipend helps cover food, clothing and rent.

“Thanks to my employment at the centre, I was able to buy a sewing machine,” she says, adding that she now sees new opportunities in the textile industry.

Like Maifrigi, 18-year-old single mother Nafisatou previously survived by selling a small range of goods. Since joining the centre, she has learned to weave and can better support herself and her child.

The two are among 10 young people retained from an initial group of 20 trainees. They learned to work with gaaraadji — the Fulfulde word for thread — made from cotton grown in Cameroon’s northern regions.

Cameroon produces about 350,000 tonnes of seed cotton annually under the supervision of the Cotton Development Company, SODECOTON, making it Africa’s fifth-largest producer. Yet little of the crop is processed locally.

According to Business in Cameroon, only about 5% of the country’s cotton is processed domestically. Around 3,000 tonnes a year were previously processed in Garoua by the Cotton Industrial Company of Cameroon, CICAM, whose operations in the city were suspended.

While West African producers such as Burkina Faso and Benin are pursuing domestic-processing strategies, Cameroon is only beginning to develop this part of its value chain.

The absence of CICAM’s operations in Garoua, together with delays in fully establishing the proposed CAMTEX industrial platform, has created room for smaller initiatives such as Gaaraadji.

Operating from premises covering more than 700 square metres, the centre has installed machinery to turn locally sourced thread into handmade cotton textiles.

“We source Cameroonian thread produced by SODECOTON through CICAM, as well as from other suppliers, depending on demand,” says Sonia Hayatou, founder of the Gaaraadji Training Centre.

Hayatou, a chemist with a passion for sewing, returned to Cameroon after working in Europe for 17 years. She hopes that, within five years, Gaaraadji will become one of the businesses processing more of the country’s cotton locally.

For now, the centre uses just over 100kg of cotton thread a month but hopes to increase production.

“We produce fabric every two days. Demand is high, especially for weddings,” Hayatou says. “We bring something new by personalising designs and ensuring quality, so customers no longer have to travel to West Africa in search of fabric. They also have the advantage of being able to monitor production.”

She believes Gaaraadji could eventually respond to larger orders, including those for uniforms.

Although its output remains modest, the centre is gaining recognition. It was selected from among 600 enterprises participating in the 2026 Cameroon International Handicrafts Fair, SIARC , organised by the Ministry of Small and Medium-sized Enterprises, Social Economy and Handicrafts, MINPMEESA, to showcase the country’s crafts.

“We recently produced a collection of 12 outfits made from 100% cotton, woven in Garoua and sewn in Yaoundé, in less than a month for the Environment, Ecosystem, Fashion and Design Forum organised by MINPMEESA,” Hayatou recalls.

Adama Habiya, MINPMEESA’s representative at Garoua II Council, says Gaaraadji was selected because of the originality and cultural significance of its work, its use of locally produced cotton and the jobs it is creating.

Since registering as a craft business with the council, Gaaraadji has also received technical and financial support through MINPMEESA’s decentralised services.

“What we appreciate about this centre is its dedication, the founder’s passion for the craft and the quality of its finished products,” Habiya says. “We encourage the centre to persevere, innovate, establish itself in national and international markets, and adapt to the changing landscape, including ICT, standards and quality requirements, intellectual property protection and business formalisation.”

When Cameroon hosted the World Trade Organization’s 14th Ministerial Conference in Yaoundé from 26 to 29 March 2026, including a side event for cotton-producing countries, Gaaraadji was invited to demonstrate its work.

“We demonstrated the journey from cotton to thread using a spinning wheel, and then from weaving to finished fabric,” Hayatou says.

Ousmanou Garba, director of the Garoua Crafts Village, says the initiative comes at a time when Cameroon needs improved weaving techniques to advance its National Development Strategy 2020–2030 and import-substitution policy, which promotes Made in Cameroon products.

Close 

The Garoua Regional Crafts Village provides Gaaraadji with technical guidance, expertise and practical advice, while also including it in trade fairs and exhibitions.

“We firmly believe that this centre will contribute to women’s empowerment through weaving, something we are already witnessing first-hand,” Garba says. “Its woven products are of high quality and meet a variety of needs within the region and beyond.”

In October 2026, Gaaraadji plans to begin offering formal vocational courses after receiving authorisation from the Ministry of Employment and Vocational Training. It will continue providing weaving instruction to women from disadvantaged backgrounds.

One challenge is promoting weaving in ways that resonate with Cameroonians and persuading consumers to see locally made cotton clothing as an investment, particularly in a market where many people rely on cheaper second-hand clothes.

Hayatou argues that the cost need not be prohibitive. The centre’s fabrics range from FCFA 2,500 (US$4.45) to about FCFA 40,000 (US$71).

She dreams of Cameroon following countries such as Burkina Faso and Mali in embracing domestic cotton processing as a way to strengthen the economy.

“Although we are still at an early stage, we are part of this movement,” she says.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Harare Vendors Given Final Deadline to Clear Streets
World.content:
The government has given illegal vendors operating in Harare until 9 September 2026 to vacate unauthorised sites ahead of a nationwide clean-up operation.

The Ministry of Local Government and Public Works said the crackdown would target illegal vending and informal trading in the Central Business District (CBD) and across the wider Harare Metropolitan Province.

In a statement, Local Government Minister Daniel Garwe said illegal vending had contributed to poor sanitation, blocked public pathways, disrupted formal businesses and increased congestion in the capital.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Whilst the Government of the Republic of Zimbabwe acknowledges the existence of informal trading as a recognized avenue of livelihood, this, however, should be within the bounds of municipal by-laws and at legally designated marketplaces," Minister Garwe said.

"The current state of disorderliness on the streets is not tolerable." he added

The government said it was particularly concerned about the impact of illegal vending on public health and security including what it described as an environment conducive to drug and substance abuse.

Minister Garwe issued what he described as a "stern and final warning" to vendors operating outside areas authorised by local authorities.

"All vendors engaging in Illegal Street and night trading have until Wednesday, September 9, 2026 to immediately vacate these unauthorised sites and relocate to lawful, designated vending markets provided by the local authority," he said.

From 9 September, the ministry, together with other government departments and agencies, will launch what the Minister described as a "comprehensive, zero-tolerance clean-up operation" targeting illegal vending sites.

Authorities said illegal structures, stalls and trading sites would be dismantled during the operation.

Municipal police will remain deployed in cleared areas to prevent vendors from returning, according to the Minister.

The government said the exercise would begin in Harare before being extended to other cities, towns and urban settlements across Zimbabwe.

The operation is being presented as part of efforts to restore public order, cleanliness and trafficability in line with the government's National Development Strategy 2 and Vision 2030 goals.

Minister Garwe urged informal traders to use the remaining time to move voluntarily to designated markets and warned that failure to comply could result in the loss of merchandise.

Close 

"We strongly urge all informal traders to take note of the advice, utilize this window, and comply with the directive voluntarily to avoid loss of their merchandise," he said.

Local authorities have also been instructed to speed up the registration and allocation of compliant traders to designated vending structures.

The government said it remained committed to creating what it described as a sustainable, orderly, clean and safe economic environment and called on residents and stakeholders to cooperate with law enforcement agencies during the operation.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Zimbabwe-Mozambique Deal to Boost Beira-Harare Fuel Pipeline Capacity
World.content:
PRESIDENTS Emmerson Mnangagwa and Daniel Chapo on Wednesday announced a major expansion of the Beira-Harare fuel corridor that will increase the pipeline's capacity by 67%, strengthening energy security in Zimbabwe and across the region.

The CPMZ pipeline's annual transport capacity is expected to rise from three million to five million cubic metres by the end of 2027.

The expansion will allow an additional two billion litres of fuel to be transported annually, benefiting Mozambique, Zimbabwe and neighbouring regional markets including Zambia, Malawi, Botswana and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

President Chapo described the project as a critical investment in regional energy security and infrastructure.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"The expansion of the CPMZ pipeline is an important investment in Mozambique's infrastructure and in the energy security of our region. By strengthening the connection between the Port of Beira and the Southern African hinterland, we are reinforcing Mozambique's role as a strategic gateway for regional trade while deepening our cooperation with Zimbabwe," he said.

He said infrastructure investments of this nature were essential for economic growth and strengthening the region's resilience.

Mnangagwa said the expansion would have significant long-term benefits for Zimbabwe and the wider region.

"The stronger Beira-Harare corridor will support Zimbabwe's energy security while creating greater capacity to serve markets beyond our borders. It shows what Mozambique and Zimbabwe can achieve through cooperation around infrastructure of shared regional importance," he said.

The expansion will involve the construction of new pumping stations at Nhamatanda in Sofala Province and Messica in Manica Province.

The project will be synchronised with the planned expansion of the Petrozim Line between Feruka and Harare, creating a higher-capacity fuel route from the Mozambican coast into the Southern African hinterland.

Authorities said construction and commissioning would be carried out without disrupting existing pipeline operations or fuel supplies.

The 294-kilometre CPMZ pipeline links the Port of Beira in Mozambique to Feruka in Zimbabwe and serves as a key fuel artery for landlocked countries in the region.

The latest expansion follows an upgrade completed in 2024 which increased the pipeline's annual capacity from two million to three million cubic metres.

António Laice, Chairman of the Board of Directors, said the project would increase capacity along one of the region's most important fuel routes while ensuring continued supplies.

"This project adds substantial capacity to one of the region's most important fuel routes without disrupting the supplies on which countries and businesses rely every day. It is an investment not only in pipeline infrastructure, but in regional trade, industrial activity and the long-term reliability of Southern Africa's fuel supply network," he said.

Close 

Beyond the latest expansion, plans are also being considered to eventually replace the existing pipeline with a larger-diameter line capable of transporting about 12 million cubic metres annually.

The proposed upgrade is projected to meet regional fuel demand through to 2050.

There are also plans being considered to extend the Harare-Lusaka fuel route into Zambia's Copperbelt, potentially further strengthening regional fuel distribution networks.

The developments are expected to cement the Beira corridor's position as a strategic gateway for fuel imports into Zimbabwe and other landlocked Southern African markets.

World.title: Kenya: President Ruto Orders Crackdown On Illegal Traders in Kenya
World.content:
Nairobi — President William Ruto has ordered a crackdown on illegal traders in Kenya amid complaints from local traders over competition from foreigners engaging in local retail businesses.

Speaking while meeting small traders at State House yesterday, the Head of State tasked State Department for Industry Principal Secretary Juma Mukhwana and Trade Cabinet Secretary Lee Kinyanjui with ensuring that illegal traders are dealt with according to the law.

President Ruto added that Parliament is already working on a Bill that will restrict foreigners from engaging in certain trades in the country.

"Kuna biashara ambayo mgeni hawezi kufanya hapa Kenya. Tayari tuko na mswada bunge. We have a bill in parliament ya mambo ya biashara. Katika hiyo bill tumependekeza ya kwamba kuna biashara ambayo mgeni hawezi kufanya hapa Kenya," President Ruto said.

".......waangalie kabisa kwa sababu hatujapitisha so that we seal all the loopholes. Isitokee ati mtu ametoka sijui China na wapi na wapi anakuja kuwa hawker. Kuja kufanya biashara ya kuuza sijui kwa duka kidogo hapo."

Over the years, local traders have raised concerns over the growing number of traders from countries such as Burundi, Somalia and Tanzania, among others, who they say are competing with Kenyans in businesses including food, mitumba and retail shops.

Federal prosecutors have charged a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with lying to investigators about the events surrounding the shooting of a Venezuelan man in Minneapolis earlier this year, Fox News Digital has learned.

The Department of Justice has charged ICE agent Christian Castro with making false statements connected to the Jan. 14 shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, who was shot in the leg. He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Minnesota on Wednesday, a source familiar with the charges said.

Castro is accused of opening fire through the front door of a Minneapolis home, hitting Sosa-Celis, and then lying about the events before the shooting. The incident came amid the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration in Minnesota.

ICE OFFICER CHARGED IN MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING RELEASED IN TEXAS AFTER JUDGE DECLINES TO INTERVENE

What followed was at least one night of unrest in Minneapolis.

The charges came after Castro was released from a Texas jail last week, following Texas Gov. Greg Abbott's refusal to sign an extradition warrant to hand him over to Minnesota authorities.

Under Texas law and barring extradition, Castro must be released after 90 days of detention. Last month, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed an unsuccessful request for a temporary restraining order in an effort to block Castro’s release or to order his return to Minnesota, The Associated Press reported.

ABBOTT TAUNTS FAR-LEFT AG WITH FIERY WARNING OVER ICE EXTRADITION FIGHT: 'SUCH BAD LAWYERS'

Castro is charged separately in that state with assault and false reporting of a crime related to the same shooting.

ICE SAYS OFFICER SHOT AND KILLED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT WHO TRIED TO RAM HIM WITH CAR IN HOUSTON

On Wednesday, ProPublica reported that federal prosecutors were barred by officials in Washington from pursuing civil rights charges against Castro.

World.title: Lawmakers press DHS in letter over Chinese forced labor allegations, flag popular Labubu dolls
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

FIRST ON FOX — The House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is requesting a briefing from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on the agency's implementation of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA), a law designed to combat the import of Chinese goods made with slave labor, according to a letter shared exclusively with Fox News Digital.

The UFLPA, passed in 2021, directed DHS' Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force to develop a strategy for quelling the importation of goods into the United States that are "manufactured wholly or in part with forced labor in the People's Republic of China."

Human rights groups began shining a spotlight on the alleged oppression and forced labor the CCP was imposing on Uyghurs, a Muslim ethnic minority in China's Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region (XUAR), a sparsely populated Chinese territory in the country's far west.

MOTHER RECOUNTS HORRORS OF BRUTAL CHINESE DETENTION CAMP WHERE INFANT SON DIED

"The Uyghurs are being politically persecuted in Xinjiang, China. They are being forced to give up their religion. They're being forced to assimilate into Chinese culture. And many of them are being forced to do labor, to work for low wages or no wages and long hours," Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., the ranking member on the House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.

Khanna argued that enforcement of the UFLPA is not just a moral issue, but one of economic and national security for Americans.

KHANNA DEMANDS ANSWERS FROM CCP-LINKED COMPANY ACCUSED OF UNDERCUTTING US MANUFACTURERS

"This is a human rights violation, but the broader problem also for Americans is that they're making steel, they're making aluminum, they're making textiles, and then they're dumping it into the U.S. market. How could U.S. Steel or Cleveland Cliffs or our aluminum manufacturers compete with slave labor? Of course we can't. So what our letter does is it says that we need more of these companies that are using forced Uyghur labor to be designated by the Department of Homeland Security," Khanna continued.

The bipartisan letter, addressed to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, asks the agency to address 10 concerns the committee has, including what work DHS and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) are doing to update the list of companies and entities on the UFLPA Entity List.

GSA FINDS CHINA-MADE TECH LABELED 'MADE IN USA' IN FEDERAL PROCUREMENT PROGRAM, ORDERS SWEEPING REVIEW

DHS added an additional 43 companies to the list in July, an action that Khanna applauded.

"I think the administration may have gotten wind that we were doing this letter and that precipitated action. You know, for a year, they hadn't done anything. Now, I give them some credit for having 44 of these companies on the list. But hopefully, once the letter goes out, we'll see more action," he said.

CHINA’S ROUTING OF BIDEN IN CHIP WAR WITH US CREATED A COMMUNIST TECH GIANT

The committee's letter highlights concerns that products produced by companies on the list and that are coming from the XUAR are still making their way to U.S. customers. Those products, the letter alleges, cover supply chains ranging from steel and aluminum to silicon-carbon materials critical to technology production.

The letter highlights a New York Times report that suggests the cotton contained in popular "Labubu" dolls comes from slave labor.

THE CCP’S NEW ‘UNITY’ LAW TURNS CHINA’S REPRESSION INTO A GLOBAL THREAT

"A lot of the textiles are coming, they come from China, are coming from Uyghurs. It's one of the easiest places to force people into labor, and that's why we included it, because of the reports that Uyghurs are involved in textile production," Khanna added.

Khanna also explained how China circumvents the import bans by outsourcing manufacturing.

TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED

"It's very challenging. I mean, obviously, conventionally, China has been evading some of the tariffs and protections by having their companies open up in Malaysia or Vietnam. Here, of course, you've got actual slave labor. And so what we're saying is identify these products back to the source. And if the source of the textile or steel or aluminum is forced Uyghur labor, then that should not be in the United States," he told Fox News Digital.

Ultimately, Khanna stressed, the problem of forced labor in China is a bipartisan issue, a statement seemingly reflected by the fact that the letter was signed by eight lawmakers, four Republicans and four Democrats.

CHINESE ESPIONAGE STEALS $600 BILLION FROM US FIRMS YEARLY. IT’S TIME FOR GOVERNMENT TO ACT

"This is about fair trade and human rights. Americans aren't concerned about fair competition. If China had laborers that were being paid a fair wage and they were making something and we wanted to buy from them and they weren't dumping, and if China were buying from us, that would be fine. But what can't happen is them using slave labor, undercutting our market and our companies, and then not allowing our companies to sell to them. That's just not fair," he told Fox News Digital.

"Most Americans believe in trade, but they want fair trade and they don't want to be competing with slave labor," Khanna concluded.

A prominent LGBT podcaster who formerly hosted a Christian reality television show was arrested by federal agents in Los Angeles Thursday for allegedly threatening to kill President Donald Trump.

Benjamin Azariah Southworth, 40, was indicted by a grand jury on federal charges for cyberstalking, making harassing interstate calls and threatening to kill President Trump, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli announced on X.

He said that Southworth led a harassment campaign against the family of one of Trump's personal attorneys.

TRUMP'S DECADE OF ASSASSINATION THREATS RUNS FROM BUTLER SHOOTING TO LATEST GOLF CLUB BREACH

"Southworth is charged with posting videos calling for President Trump’s assassination, then targeted the family of the President’s personal attorney by publishing their home address and phone numbers, and leaving voicemails threatening 'justice comes to your door," Essayli said.

The act of publicly revealing personal information of public officials and celebrities without their consent is known as 'doxxing' and is usually done with the intent to harass, shame or cause harm.

"Threats against the President of the United States are federal crimes. We will not tolerate threats of political violence in the United States. My office will prosecute anyone who crosses that line to the fullest extent of the law," the U.S. Attorney wrote in a statement on X.

On Southworth's website "Holy Menace", which is still live at time of publication, the podcaster sells $5 stickers that say "Kill Trump."

While being taken into custody by agents, Southworth yelled, "Donald Trump is a pedophile. The country has fallen!" according to the New York Post, which had a photographer present at the time of his arrest.

Court documents obtained by the publication allegedly state that on April 7, 2026, Southworth posted a video on his Instagram account that contained a series of threats against Trump.

"I have been vocal in calling for the execution of Donald Trump," he allegedly said. "This government is illegitimate and out of control. It’s time for course correction. Kill Donald Trump."

The documents allegedly include a myriad of other examples of Southworth making threatening comments against the president, but the papers are not publicly available.

MAN INDICTED FOR ALLEGEDLY POSTING GRUESOME DEATH THREATS AGAINST KRISTI NOEM, PAM BONDI ON SOCIAL MEDIA

"Anyone who engages in or endorses political violence or assassination culture must be condemned in the harshest terms possible," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital.

"They should also immediately seek psychiatric help to treat their severe and debilitating case of Trump Derangement Syndrome that has warped their brains and made them sick in the head."

In the late 2000s, Southworth hosted the Christian reality TV show "The Remix", which aired on some of the largest Christian networks in the country, including National Religious Broadcasters TV. The show featured Christian musicians and bands.

In 2008, Southworth came out as gay. He was subsequently the opening act for gay Christian singer Ray Boltz on the singer's nationwide tour in 2010.

In 2020, he started a podcast called "Yass, Jesus!'" which is described as "an interfaith and sexuality affirming comedy podcast that believes you don't have to pick between gay and God." He cohosts the show with "Mean Girls" actor Daniel Franzese, who is also gay.

The Southeastern Conference (SEC) blitzed LSU on Thursday with a lawsuit as Commissioner Greg Sankey and others were in court over NCAA eligibility for professional athletes.

Sankey provided an affidavit that stated that SEC presidents voted unanimously (15-0) in favor of the new rules with Rousse abstaining.

On the somber anniversary, and in the days leading up to it, Fox News personalities and correspondents will present commemorative packages and interviews while reporting live from locations across New York, Washington, D.C., and Pennsylvania.

"FOX & Friends" will spend the week of Sept. 7 broadcasting live from several locations tied to the horrific day. Co-host Steve Doocy, who was broadcasting live alongside co-host Brian Kilmeade on the morning of the attacks in 2001, will host the program’s flagship "Breakfast with Friends" series live from the historic O’Hara’s Pub in New York City just two blocks from Ground Zero.

MASSIVE PIECE OF 9/11 HISTORY MAKES STUNNING 10,500-MILE JOURNEY ACROSS AMERICA

Doocy will then travel to Washington, D.C., on Tuesday and speak with Tunnel to Towers Foundation chairman and CEO Frank Siller. The show will also feature the Steel Across America tour — a historic coast-to-coast campaign honoring those who sacrificed their lives on 9/11 — arriving at the White House.

Doocy will broadcast live from Shanksville, Pennsylvania, the crash site of United Airlines Flight 93, on Thursday.

On Friday, Fox News Channel’s special coverage will commence with "FOX & Friends" co-hosts Kilmeade, Ainsley Earhardt and Lawrence Jones broadcasting live from the Hyatt House in Jersey City, overlooking the New York City skyline. Doocy will contribute live from Ground Zero.

"America’s Newsroom" co-anchors Bill Hemmer and Dana Perino will broadcast live from Brookfield Place overlooking the World Trade Center campus in downtown Manhattan. The reading of the victims’ names from the National September 11 Memorial & Museum is also expected to air during "America’s Newsroom."

TRUMP CONFIRMS PENTAGON PLANS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS, DISPUTES REPORT ON GROUND ZERO ABSENCE

"The Faulkner Focus," "Outnumbered," "America Reports" and "The Will Cain Show" will all feature special segments and interviews tied to 9/11, while Martha MacCallum’s "The Story" will report live from the Hyatt House and feature interviews with Cardinal Timothy Dolan and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch.

Throughout the day, Fox News senior correspondent Eric Shawn, who reported from Ground Zero on the day of the attacks, will contribute live from downtown Manhattan and correspondent Alexis McAdams will report live from Shanksville.

Chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin will contribute from the Pentagon and senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy will be stationed at the White House.

On FOX Business Network, "The Claman Countdown" anchor Liz Claman will commemorate the 658 Cantor Fitzgerald employees lost in the 9/11 attacks on Sept. 10. The following day, Claman will feature an interview with Silverstein Properties CEO Larry Silverstein from the World Trade Center, which he helped rebuild following the attacks.

AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS

Fox News Digital will publish multiple retrospective and feature stories focused on survivors, first responders, victims’ families and those carrying the legacy of 9/11 forward 25 years later. Fox News Digital will also provide day-of coverage of the commemorations at Ground Zero, the Pentagon and Shanksville, including livestream embeds from all three ceremonies.

Fox News Digital will also feature interviews with National September 11 Memorial & Museum CEO Elizabeth L. Hillman and former Navy SEAL Robert O’Neill, among others. The platform will publish a "Never Forget" archival photo retrospective, including a look at how Ground Zero and the Manhattan skyline have changed since the attacks.

FOX Nation will debut two new specials ahead of the anniversary, starting with "Paul Mauro’s Notes from Ground Zero" on Sept. 4. The special spotlights Fox News contributor and former NYPD Inspector Paul Mauro, who was working the morning of 9/11 and scribbled down notes in the days following the attacks, as he returns to Ground Zero for the first time in 25 years.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

On September 8, FOX Nation will launch "Born on 9/11: 25 Years with Harris Faulkner," exploring the lives of people born on September 11, 2001. FOX Nation will also livestream the official ceremonies at the NYC memorial site and the Pentagon next Friday.

FOX News Audio and FOX News Podcasts will present extensive coverage of the anniversary as well, including an eight-part documentary series entitled "FOX News Rewind: 9/11," that features a variety of Fox News personalities.

On YouTube, "The Brian Kilmeade Show" will provide access to some of Kilmeade’s most notable 9/11 interviews and affiliates will be offered an anniversary special from Kilmeade that reflects on how America has evolved over the last 25 years.

World.title: Fox News parts ways with Maria Bartiromo
World.content:
Fox News Media, the parent of Fox News Channel and Fox Business Network, said Thursday that it had parted ways with longtime anchor Maria Bartiromo.

“We thank Maria for her work over the lasts 12½ years and wish her all the best on her next chapter,” a spokesperson said in a statement that did not elaborate further.

Bartiromo has been Fox Business Network’s global markets editor since joining it in 2014. She hosted “Mornings with Maria” and “Maria Bartiromo’s Wall Street” on Fox Business, while also anchoring “Sunday Morning Futures,” a business-focused show on Fox News Channel.

Bartiromo joined Fox from CNBC, where she hosted one of the network’s highest-profile programs, “Closing Bell” and was the first person to report live from the floor of the New York Stock Exchange.

Bartiromo’s departure was “effective today,” the Fox spokesperson also said.

Long seen as a trailblazer for women in financial media, Bartiromo’s reporting took a more openly conservative turn after she left CNBC, where her reporting had been viewed as largely apolitical.

Many of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet secretaries appeared regularly on her shows during both of his terms in office. Fox also regularly touted Bartiromo’s shows as ratings winners.

In 2021, Bartiromo’s comments and shows were cited as exhibits in a defamation lawsuit filed by the voting machine maker Dominion Voting Systems against Fox News. Dominion alleged that the cable network operator had knowingly broadcast false claimed that Dominion had rigged the 2020 presidential election.

Fox News and Dominion eventually settled the lawsuit in 2023 for $787 million.

During her nearly 21 years at CNBC, Bartiromo appeared regularly on national broadcast programs, including NBC’s “TODAY” and “Nightly News” during the 2007-2008 financial crisis.

Comcast, the parent company of NBC News, spun off CNBC in 2025.

Bartiromo did not immediately reply to an email seeking comment on her departure.

Bartiromo has not appeared on FBN’s air since Aug. 9, according to a review of archived episodes of her shows. Her biography page and show pages had already been removed from Fox’s websites Thursday.

Bartiromo was one of the first financial journalists on cable TV whose influence extended beyond Wall Street.

Early in her career, Bartiromo had been dubbed the “Money Honey,” a nickname she later said she had misgivings about.

In the early 1990s, The Ramones’ Joey Ramone released a song titled “Maria Bartiromo.”

She also appeared in the 2010 film “Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps,” where she played herself alongside Michael Douglas’ Gordon Gekko in a scene set at a fictional CNBC interview.

World.title: In Nepal, mourners hold symbolic cremation for missing loved ones
World.content:
The wall of ice, water and rock that tore through Nepal last week has claimed more than 1,200 lives and left more than 4,000 missing, depriving many grieving families of a basic rite: funerals.

The scale of the disaster has proved challenging for authorities, with morgues overwhelmed by a large number of unidentified remains. In many cases, bodies have been washed far downstream and rendered unrecognizable, while others still missing are feared to have been buried in the torrent of thick mud.

Ezra Acayan / Getty Images

As hopes fade that survivors will be found, a week on from the disaster, family members without the remains of their loved ones have begun to hold symbolic cremations.

The ceremonies provide an outlet for the grief and uncertainty that have gripped so many in Nepal, and ensure that a key religious rite is afforded to the dead.

Ritesh Shukla / Getty Images

At Kathmandu’s Pashupatinath Temple, the most revered Hindu temple in Nepal, mourners gathered Wednesday to mark the loss of missing loved ones. On the banks of the holy Bagmati River, they burned effigies made of kusa grass, also called darbha, a plant used in Hindu rituals, on miniature funeral pyres.

The small stick figures, wrapped in orange cloth, were rubbed in paste and covered in garlands of orange flowers.

World.title: Colin Kaepernick is done with the NFL. He isn’t done fighting.
World.content:
The same league that let Michael Vick play again after he went to prison for dogfighting, and allowed Deshaun Watson to sign a contract for $230 million following accusations of sexual misconduct by more than 20 women (Watson has maintained his innocence), was keeping Kaepernick out.

“There’s not a definitive moment that I would point to,” Kaepernick says about when he realized what was happening.

Instead, it was more of a culmination.

“Coming on the back of going to a Super Bowl, going to an NFC Championship, setting records, and not a single team would bring me in, even for a workout?” Kaepernick says.

In August 2017, the Miami Dolphins — whose owner Stephen Ross previously launched a nonprofit to fight systemic racism — signed quarterback Jay Cutler after an injury to starter Ryan Tannehill, even though Cutler had already retired. NFL team executives, meanwhile, used the media to try to throw water on the idea that Kaepernick was blackballed.

Some coaches and GMs did reach out, Kaepernick says, and explicitly told him, “Yeah, we want to bring you in, but it’s getting shut down above us.”

One of those coaches, Kaepernick writes in his book, was John Harbaugh, the then-head coach of the Baltimore Ravens. Kaepernick spoke extensively with Harbaugh during the summer of 2017. Harbaugh’s brother Jim was Kaepernick’s coach during the 49ers’ run to the Super Bowl.

Kaepernick writes that Harbaugh was “pushing” to sign him, but was “shut down from above.”

In October 2017, Kaepernick filed a grievance against the NFL under the terms of the league’s and players’ collective bargaining agreement, alleging that owners were colluding against signing him due to his protest.

“Everybody believes that he was blackballed,” says one former player who was in the league during 2016. “Players knew that this would happen. That was a firm belief around the league.”

Goodell pushed back on the notion of organized collusion to keep Kaepernick out of the NFL.

“Those are decisions that each individual owner has to make and their clubs, coaches, GMs,” Goodell told NBC in 2020. “And I’ve talked to a lot of our clubs about it and I’ve encouraged them. I’d love to see him play again.”

Jesse Dittmar for NBC News

In November 2019 — months after the NFL settled Kaepernick’s lawsuit — the league tried to arrange a midseason workout for him in front of all 32 teams. The details of this day are now infamous, as Kaepernick ultimately called off the NFL’s workout the morning of due to an extensive waiver he refused to sign — a waiver Kaepernick believed would sign away his employment rights and potential future claims — and instead managed to organize a workout of his own.

The dissolution of the workout drew another round of skepticism, with many claiming Kaepernick was pulling a media stunt or was not serious about wanting to play again.

While Kaepernick was out of the league, the NFL went about trying to turn the temperature down on his protest, battling the aftermath of an especially divisive election and a ratings slide some attributed to the player demonstrations.

The league partnered in 2017 with the Players Coalition, a group founded to address systemic racism, and has since committed more than half a billion dollars to various social justice causes. Kaepernick wasn’t part of the group. (Reid said in 2017 that Kaepernick was kicked out of communications with the group by co-founder Malcolm Jenkins, which Jenkins denied.)

The NFL did whatever it could to stop the kneeling, the former player says, believing the league wanted to weed out players who kneeled: “What happened was the league and the Players Coalition came to a deal, and then the league did what they were going to do … They wanted their games to go back to normal.”

Kaepernick’s protest likely cost him tens of millions of dollars, even accounting for whatever he got from the NFL in the settlement.

But as his career was sacked, as television pundits continued to make personal attacks, and as 986 people were killed by police in 2017, Kaepernick stayed largely quiet.

He says that was by design.

“No individual should be speaking for everyone across the country. I don’t think that’s a responsible way to approach things,” Kaepernick says. “It’s also being able to enable other people to step into leadership positions, because that’s what movements actually are. It’s not one person just driving things.”

Months after his workout snafu, events unrelated to Kaepernick raised the volume on his protest once more.

On May 25, 2020, 46-year-old George Floyd was killed by police officer Derek Chauvin in Minnesota.

Video revealed Chauvin kneeled on Floyd’s neck for over nine minutes, killing him. Chauvin was convicted on multiple murder charges in 2021.

Nearly four years after Kaepernick kneeled in response to police brutality, worldwide protests emerged in the wake of Floyd’s killing. Kaepernick says seeing the protests around the world made him hopeful in the moment, especially as people in some cases risked their own well-being to be heard in the middle of the pandemic.

Nike included Kaepernick in its 30th anniversary "Just Do It" campaign in 2018. Supporters gathered outside NFL headquarters in New York City after Kaepernick filed a grievance against the league alleging that owners were colluding against signing him because of his protest. Getty Images file

“There was a significant portion of the population that previously was disconnected from these realities,” Kaepernick says. “It was like, oh, actually I have to sit with this now and I have to grapple with this. And am I OK with this? And what is my role within this? Am I complicit?”

Corporations also scrambled to meet the moment, including the NFL. In June 2020, several NFL players coordinated social media posts asking for the league to condemn racism and “admit wrong in silencing our players from peacefully protesting.”

The next day, Goodell responded in a video message.

“We, the National Football League, condemn racism and the systematic oppression of Black people,” Goodell said in the video, echoing the words players demanded from him. “We, the National Football League, admit we were wrong for not listening to NFL players earlier and encourage all to speak out and peacefully protest. We, the National Football League, believe Black lives matter.”

Kaepernick wasn’t impressed.

“His response through that video was only because of pressure from players, not because it was altruistic,” Kaepernick says.

The idea that the league should have listened to protesting players “is so laughable in my mind, and so disingenuous,” Kaepernick says. “We had been trying to address the issue that the NFL created with blackballing me for years. To come out and say we should have listened on the back of that — while I’m still actively trying to play in the NFL — it’s so performative.”
