World.title: Israel prepared to remove Palestinians from Gaza if U.S. approves, defence minister says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Israel is waiting for U.S. approval to remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Wednesday, resurfacing a plan that has been widely condemned as forced displacement and described as ethnic cleansing.

Katz, speaking at a news conference hosted by Israeli news site Ynet and newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, said Israel is ready to facilitate what has been described as "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians in Gaza "by any means."

Palestinians in Gaza have mostly rejected the idea, fearing it will result in their forced expulsion.

Yedioth Ahronoth reported that Israeli National Security Minister and far-right Jewish Power party leader Itamar Ben-Gvir will unveil the plan on Thursday, which will reportedly remove Palestinians over the span of seven years.

Ben-Gvir — who has been sanctioned by Ottawa over repeated incitements of violence against Palestinian communities — is expected to present the plan dubbed "Disengagement 710" as part of his campaign in October's legislative elections.

Pending U.S. backing, Katz described the move as necessary, insisting the issue at hand is finding countries to take the Palestinians in.

"There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration," Katz said.

Katz said the Israeli government "is organized and prepared to get them out — by sea, by air, by every way possible," according to the Times of Israel.

Palestinians walk past the rubble of residential buildings destroyed, in Gaza City on Wednesday. (Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters)

The comments come nearly three years since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel, which killed 1,200 people and led to about 250 being taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies. Israel's ensuing assault on Gaza has killed more than 73,400, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, and left much of the enclave in ruins.

In February 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump pitched the idea of taking ownership of the territory and permanently displacing its residents before turning it into the "Riviera of the Middle East," which at the time was met with unified anger and concern.

Trump later appeared to abandon the idea, and in January 2026 established the "Board of Peace" to ostensibly handle the resolution of violence and reconstruction in Gaza, although the board has made little progress.

Katz claims Trump has not abandoned the plan, but has merely "frozen it" due to pressure from Arab states, the Times of Israel reported.

Forcible deportation 'manifestly illegal': UN

In response to Trump's remarks in February 2025, United Nations experts warned that moving or forcibly relocating Palestinians would violate international law.

"It is manifestly illegal to invade and annex foreign territory by force, to forcibly deport its population, and to deprive the Palestinian people of their inalienable right to self-determination," they said in 2025.

The UN Office of the High Commissioner raised concern over ethnic cleansing by Israeli authorities in both Gaza and the West Bank this past February. It said the increase of reported attacks and forcible transfers "appear aimed at a permanent displacement of Palestinians throughout the occupied territories."

Many Palestinians in Gaza refuse to leave their homes despite dire living conditions after Israel's two-year offensive in the enclave left roughly two million people displaced and living in crowded makeshift tent camps. Families have been left to deal with widespread destruction, severe water shortages and acute food insecurity.

"We were born and raised in Gaza, we will die and be buried in Gaza," Umm Yusuf Shabat, a 55-year-old mother and grandmother, told a freelance videographer with CBC News in the legislative district west of Gaza City.

"There is no immigration by any means. It is enough, the displacement we went through. No matter what happens, we will not [be displaced] again."

Muhammad Abu Jibbeh, 39, echoed Shabat's remarks, saying he refuses to leave.

"Ultimately, this is our homeland … we are going to remain steadfast and we will not leave our land and we utterly reject the idea of leaving the country or migrating," Abu Jibbeh said.

WATCH | Gaza described as 'humanitarian purgatory' in July: Gaza stuck in ‘humanitarian purgatory’ 9 months into ceasefire | Duration 5:01 Nine months after a ceasefire brought an end to Israel’s heaviest attacks, large parts of Gaza are still in crisis. For The National, CBC’s Chris Brown breaks down how a collapsed water grid, severe food shortages, and ongoing military activity have left the territory frozen in what’s been described as ‘humanitarian purgatory.’

Others say the living conditions have made it impossible to bear or envision a future in the war-torn territory. The Israel Defence Forces currently control up to 70 per cent of Gaza, according to Israeli sources cited in a July report.

Abdul Rahman Al-Turk, 28, says he has been displaced seven times within Gaza since the war began in October 2023. He says water and bread shortages persist, making it difficult to get by.

"We are tired. When we have the first chance to leave the country, we will take it," Al-Turk told CBC News.

"There is no future here. There is no work, no construction, nothing. What do we want to do in this country? If the solution is migration, then get us out."

Latest Trump plan notes no displacement

Despite a U.S.-backed ceasefire that took effect in October 2025, which halted the large-scale fighting that had devastated the enclave, Israeli strikes and raids continue in Gaza. The Gaza Health Ministry said more than 1,300 civilians have died since then.

The 20-point peace plan, agreed upon by Israel and Hamas in October 2025, did not call for Palestinians’ displacement.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected Trump's new 15-point peace plan last month, saying Israel will not withdraw forces until Hamas ⁠⁠fully disarms. Trump's plan states that nobody will be forced to leave the Gaza Strip under Clause 13, which calls for a phased Israeli withdrawal.

WATCH | Netanyahu rejects Trump's 15-point peace plan last month: Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point Gaza peace plan | Duration 1:45 Israel has rejected U.S. President Donald Trump’s 15-point Board of Peace plan for Gaza. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu signalled Israeli forces will not withdraw until Hamas 'genuinely' disarms.

Hamas formally dissolved its primary civilian governing body in July but maintains it will only disarm after a complete Israeli withdrawal from the territory.

Katz's remarks this week drew a sharp rebuke from Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who condemned the plan.

"After our trip to the Gaza-Egypt border last year, [Sen. Jeff Merkley] and I released a report entitled, 'The Netanyahu Government is Implementing a Plan to Ethnically Cleanse Gaza of Palestinians,'" Van Hollen said in a post on X.

"Now the Israeli [Ministry] of Defence confirmed that's the goal. We must end our complicity."

World.title: Vaccine-preventable illnesses on the horizon again as Canadian kids head back to school
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With millions of Canadian kids heading back to school and temperatures set to drop, it’s time to brace for another fall of seasonal illnesses — and medical experts say staying healthy takes more than just a flu shot.

The latest federal surveillance report , which tracks influenza, COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), shows it’s likely the calm before the storm, with low and stable levels of all three respiratory threats that are set to come roaring back in the months ahead.

“As we transition to colder weather and we’re inside more, that’s when the bugs spread … and that’s when we see our emergency department visits start to go up, and then kids in the hospital more,” said Saskatoon-based pediatrician Dr. Ayisha Kurji, an assistant professor at the University of Saskatchewan.

McMaster University immunologist Matthew Miller says Canadians should already start assessing their options to get seasonal vaccines. For flu specifically, he noted that last year included a “really unusual severe early peak��” in influenza circulation.

“We saw really high case counts in … early December, which is about a month in advance of when we normally see flu season peak,” Miller said.

“What that means is that it's really important to be immunized in a timely manner in the fall to ensure that our immune systems have time to respond to the vaccine and mount that protective immunity.”

It typically takes around two to four weeks for the body to hit a peak immune response to the shot, he said.

And Miller stressed that a fall flu shot — which is recommended for all Canadians aged six months and up — is just one piece of the “suite of vaccines” families should consider.

Measles, for example, has continued circulating, and this fall may see further spread.

“Coming out of the summer months where families have often travelled ... puts everybody at increased risk when the school year starts again,” said Miller, “and all these young children, who have been to all kinds of different places, are now in close quarters again in classrooms.”

WATCH | Mother urges parents to vaccinate kids after daughter's measles death: Mother urges parents to vaccinate kids after daughter’s measles death | Duration 2:07 Measles may start like a bad cold — with symptoms like a high fever and cough — but in rare cases, it turns deadly. For one child, complications emerged about a decade later, robbing her of speech, movement and, eventually, her life.

Flu, COVID, RSV shots available for fall

Canada’s national vaccine advisory body recommends a COVID shot for higher-risk individuals , including older adults 65 and up and anyone who is pregnant or has underlying medical conditions.

“I still recommend the COVID vaccine because it’s still something that’s around, and still sends people into hospital,” said Kurji.

RSV vaccines are also available for older adults and pregnant individuals, to combat what Miller called an “extraordinarily dangerous virus to newborns.”

Real-world research has shown these relatively new shots are making a huge difference in serious RSV-related illness, with one large study showing the vaccine given during pregnancy cut babies’ hospital risk by more than 80 per cent .

“It's really having a profound impact on reducing rates of infection and particularly severe infection in these age groups — older adults and, in particular, newborns,” Miller said.

Beyond seasonal vaccines, experts stress Canadians need to stay up to date on their routine shots as well, given the resurgence of a range of vaccine-preventable diseases like measles, which can lead to flu-like symptoms and a blotchy rash, or in more serious cases, pneumonia, brain swelling, or even death.

“We have seen, since the pandemic, a decrease in uptake in the basic regular childhood vaccines,” said Dr. Joss Reimer, Canada’s chief public health officer.

“The recent spread of measles really shows us exactly what we need to be worried about,” she added.

“As soon as our numbers dip below a certain level, we do start to see these viruses come back and put children at risk, especially those kids who are either too young or, for some other health reason, can't get vaccinated.”

WATCH | Calls for B.C. to adopt universal infant RSV immunization program: Group calls on B.C. government to adopt a universal infant RSV immunization program | Duration 3:32 A national organization of women physicians is calling on B.C. to adopt a universal infant RSV immunization program ahead of this year's cold and flu season. Currently, pregnant people can elect to get the maternal RSV vaccine but they must pay out of pocket. The Federation of Medical Women of Canada is calling for a provincial program that would cover the costs for all. We spoke with Dr. Shelley Ross, who co-chairs the RSV task force.

Measles resurgence across Canada, U.S.

Just 85 per cent of two-year-olds in Canada were fully vaccinated against measles, mumps and rubella by the end of 2025, federal data shows — a far cry from the 95 per cent medical experts say is needed population-wide to keep measles at bay.

The same data shows less than 80 per cent of children that age were fully vaccinated with the shot targeting diphtheria, tetanus, and whooping cough.

Middling vaccination rates in recent years have contributed to an explosion of measles, one of the world’s most contagious viruses, across North America.

The U.S. has seen 37 new outbreaks so far in 2026, involving thousands of cases, while Canada lost its official measles elimination status last November after racking up more than 5,000 infections since late 2024, and more than 1,000 new cases just this year.

B.C.'s provincial health officer Dr. Bonnie Henry recently said most of the 30 people hospitalized since the start of that province's outbreak last year have been unvaccinated children.

“It’s sad to me that’s that where we are,” Kurji said. “Measles is an illness that is highly preventable [through vaccines]… one dose is great, two doses is almost perfect.”

Most modern clinicians haven’t even witnessed a real measles infection in their lifetime, Kurji added, which means cases can be tougher to spot and precautions to prevent onward transmission may not be put in place fast enough.

World.title: Feds announce $4.7B for new VIA Rail cars to be built in Ontario, Québec
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced an investment of $4.7 billion to build and maintain more than 300 rail cars for VIA Rail in Canada rather than in the U.S. Carney said the investment is predicted to generate more than $1.6 billion in economic benefits.

Carney announces $4.7B to build rail cars in Canada instead of U.S.

In the latest push of its Buy Canadian Policy, the federal government is spending more than $4.7 billion for Via Rail to acquire and maintain 313 new passenger rail cars from Alstom Canada.

This will be the first time in four decades that Via Rail passenger cars will be built entirely in Canada. Much of its existing fleet was built in the United States.

“They'll be Canadian electricians that install the wiring, Canadian machinists that will make the precision parts, Canadian welders will build the steel frames from Canadian carbon steel," Carney said at the Alstom Plant in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Thursday morning.

“That work reaches well beyond the factory floor into communities across our country.”

These cars will be manufactured and assembled in Thunder Bay and La Pocatière, Que., with design and engineering work taking place in Saint-Bruno-de-Montarville, Que.

The government projects the project could generate more than $1.6 billion for the economy and support nearly 700 jobs across Ontario and Quebec.

Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks at the Alstom Plant in Thunder Bay, Ont. on Sept. 3 after announcing a $4.7 billion contract to build 313 new passenger cars for Via Rail. (David Jackson/The Canadian Press)

“We've announced the contract of the decade,” said Michael Keroullé, president and CEO of Alstom Americas.

“This is actually kind of the first time we get the opportunity to work with the national railroad, with Via Rail. But more importantly, we are replacing cars that are now 70 years of age, very old, long overdue in terms of replacement.”

The announcement comes on the heels of another big project underway at the plant, which will handle the final assembly of new subway cars for the Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) — each of which will include 55 per cent Canadian content.

More to come.

World.title: Is Quebec actually the most taxed jurisdiction in North America?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With the rising cost of living front and centre in the Quebec election campaign, a familiar refrain has emerged: Quebec is the most taxed jurisdiction in North America.

Conservative Party of Quebec Leader Éric Duhaime is leaning on that claim to justify his promise of deep income and corporate tax cuts to help address the cost of living.

"Quebecers face the highest tax burden in North America. It is now the government's turn to tighten its belt,” Duhaime said in a news release last Friday.

He repeated that point during a news conference the same day, saying Quebec is "the worst one" among 60 states and provinces across Canada and the U.S.

But is the claim actually true? We took a closer look.

An overall heavy burden

The short answer is yes — with an asterisk. It depends on what exactly is being measured, according to Luc Godbout, a professor and the research chair in taxation and public finance at the Université de Sherbrooke.

One way to answer this question is through what economists call the "overall tax burden." This involves adding up all taxes paid to federal, provincial and local authorities by individuals and businesses, and then expressing that as a percentage of the gross domestic product (GDP).

By that measure, Quebec does indeed have the highest taxes among all 10 Canadian provinces, sitting at 38.6 per cent of its GDP for 2024, according to an annual study prepared by Godbout and other researchers at the university.

Quebec also has a higher overall tax burden than the United States and Mexico.

As this chart shows, the province's tax burden sits closer to the average of advanced countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Another way to measure the tax burden is by analyzing it at the individual level and looking at personal income taxes, social contributions and consumption taxes, Godbout explained to CBC News.

On that front, Quebec’s gross individual tax burden is heavier than all other provinces except one: Nova Scotia, Godbout pointed out.

On the whole, if Nova Scotia's tax system were applied to Quebecers, they would actually pay more.

LISTEN | This is Montreal: Should Quebec cut taxes to tackle the cost of living?: This is Montreal 15:16 Should Quebec cut taxes to tackle the cost of living? It’s often repeated that Quebecers pay the highest taxes of any jurisdiction in North America. CBC reporter Ben Shingler breaks down how the tax burden on Quebecers compares to elsewhere and what we get for it. And we’ll hear why some economists are saying that any government intervention to help with the cost of living needs to be targeted to the people who need it the most.

Taxes shrink wealth gap

The picture becomes more nuanced when evaluating what's called the "net tax burden."

This measure takes into account not only what individuals pay in taxes, but also what they get back through refundable tax credits and family allowances paid directly to households.

By this metric, the tax system in Quebec actually results in a lighter burden for individuals than in four of the nine other provinces. Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador, and New Brunswick all have a higher net tax burden, Godbout pointed out.

For example, a single-parent family earning $56,714 (which is two-thirds of the average wage) in Quebec gets back 12 per cent more in government transfers than they pay in total taxes — the lowest net burden in Canada, according to the annual study.

On the flip side, high-income earners with no children are heavily taxed in the province.

A single person earning $141,362 (which is two-thirds more than the average wage) faces a net tax burden of nearly 35 per cent, the highest in the country.

As the chart below illustrates, Quebec's tax system significantly shrinks the wealth gap.

Before taxes, Quebec's Gini coefficient, which measures inequality, is 0.43, but government transfers drop it to 0.27, leaving the province with some of the lowest income inequality in the country.

Colin Pratte, a researcher at the Institut de recherche et d’informations socioéconomiques (IRIS), argues higher tax collection in Quebec serves as an effective mechanism for wealth redistribution.

He points to the latest numbers from Statistics Canada, that show Ontario’s poverty rate is 50 per cent higher than in Quebec.

“It is actually the main tool for a given government, a given society, to make sure that wealth is well distributed among people of that society,” he said.

So, while Duhaime’s campaign rhetoric rings true for corporations, high-income earners, and childless individuals, Quebec's system of government transfers means lower-income families actually face some of the lightest net tax burdens on the continent.

World.title: Interior design: A new angle on tile
World.content:
Article content

Tile is breaking out of the kitchen and bathroom. The familiar finish is moving into living rooms, bedrooms, home offices and entertaining spaces, proving its potential extends far beyond traditional wet zones. With an extraordinary range of colours, formats and tactile effects available, it can anchor a room, define its architecture or introduce a quiet layer of personality. Its durability adds another compelling advantage, meeting the growing desire for interiors that feel elevated yet can handle the realities of daily life.

World.title: Colombia’s education minister resigns after less than a month
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella replaced his education minister after she resigned, claiming “an unexpected family situation.”

De la Espriella announced on social media platform X that he had accepted the resignation of the evangelical Education Minister Viviane Morales, who took office on August 7, the first day of the administration.

I bid a nostalgic farewell to my dear friend Viviane Morales. God’s designs are inscrutable, and she must leave us early to take charge of a personal situation that I sincerely hope she can resolve very soon. President Viviana Morales

In the same post, De la Espriella said he had appointed Ilva Myriam Hoyos, stressing that “I am confident that she will be an outstanding minister and that she will serve Colombia with dedication, character, and conviction.”

While in office, Morales lead the government’s Culture War in education and vowed to remove “gender ideology” from Colombia’s classrooms, and proposed a law that would allow churches to provide public education services.

Hoyos, a catholic, warned in 2016 that a peace deal between the government of President Juan Manuel Santos and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC promoted gender ideology.

The new education minister used to work with Alejandro Ordoñez, Colombia’s notoriously far-right former Inspector General and the country’s current ambassador to the Organization of American States.

World.title: De la Espriella claims Colombia’s military killed 23, arrested 6 EMC guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella claimed Wednesday that Colombia’s armed forces killed at least 23 members of FARC dissident group EMC and captured another six.

In a video, De la Espriella said that “Operation Azarias,” targeted the EMC’s Carolina Ramirez Front and killed one of its commanders, a man called “Tigre” or “Pintado,” in the south of the Guaviare province.

A second guerrilla commander, “Victor,” was among the six alleged EMC members who were arrested during the operation, which included air strikes.

The president claimed that Victor carried out attacks against the military “during the elections, as part of the ‘gunpoint vote’ strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict.”

That narcoterrorist, whom we have now taken out of circulation, carried out attacks against members of the National Army and the Navy. During the elections, as part of the “gunpoint vote” strategy launched by the previous regime to skew the popular verdict, this criminal ambushed a unit that was on the move precisely to protect citizens’ right to vote freely. President Abelardo de la Espriella

There is no evidence to suggest that De la Espriella’s predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro, employed illegal armed groups to coerce voters into voting against his would-be successor.

One minor allegedly survived the attack and was surrendered to family welfare agency ICBF. The Medical Examiner’s Office is expected to investigate how many minors were among the alleged “narcoterrorists.”

At least three minors were killed in a previous operation in Guaviare that killed at least nine alleged members of the EMC’s main rival, FARC dissident group EMBF, the Medical Examiner’s Office said earlier this week.

Air strikes against illegal armed groups are controversial as they could imply the blanket killing of victims of child recruitment, a war crime according to international humanitarian law.

The government has long insisted that those recruiting children and minors are responsible for the deaths of their victims.

World.title: 1 killed, 15 injured in northeast Colombia car bomb attack on police station
World.content:
At least one person was killed and another 15 injured in a car bomb attack on a police station on the outskirts of Cucuta, the capital of Norte de Santander.

According to the National Police, the bomb exploded on Monday evening outside of the police station in Los Patios, a municipality that is part of Cucuta’s metropolitan area.

Apart from the casualties, the blast also damaged buildings and vehicles that were parked near the police station, police told local media.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had convened a security council meeting “with the entire top brass of the security forces.”

“Wherever the terrorists try to sow fear, that is where the State will be with all is might,” said De la Espriella.

We will pursue with an iron fist those who threaten Colombians, until we capture them, dismantle their networks, and restore peace to our communities. Abelardo de la Espriella

In the region around Cucuta, guerrilla organizations ELN and EMBF have been fighting each other. Organized crime groups operate mainly inside the urban area of the capital of the Norte de Santander province.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.

World.title: Vote to move Uribe’s massacre probe to Congress triggers infighting among Colombia’s left
World.content:
Internal fractures within Colombia’s leftist opposition burst into the open following a vote by five representatives of the Historic Pact (PH) party to transfer a criminal investigation against former President Alvaro Uribe to Congress’ Accusations Commission.

The controversy erupted after the five PH members of the committee backed a motion of Uribe’s Democratic Center (CD) party to assert legislative jurisdiction over long-standing criminal cases against Uribe, including investigations into the massacres of El Aro (1997) and La Granja (1996), and the 1998 assassination of human rights defender Jesus Maria Valle.

PH members

David Alejandro Toro

María del Mar Pizarro

Heráclito Landínez

Jorge Bastidas

Gabriel Becerra

As the former governor of Antioquia, Uribe would have been in on the massacres carried out by the Bloque Metro and AUC paramilitary groups, according to the Prosecutor General’s Office, which refused to turn over the investigations.

The commission claimed jurisdiction over the Uribe file because the paramilitaries didn’t demobilize until after 2002, when he became president.

Critics of the decision, including the prosecution and PH Senate chief Ivan Cepeda, argued that Uribe’s alleged involvement in the crimes happened years before he was granted presidential immunity.

Cepeda spent much of his career fighting Uribe in court over his alleged ties to the AUC.

Because of the committee vote, the Constitutional Court will have to rule on who gets to investigate Uribe’s alleged crimes against humanity, which could delay the investigation.

Journalists who reported on the PH support for the fabricated conflict suggested that this may be part of a political deal between congressmen political deal between Uribistas and Petristas, supporters of former President Gustavo Petro.

Becerra, who is close to Cepeda, said in a statement that there “existed nor will there exist any political deal that would compromise justice, truth or the rights of victims.

According to the house representative, the PH lawmakers “initially considered it reasonable and legally appropriate to clarify the jurisdiction of the authority responsible for conducting the investigation,” but changed their mind in response to the controversy and calls for their resignation.

Lawyer Miguel Angel del Rio, the victims representative in the Uribe case, told Tercer Canal that “the ethic committee of the Historic Pact should investigate these five congressman,” adding that “what we have here is solidarity with impunity and this cannot be allowed.”

The Historic Pact became Colombia’s largest political party after congressional elections in March, but has seen an increase in internal tensions after Cepeda’s failure to win the presidential election in June.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.

My first encounter with Steve came in late 2002, after he had offered me the editor’s job—sight unseen, via e-mail—and I accepted, knowing only that I’d earn about US$500 a month and should show up in Santiago with an AP style guide and a copy of Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style. That it all seemed a bit rushed and loosey-goosey gave me pause for concern, but I was eager for an excuse to return to Chile, so hopped on a plane and flew down from Costa Rica.

Still, after our first meeting, I wondered just how wise my decision really was. It was then that I realized the Santiago Times wasn’t, as I’d imagined, a print paper. It was Internet-based, with a rudimentary website that was only half functioning. “We got hacked,” Steve told me. He also explained that he was living at that moment in Puerto Montt—1,000 kilometers to the south—and that he was recovering still from a recent and quite serious car accident. It had been a very bad year, he said.

I gave the gig a chance, though, and things gradually improved. Some energetic new interns trickled in, as they always did at the Santiago Times. A talented British/Australian writer showed up too, and I asked Steve to hire him as a kind of co-editor. The business couldn’t really afford another paid staff member, but Steve honored my request, and for the next year or so we had a great run. Then the money ran out.

“I can’t afford to pay you both, so one of you has to go,” Steve told us one morning. “I’ll leave it up to you two to decide which one.” And so we did—over a liter of beer, even though it was like nine-something in the morning. The co-editor (still a dear friend of mine) offered to go. But I’d leave too, I decided. A month or so later. The job had run its course, I thought.

We were frustrated and certainly taken aback—especially by the “decide amongst yourselves who stays and goes” part of the equation. And yet, neither of us was really surprised, because even then, we’d seen enough of Steve and his herky-jerky management style to know that this was precisely the kind of situation that could and would, as it turned out, unfold.

We couldn’t really be angry either. Or at least not stay angry. Because again, with Steve, what you saw is what you got. He was passionate about his project, but not always clear about how to make it grow. Often he’d have a new idea, and then charge ahead. And in those cases, there’d be a flurry of positive changes—new computers maybe, a new paid staff person, a larger office space. But then a particularly capable group of interns would move on, money would run scarce, the whole operation would contract, and we’d be back to square one, or so it felt.

I know this because later I joined Steve for a second, longer stint. What never varied, though, was his fighting spirit. A feisty advocate for the underdog, he was always chomping to champion a good cause—demanding accountability for human rights violations, defending the environment, shining a light on corruption and hypocrisy.

The Santiago Times was his platform, and he committed himself tooth-and-nail to making it survive, if not prosper. And in the meantime, the interns, editors, photographers and other collaborators kept coming through. They kept using Steve’s office and humble little publication as a landing point for early-career, working-abroad experiences, and as a launching pad for further adventures and professional endeavors.

If there was a method to Steve’s madcap approach, it was that with each new idea he had for the Santiago Times, with each new push to improve or revive it, he bought the business a little more time. Months turned into years and then decades. And all the while, people like myself were given an opportunity to work and learn—in large part through trial and error, because although Steve had things to teach, he also gave us space to teach ourselves.

It was his special tenacity, though, that kept the whole thing going, that gave so many people the chance, year after year, to develop their skills. We had fun too. So much fun. The office on Av. Santa María produced lasting, globe-spanning friendships, even love stories. And that was also part of Steve’s gift to us all.

He was an unabashed eccentric. Smart. Complicated. He had an entrepreneurial spirit but no real nose for business. Steve was a lawyer who wrote about politics and fruit exports. An editor with a penchant for typos. Part idealist, part cynic. A campaigner with no patience for diplomacy. He was perpetually cash-strapped, but generous. He was impulsive and impatient at times, but also deeply committed—to his various projects and causes, and to his family and colleagues. He was a teacher and a mentor. A doting father. A friend.

Goodbye Steve. Paz. And thank you.

World.title: Anti-vaccine mandate protests spread across the country, crippling Canada-U.S. trade
World.content:
Speaking to reporters at a press conference in Ottawa, Emergency Preparedness Minister Bill Blair said the blockade at Windsor’s Ambassador Bridge is particularly alarming because a quarter of all Canada-U.S. trade moves through that one crossing, which connects Canada with Detroit and points beyond.

Hundreds of millions of dollars worth of products have been held back for three days as 50 to 75 vehicles and about 100 anti-mandate protesters camp out on the main road that leads on and off the bridge.

The Canada Border Service Agency (CBSA) has closed the bridge to commercial traffic temporarily, diverting trucks to the Blue Water Bridge in Sarnia, Ont. instead. CBSA is reporting wait times in excess of four hours to make the short trip across to Port Huron, Mich.

We’ve seen the criminal acts, acts of thuggery and the obnoxiousness that they’ve inflicted on the people of Ottawa. Now they’re blocking the highways leading into our ports of entry. They’re putting their foot on the throats of all Canadians.

Labour unions representing auto workers have reported some idled Windsor plants have sent workers home while the trucker convoy holds up much-needed parts coming from the U.S.

Transport Minister Omar Alghabra said central Canada could soon see empty store shelves because so much of the region’s fresh food and produce comes into the country across that bridge.

To be honest, I find it ironic that the same people who were trying to sell Canadians fake stories about empty shelves are now causing those shelves to go empty, Alghabra said.

Windsor Mayor Drew Dilkens said the protesters appear to be determined to stay. They feel such a passion for this particular cause that they’re willing to die for it, he said.

Speaking briefly to reporters before question period, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said his government is working with Ontario and the City of Windsor to put an end to the blockade.

World.title: Excellent prospects for Mercosur beef exports, except Argentina
World.content:
The Argentine beef industry is optimistic about world meat production and global demand this year, with China again playing a leading market role. A report issued by Argentina’s Rosario Stock Exchange (BCR) and the Mercado Ganadero Department (Rosgan), world beef production will reach 58 million tons, representing a 1% increase over 2021.

This prospect would reverse the downward trend seen in 2021, mainly because of the recovery of the meat-packing industries in Brazil and Australia, the world’s first and third-largest meat exporters, respectively.

As for the global flow of imports, the expected average, according to analysts at BCR/Rosgan, is 10 million tons, which would imply an increase of 2.7% compared to last year.

China, which reduced the pace of international beef purchases in 2021 to 950,000 tons compared to more than 1.1 million tons in 2020 will once again represent 32% of global consumption. According to BCR/Rosgan, China accounted for 13% of global meat demand in 2017.

At that time, Argentina was in the top five beef exporters, having previously been in the top three. But Argentina has dropped out of the top ten beef exporters in recent years, owing to government restrictions on beef exports with the purpose of supporting the domestic market and helping with lower prices.

Nevertheless the Brazilian and Argentine beef markets had an unusual year in 2021. Traditional animal protein producers, the two countries witnessed declines in their exports, particularly in the last months of the year. Overall compared to 2020, Brazil beef sales dropped 9,92% while Argentine exports decreased 13,84%.

The reduction experienced by Brazil can be explained by the beef embargo imposed by China. In effect on September 2021, Brazil voluntarily suspended exports to China after the identification of two cases of mad cow disease in the country.

The World Organization for Animal Health (OIE) recognized that these were atypical episodes and that the risk to the national herd was negligible. Despite this, China insisted in freezing Brazilian beef exports for over three months until December 15.

The drop in Argentine beef shipments were motivated by the high price of the product in the domestic market, and thus the government suspended all exports in May 2021. ” As a consequence of sustained increases in the price of beef cuts in the domestic market, the national government decided to implement a set of emergency measures to better organize the sector, restricting speculative practices, improving the traceability of exports and avoiding tax evasion,” said the decree issued at the time.

Further measures were implemented, and given the deteriorating economic situation of Argentina and its impact on inflation, the country’s export ban on certain beef cuts was extended until the end of 2023.

As a result of this situation, Mercosur junior member Uruguay strongly benefitted and saw beef shipments increase 35%. The same can be said of the other Mercosur member, Paraguay, that also experienced a record year of beef exports in 2021.

World.title: Unemployment in Chile almost back at 2019 levels
World.content:
Chilean authorities have reported Monday that unemployment nationwide had fallen in 2021 to 7.2% while in the same period of 2020 it had hit 10.3%. In the middle of the social uprisings of 2019 it had been recorded at 7.1%.

“It is the eighth consecutive annual decrease in the unemployment rate,” said Leonardo González of the National Institute of Statistics (INE), which also reported the unemployment rate for women stood at 7.4%, and for men at 7.1%.

In the quarter of the year, 119,930 jobs were created compared to the previous quarter. With seasonal adjustment, González specified, the number of jobs recovered quarterly reached 49,625.

Around 1,436,000 jobs have been recovered, which represented 77.5% of all jobs lost during the worst part of the COVID-19 pandemic, with 81.8% accounting for jobs held by men and 73.1% for those carried out by women.

The INE also said 80.1% of formal jobs and 94.5% of informal jobs had been recovered.

“If we continue at this rate, we estimate that we will soon be able to recover all the jobs that were lost in the worst moment of the pandemic,” González stressed. He warned, however, that “we have been consistently seeing these rates rise, but we are not yet seeing pre-pandemic levels.”

Employment ended 2021 at 54.3%, while the labor force participation rate ended at 58.5%, an 8.1% yoy increase, driven by women (11.7%) and men (5.7%).

Jobs were boosted by construction (22.2%), commerce (8.5%) and the hotels and restaurants (30.9%).

Economy Minister Lucas Palacios said that during “2021 we met the goal of strongly recovering economic activity and also employment.”

“We have recovered 80% of the jobs that the pandemic and recession destroyed. It was necessary to create health, operational security and certainty conditions to reactivate the economy and especially investment, which is the main source of opportunities,” Palacios said.

Palacios also highlighted joint efforts by the public and private sectors. “Incentives from the State can be very relevant to promote investment and employment,” the minister explained.

Labor Minister Patricio Melero agreed the unemployment figures meant “great news” and praised “the measures adopted by the government, both in economic and health matters,” which were yielding “results which are very positive for the country.”

(Source: ANSA)

World.title: Argentine analysts rule out a real shift by Washington on the Falklands
World.content:
Argentine analysts rule out a real shift by Washington on the Falklands

3rd Thursday, September 2026 - 17:50 UTC Full article

Political scientist Andrés Malamud, of the Institute of Social Sciences in Lisbon, summarised his forecast by saying the same thing will happen as with Greenland, namely nothing

Argentine specialists in international affairs consulted this week agree that Donald Trump's statement about a possible review of the US position on the Falklands responds to pressure on London rather than to any substantive change on sovereignty over the archipelago.

The US president replied on Monday, when asked about the matter in the Oval Office: “I always review every position. That's just one of many.” Argentine President Javier Milei described the remarks as “very significant” and announced an address to the nation for Thursday.

Political scientist Claudio Fantini argues it should be read “as a warning, not an announcement”. In his view the motive is not the debate over NATO defence spending but Britain's refusal to authorise the use of bases on its territory for operations against Iran, with an added ideological element, given that both governments are Labour. He recalled that when South Korea declined to cooperate in the same conflict, Washington threatened to scale back joint military exercises on the peninsula. Even so, he believes Argentina should highlight the statement rather than let it pass.

Gabriel Puricelli, of the Public Policy Laboratory, describes the archipelago as “the handiest pretext” to force Andy Burnham's government to raise military spending to 3% of gross domestic product. “Argentina's interests do not come into consideration at all in his possible review of the position on the legal status of the South Atlantic islands,” he said.

Political scientist Andrés Malamud, of the Institute of Social Sciences in Lisbon, summarised his forecast by saying the same thing will happen as with Greenland, namely nothing. Former ambassador Diego Guelar, who represented Argentina in Washington, Brasília and Beijing, argues that a strategic change of that nature would require consulting the US Congress and that “his opinion alone is not enough”, though he accepts that if it happened it would weaken the British position.

Different registers coexist within the Argentine government. Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno adopted a restrained tone: “On what we do not control, we do not operate,” he said, adding that the task is to “do our homework” so the claim is heard. Presidential adviser Santiago Caputo, by contrast, posted on social media that “England is the past, Argentina is the future” and that it would be odd if the United States did not review its stance.

Argentine diplomats cited by the newspaper Infobae qualified that a favourable US vote at the United Nations would be “more symbolic than political” and that “in practical terms it changes nothing”. In June, the Decolonisation Committee approved by consensus a resolution urging the United Kingdom to negotiate, the same one London has disregarded since 1965.

The British government has reiterated that its position has not changed and that its commitment to the islanders is “unwavering”.

World.title: Trump hints he would not back the UK and doubts its "capacity" to retake the Falklands
World.content:
Trump hints he would not back the UK and doubts its “capacity” to retake the Falklands

3rd Thursday, September 2026 - 17:38 UTC Full article

“I don't know if you're prepared to do that. I just don't know if you have the capacity to do that,” he said

US President Donald Trump has suggested his country would not come to Britain's aid in a possible conflict with Argentina over the Falklands, linking that position to the lack of British support in Washington's war with Iran.

Asked in an interview with GB News whether he would “come to the aid” of the United Kingdom in a territorial dispute, he replied: “Well look, I was there when they had the first war. That was a long time ago and I watched it so carefully, and you comported yourselves very well. You took it back pretty strongly, but it's a long way away. That's a big trip.”

He then questioned Britain's current military capacity. “The Falklands is very interesting because your country is not the same country it was 20 years ago, 25 years ago. And you went there and you just took it back very quickly and there was no games. So I don't know if you're prepared to do that. I just don't know if you have the capacity to do that,” he said.

The president then turned to the Middle East conflict. “Your country's not doing well. Don't forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and you weren't there to help me. Your country was not there to help me. We didn't need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, 'why didn't you send a couple of ships?'” According to his account, then prime minister Keir Starmer replied that none were available, which he called “pretty sad”. He added that NATO had also been absent despite most members' reliance on that route for supplies.

The record qualifies that account. The United Kingdom initially refused the use of its bases for offensive strikes against Iran, but later authorised their use for defensive action, had minehunters deployed in the region and sent the destroyer HMS Dragon and helicopters to Cyprus after a drone struck the Akrotiri base. What it declined was the specific request to send vessels to reopen the strait.

The remarks come days after Trump told the BBC, when asked whether he was reviewing the US position on the archipelago: “I always review every position. That's just one of many.” He had previously warned that Washington could revise its neutrality if London failed to raise defence spending.

A British government spokesperson said the islanders “are British with a right to determine their own future”, and have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain an overseas territory, with London's commitment “unwavering”.

Previous US administrations have formally recognised de facto British administration of the archipelago without taking a position on sovereignty. Argentina and the United Kingdom fought a 74-day war in 1982 that left 255 British service personnel, 649 Argentines and three islanders dead. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters backed retaining British overseas territory status, with three votes against.

Argentine President Javier Milei is due to address the nation on Thursday night on the sovereignty claim. The Falkland Islands Government has not commented.

World.title: Investment banks warn the Venezuela deal will not bring down fuel prices
World.content:
Investment banks warn the Venezuela deal will not bring down fuel prices

3rd Thursday, September 2026 - 08:41 UTC Full article

UBS argues that Venezuelan output will take years to recover and that the impact on prices will be limited in the short term

Leading financial analysis firms have tempered the White House's forecasts on the Venezuelan oil agreement announced by Donald Trump on Friday, which grants a company part-owned by the US government control of seventeen fields holding some 65 billion barrels of reserves for a hundred years.

UBS argues that Venezuelan output will take years to recover and that the impact on prices will be limited in the short term. The Swiss bank says prices “continue to react mainly to developments in Hormuz” and has not revised its forecasts for the sector as a result of the deal. The White House had maintained the transaction would substantially reduce petrol prices for American consumers.

Timelines are the main obstacle. The consultancy Rystad Energy calculates that Venezuela will not recover its historic production peak — three times current levels — until 2050, and that doing so would require investment of 85 billion dollars. UBS adds that new transport infrastructure, technical capacity and a stable environment will be needed after years of underinvestment, sanctions and power cuts.

Despite holding the world's largest proven reserves, some 300 billion barrels, Venezuela extracts around 1.1 million barrels a day and ranks twentieth among world producers, behind Angola and level with Colombia, according to the International Energy Agency. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Wednesday in Caracas that output would more than double in the coming years.

Companies are responding unevenly. Chevron, which never fully left the country, announced on Wednesday an investment of 7 billion dollars over five years aimed at doubling its production by 2031, the largest commitment by a US company since January. Spain's Repsol, mentioned by acting president Delcy Rodríguez when she set out the terms of the deal, expects to triple its own. ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips, which left in 2007 after part of their assets were nationalised, maintain that conditions for a return do not exist.

Doubts also persist over the deal's durability. Citi considers that greater transparency and broader political legitimacy will be needed for it to survive a future change of government in Washington. UBS warns of possible litigation, given that the agreement provides for US companies to take over projects previously operated by Russian and Chinese firms. Both the Venezuelan opposition and sections of chavismo have criticised the operation.

On Venezuela's possible departure from OPEC, analyst Homayoun Falakshahi of the firm Kpler said it “would be a great victory for Trump”, though it could increase internal pressure on the interim government.

World.title: Lenín Moreno and a former Chinese ambassador convicted over bribes at Ecuador's largest dam
World.content:
Lenín Moreno and a former Chinese ambassador convicted over bribes at Ecuador's largest dam

3rd Thursday, September 2026 - 08:11 UTC Full article

The ruling is a first-instance decision and is not final. Moreno, 73, announced he will appeal, remains in Ecuador and has not been detained

A court of Ecuador's National Court of Justice on Friday sentenced former president Lenín Moreno to five years in prison for bribery, in the case over kickbacks linked to the construction and financing of the Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric plant. The same sentence was handed to China's former ambassador in Quito, Cai Runguo, and to former representatives of the Chinese state builder Sinohydro, Yang Huiju and Song Dongsheng.

The ruling is a first-instance decision and is not final. Moreno, 73, announced he will appeal, remains in Ecuador and has not been detained. “I have not received a single cent from Sinohydro,” he said outside the court. If the conviction is upheld, his paraplegia and age would mean he serves house arrest. The ruling also imposes a lifetime ban from holding public office.

The court, made up of judges Manuel Cabrera, Daniella Camacho and Julio Inga, found it proven that Moreno acted from the vice-presidency, which he held between 2007 and 2013 under Rafael Correa, to favour the awarding and financing of the project. According to prosecutors, Sinohydro channelled some 76.1 million dollars in bribes between 2009 and 2018, equivalent to 4% of the contract's value. The company Comercial Recorsa, linked to businessman and Moreno family friend Conto Patiño, received more than 75 million dollars from Panama.

Of the twenty-one defendants, twenty were found guilty. Patiño received five years. Moreno's wife, Rocío González, his daughter Irina, his brothers Edwin and Guillermo and his sister-in-law Martha González were convicted as accomplices and sentenced to two years and six months each. Former Coca Codo Sinclair managers Luciano Cepeda and Henry Galarza received three years. Financial reparations imposed on those convicted total more than 163 million dollars.

The trial ran for 31 sessions, with 29 witness statements, twenty expert reports and ninety documentary exhibits. Former vice-president Jorge Glas, who is serving a sentence in a maximum-security prison, testified for the prosecution and said he had received calls from Moreno about the project's progress and financing even though, in his account, those matters fell outside his remit. Moreno placed responsibility for the contract on Glas and argued that without charges against a senior official in charge of it the bribery case has no basis.

Coca Codo Sinclair, with 1,500 megawatts of installed capacity, supplies around 25% of Ecuador's electricity demand. Construction began in 2010 and it was inaugurated in 2016. The state took delivery despite 17,600 documented fissures, and regressive erosion of the Coca river threatens its facilities. Neither Sinohydro nor the Chinese government has commented on the ruling.

World.title: China's embassy accuses a senior Argentine official of spreading “rumours” about the Nepal flood
World.content:
China's embassy accuses a senior Argentine official of spreading “rumours” about the Nepal flood

2nd Wednesday, September 2026 - 21:22 UTC Full article

Juan Pablo Carreira, digital communication director at Argentina's presidency, blamed a Chinese state company for the Nepal disaster

China's embassy in Buenos Aires has accused an official in Javier Milei's government of spreading “malicious rumours” and seeking to “stain the international image” of the Asian country, after he attributed to a Chinese state company responsibility for the flood that devastated the border corridor between Nepal and Tibet on August 26.

The disaster began when a mass of ice and rock broke away from a glacier front on the northern slopes of Langtang Lirung, in Nepali territory, and fell some 1,200 metres to the valley floor. The material temporarily blocked the Lhende Khola river, forming a lake that later burst through, generating a surge of water and mud that swept away the Gyirong border crossing and descended along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. The United States Geological Survey initially recorded the signal as an earthquake and later reclassified it as the trace of the glacier collapse. The current toll stands at at least 1,050 dead and 3,916 missing in Nepal, and 16 dead and 546 missing on the Chinese side. Among those unaccounted for are more than 900 workers at hydropower plants in central Nepal.

Juan Pablo Carreira, national director of digital communication at the Argentine presidency, wrote on August 30 from his personal account on X that a Chinese state company was building a hydroelectric installation beside a glacier on the border and that failures in state organisation of industrial activity had caused the collapse. He linked the episode to other disasters he attributed to communist governments and concluded by asserting that communism kills.

Records of the episode note that attribution of the disaster to Chinese infrastructure circulated on social media during the first hours and was ruled out by subsequent satellite imagery and scientific analysis, which identified the glacier collapse on the Nepali side as the immediate source.

“A certain Argentine official, driven by biased ideological prejudice, is maliciously spreading rumours,” the Chinese mission said, calling for an end to speculation and urging him to “stop politicising or instrumentalising natural disasters”.

Declaración de Portavoz de la Embajada China en Argentina pic.twitter.com/hwciHJIXCo — Embajada de China en Argentina (@ChinaEmbArg) September 1, 2026

Presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier said the government answers only for the content of its official accounts and that “there is no official that we know of who has made any statement on the matter”. Opposition deputies have requested that Carreira be summoned to Congress.

The episode comes as Buenos Aires negotiates with Beijing. China is Argentina's second trading partner after Brazil; the currency swap between the two central banks was renewed at the start of the month, and Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno has confirmed preparations for a trip to China with the economy minister and the presidency's general secretary, with no date set.

World.title: Trump says Venezuela is “not ready” to hold elections and sets no timetable
World.content:
Trump says Venezuela is “not ready” to hold elections and sets no timetable

2nd Wednesday, September 2026 - 21:00 UTC Full article

“Delcy wants it, but they are not ready yet,” he said in the Oval Office, referring to acting president Delcy Rodríguez

US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that Venezuela does not yet meet the conditions to call elections, five days after announcing the agreement granting Washington majority control over a fifth of the country's oil reserves for a century.

“I don't think they're ready yet. It's very new, we got them out of a dictatorship and we get along very well with the government. Delcy, as you know, is doing a very, very good job. She is very respected and we want that and they want it too. Delcy wants it, but they are not ready yet,” he said in the Oval Office, referring to acting president Delcy Rodríguez. He added that he hopes elections can be held soon, but did not specify what conditions must be met or set out any timetable.

A senior US administration official, speaking to reporters on condition of anonymity, expressly ruled out setting a date. “It would be an artificial deadline,” he said. “But we want it to be as soon as possible, once the conditions are in place.” He urged patience and argued that Venezuelan institutions were degraded over the previous two decades and must be rebuilt before elections can be considered free and fair.

The same official listed the prerequisites Washington considers necessary: economic and legal stability, a free press, political parties with sufficient time to organise, a credible electoral process and a legal system “that does not disqualify candidates”. The agreement reached on August 12 between the interim government and a section of the opposition, which annulled and restarted the process for appointing Supreme Court justices, made no reference to the National Electoral Council or to political prisoners. The talks will hold further sessions in mid-September.

The US position follows a three-stage roadmap set out after the military operation that captured Nicolás Maduro in Caracas on January 3 and took him to New York, where he awaits trial on drug trafficking charges. The first two phases cover reconstruction of the oil sector and economic stabilisation; elections belong to the third.

The agreement announced last week grants a joint venture between the US government and the Venezuelan company North American Blue Energy Partners hundred-year rights over seventeen fields holding some 65 billion barrels. The firm belongs to businessman Alejandro Betancourt, who is under investigation in Switzerland and Spain without any conviction against him. Critics argue the deal may create an incentive to prolong the interim government's tenure and delay the transition. The US administration maintains it continues to seek elections, but that the Venezuelan economy must be revitalised first.

World.title: A Brazilian Supreme Court justice lifts secrecy on a banker's messages to another judge
World.content:
A Brazilian Supreme Court justice lifts secrecy on a banker's messages to another judge

2nd Wednesday, September 2026 - 20:56 UTC Full article

The report contains only what the banker sent. Forensic examiners recovered 52 files saved automatically by his phone, but not the judge's replies

Brazilian Supreme Court justice André Mendonça, rapporteur in the Banco Master case, on Tuesday lifted the secrecy order on a Federal Police report of more than two hundred pages containing messages sent by businessman Daniel Vorcaro, the bank's owner and currently in pre-trial detention, to his fellow justice Alexandre de Moraes.
