The report contains only what the banker sent. Forensic examiners recovered 52 files saved automatically by his phone, but not the judge's replies. Vorcaro wrote the texts in the notes application, took a screenshot and sent the image via WhatsApp using view-once mode, a method that prevents any record being kept. Moraes has not commented on the conversations and has not been charged; Vorcaro is in pre-trial detention and has not been convicted.

Among the messages is one sent two days before his arrest, in November 2025, asking whether he should be outside the country the following Monday. That night he was detained as he prepared to board a private plane. In another, he suggests pressing the head of the Federal Police and the prosecutor general “so that nobody below them does something outrageous”. The document also records in-person meetings between the two in Brasília and São Paulo between 2024 and 2025, including one at the businessman's home.

The report further details a contract signed in January 2024 between Banco Master and the law firm of Viviane Barci de Moraes, the justice's wife, for 108 million reais in 36 monthly instalments, and a second agreement dated May 2025. According to the technical analysis, the last modification to the draft was recorded under the name “Minister Alexandre de Moraes”. The couple responded in a statement that the judge had access to the document but denied he edited it.

Operation Compliance Zero is investigating a 12 billion reais fraud linked to the transfer of credit portfolios, with assets frozen worth 22 billion. Public pension funds are among those affected. Mendonça announced he will take the matter to the court's full bench regardless of any ruling by the Prosecutor General's Office, to which he sent the material. The Brazilian Bar Association expressed “extreme concern” over the institutional situation.

The disclosure comes five weeks before the presidential elections of October 4. Moraes is the justice who oversaw the case in which former president Jair Bolsonaro was convicted. The winner of the elections will appoint judges to the three seats that will fall vacant during the term. Candidate Flávio Bolsonaro called on Tuesday for Moraes to resign.

World.title: The UK dismisses Trump's remarks and reaffirms its sovereignty over the Falklands
World.content:
The UK dismisses Trump's remarks and reaffirms its sovereignty over the Falklands

2nd Wednesday, September 2026 - 07:50 UTC Full article

“The people of the Falkland Islands are British and have the right to determine their own future,” said a spokesperson for Prime Minister Andy Burnham

The British government on Tuesday dismissed US President Donald Trump's remarks about a possible review of Washington's position on the Falklands, and reiterated its commitment to the archipelago's status.

“The people of the Falkland Islands are British and have the right to determine their own future. They have expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering,” said a spokesperson for Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as reported by The Guardian. It is Downing Street's first statement since Trump replied on Monday, when asked about sovereignty over the archipelago: “I always review every position, that's just one of many.” The US president confirmed no decision.

The remarks follow a report in The Telegraph that senior Pentagon officials are considering a review of the US stance on the islands as a means of pressing London to raise military spending to the 5% of gross domestic product demanded by NATO. British Chancellor John Healey said on Monday he had received no such suggestion from his US counterparts.

In Buenos Aires, President Javier Milei described Trump's words as “very significant” and defined the sovereignty claim as Argentines' “most important and sacred cause”. He announced he will address the nation on Thursday on the matter and argued that the United States needs “a reliable ally on the passage from the Atlantic to the Pacific”, a condition he says Argentina meets. On social media he used crude language to disparage journalists who questioned his use of a national broadcast.

The shift contrasts with the president's earlier positions. He has expressed admiration for Margaret Thatcher, the British prime minister during the 1982 conflict, and has defended the islanders' right to self-determination, arguing that Argentina must persuade them to “prefer to be Argentine”. Until players unfurled a banner asserting the Argentine claim after the World Cup semi-final against England, the presidency was preparing a trip by Milei to London, which would have been the first visit by an Argentine president this century.

The United Kingdom has administered the archipelago since 1833 and Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim. In the referendum of March 2013, 99.8% of voters backed retaining British overseas territory status, with three votes against out of 1,517 valid ballots and a turnout of 92%. The Falkland Islands Government has not commented on Trump's remarks.

World.title: Sheinbaum touts Mexico’s trade position amid US tariff talks: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🕯️ Sheinbaum addresses Atizapán family murders: The president called the killing of musician Jonathan Meléndez, his pregnant wife, their three-year-old daughter and a domestic worker a “very sad, terrible situation.” She noted that two alleged perpetrators had been arrested and said the motive for the crime was a dispute between two families.

🏭 Mexico seeks lower US tariffs: Sheinbaum said her government is working hard to secure a better agreement with the Trump administration on tariffs affecting Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles. Her remarks came after Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard met with U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday.

💬 Sheinbaum discusses politics and AI with Petro in CDMX: Sheinbaum said former Colombian president Gustavo Petro spoke to her about a book he is writing on attempted influence over elections by “the international right.” She said they also spoke about artificial intelligence and its potential impacts. During the meeting, Sheinbaum said she outlined Mexico’s political context and invited the leftist politician to return for a talk at a federal historical institute.

Why today’s mañanera matters

A multiple homicide case and the United States’ trade barriers were among the significant issues President Claudia Sheinbaum spoke about at her Thursday morning press conference.

Official statistics — disputed by some — show that homicides have declined significantly during the term of the current government, but, violence remains a major problem in Mexico, where, on average, more than 48 people were murdered on a daily basis in the first seven months of 2026.

The killing of four people in a México state apartment this week has attracted more attention than many other homicides as one of the victims was a well-known musician.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s comments about her meeting on Wednesday with Gustavo Petro, who served as the first leftist president of Colombia until his four-year term ended last month. As president, Petro held face-to-face talks with Sheinbaum on several occasions, including at Mexico’s National Palace in December 2024.

Sheinbaum comments on multiple homicide in México state

A reporter asked Sheinbaum about the murder of a family in Atizapán de Zaragoza, a municipality in México state that is part of greater Mexico City.

Jonathan Meléndez, keyboard player with the well-known band Camilo Séptimo, his pregnant wife, their three-year-old daughter and a domestic worker were found dead on Tuesday in an apartment in an affluent area of Atizapán. A golden retriever was also found dead in the apartment.

Sheinbaum said she was briefed on the case on Wednesday.

“It’s a very sad, terrible situation,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that arrests have been made in connection with the crime. Authorities on Wednesday reported the arrest of two men who are alleged to have committed the murders.

Sheinbaum said that the murders were related to a dispute between two families. She also said that the México state government is supporting relatives of the victims and that the federal Interior Ministry is also ready to provide assistance.

Mexico seeks reduction of US tariffs on steel, aluminum and vehicles

Asked about the meeting on Wednesday between Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard and U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, Sheinbaum said her government is working very hard to reach an agreement with the Trump administration that results in a reduction of the U.S. tariffs that currently apply to Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles.

“There is ongoing dialogue,” she said, noting that Ebrard is a frequent visitor to Washington, D.C.

“… We’re seeking the best possible agreement for Mexico,” Sheinbaum said. “… We’re doing well and we hope to be able to reach a beneficial agreement.”

Sheinbaum reiterated that Mexico is among the “best-positioned countries” in terms of trade with the United States, as its exports — most of which enter the U.S. duty-free under the USMCA free trade pact — are subject to lower tariffs than those from other nations.

“The majority of [Mexican] goods that are exported to the United States don’t have tariffs, but we want an even better agreement on steel, aluminum and automobiles,” she said.

Sheinbaum summarizes her meeting with Gustavo Petro, former president of Colombia

Asked about her meeting in Mexico City on Wednesday with Gustavo Petro, Sheinbaum told reporters that the ex-president of Colombia spoke to her about a book he is writing.

She said that Petro, in the book, “touches on some issues that we’ve spoken about here.”

“But obviously it’s from his perspective,” Sheinbaum said. “… It has to do with the use of digital platforms [e.g. social media] to externally influence election results.”

She said Petro is writing about how the “international right” has organized itself to exert influence in different parts of the world.

Acabo de salir de hablar con la presidenta de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos, @Claudiashein pic.twitter.com/e9msOf0CZd — Gustavo Petro (@petrogustavo) September 2, 2026

Earlier this year, Sheinbaum agreed with a reporter who suggested that an “international media” campaign designed to “impose narratives in Mexico” was taking place.

“There are a lot of people who have come to an agreement. This international right-wing movement we talk about moves in many places in the world and there are a lot of people who are betting on the defeat and failure of the Mexican government for ideological reasons and for political reasons,” she said on May 13.

On Thursday morning, Sheinbaum said that Petro is also writing about artificial intelligence and “the impact it could have at a national and international level.”

“We spoke about that, about the reflection he’s making in his book [and] I spoke to him about Mexico,” she said.

“[I told him that] our perspective is very different because here there is a large majority of Mexican people who support the transformation and the results we’ve achieved, and the people are happy with the work the government is doing,” Sheinbaum said.

“… They were some of the issues we spoke about,” she said, adding that she had invited Petro to return to Mexico to speak at the National Institute of Historic Studies of the Revolutions in Mexico.

World.title: Mexico and My Money: How to move money into Mexico from abroad without losing a bundle
World.content:
Most foreigners who relocate to Mexico arrive with most of their liquid assets sitting in a bank outside of Mexico’s borders. Before long, they are wondering about the best ways to move money from there to here to fund everyday expenses.

Whether it is money for rent and groceries, or a big-ticket item like a car or real estate, finding the most economical way or ways to move money across borders is not necessarily intuitive.

Below are the best — and worst — ways to accomplish this boring but necessary task.

Factors to consider before choosing a money transfer method

If you’re new to living abroad and have never done a cross-border money transfer, it is natural to feel fear and uncertainty about the safety and reliability of the transaction. And that is before you even consider cost.

The truth is, there is no “one size fits all” best method for moving money across borders. The best option depends on three things. How much you need to transfer? How soon you need the money? In what form do you want the funds?

The best ways to move small amounts across borders

When you have no bank account in Mexico and only need to access small sums from a foreign bank account, a Mexican bank ATM is your best option.

At a Mexican ATM, two different fees are applied to cash withdrawals. The first is a “convenience” fee, which ranges from 30 to 200 pesos per transaction. The second is the exchange rate commission applied when converting money from your home country’s currency to Mexican pesos.

As a non-bank customer, it is wise to test out different brands and locations. BBVA and HSBC tend to charge larger transaction fees to out-of-network users, while fees from Banorte and Santander are typically lower. Even within the same bank, ATMs in touristy areas often have higher fees than those in non-touristy neighborhoods.

While the ATM’s convenience fee cannot be avoided (though some U.S. banks will refund them), foreigners can avoid exchange rate markups at Mexican ATMs that can reach 6%. To protect yourself, always decline the Mexican bank’s conversion rate when withdrawing funds. The transaction will still process, but at your foreign bank’s exchange rate, which is almost certainly better.

In addition, take care to avoid standalone ATMs that are not tied to major banks, such as those in convenience stores, gas stations and other public venues. These are easy for criminals to tamper with and can also apply exorbitant fees.

How to move large sums across borders

Because the daily limit on ATM withdrawals in Mexico is about 11,000 pesos (US $645), there are times when this method will not meet your needs. For transfers exceeding ATM limits — such as US $1,000 to US $50,000 — electronic transfers (also called EFTs or ACH transfers) are the most cost-effective option.

Money transfer specialists like Wise, Remitly, Revolut and others handle a large volume of these transactions. But they are not all the same.

Transaction fees and wait times from one provider to the next vary widely, so it pays to shop around. While Wise can move US $1,000 to Mexico in seconds, with Remitly it could take three to four days. Exchange rate markups with these services can range from 0.8% to as much as 3% over the mid-market rate.

In addition, while most who use these services have a Mexican bank account to receive the funds, some providers like Western Union or Remitly allow senders to pick up cash at Mexican retail chains like Oxxo or Walmart. Others give customers the option to send money to a mobile wallet.

Besides helping foreigners living in Mexico access their funds in overseas banks, these service providers also handle a large share of the nearly US $62 billion in annual remittances sent home by Mexicans working abroad.

In rare cases when a foreigner might need to move an even larger sum of money to Mexico — such as US $500,000 for a home purchase — a standard money transfer service may not suffice.

Among top specialists, platforms like OFX and Wise can accommodate high-value transactions of this size. Even when they do, it is common to experience longer wait times.

International wire transfers

In these cases, the most reliable option is an international bank-to-bank wire.

International wires use the SWIFT payment system and a unique code for each banking institution, ensuring funds reach the correct destination. They may also require a phone call to verify the sender’s identity.

This method is considered the safest of all, though keep in mind that international wires may take several days to reach the destination bank. Additionally, traditional banks add big exchange rate markups (2% or more) and fees (up to US $50) on international wires.

Due to these shortcomings, international wires only make sense when an ACH transfer does not satisfy your needs, or when you insist on having a person assist you for peace of mind.

How to lose a lot of money while moving it into Mexico

Convert physical cash you carried to Mexico

This old-school method of moving cash across borders carries some of the highest commissions. At money changers in Guadalajara, exchange rate markups can reach 5%. At a kiosk inside the arrivals hall of an international airport, it is even worse, with markups reaching 10% to 20% over the spot exchange rate. These places tend to target desperate travelers and should be used only in an emergency.

Choose a money transfer service without comparing fees first

Because quality and reliability are a moving target with money transfer specialists, it pays to collect multiple quotes and periodically check customer reviews. That said, some providers routinely fall short, hitting customers with 3% or higher fees, such as PayPal and its subsidiary, Xoom.

Fail to manage exchange rate risk

For anyone who needs to send large sums of money to Mexico with an uncertain time horizon, managing exchange rate risk is critical. In the case of a foreigner buying Mexican property with funds sourced from abroad, if the peso strengthens against your home currency while you wait months for paperwork to finish, you could end up paying tens of thousands more than intended.

Fortunately, there are now services for this, too.

With MexEdge, it is possible to purchase a forward contract for a fee of about 1% that locks in the current exchange rate for up to two years. While forward contracts do not make sense for small transactions, the savings can add up on larger ones.

Conclusion

No matter which service you use, U.S. citizens should know that banks and money transfer services are legally obligated to report cross-border transfers exceeding US $10,000 under the Bank Secrecy Act. The law applies to U.S. financial firms as well as foreign banks with branches in the U.S. to combat money laundering.

For foreigners living in Mexico without a local bank account, many of the best money transfer options will not be available. It is a key reason to consider opening a local account, which will be the topic of the next article in the “Mexico and My Money” series.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Born in the USA to a Mexican parent? There’s help for clarifying your dual nationality
World.content:
“Soy México 2026,” a campaign to help children and adolescents born in the United States to Mexican parents obtain recognition of Mexican nationality, has kicked off in Tijuana and San Felipe, Baja California, and will run throughout September.

Tecate, Ensenada and Playas de Rosarito will then run the program starting in October.

The move is aimed at children and adolescents aged under 17 who have a Mexican parent and reside or attend school in Baja California. Its purpose is to eliminate the documentation barriers often faced by binational families along the border region between Baja California and California.

ATENCIÓN FAMILIAS EN LA FRONTERA: Niñas, niños y adolescentes nacidos en EE. UU. que viven en Baja California podrán obtener su acta mexicana y CURP sin costo de apostilla ni traducción mediante ‘Soy México 2026’. pic.twitter.com/hV2ADwnapy — Alfredo Alvarez (@alfredoalvarez1) August 15, 2026

The process allows for the birth registration in Mexico of minors originally registered in the U.S. through the electronic validation of their U.S. birth certificate. With this process, families are not required to submit an apostille, an official translation, or a letter certifying the absence of a Mexican birth record — requirements that typically increase the cost and duration of the process.

Upon completion, beneficiaries will obtain a Mexican birth certificate and a Unique Population Registry Code (CURP).

In Tijuana, the process will be free of charge, while in San Felipe, a 50% discount on the associated fees will apply. Civil Registry offices in both municipalities will provide guidance as part of a coordinated effort involving the state government, local governments, and the National Population and Identity Registry (Renapo).

To initiate the registration process, parents must submit an application, a legible copy of the minor’s U.S. birth certificate, the parents’ Mexican birth certificates (with QR code), official identification documents, and the certified CURP of one or both Mexican parents.

The campaign takes on particular significance in Baja California due to the region’s intense cross-border mobility and the presence of a large foreign-born population.

Data cited by the newspaper Excelsior based on figures from the National Population Council (Conapo) and the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI), indicate that in 2020, 142,707 people born outside Mexico resided in Baja California — the highest figure among the entities featured in that count, including Mexico City, Chihuahua and Jalisco.

The demand for the dual nationality process was particularly high in Tijuana last year, which broke all-time records after processing 14,345 applications through this campaign — a 600% increase over the figures from the previous edition.

In contrast, data from the Civil Registry Coordination office of Chihuahua, revealed that the 2025 edition of “Soy México” concluded with 3,816 Mexican nationality applications processed in Ciudad Juárez; double the figure from the previous year.

With reports from Diario Tijuana

World.title: Mexico’s National Search Commission for Missing Persons has a new canine comrade
World.content:
Mexico’s National Search Commission for Missing Persons (CNB) has introduced Molly — its first canine member — to help locate missing people in a country where disappearances remain a major national crisis.

Molly and her handler form a K9 team the commission said is trained to search on land as well as in and around bodies of water, according to a Monday press release written in the dog’s voice.

“Starting today, I’m a member of the K9 unit of the CNB, and I have a very important mission: to search for people,” Molly “said” in the release. She said she will contribute her “sense of smell” and other talents.

The CNB, a federal body within the Interior Ministry (Segob), coordinates and carries out searches for disappeared and missing people, working with search agencies in Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

The commission said Molly will work alongside personnel who plan operations, coordinate logistics and analyze information. It did not provide details on her breed, training history or deployment schedule.

“Every search is the result of many hours of preparation and dedication,” said Molly, who appears to be a Belgian Malinois, a high-energy Belgian Shepherd variety.

Her arrival could offer the commission an important ally.

In Guanajuato, a search-collective leader recently said canine teams have helped confirm about eight of every 10 positive findings in the search for clandestine graves.

Norma Patricia Barrón Núñez, who leads the Una Luz en Mi Camino (A Light on My Path) search collective in Irapuato, Guanajuato, told the newspaper Milenio that when dogs find a possible site, they scratch the ground, prompting authorities to investigate further.

The Guanajuato Attorney General’s Office has 17 dogs, including nine trained in forensic search and detection. The state’s Security and Peace Ministry has two dogs assigned to search for people, while the National Guard has five assigned to search-and-rescue operations, Milenio reported.

Dogs have long held public-facing roles in Mexican security agencies.

Famed Navy search-and-rescue dog Frida assisted in searches after earthquakes and explosions from 2010 until her 2019 retirement. The late yellow Labrador became an international symbol of Mexico’s response to the devastating September 2017 earthquake in central Mexico.

More recently, Comando, a small mixed-breed dog adopted by National Guard personnel in Chihuahua, has become a familiar presence at the force’s state headquarters. And in San Luis Potosí, a former stray named Coyotito accompanies Civil Guard officers on patrol.

As for Molly, the CNB said it would later release more information about her training and fieldwork. She will wear a tactical harness with a K9 badge and a Mexican flag patch.

The CNB listed 132,534 people as disappeared or unaccounted for nationwide as of March 2026, federal authorities said.

With reports from El Financiero, Milenio and Reforma

World.title: Ebrard presses US commerce secretary over tariffs at G20 meeting
World.content:
Mexico Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick met Wednesday on the sidelines of a G20 gathering in North Carolina, where they discussed the troubled negotiations on the U.S.-Mexico-Canada (USMCA) trade agreement.

Ebrard is pushing back on U.S. tariffs on cars, steel and aluminum, which have been a sticking point in the negotiations. Mexico says the tariffs on these sectors are unjustified ⁠and at odds with the spirit of ⁠North America’s closely integrated manufacturing supply chains.

The United States is hosting the two-day G20 “Innovation Ministerial,” led by Lutnick and White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios, with representatives from Mexico, China, Brazil, Canada, Germany, and other G20 nations in attendance.

The summit focuses on innovation policies and the deployment of technologies to boost the economic prosperity of member countries. These topics were also discussed by Ebrard and Lutnick as they apply at the regional level.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has been one of the central topics of G20 discussion, alongside industrial innovation in supply chains and the development of a skilled workforce to meet growing global technological demands.

Several business leaders are attending the event, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Tesla/SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

The US goes its own way on Artificial Intelligence

While Mexico has yet to forge an official national AI plan, the clash of views between the United States and the European Union on AI regulation has been apparent at the G20 Innovation Ministerial.

U.S. representatives voiced opposition to technology-specific AI regulations found in the EU’s AI Act. Trump’s tech adviser, Michael Kratsios, encouraged countries to embrace the so-called Carolina Principles instead, which advocate regulations that do not single out specific technologies.

Meanwhile, the European Commission confirmed this week it had sent requests to over 30 AI companies worldwide to better understand whether they are complying with the EU’s AI Act.

The Act has been billed as the world’s first comprehensive effort to regulate AI and would prohibit any AI activities deemed to pose an “unacceptable risk.” It also imposed transparency standards that took effect in August.

With reports from Reuters, La Jornada, CNBC and Al Jazeera

World.title: Suspect arrested in the murder of Paola Buenrostro, a landmark case that made transfemicide a crime
World.content:
A man accused of murdering a transsexual sex worker in Mexico City almost 10 years ago was arrested in México state on Monday, authorities said.

The case of Paola Buenrostro — who was shot dead in an inner-city Mexico City neighborhood on Sept. 30, 2016 — was the first to be recognized as a transfemicide by the Mexico City Human Rights Commission.

In 2024, the Mexico City Congress passed a law, known as the “Paola Buenrostro Law,” that made transfemicide a crime with a prison sentence of up to 70 years. Buenrostro’s case thus became even more emblematic for members of the trans community in Mexico, many of whom are victims of crimes themselves.

Arturo Felipe Delgadillo Olvera, the man accused of killing Buenrostro after picking her up on a Mexico City avenue known for sex work, was detained in the México state municipality of Nicolás Romero on Monday, the Mexico City Attorney General’s Office (Fiscalía CDMX) said in a statement.

Fiscalía CDMX said that Delgadillo (referred to as Arturo “N” in the statement) was arrested for “his probable involvement in the transfemicide of Paola Buenrostro.”

“According to the investigation, in the early morning hours of September 30, 2016, Paola got into Arturo ‘N’s’ vehicle after he hired her services. Moments later, she called out for help to her colleagues, and immediately after, two gunshots were heard. Her colleagues approached the car, where they found Paola unconscious in the passenger seat and the accused holding a firearm. Paola died as a result of her gunshot wounds,” Fiscalía CDMX said.

Delgadillo was detained the day he allegedly murdered Buenrostro, but was later released due to the arresting officers’ failure to present sufficient evidence against him. He evaded recapture for almost a decade.

Fiscalía CDMX noted that in 2023, it offered a reward of up to 500,000 pesos (US $29,400) for information leading to Delgadillo’s arrest. In efforts to locate the suspect, Mexico City investigative police pursued various lines of inquiry, carried out field work in the capital and in México state and requested “collaboration” with the Baja California Attorney General’s Office, Fiscalía CDMX said.

“These actions made it possible to rule several locations out and to focus the search on the El Tráfico neighborhood in the municipality of Nicolás Romero, … where agents located and apprehended Arturo ‘N,'” the Attorney General’s Office said.

Mexico City Attorney General Bertha Alcalde Luján said on Monday that, “with this arrest, we take a decisive step toward taking Paola’s case to court.”

“We acknowledge the struggle of her family and the trans community, who kept the demand for justice alive,” she said.

“At the Mexico City Attorney General’s Office, we will handle this case with rigor and a gender perspective,” Alcalde said.

Delgadillo accused of homicide, not femicide, in initial court hearing

In a separate statement on Tuesday, Fiscalía CDMX noted that a warrant issued in 2016 for the arrest of Delgadillo was for the crime of homicide rather than femicide. For that reason, the suspect’s first hearing on Tuesday was for homicide, Fiscalía CDMX said.

The Attorney General’s Office noted that “victims and activists” have requested that the murder of Buenrostro be reclassified as femicide. It said that a reclassification in “later stages” of the criminal process remained possible.

Fiscalía CMDX said that in 2016, the grounds for proving femicide were “more restrictive,” while the crime of transfemicide “didn’t yet exist.”

However, it said that “the identity of Paola Buenrostro as a trans woman” is now “fully recognized.”

Witness slams prosecutors

After Tuesday’s initial hearing, trans activists including Kenya Cuevas — a trans woman who was with Buenrostro just before she was allegedly murdered and saw her lifeless friend in Delgadillo’s vehicle — complained that Buenrostro was identified as a man by prosecutors in court.

“They showed up before a judge saying my male name the whole time, the name I had before my change of identity,” Cuevas told reporters.

She said that prosecutors also used Buenrostro’s previous “male name” and the previous male names of other “witnesses” — i.e., other transsexual sex workers who were with Buenrostro on the night she was murdered.

Cuevas said that she and other trans activists weren’t seeking the reclassification of the murder of Buenrostro as “transfemicide,” but they do, “at least,” want the crime to be reclassified as femicide given that that offense “already existed” in the Mexico City criminal code at the time.

According to a report by the EFE news agency, the complaint about prosecutors’ use of previous male names of Buenrostro and other transsexual sex workers “escalated into a protest” at the headquarters of the Mexico City Attorney General’s Office, where activists “denounced institutional transphobia and demanded the reclassification of the crime.”

In its statement on Tuesday, Fiscalía CDMX said that it would “provide the necessary evidence to request that the judge consider reclassifying the crime.”

It also said that it “fully recognizes the right of victims, and the activists who stand with them, to protest and demand justice.”

“We understand the pain and anger that have built up over nearly a decade, and we reiterate our willingness to keep channels of dialogue and support open, even when there are differences regarding the legal aspects of the process,” Fiscalía CDMX said.

“At the same time, the Mexico City Attorney General’s Office is clear: no protest, however legitimate, can justify attacks against public servants or damage to the institution’s facilities,” Fiscalía CDMX said.

“Regarding the allegations about the treatment received during the hearing, the Mexico City Attorney General’s Office takes them seriously. Any error in the manner of addressing the victims does not meet the standards of care that the institution requires of its personnel. However, this does not imply that there is any institutional practice, directive, or intent of a transphobic nature.”

With reports from El Financiero, Animal Político and EFE

World.title: El Jalapeño: US, Mexico near trade war over right to misname European cheese
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

WASHINGTON, District of Columbia — Binational relations reached a delicate impasse Tuesday as diplomatic envoys from the United States and Mexico threatened to derail billions of dollars in North American commerce over which nation holds the ultimate authority to label domestic dairy after municipal districts in Western Europe.

The trade dispute escalated following Mexico’s recent accord with the European Union, which grants strict geographical protections to heritage products like Parmigiano Reggiano and Manchego. U.S. negotiators immediately pushed back, insisting that American dairy producers possess an unassailable right to market Wisconsin-made cow’s milk products using the names of ancient Italian and Spanish provinces.

“This is a fundamental issue of economic heritage,” said senior U.S. trade representative Harold Vincent, who spent the morning defending the cultural necessity of shelf-stable shaker canisters named after the Emilia-Romagna region. “Our position is clear: no foreign continent should be allowed to restrict North American companies from using names of towns that no one working for those companies has ever visited.”

Mexican officials attempted to maintain the high ground, emphasizing their commitment to international law — while simultaneously fighting to preserve domestic production of Mexican “Manchego,” a cow’s milk cheese that bears little relation to the sheep’s milk variety produced in La Mancha, Spain, since the Middle Ages.

“We respect European tradition,” noted one Mexican trade official who requested anonymity. “However, we also respect the time-honored Mexican tradition of taking a completely different cheese, giving it the exact same name, and putting it in a sincronizada.”

The European Commission, meanwhile, issued a stern statement reminding both nations that European towns are actual geographic locations containing human beings, not trademarked adjectives designed to sell processed dairy products across the Western Hemisphere.

Trade analysts warn that if negotiations under the USMCA break down over these dairy semantics, the retaliatory tariffs could be catastrophic. “We are looking at a dark timeline where the entire North American automotive supply chain is completely paralyzed because neither side can agree on whether a brick of pale orange paste produced in Ohio is allowed to call itself ‘Feta,'” noted chief economist Mark Higgins.

World.title: Meet Ana Valdez, a Forbes ’50 over 50′ illuminating the Latino narrative in the United States
World.content:
At MND, we’re always looking for new perspectives on the United States-Canada-Mexico relationship from leaders and organizations working to improve trilateral relations through fact-based data and reporting.

One of those leaders is Ana Valdez of the Latino Donor Collaborative (LDC), a non-profit organization and think tank she has led as president and CEO since 2014.

Valdez, a Mexico City native, emigrated to the United States in the 1990s and got a volunteer job in the White House when Bill Clinton was president. Fast forward to today, and she is on Forbes’s “50 over 50” list — a selection of women aged over 50 who are doing ambitious, influential and powerful work in the United States.

The LDC, according to the organization’s website, is “dedicated to reshaping the perception of Latinos as part of the American social mainstream.”

This is very important work, Valdez told Mexico News Daily during a recent interview.

“When I [first] came here, I saw a huge disconnect between the perception of who Latinos are in the United States and the reality of who they are,” she said.

“One misconception is that everybody is an immigrant. That matters because about 70% of Latinos in this country have been here for many generations. Some were here even before this [land] was the United States,” Valdez said.

CDMX to LA via Spain and Switzerland

“Since taking the helm of the Latino Donor Collaborative in 2014, Ana Valdez has led an organization that represents the economic interests of all Latinos in the U.S,” states a brief profile of the 64-year-old that Forbes published as part of its “50 over 50” list.

“In 2023 she launched the nonprofit’s Latino Data Collective, which puts economic data and market information about Latinos into the hands of more than 650,000 CEOs, politicians, board directors and media executives.”

Before moving to the United States close to 30 years ago, and joining the Los Angeles-based LDC more than a decade ago, Valdez studied and worked in Europe for a period. Before that, she completed a bachelor’s degree in business and marketing at Mexico’s Tec. de Monterrey university.

“I was born and raised in Mexico City,” she told MND, beginning a highly condensed version of her life story.

Valdez noted later in our interview that she completed a master’s degree in international relations in Spain and subsequently worked with the United Nations in Switzerland.

“After living in Europe for four years, I came to the United States and found the Latino community. I didn’t know about it growing up in Mexico City, and I didn’t know about it in Europe,” she said.

Valdez explained that she traveled to the United States to work on a PhD thesis, but ended up getting a volunteer job at the White House, “and after three months they hired me.”

“I stayed and never finished my PhD,” she said.

In addition to working at the White House in both a volunteer and paid capacity, Valdez held positions at Nielsen and Banamex before her appointment as CEO of LDC.

“My first job was at Nielsen, so I’m a nerd — [I love] using data … to do anything [related] with business,” she told MND.

“I’ve been madly in love with data ever since,” Valdez said before correcting herself to note that her passion for statistics actually dates back to her college days.

The LDC’s mission and vision

The LDC, the organization says on its website, “was founded in 2010 after a group of national business leaders identified a critical gap: the lack of an accurate narrative about Latinos, resulting in the perpetuation of harmful stereotypes.”

“This gap in understanding about U.S. Latinos was particularly troubling, as some states began passing laws that allowed for the arbitrary arrest of individuals based on these stereotypes,” the LDC says.

“In response to these alarming developments, co-founders and national leaders Sol Trujillo and Henry Cisneros [a former U.S. secretary of housing] recognized the urgency of creating a bipartisan non-profit organization and producing reputable data and statistics that accurately reflect the identity of Latinos in America and their contributions to the nation.”

The LDC says it “produces the most reputable data on Latinos in the United States,” much of which is compiled from official U.S. government stats, according to Valdez.

The organization says that the statistics it presents are “critical to the U.S. economy, workforce, business development, entertainment, and several other key aspects of American prosperity” given that members of the U.S. Latino community account for 20% of the entire U.S. population and more than one-quarter of Americans aged 18 and under.

The organization says its mission is to “reframe and advance an accurate perception, portrayal, and understanding of the important contributions that American Latinos make to American society,” while its vision is for “American Latinos to be recognized as valued, patriotic Americans in all facets of American life.”

A central element of the LDC’s strategy to reframe perceptions of Latinos in the United States — including some 40 million people of Mexican origin — is the publication of data-heavy reports focusing on the Latino population’s contributions to the U.S. economy and society. Among the more than 60 reports the organization has published are the “2026 LDC U.S. Latino Economic Impact Report” and “Data Beyond Demographics: U.S. Latinas’ Economic Power, Influence, and Growth.”

Mexico News Daily will soon begin presenting some of the key data in LDC reports in articles with an easy-to-read, visually engaging format.

“For us, collaboration is amplification,” Valdez said, referring to a partnership with MND.

“We believe from the bottom of our hearts and minds that this information helps everybody. It helps Americans in Mexico, too. There are so many Americans living in Mexico right now, and it would be a blind spot not to inform them about people who are doing exactly the opposite,” she said.

Changing Latinos, changing perceptions

Valdez told MND that Latinos made up around 7% of the U.S. population in 1960, whereas they account for 20% today, an increase attributable to both immigration and the birth in the United States of millions of Latino babies.

“People didn’t know Latinos before because they were only 7% [of the U.S. population],” she said.

“The preconceived idea of Latinos was perhaps someone seen as a valet parker, a housekeeper or a gardener.”

Valdez acknowledged that many Latinos worked — and continue to work — such jobs. However, she emphasized that many Latinos are now business owners or work in professional fields. In a 2025 infographic, the LDC highlights that there are “approximately 5.7 million U.S. Latino enterprises in the U.S.”

Valdez noted that many recent — and in some cases undocumented — Latino immigrants to the United States have attempted to maintain a low profile while the Trump administration carries out an aggressive deportation agenda. However, U.S.-born Latino “kids” are “completely different,” she said.

“…[Market research company] Kantar calls these young people ‘200 percenters,'” Valdez said.

“They feel 100% American and 100% Latino too. Contrary to their parents, they are not ashamed or embarrassed. They are unapologetic about being Latino. They’re proud, comfortable and confident. Their friends and peers want to know more [about Latino culture], want to learn Spanish, want to dance to Bad Bunny,” she said, providing one example of how U.S. perceptions of Latinos, and Latino culture, have changed.

“… Every year, thousands or hundreds of thousands of Latinos turn 18. They vote. They go to college. If they don’t go to college, they work in much better environments than the fields where their parents worked. They are assertive [and] speak English perfectly,” Valdez said.

She subsequently noted that her husband is Mexican-American, “from one of the families that came to what is now the United States when it was still Mexico.”

“… The border crossed them when the United States took over New Mexico and many other states,” Valdez said.

“… When my husband was growing up in Colorado, people were bullied for speaking Spanish. He remembers his mother putting burritos in his lunch. He was embarrassed when he opened it and it smelled, so he would put it away, not eat it and throw it out. He was bullied because of it,” she said.

“Fast-forward to our kids in a school on the west side of Los Angeles. We realized that one of them was charging his friends to bring them home for lunch because everyone wanted real Mexican food. His white friends wanted it,” Valdez said.

“So it is a complete change,” she said.

Beyond greater acceptance in the U.S. of Mexican food and the cuisines of other Western Hemisphere countries — and indeed increased desirability and “trendiness” of such food — there is growing recognition of the immense contribution Latinos make to the United States.

Unfortunately, however, there is still discrimination against Latinos in the U.S., while certain stereotypes and misconceptions persist. The LDC, as it has done since its foundation, will continue to work to counteract those enduring problems.

It’s not just Forbes taking notice of Valdez’s work

Forbes is by no means the only prominent media organization that has taken notice of LDC’s work under Valdez’s leadership. Among the others are CBS News, CNBC, Variety and Axios.

Valdez has also come to the attention of the Mexican government, leading to invitations to speak at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s morning press conferences.

At Sheinbaum’s May 22 mañanera, the LDC CEO presented a range of data about women of Mexican origin in the United States, including one particularly striking statistic — that those women contribute US $1.1 trillion to U.S. GDP on an annual basis.

When we asked Valdez why she — a Los Angeles-based data expert focused on Latinos in the U.S. — had been invited to speak at the president’s mañanera on numerous occasions, she noted that Sheinbaum is a scientist who “likes numbers.”

“When a scientist realizes that there are almost 40 million nationals or people with Mexican national background living in the United States, and that Mexico was not in touch with them, she wanted to know more about them and begin engaging them,” Valdez said, noting also that Sheinbaum has been a strong supporter of Mexican deportees and the Mexican community in the U.S., including people at risk of deportation.

World.title: IHG Brings Its voco Brand to the Cancun Lagoon Side
World.content:
Mexico · TRAVEL

Key Facts — What happened IHG will convert a former Real Inn into a voco hotel in Cancun, two Mexican trade outlets reported.

— How big The hotel has 160 rooms with views of the Nichupte lagoon.

— Location It sits at kilometre 5.5 of Cancun’s hotel zone.

— What comes next Opening is scheduled for October 2026; the hotel was not yet open as of early September.

— The catch The hotel is on the lagoon side, not the beach side.

IHG Hotels & Resorts will open a voco hotel in Cancun in October 2026. The property, a former Real Inn, overlooks the Nichupte lagoon.

The beach and hotel strip at Cancun. The new voco hotel faces the Nichupte lagoon rather than the sea. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

IHG Hotels & Resorts will bring its voco brand to Cancun with a 160-room hotel on the Nichupte lagoon. The property, a former Real Inn, is set to open in October 2026.

IHG Announces voco Cancun

IHG Hotels & Resorts will open a voco hotel in Cancun, Mexico, in October 2026. The Mexican trade outlet REPORTUR reported the news on 3 September 2026.

The hotel will occupy the former Real Inn building at kilometre 5.5 of Cancun’s hotel zone. It will have 160 rooms with views of the Nichupte lagoon.

A Second Source Confirms the Details

REPORTUR is not the only outlet on this story. Quintafuerza.mx reported the same 160-room count, location, and October opening on 31 August 2026, citing local outlet Novedades de Quintana Roo.

That second report also said the conversion should create about 100 new jobs. Two Mexican outlets now agree on the hotel’s size, site, and timing.

What Is voco?

voco is an upscale hotel brand within IHG’s portfolio, often used for converting existing hotels. It sits above midscale brands but below IHG’s luxury names.

IHG’s own materials describe voco hotels as offering a warm, distinctive style at a premium level. The brand has grown quickly since IHG launched it in 2018.

Location and Lagoon Views

The hotel overlooks the Nichupte lagoon, an inner lagoon opposite the Caribbean-facing beaches. Guests will see water, but not the open sea.

The lagoon side offers a different experience from the beach side. It sits closer to Cancun’s mangrove ecosystem and away from the busiest beach strip.

Former Real Inn Building

The building previously operated as a Real Inn, a midscale hotel brand. Both REPORTUR and Quintafuerza.mx report that it will now run under the voco flag.

REPORTUR said the property was “previously known as Real Inn.” It will now operate under the voco name from IHG Hotels & Resorts.

IHG’s Own Announcements

IHG did announce this Cancun conversion, contrary to an earlier claim in this article. A 2025 IHG press release listed a 160-room, lagoon-view voco for Cancun as part of a six-hotel Mexico deal.

That original release projected a 2027 opening for the wider group of hotels. The October 2026 date now reported by REPORTUR and Quintafuerza.mx suggests this property is opening ahead of that broader schedule.

Opening Timeline

The hotel is scheduled to open in October 2026, per REPORTUR and Quintafuerza.mx. As of 3 September 2026, it was not yet open.

Neither outlet gave an exact calendar date within October. Travelers planning October trips to Cancun should confirm the exact date closer to the time.

Target Guests

The hotel will target both business and leisure travelers, according to REPORTUR. It called the property an option for those visiting for work or rest.

The lagoon location may appeal to travelers seeking a calmer setting. It remains close to the hotel zone’s main attractions.

Global voco Expansion

voco is growing fast worldwide. TOPHOTELNEWS reported on 28 August 2026 that the brand has had “a slew of openings around the world,” including in Asia Pacific.

IHG has also signed a voco hotel for Karjat, in India’s Maharashtra state, under a separate 2026 announcement. That shows the brand’s expansion beyond Latin America.

No Investment Details

No investment figure has been reported for this project. Neither REPORTUR nor Quintafuerza.mx mentioned any cost, budget, or room rate.

The absence of financial details is normal for early hotel-conversion news. Such figures often emerge later, closer to a property’s opening.

What This Means for Cancun

Cancun’s hotel zone will gain a new upscale option once voco opens. The brand adds variety to IHG’s growing presence in Mexico.

Converting an existing building is generally faster than new construction. It also gives the property a fresh identity under a different brand.

Nichupte Lagoon vs. Beach

The hotel faces the lagoon, not the ocean, so it has no direct beach access. Guests would need to cross the hotel zone to reach the sand.

The lagoon still offers water views and a different, quieter setting. That may suit travelers who prioritize calm over beachfront convenience.

Cancun’s Hotel Zone

Cancun’s hotel zone is a narrow strip of land between the Caribbean Sea and the Nichupte lagoon. Most large hotels there face the ocean side.

A voco hotel on the lagoon side is less common than a beachfront property. It gives IHG a foothold in a quieter part of the same strip.

IHG’s Wider Push in Mexico

The Cancun voco is one of six hotels IHG has signed for conversion to the voco brand in Mexico. The others are planned for Guadalajara, Ciudad Juarez, San Luis Potosi, Torreon, and Nuevo Laredo.

That six-hotel plan shows IHG betting on conversions, not just new builds, to grow voco in Mexico. Cancun appears to be moving fastest among the group.

Future of the Property

The former Real Inn will finish its rebrand to voco around the October 2026 opening. Until then, it is not operating under the voco name.

Travelers should wait for an official date before booking around the opening. Details may still change before the hotel welcomes its first guests.

Sources and Verification

This article draws on REPORTUR, Quintafuerza.mx (citing Novedades de Quintana Roo), IHG’s own 2025 and 2026 press releases, and TOPHOTELNEWS. All confirm the core details of this project.

An earlier draft cited Construction World for the Karjat, India voco news. That citation could not be confirmed and has been removed.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will the voco Cancun hotel open?

The hotel is scheduled to open in October 2026, according to REPORTUR and Quintafuerza.mx. As of early September, it was not yet open.

Where is the voco Cancun hotel located?

It sits at kilometre 5.5 of Cancun’s hotel zone. The hotel overlooks the Nichupte lagoon.

What was the building before?

The building previously operated as a Real Inn hotel. It will now run under IHG’s voco brand.

Is the voco Cancun project confirmed by more than one source?

Yes. REPORTUR, Quintafuerza.mx, and IHG’s own press releases all describe this Cancun voco project.

Sources: REPORTUR; Quintafuerza.mx (Novedades de Quintana Roo); IHG Hotels & Resorts; TOPHOTELNEWS.

World.title: Grupo Sura Shares Surge to Fresh Highs in Bogota
World.content:
Colombia · MARKETS

Key Facts — What happened Grupo Sura shares rose 3.87% on 1 September 2026, then another 5.12% in the next session, Colombian outlets reported.

— How big The stock closed at 62,840 pesos (US$19.89) on 1 September, then climbed to about 65,700 pesos.

— The catch That price sits above the 63,940-peso high of 30 January that data providers had listed.

— Who it hits Grupo Sura is a Colombian holding company for insurance, pensions, and financial services across Latin America.

— What comes next No source gives a confirmed reason for the rise, and small price gaps remain between different data pages.

Grupo Sura shares jumped in two straight Bogota sessions, and Valora Analitik called the close a record. The available price data backs that up, showing a close above the previous January high.

The downtown Bogota skyline. Grupo Sura shares rose more than five percent to fresh highs. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

Grupo Sura shares jumped again in Bogota, and Valora Analitik called the close a record. The available price data backs that up: the close topped the previous high from January.

A Two-Day Jump in Bogota

Grupo Sura shares rose 3.87 percent on 1 September 2026, closing at 62,840 pesos (US$19.89) a share. Investing.com reported that Grupo Sura was the best performer on the Colcap index that day.

The Colcap index itself gained 1.86 percent that same day. Grupo Sura led a broadly positive session for Colombian shares.

A Bigger Jump the Next Session

In the following session, Grupo Sura shares climbed a further 5.12 percent, according to Colombian outlet Valora Analitik. The outlet said the shares had closed at “historic highs” for the stock.

Valora Analitik’s report did not give an exact peso price. A separate market-data page, La República, showed a close of about 65,700 pesos (US$20.80) for that same move.

That comparison supports Valora Analitik’s “historic highs” description. It suggests the shares did set a fresh record, not just a recent high.

Why the Numbers Differ Slightly

La República’s page showed a previous close of 62,500 pesos before the 5.12 percent move. That figure is close to, but not identical to, the 62,840-peso close reported for 1 September.

Small gaps like this are common when different market-data pages update at different times. The overall direction, a sharp two-day rise, is consistent across every source checked.

What Grupo Sura Is

Grupo de Inversiones Suramericana, known as Grupo Sura, is a Colombian investment holding company. It focuses on insurance, pensions, asset management, and other financial services.

It operates in several Latin American countries and holds major stakes in regional financial groups. Its stock is a key proxy for the Andean financial sector.

No Confirmed Reason for the Rise

No source gives a confirmed reason for the recent jump in Grupo Sura shares. Valora Analitik’s report did not include analyst commentary or corporate news.

Investing.com’s market wrap for 1 September also gave no explanation for the move. Without a named source, any reason would be speculation.

The Colcap Index in Context

The Colcap is Colombia’s main stock index, and Grupo Sura is one of its components. Strong moves in the stock can shift the whole benchmark.

On 2 September 2026, financial firm Acciones y Valores reported the index at 2,489 points, up 0.77 percent. The Rio Times reported the same level, 2,489.31 points, that day.

A Claim We Could Not Confirm

An earlier version of this article cited a euro-priced Grupo Sura instrument on MarketScreener. Repeated checks of MarketScreener’s own listings for the company found only peso-priced shares on the Colombian exchange.

That euro figure could not be confirmed, so it has been removed. Grupo Sura’s main listing remains its peso-priced shares in Bogota.

How Big Was the Move in Dollars

In dollar terms, the 1 September close of 62,840 pesos was worth about US$19.89. That used the peso-to-dollar rate Infobae reported for 3 September 2026, 3,159.04 pesos per dollar.

The later close of about 65,700 pesos was worth roughly US$20.80 at that same rate. Both dollar figures depend on the exact exchange rate used at the time of trading.

The Importance of Exact Prices

Exact prices matter for judging record claims like this one. Different pages gave slightly different numbers for the same days, which made this story harder to pin down.

Even so, every source pointed the same way: Grupo Sura shares rose sharply and closed above their prior known high. That is the core, verified fact.

Market Backdrop in Early September

The Colcap index rose in both early September sessions checked for this article. On 1 September it gained 1.86 percent, and on 2 September it added 0.77 percent.

Grupo Sura was among the market’s clear leaders during that stretch. The broader rally in Colombian shares helped lift the stock alongside its own gains.

What Investors Should Watch

Investors should watch for the Colombian exchange’s own official closing prices in the days ahead. Those would settle any remaining gap between the figures reported here.

Watch, too, for any analyst note that explains the rally. None had appeared in the sources checked for this article.

Background on Colombia’s Stock Market

Colombia’s main stock exchange, the Bolsa de Valores de Colombia, lists shares of the country’s largest companies. The Colcap index tracks the most heavily traded names on that exchange.

Grupo Sura has long been one of the exchange’s largest and most watched stocks. Its size means its price swings often move the whole Colcap index.

Sources and Verification

This article relies on reporting and data from Valora Analitik, Investing.com, TradingView, La República, and Acciones y Valores. The Rio Times also supplied the 2 September Colcap level.

Where sources gave slightly different peso figures for the same session, this article notes the gap instead of picking one as certain. Readers should treat the exact peso totals as approximate.

The Bottom Line

Grupo Sura shares rose sharply on 1 and 2 September 2026, and Valora Analitik called the close a record. Available price data backs that description.

The close reported by La República, 65,700 pesos, sits above the 63,940-peso high from January. On the numbers available, the record claim holds up.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Grupo Sura shares hit a record high in September 2026?

Valora Analitik said yes, and available price data agrees. A close of about 65,700 pesos on 2 September sits above the prior high of 63,940 pesos from January.

What is Grupo Sura?

Grupo Sura is a Colombian investment holding company. It focuses on insurance, pensions, and financial services across Latin America.

Why did Grupo Sura shares rise?

No confirmed reason is available. Sources reported the price moves but did not explain them.

What was the previous high for Grupo Sura shares?

TradingView and Investing.com listed 63,940 pesos (US$20.24) per share on 30 January 2026 as the prior high. The September close appears to have topped that level.

Sources: Valora Analitik; Investing.com; TradingView; MarketScreener; La República; Acciones y Valores; The Rio Times.

World.title: Foreign Investors Pulled Billions From Brazil’s Shares in August
World.content:
Brazil · MARKETS

Key Facts — What happened Foreign investors withdrew about 18.1 billion reais (US$3.5 billion) from Brazilian shares in August 2026, InfoMoney reported.

— How big JPMorgan put the outflow at 22 billion reais (US$4.2 billion), the third largest since 2008.

— The catch The outflow reversed a positive July, when foreign investors added 4.3 billion reais (US$0.8 billion) to Brazilian shares, per InfoMoney.

— Who it hits Foreign investors are major players in Brazil’s stock market, so their August retreat pressured shares for weeks.

— What comes next The Ibovespa index fell slightly in August, then rose for nine straight sessions into September.

Foreign investors pulled billions from Brazilian shares in August 2026, the worst month of the year. The Ibovespa index dipped slightly for the month, then rallied hard in its final two weeks.

Traders watch the quote boards at the Sao Paulo exchange. Foreign investors were net sellers through August. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

Foreign investors pulled billions from Brazilian shares in August 2026, the worst month of the year. The Ibovespa index still dipped slightly, before rallying hard in the final stretch.

August Outflow

Foreign investors withdrew about 18.1 billion reais (US$3.5 billion) from Brazilian shares in August 2026. InfoMoney called it the worst month of the year for foreign investors, citing data from B3, Brazil’s main stock exchange.

B3 runs Brazil’s stock market and clearing systems. It publishes data on investor flows that Brazilian media report on.

Preliminary Numbers, Different Methods

Media outlets reported different figures during August, since B3 data updates daily. InfoMoney’s early tally, through 27 August, showed a negative balance of 18.4 billion reais (US$3.6 billion).

A separate JPMorgan analysis, reported by Revista Oeste, put August’s outflow at 22 billion reais (US$4.2 billion). JPMorgan called it the third-largest monthly outflow from Brazilian shares since 2008.

The Final Tally

By early September, InfoMoney reported the full month’s total: a net outflow of 18.1 billion reais (US$3.5 billion). It called this the worst month for foreign investors in all of 2026.

The gap between InfoMoney’s estimates shows how B3 data shifts as more trading days close. The final total still marked the deepest monthly loss of the year.

A Rough Start, Then a Reversal

Early in August, foreign investors sold heavily, pulling out about 23 billion reais (US$4.4 billion) by 20 August. CNN Brasil reported that outflow using B3 data through that date.

After that, roughly 5 billion reais (US$1.0 billion) flowed back in during the rest of the month, CNN Brasil said. That reversal trimmed the final outflow to about 18 billion reais (US$3.5 billion).

One Day Turned Positive

Not every day in August was negative for foreign investors. On 27 August alone, B3 data showed a net inflow of 208 million reais (US$40 million).

That single day of buying was small next to the month’s losses. But it hinted at the partial recovery that followed in late August.

Why Foreign Investors Sold

Analysts pointed to caution ahead of Brazil’s elections and worries about the government’s fiscal plans. Money Times reported that JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley both grew more cautious on Brazilian shares in August.

Both banks cited a slowing economy and rising credit risks in their notes. Those views likely fed into the foreign selling that outlets tracked through the month.

The Ibovespa’s Bumpy August

Brazil’s benchmark stock index, the Ibovespa, actually fell about 0.3 percent in August 2026, InfoMoney reported. That is a small move, but it followed a wild month for foreign investors.

The index fell for 11 straight sessions from 4 to 18 August, tracking the heaviest foreign selling. It then rose for nine sessions in a row into September, InfoMoney said.

Not the First Swing This Year

August was not the first month with unusual foreign flows in 2026. In July, foreign investors added 4.3 billion reais (US$0.8 billion) to Brazilian shares, InfoMoney reported.

Earlier in 2026, foreign investors had also poured large sums into Brazilian shares, especially in January, according to Money Times.

A Record Streak of Selling

The consultancy Elos Ayta tracks B3’s foreign investor data back to January 2022. ADVFN reported that August’s outflow became one of the two largest in that entire record, alongside May 2026.

Einar Rivero, the consultancy’s founder, compiled the analysis using B3’s own trading data. It excluded new share offerings, focusing only on shares already listed on the exchange.

Foreign Investors’ Role on B3

Foreign investors have long been one of the biggest groups trading shares on B3. That is why their August retreat drew so much attention from Brazilian financial media.

When foreign investors sell heavily, it can weigh on share prices even if local buyers step in. Their August exit tested how much the market could rely on domestic demand alone.

The Brazilian Real

The US dollar closed at about 5.18 reais on 31 August 2026, according to CNN Brasil and InfoMoney. That is a reference point for the size of these flows.

A weaker real can make imports pricier for Brazilians and change returns for foreign investors. Currency moves depend on many factors, not just stock flows.

What Comes Next

Investors will watch whether foreign investors keep selling or return to buying in September. Early September data already showed the Ibovespa extending its winning streak.

If foreign investors come back, it could support further gains in Brazilian shares. If they keep selling, the rally may depend more on local buyers.

Background on B3

B3 is Brazil’s main stock exchange and clearing house, based in São Paulo. It lists shares of the country’s largest companies and publishes daily investor flow data.

Brazilian and international media routinely summarize this data. Because B3 updates its figures as more trades settle, early estimates often change once a full month closes.

Methodology Differences

B3’s own daily data, InfoMoney’s tallies, and JPMorgan’s bank research are three different ways to measure the same trend. Each uses a different cut-off date or counting method.

That is why one report said 18.4 billion reais and another said 22 billion reais for roughly the same period. Both describe real selling by foreign investors, just measured differently.

Sources and Verification

This article relies on reporting from InfoMoney, CNN Brasil, ADVFN News, Money Times, and Revista Oeste, all citing B3 or JPMorgan data. Figures for August varied slightly by date and methodology.

The final, most complete figure for August is InfoMoney’s 18.1 billion reais (US$3.5 billion) total. That is the number this article treats as most reliable.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did foreign investors pull from Brazilian shares in August 2026?

Foreign investors withdrew about 18.1 billion reais (US$3.5 billion) from Brazilian shares in August 2026, according to InfoMoney. That made it the worst month of the year.

Why did foreign investors sell Brazilian shares in August 2026?

Analysts pointed to caution before Brazil’s elections and fiscal worries. Money Times reported that JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley both grew more cautious on Brazilian shares.

Did the Ibovespa fall because foreign investors were selling?

The Ibovespa dipped about 0.3 percent in August, then rallied for nine straight sessions into September. Foreign selling likely contributed to the index’s rough start to the month.

What is B3?

B3 is Brazil’s main stock exchange and clearing house. It publishes daily data on investor flows, including how much foreign investors buy and sell.

Sources: InfoMoney; CNN Brasil; ADVFN News; Money Times; Revista Oeste.

World.title: Bogota Metro Line 2 Bids Are Due Monday After a Failed First Tender

Colombia · INFRASTRUCTURE

Key Facts — What happened Bogota’s city government reactivated the international tender for Metro Line 2.

— The deadline Groups must submit for the Line 2 tender by Monday, 7 September 2026, La República reported.

— How big The contract award is targeted for 2027, before construction starts.

— The catch Line 2 is still in planning, not construction; Line 1 is being built.

— Who it hits Commuters in Bogota, who await an expanded metro network.

— What comes next Interested parties will be announced in the coming days, says the president.

Groups bidding to build Bogota’s Metro Line 2 face a Monday deadline, La República reports. It is the next step since the city’s first tender for the line failed.

The first train for the Bogota metro. Line 1 is under construction while Line 2 goes back out to tender. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

Groups bidding to build Bogota’s metro line 2 must submit by Monday, 7 September 2026, La República reported. The city government aims to award the contract in 2027.

Tender Restart

Groups bidding for Bogota’s Metro Line 2 must submit their offers by Monday, 7 September 2026, La República reported. This closes the second round of an international tender for the line.

Bogota’s first Metro Line 2 tender was declared void in January 2026, after no group submitted a final offer. The city government reopened the international tender in February 2026, Infobae reported.

The goal is to award the contract in 2027, before construction begins. The city is seeking broader participation from international firms.

President’s Statement

On 2 September 2026, President Abelardo De La Espriella visited the Bogota Metro and said the structuring is in its final stage. He added that interested parties will be known in the coming days.

La República reported his words. “The structuring is entering its final stage,” he said.

He added that the interested parties in the tender would be known in the coming days.

Current Status of Metro Lines

Metro Line 2 is still in planning, not construction. Lines 2 and 3 are in structuring phases, while Line 1 is under construction.

President De La Espriella has committed to finishing Line 1 and advancing Lines 2 and 3. He also mentioned structuring studies for a future Line 4.

Why the First Attempt Failed

The first Line 2 tender closed with no valid offers, so the city declared it void in January 2026, Infobae reported. The prequalified groups did not submit final proposals by the deadline.

The city government then reopened the process to attract more international companies. It is now working to ensure a successful second tender.

Timeline and Next Steps

Offers for the Line 2 tender are due Monday, 7 September 2026, according to La República. The contract award is still targeted for 2027.

Interested parties will be revealed in the coming days, the president said. This report does not name any bidders.

Political Context

President De La Espriella has made the metro a priority. His promises include finishing Line 1 and pushing forward Lines 2 and 3.

This political support adds pressure but does not change the formal tender calendar. The city government leads the process.

International Participation

The city is seeking to expand participation from international firms. This is part of the reactivated tender process.

More international interest could bring expertise and competition. The city hopes this will lead to a successful award.

Funding and Costs

No verified contract value for Line 2 has been disclosed. Reports do not provide cost estimates for the new tender.

The national and Bogota governments do have a co-financing deal for the metro network as a whole. Its size has not been confirmed for this article.

Technical Details Unknown

Line 2 is planned to run 15.5 kilometers, with 11 stations. Ten stations will be underground and one elevated, according to the Bogota city government and Empresa Metro de Bogota.

The line will also have one maintenance yard, in the Fontanar del Rio area. These figures come from official city planning documents, not the new tender itself.

Challenges Ahead

The tender process faces challenges, including ensuring transparency and attracting qualified bidders. The city must also manage public expectations.

The failed first attempt adds pressure to get this right. A successful tender is crucial for Bogota’s metro expansion.

Public Expectations

Residents of Bogota have long awaited an expanded metro system. Line 1 is under construction, but Lines 2 and 3 are still years away.

The reactivated tender brings hope for progress. However, the timeline remains uncertain.

What to Watch

Watch for the announcement of interested parties in the coming days. This will show which companies are competing.

Also watch for the tender schedule and any official notices. The city has not yet published a detailed timeline.

Conclusion

Bogota’s metro line 2 tender is back on track after a failed first attempt. The city aims to award the contract in 2027.

The coming days will reveal interested parties, marking a key step. The process remains in early stages.

What the President Said

On 2 September 2026, President Abelardo De La Espriella said the structuring of Line 2 is entering its final stage. He added that ‘in the coming days the interested parties in the tender will be known.’

This quote was reported by La República. It shows the president’s direct involvement in the project’s progress.

The Failed First Attempt

The current tender process is a second try. The first attempt was declared void in January 2026, according to Infobae, after no group submitted a final offer.

The city government reopened the international tender in February 2026. They now aim to attract more international companies.

Who Is in Charge

The Bogotá city government, known as the Alcaldía de Bogotá, is leading the tender. They are the authority that reactivated the process.

The president supports the project but does not run the tender. The city government will make the final contract award.

What Happens Next

The stated goal is to award the Line 2 contract in 2027, according to Infobae and El Espectador.

Before that, the city will reveal interested parties in the coming days. Then they will proceed with the formal tender steps.

Other Metro Lines

President De La Espriella also promised to finish Line 1 and push forward Lines 2 and 3. He wants to start studying a future Line 4.

This was reported by La República and Infobae on 2 September 2026. Lines 2 and 3 are still in planning, not construction.

What Is Not Known Yet

This report does not name the bidders for the Line 2 tender. The groups that dropped out of the failed first tender are also not named here, to avoid unfair blame.

No contract value for Line 2 has been disclosed yet. That figure should emerge once the city picks a winner.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the status of Bogota’s Metro Line 2 tender?

The tender has been reactivated after a failed first attempt. The city government is leading the process and aims to award the contract in 2027.

When will interested parties be announced?

President Abelardo De La Espriella said on 2 September 2026 that interested parties will be known in the coming days. The structuring is in its final stage.

Is Metro Line 2 under construction?

No, Metro Line 2 is still in planning. Only Line 1 is under construction, while Lines 2 and 3 are in structuring phases.

Why did the first tender attempt fail?

No group submitted a final offer, so the city declared the tender void in January 2026, Infobae reported. The city reopened the process to attract more international firms.

Sources: Infobae; La República; El Espectador.

World.title: Chile Traders See the Key Rate Stuck at 4.5% for Two Years
World.content:
Chile · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Chile’s central bank survey shows traders expect the key rate at 4.5% for two years.

— How big The policy rate is 4.5%, held since December 2025.

— The catch The bank has not committed to two years; it’s only a market expectation.

— Who it hits Borrowers and businesses face stable loan costs for now.

— What comes next No change is expected at the September 8 meeting.

Market operators in Chile expect the central bank to keep its benchmark interest rate unchanged for the next two years. The forecast comes from the bank’s own survey of financial operators.

Santiago’s financial district, with the Andes behind. Traders expect the key rate to stay at 4.5 percent. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)
