World.title: Trump's Iran strategy: Could this become a forever war?
World.content:
The US has launched fresh attacks on military targets in Iran. It wants to prevent Tehran rebuilding its destroyed capabilities, but risks triggering a sustained downward spiral of reconstruction followed by new attacks.

US president Donald Trump has given a fairly clear description of what the next phase of the Iran war could look like. The Iranians had tried to rebuild their radar equipment, Trump stated after the most recent wave of US strikes. "We waited until it was almost built, and then we hit it," he said.

On Tuesday, American forces once again attacked several targets in Iran. According to US Central Command (CENTCOM), the targets destroyed included "air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites."

"Mowing the grass"

Iran responded by firing rockets and drones at US facilities in the region. With this, the war moved on to what CENTCOM had indicated just a few days earlier could be the strategy for the next phase.

What strategy will Donald Trump choose to pursue next in the war with Iran? Image: Ken Cedeno/REUTERS

According to the news portal Axios, it was considering limited strikes, at regular intervals if necessary, to prevent Iran from reconstituting its military capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz. An American government representative used a concept from Israeli security policy to describe this idea: He called it "mowing the grass."

The metaphor refers to a strategy that doesn't even attempt to promise that an opponent will be defeated once and for all. It is enough to regularly reduce the enemy's military capabilities to the point where the threat remains manageable. When the grass grows back, you "mow" it again.

Applied to the situation in Iran, this would mean the US keeping an eye on which military capabilities the enemy is reconstituting, and attacking once it crosses a certain threshold.

Successes that won't last

In the past few months, the US has scored some military successes. US forces have significantly reduced Iran's military capabilities in the Strait of Hormuz, and have begun clearing Iranian sea mines.

However, these successes will not last. Tehran is repairing or procuring new radar installations, anti-aircraft positions, and anti-ship missiles. US bombs could certainly destroy important Iranian positions with targeted strikes. But the knowledge and the industrial basis of Iranian military technology would remain.

An image issued by US CENTCOM of a precision strike against an Iranian military target in July 2026 Image: US Central Command/AFP

Reconstruction can therefore be delayed, but not prevented. The US will repeatedly be confronted with the same choice: whether to accept that Tehran is regaining its capabilities, or to attack again and destroy them.

Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) in Washington, warned as early as April that this development could lead to an "enduring low-intensity conflict punctuated by more intensive interventions."

Trump's belligerent warnings

The fact that the strategy of "mowing the grass" is reaching its limits is also because it was never designed for a war with a state. Israel developed the strategy to combat non-state actors likeHamas.

However, as Yacoubian pointed out in her article, the Israeli academics who initially coined the term warned that if the opponent had "statist characteristics and/or more powerful capabilities, 'mowing the grass' might become an outdated military strategy." This is clearly the case with the Strait of Hormuz.

The US needs to keep the strait reliably open. Iran, on the other hand, only needs to make people believe that the passage remains dangerous. In this way, even a significantly weakened opponent can impose substantial costs on Washington.

Keeping the vital shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz open is a priority for the US Image: Atta Kenare/AFP

Another problem for the US is that, while Washington can determine the intensity of its own attacks, it has no control over Tehran's response. This week, US president Trump warned Tehran not to launch a retaliatory strike, threatening that Iran would be "totally wiped out as a country" if it did.

Nonetheless, the regime in Tehran immediately fired missiles against American facilities in the region. Jordan alone reported 13 ballistic missiles in its airspace, 10 of which it was able to intercept.

The nuclear question

But Mona Yacoubian believes that repeated American attacks carry a far greater risk. She warns that they may lead Tehran to conclude that "pursuit of a nuclear weapon" is the only way to achieve "lasting deterrence." This suggests that, by attacking Iran, the US and Israel could actually accelerate the precise development they sought to bring under control.

The Natanz nuclear facility in Iran was one of the first sites targeted by the US and Israel Image: Planet Labs

From Washington's perspective, the alternatives available to Trump don't look much better. If the president accepts Iran rebuilding its military strength around the Strait of Hormuz, he risks renewed attacks on shipping and disruption of one of the world's most important energy routes.

The consequences for the global economy are well known. In spite of the upheaval and repeated negotiations, a political agreement between Washington and Tehran has so far failed because of apparently insurmountable differences.

The next "forever war"?

For Donald Trump, "mowing the grass" has domestic appeal, in spite of the uncertainty it brings to foreign policy. The US president would be able to avoid occupation, nation building, and deploying large numbers of American ground troops. At the same time, it allows him to distance himself from the so-called "forever wars" he repeatedly accused his predecessors in the White House of pursuing.

Ultimately, though, this supposed way of avoiding a forever war could become one of its own. Yacoubian describes it as a "Sisyphean attrition strategy without end." As long as Washington is not prepared at some point to accept the rebuilding of Iran's capabilities, each successful attack merely creates the justification for the next one.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Berlin BER airport Terminal 1 evacuated after security scare
World.content:
Authorities have emptied Terminal 1 at BER airport in Berlin, at least as a precaution. The federal police confirmed reports that had started to emerge on social media from people at the scene.

Germany's federal police, responsible for transportation security, evacuated Terminal 1 of Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) on Thursday evening.

Preliminary reports suggested a luggage security scare. It was not immediately clear whether or not it posed a real threat.

What do we know about the evacuation?

A spokesman told Germany's DPA news agency that passengers had been asked to leave the building. He said that a woman had told security staff at a service point that she had a dangerous substance.

"A potential threat from the unidentified substance could not be ruled out," the spokesperson said.

He said that as a result a dangerous item alert was issued and declined to comment further at the early stage.

Prior to this, travelers and a German reporter had posted corresponding social media accounts from the scene about the terminal building being emptied, including footage either of crowds waiting outside or of emergency vehicles parked near the lower level entrance.

What did the airport say about departures and arrivals?

The airport also confirmed the incident slightly later on Thursday.

"Because of the suspicion of a dangerous substance, the federal police issued a dangerous item alert at around 17:45," a spokesman said, leading to the "public area of Terminal 1 being cleared."

He said that planes that were already prepared to depart could take off as normal and incoming arrivals could also continue to land.

Passenger processing was being "relocated to Terminal 2 to the extent that it's possible," he said. "The degree to which this could lead to delays or cancellations is not yet foreseeable."

Many but not all flights departing Terminal 1 from around 7 p.m. local time were marked as at least slightly delayed on the airport's website.

BER or the "Willy Brandt Airport" in Schönefeld is Berlin's busiest and Germany's third-busiest airport since it opened in 2020. It also serves as the primary airport for many federal government flights. Some 26 million passengers travel through it each year.

This is a developing story, more to follow...

World.title: Norway seizes Russian ship in Svalbard to compensate Ukraine
World.content:
Authorities in Norway have seized a Russian ship, the Professor Molchanov, on a court order sought and obtained by Naftogaz in Ukraine. Russia has protested the move, which stems from its refusal to pay Naftogaz damages.

Norwegian courts have ordered the seizure of a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce part of a $4.22 billion (roughly €3.6 billion) compensation claim won by Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz after Moscow's seizure of its assets in Crimea, which Russia illegally annexed in 2014.

Officials announced that the ship had been stopped from departing the port in the Russian coal mining settlement of Barentsburg in the Svalbard archipelago late on Wednesday.

Svalbard has been Norwegian territory since 1925 but is a demilitarized zone where people from dozens of countries, Russia included, can settle without visas under certain conditions.

Russia's ambassador to Norway said that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels.

Around two thirds of Svalbard is designated as national parks and nature reserves, but the coal mining settlement of Barentsburg is home to about a tenth of the archipelago's population Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance

What do we know about the Professor Molchanov ship being impounded?

The first group to announce the ship's seizure was Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz as it tries to secure the compensation awarded to it by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague in 2023.

Russia had refused to pay the fine plus legal fees and interest amid its ongoing war with Ukraine, and Naftogaz has since begun trying to secure the seizure and forced sale of Russian commercial assets via local courts instead.

"Russia cannot evade ​responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko.

Covington said it had been tracking the ship, the Professor Molchanov, for months. It said its application was approved on Monday by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court, which ordered Svalbard's governor to ensure the ship stayed in dock once it arrived.

The end of coal mining in Svalbard To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Svalbard governor's office later issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held in Svalbard.

"The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel in collaboration with Trust Arktikugol," it said, referring to the Russian enterprise (meaning "Arctic Coal") that administers the Barentsburg mining settlement.

Norway's Justice Ministry, meanwhile, said the issue did not directly concern the government in Oslo.

"Russia can demand that ​the district court reassess the case," the Justice ‌Ministry said.

How did Russia respond?

Russia's ambassador to Norway, Nikolai Korchunov, said in a statement on Thursday that Moscow would pursue the ship's release through legal channels.

"We insist on the immediate release of the vessel and on ensuring the safety of its passengers and crew," he said.

The Kremlin also summoned Norway's ambassador in Moscow to lodge a formal complaint.

Is Svalbard Russia's real leverage in the Arctic? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Professor Molchanov, a repurposed research vessel, arrived in Barentsburg on Tuesday with a party of Russian scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying them.

"The seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship's crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual," Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda (KP) radio wrote on KP's website.

He said that for the time being, "the Professor Molchanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port of Barentsburg," adding it was unclear how long this would remain the case.

Prior to the war in Ukraine Barentsburg was also home to Ukrainian and other foreign nationals. But most have since left, Ukrainians in particular were told to accept an offer of Russian citizenship or leave. Image: Sergei Malgavko/TASS/picture alliance

What is behind Svalbard's special status, and why is it home to the Barentsburg settlement?

Svalbard is an archipelago well to the north of mainland Norway in the Arctic Circle, sparsely populated and thought to be home to slightly fewer than 3,000 people.

It was a whaling base in the 17th and 18th centuries and became a coal mining site at the beginning of the 20th century.

The territory was recognized as part of Norway in 1925, but only after the 1920 establishment of an international treaty — which nowadays has dozens of signatories — designating the area a demilitarized zone where anybody from a signatory state was permitted to settle and work without a visa, provided they met certain conditions.

The Soviet Union eventually acquired three sites and developed them as company towns: Barentsburg, with a remnant population of around 300 mostly Russian nationals, the nearly-abandoned settlement of Pyramiden, and Grumant, which has been left as a ghost town for decades.

Tourism has become a growth industry on the stark but stunning polar archipelago.

World.title: Germany: From emigration to immigration destination
World.content:
Migration is a sensitive topic in Germany, with public debate dominated by the fear of uncontrolled immigration. People forget that, over two centuries, millions of Germans emigrated in search of a better life.

"Why should [they] be suffered to swarm into our Settlements, and by herding together establish their Language and Manners to the Exclusion of ours? [...] [They] will shortly be so numerous [...] and will never adopt our Language or Customs."

These defamatory comments about refugees and asylum-seekers sound as if they might have been made today by the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD). Yet in this instance, the people vilified and accused of refusing to integrate are Germans — and the harsh judgement was made in the 18th century by none other than Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States.

The pursuit of happiness and a better life are mentioned in the American Declaration of Independence, which Franklin helped write. Over the centuries, they have been the motivation for countless people to turn their backs on their respective homelands.

Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States, warned against accepting German immigrants Image: Public Domain

The Germans who emigrated to America in Franklin's lifetime were actually fairly limited in number. By 1820, only about 150,000 had successfully made the journey. Often, they were persuaded by compatriots who told tales of their tremendous success in their new homeland and celebrated the prosperity they had supposedly attained in a very short space of time. What most people back home didn't know was that these recruiters received a commission for every migrant.

"The crossing on a sailing ship cost about what a tradesman would earn in a year," said Simone Blaschka of the German Emigration Center in Bremerhaven . "To be able to afford that, families had to sell all their worldly goods."

A journey into the unknown

They would have had no idea what awaited them on board the ship. During the crossing, which took several weeks, they were packed together below deck in a very confined space, plagued by bedbugs, fleas and rats. Many fell sick with dysentery, typhoid, smallpox or scurvy.

In his book "Journey to Pennsylvania in the Year 1750," the schoolmaster and organist Gottlieb Mittelberger described what he had experienced on the voyage: "Many people whimper, sigh and cry piteously for their homes; most of them get home-sick. Many hundred people necessarily die and perish in such misery, and must be cast into the sea."

Many European immigrants who came to the US in the 20th century arrived by boat in New York Image: Raimund Franken/imageBROKER/picture alliance

On arrival in America, Mittelberger wrote, the majority of his fellow passengers were effectively auctioned off. These were people without means who were granted free passage after undertaking to work for years as bonded laborers in exchange. In the US, their contracts were sold off. Mittelberger saw families torn apart and parents forced to sell their children.

An invitation from Russia

As these early migrants were traveling to America, there was simultaneously a big wave of emigration from Germany to the east. People followed the call of the Russian czarina, Catherine the Great, herself a German princess by birth.

On July 22, 1763, she issued a manifesto inviting people to come to Russia, with the aim of cultivating uninhabited regions for arable farming. She promised the new arrivals free transport to their chosen place of residence, land, also free of charge, the first year tax-free, schooling, exemption from military service, and a special political status that would allow them to maintain the German language and, for the most part, govern themselves.

Catherine the Great officially invited Germans to immigrate to Russia in the late 18th century Image: akg-images/picture-alliance

However, in the 19th century the American continent once again became the dream destination. "The German population almost doubled in the 19th century, so you can imagine what the job market was like," said Blaschka from the German Emigration Center. The situation was exacerbated by failed harvests and famines.

"People didn't see any future for themselves or their children, and decided to emigrate," she said. In this way, around 6 million Germans were drawn to the New World.

Migration: A burden or an asset?

Germans were far from the only ones who left their homeland.

"Between the beginning of the 19th century and the World War I, there were probably around 60 million Europeans who left their homes," said Jochen Oltmer, a professor at the Institute for Migration Research and Intercultural Studies in Osnabrück. Then, in the mid-20th century, this trend reversed and Europe went from being a continent of emigration to one of immigration.

Migration researcher Jochen Oltmer has studied the immigration waves to and from Europe in the 19th and 20th centuries Image: Michael Gründel/NOZ

In the 1950s and '60s, the future looked rosy for postwar West Germany and its "economic miracle." From 1956 onward, so-called "guest worker trains" arrived in stations like Stuttgart, Dortmund and Cologne, carrying Italians, Greeks, Spaniards, Portuguese, Yugoslavs and Turks, attracted by the promise of well-paid jobs in the new Federal Republic.

By the time the ban on recruiting foreign labor came into force in 1973, around 14 million people had come to West Germany as "guest workers." Around 3 million stayed permanently.

Yet Germany still did not consider itself an immigration country. "For a very long time, we were dealing with the mindset: It doesn't matter why people came to the Federal Republic; they don't belong, because in any case they'll leave the country again and disappear," said Oltmer.

Between 1956 and 1973, around 14 million 'guest workers' came to Germany from other European countries Image: Hans Heckmann/dpa/picture alliance

In 2025, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, more than 30% of Germany's total population had a migrant background. Yet many third- and fourth-generation citizens still don't feel they belong, which has to do with the perspective of the society in which they live.

Who's welcome – and who isn't?

These days, Germany is keen to attract skilled workers, but refugees are only granted asylum if they are politically persecuted in their homeland, or are fleeing war.

As a migration researcher, Oltmer is constantly examining the reasons why some migrants are accepted and others are not. This question was especially relevant in 2015, when refugees came to Germany in very large numbers.

"The attitude was: 'OK, you people from Syria, in light of the Syrian civil war, you are entitled to protection.' But at the same time this society says of people from Afghanistan, 'In your case, we're a bit more sceptical,'" he said.

Germany took in hundreds of thousands of refugees in 2015, above all people fleeing the civil war in Syria Image: Johannes Simon/Getty Images

Yet asylum accounts for barely 10% of immigration to Germany, Oltmer explained. The majority of immigrants are not people fleeing their country. "This means that when it comes to scandalization and the creation of certain negative images, we are seeing a massive distortion of the debate." And the descendants of the German emigrants Benjamin Franklin once reviled as "Palatine boors" have long since perfectly integrated into American society.

In Germany, however, integration is taking much longer. "Many people have no possibility of regularizing their status and obtaining a stable residence permit, even though everyone involved knows they can stay, and will stay," said Oltmer. He believes people urgently need to sit down and clarify how they want German society to look in future.

"It may be a very hard, even hurtful discussion. But it's the only way."

Berlin initiative helps immigrant moms find their feet To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: US sanctions halt TOEFL and GRE tests in Iran, disrupting study plans
World.content:
Students in Iran can no longer take English-language proficiency exams after the suspension of a US sanctions exemption. Applicants say the move threatens university deadlines and adds costly travel obligations.

Iranian students hoping to study abroad are facing a new obstacle after TOEFL and GRE testing was suspended inside the country following changes to US sanctions regulations.

"My entire plan was built around taking this exam," a TOEFL candidate in Tehran told DW.

She said she had spent months preparing applications for a Ph.D. program, contacting professors and gathering documents despite internet disruptions and other challenges.

ETS, the US-based organization that administers both English-language proficiency exams, announced it suspended testing in Iran after the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) froze General License G, which had allowed certain educational services to continue in Iran.

"Following OFAC's suspension of General License G, ETS has paused administration of the TOEFL and GRE tests in Iran effective immediately," the organization said in an official notice.

ETS added that Iranian nationals can still take the exams outside Iran and that it is exploring options to restore testing.

TOEFL is a US-based English-language proficiency test accepted by universities worldwide. The GRE is a standardized test required by some graduate programs, particularly in the United States and Canada.

Since the Iran war began in late February, the US has increasingly expanded sanctions targeting Iranian trade and exports, contributing to broader disruptions throughout the Iranian economy.

No timeline for testing to resume

An Iranian institution that administered TOEFL exams told DW that new registrations had stopped following the latest sanctions changes.

The institution added that the suspension could be temporary, but no date had been given for exams to resume.

That uncertainty is particularly serious for students approaching university and scholarship deadlines who have spent months preparing and paying application-related costs.

The suspension follows earlier problems with IELTS (British equivalent of TOEFL) testing in Iran. An IELTS center in Tehran told DW that sanctions-related difficulties transferring money had become one of the main obstacles to continuing exams.

Some Iranian applicants had already been traveling to countries such as Turkey and Armenia to take IELTS. TOEFL and GRE candidates may now have to do the same.

Can Iran survive Trump's new sanctions? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rising costs for applicants

Alireza, who is preparing to apply to a university in Italy, said the suspension of TOEFL had disrupted a backup plan he had arranged after IELTS testing became unavailable.

"European universities usually accept IELTS. But because IELTS has been suspended in Iran, after extensive correspondence with the university, they agreed to let [Iranian students] meet the required score through an equivalent TOEFL result," he told DW.

"But now TOEFL has also been suspended in Iran. Traveling to a neighboring country just to take the exam is very expensive, especially given Iran's current economic situation," added Alireza.

Another candidate told DW that taking the exam in Turkey or Armenia would mean paying for travel and at least one night's accommodation on top of the test fee.

For students hoping to secure scholarships or full funding, those additional expenses can be significant.

Many Iranian students pursue post-graduate education abroad Image: Sigrid Gombert/Image Source/IMAGO

Students launch petition

Iranian TOEFL and GRE candidates have launched an online petition urging ETS to restore access to the exams.

The petition says thousands of students are losing access to tests required for university admissions, scholarships, graduate programs and other academic opportunities. Many, it says, have spent months preparing, paid exam-related costs and built their application schedules around specific test dates.

"Students should not lose years of preparation or their chance to pursue higher education because access to required examinations has suddenly been removed," the petition states.

Narges, an Iranian applicant affected by the suspension, said she had seen the petition circulating in Telegram groups used by language learners and students applying to foreign universities.

"I doubt it will have any impact," she said. "Still, I'm going to sign the petition."

Experiences of international Ph.D. students in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The organizers are calling on the US Treasury Department's OFAC to provide a specific exemption for standardized academic testing, and on ETS to restore TOEFL and GRE services in Iran as soon as legally possible.

They argue that sanctions aimed at the Iranian government should not restrict educational opportunities for ordinary citizens who have no role in state policy.

When sanctions impact education

Until recently, the General License G had provided a legal channel for certain academic exchanges and educational services despite broader US sanctions on Iran.

For many students, the suspension is the latest in a series of barriers to studying abroad.

Bahar, who is applying for Ph.D. programs, said many Iranian students had already shifted their focus from the United States because obtaining visas had become increasingly difficult.

"American universities were our first choice because they generally offer funding for Ph.D. programs more readily than European universities," she told DW.

Now, she said, applicants are increasingly turning to Europe and Australia, but the testing suspension has created a new hurdle.

Missing a required exam can add months, or even a year, of waiting for affected applicants Image: Ahmad Halabisaz/Xinhua/IMAGO

"There is effectively no difference between IELTS and TOEFL for us now, because in either case, we have to leave Iran to take an English language test," Bahar said.

For students approaching admissions deadlines, postponement may not simply mean waiting a few months. It can mean missing an entire admissions cycle, losing scholarship opportunities or delaying academic plans by a year or more.

While ETS says it is examining possible ways to restore testing in Iran, there is currently no indication of when that might happen. For many applicants, the immediate choice is limited: wait without knowing when testing will return, or spend considerably more to take the same exam abroad.

Edited by: Ole Tangen Jr

World.title: Putin denies fresh mobilization campaign in Ukraine war
World.content:
The Russian president said there was no present need to mobilize more men, describing the reports as Ukrainian "disinformation." Putin was speaking during an economic forum in Russia's east.

Russia is not preparing to mobilize more men to fight, President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, describing such speculation as Ukrainian "disinformation."

In 2022 and a few months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Putin ordered the unpopular "partial mobilization" of reservists amid a string of military set backs.

The decision prompted an exodus of draft-age men from Russia and the Kremlin has since repeatedly denied plans for another mobilization.

"There is no scenario today that would require mobilization," Putin told a plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.

"This is a disinformation campaign by the enemy in the run-up to the State Duma elections, aimed at influencing the outcome," he added, referring to Russian parliamentary elections later this month. "As is well known, our people enlist voluntarily and sign a contract."

Putin had already dismissed mobilization speculations earlier this week, calling such reports "utter nonsense" and an "information attack" against Russia.

What did Putin say about peace in Ukraine?

Putin once again claimed there was a chance for peace with Ukraine, but stressed the conflict must be resolved by Moscow and Kyiv.

His statements come amid intensified Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital. Meanwhile, Kyiv has intensified its attacks deeper within Russia, striking online retailers and other civilian targets.

Russia launches missile and drone barrage on Kyiv To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Putin thanked countries which were making an effort to mediate a resolution to the conflict. He said the US and China, among others, were ready to support a peace settlement.

"Ultimately, however, the problem must be resolved ​by the countries involved in the conflict — Russia and Ukraine. ⁠This ​is the correct ​approach. Yet, we are grateful ​to everyone attempting to ‌ contribute to a settlement. Is there ​a ⁠chance? In my view, yes, there is," Putin said.

Still, he went on to condemn Ukraine, saying warnings about risks to planes in Russian airspace amount to "state terrorism." On Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that his country's drones have made Russian airspace unsafe for planes.

Putin was speaking during the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/AFP

How has Moscow responded to Zelenskyy's airspace warning?

On Thursday, Russia's Transport Ministry said it has provided clarifications to foreign airlines about Russian airports' and airspace safety measures.

"They work very closely with us and ​understand all our rules, standards and how we ​ensure flight safety," Russian news agency Interfax ​quoted ‌Transport Minister Andrei Nikitin as saying.

He added that the clarifications were given in response to requests from foreign carriers.

On Wednesday, Russian aviation watchdog Rosaviatsiya stressed in a statement that the country's "air transport, its ground infrastructure, continue to operate ​normally, receiving and dispatching flights, including those of foreign airlines."

European and US carriers have avoided Russian airspace since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. However, other airlines from China, Turkey and the Gulf states still use it.

World.title: Can Hichilema heal Zambia's political divide?
World.content:
The Zambian president starts a second term after a contested election exposed deep political divisions. His challenge now is to unite the country while addressing concerns over political freedoms.

Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema was sworn in for a second five-year term on Tuesday.

For decades, Zambia has worn its peaceful transfers of power almost like a badge of honor in a region where elections have too often ended in disputed results, violence or leaders refusing to leave. Hichilema's own victory in 2021 appeared to strengthen that reputation.

Five years later, the picture is more complicated.

Hichilema begins his second term after a disputed election, with his main challenger facing treason charges, opposition supporters questioning the credibility of the vote and controversy surrounding the closure of courts during the crucial window for election petitions.

Hichilema has promised reconciliation. But for a president who once sat on the other side of power as an opposition leader and treason suspect himself, the test now is whether those words will be matched by the political space he gives his opponents.

Ngobola Cengelo Muyembe, a political, business and social analyst, told DW that reconciliation must begin by recognizing that a significant part of the electorate backed someone else.

"You have to remember that in every 10 people that voted, four people voted for the other side," Muyembe said, noting that during the president's inaugural address, he spoke about reconciliation and uniting people. "But that message can only resonate if what is on the ground reflects what is being spoken about."

Can Hichilema reunite a divided country?

Raymond, a self-employed Zambian who asked that his full name not be used, told DW that Hichilema should look beyond who supported him at the ballot box and govern across Zambia's political and ethnic divisions.

"The president, congratulations! Don't think about people who voted for you, didn't vote for you. One Zambia, one nation, one city," Raymond said. "Real change in mines and agriculture. The mines want us Zambians to be benefiting. Even your Tonga, your Bemba, you are all Zambians."

Zambia has held largely peaceful elections since it returned to multiparty democracy in 1991 Image: Jean Mandela/REUTERS

Artist Mazuba Nzabuka told DW he also wants Hichilema to govern those who supported him and those who did not, while giving young people a greater voice.

"Going forward, he is going to do the promises left behind. He is a president for all people," said Nzabuka. "Those who did not vote for him, those who voted for him. We are the same people. The five years going forward, our voices can be heard. Look after the youths."

But reconciliation will have to contend with the political fallout from the election.

Zambia returned to multiparty democracy in 1991 and has since witnessed several changes of governing parties through elections. Hichilema himself benefited from that tradition when he defeated incumbent President Edgar Lungu in 2021.

The latest election prompted debate about whether that image remains intact.

Democracy faces a new test

The independence of Zambia's institutions may feature prominently during Hichilema's second term.

Critics said their concerns intensified after courts were closed on the final day available for presidential election petitions. Interruptions during the announcement of election results prompted some opposition supporters to question the process.

Can Zambia trust election referee? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Analyst Muyembe said that protecting political speech and allowing opponents to openly challenge the government will be crucial to rebuilding confidence.

"If you really respect the people that voted against you, allow them to speak, engage them in a debate, not where you just have to bring in only the people that agree with you and the ones that are talking to themselves on TV, and encourage this national dialogue," Muyembe said.

"Allow the opposition who lost to complain about it the way they want, and then from there you can chart a way forward. But to stifle debate and fudge facts, this is not really helping our democracy."

The arrest of Hichilema's main challenger, Brian Mundubile, and his running mate on treason charges linked to allegations of plotting an armed uprising has become another point of political controversy.

Authorities maintain the case concerns national security, while opposition supporters have questioned the timing of the arrests.

The situation has drawn attention because Hichilema himself once faced a treason charge while in opposition.

The question of whether the institutions that once wielded enormous power over him can operate independently when dealing with his own political opponents is likely to remain part of the debate surrounding his second term.

From economic stability to household relief

Political freedoms are not the only test. Hichilema enters his second term pointing to progress in stabilizing Zambia's economy, including lower inflation and the restructuring of the country's external debt.

But many Zambians are waiting for those gains to reach their homes.

Mutinta Mushabati, who attended Hichilema's inauguration at Heroes Stadium in the capital, Lusaka, told DW that she was encouraged by what she heard from the president.

"That he is going to increase everything, new allowances for school-going children, social cash transfer, CDF," she said, referring to Zambia's expanded Constituency Development Fund, which allocates public money directly to each of the country's constituencies to finance community-driven local development projects and infrastructure.

"I'm very excited right now. I don't even know what I can say. I'm very happy."

Muyembe told DW that the gap between positive national economic indicators and the experience of ordinary households represents a key challenge for Hichilema's second term.

He compared the economy to a reservoir that may be full while the pipes carrying water to individual homes remain blocked.

"Imagine that you got a giant command reservoir that distributes water to houses in the village," the analyst said.

"When the reservoir is full, you have stabilized your macroeconomic arrangement. But if the pipes that take water to the small little villages, the small little houses in these villages, are clogged and blocked, then you haven't really solved the issue because the people need to have the water in their individual houses."

Making Zambia's minerals work for Zambians

Copper and mining remain central to Zambia's economy and could provide one route for translating economic growth into household gains.

Muyembe told DW that Hichilema's government should focus not simply on attracting billions of dollars in investment, but also on ensuring Zambian businesses participate in the supply chains created by that investment.

"If a mine is going to spend $2 billion or $3 billion [€1.7 billion to €2.6 billion] to expand that mine, that $3 billion has to go to the people, the people that are small businesses."

Greater local participation, Muyembe argued, could help create businesses and employment while allowing Zambia to retain more of the wealth generated from its natural resources.

The challenge is particularly important for young Zambians, whose expectations extend beyond political stability to jobs and opportunities.

Five years to shape a legacy

Despite his criticism of the political environment surrounding the election, Muyembe told DW that Hichilema still has an opportunity to determine how his second presidency will ultimately be remembered.

He pointed to former Zambian President Levy Mwanawasa, whose disputed 2001 election was followed by a presidency that later gained broader respect.

"I think he has a chance, basically, to redeem himself from the dent of these elections because it also happened with Mwanawasa. I think Mwanawasa's elections were also looked at funny, but he redeemed himself in the way he governed the following year."

That leaves Hichilema with two closely connected tests over the next five years.

One is economic: whether improving headline indicators can translate into jobs, stronger local businesses and better living standards.

The other is democratic: whether opposition voices can operate freely, institutions can command public trust and political competition can take place without eroding Zambia's long-standing tradition of peaceful transfers of power.

The crowds celebrating at Heroes Stadium showed the hope that still surrounds Hichilema among his supporters. The disputed election and its aftermath revealed the mistrust that exists among many other Zambians.

How he governs both groups may ultimately determine not only Hichilema's legacy, but the kind of democracy Zambia carries into its next political chapter.

This article has been adapted from an episode of DW's AfricaLink podcast.

World.title: Que nadie se quede fuera
World.content:
La voluntaria Pepi Solana durante una clase de refuerzo a niños en en la asociación Juniors en el barrio de la Viña (Cádiz), en uno de los programas de acción social de CaixaBank.

Personas mayores activas, emprendimiento local, población que vive en el entorno rural... La sociedad cambia y los servicios financieros se adaptan a colectivos con las mismas necesidades que el resto. El compromiso social de CaixaBank pone el foco en la atención al cliente esté donde esté y la integración de personas en situación de vulnerabilidad

“Son cuestiones básicas que pueden cambiar la vida de una persona”. Así resume Pepi Solano (San Fernando, Cádiz, 58 años) lo que supone aprender conceptos y poder adoptar costumbres de economía básica entre los más jóvenes. Solano, a través de Voluntariado CaixaBank, participa desde 2015 en distintos programas sociales en Cádiz, desde apoyo escolar hasta acompañamiento a personas mayores, y este tipo de consejos los imparte a alumnos de 4º de la ESO. Por ejemplo, que el ahorro comienza si guardan dos de los cinco euros de su paga, o que “las tarjetas no se prestan a nadie”. “Alguno se queda con cara de: ‘¿Cómo?’. Otros directamente se justifican: ‘Bueno, es que es mi amigo...’. Y rápidamente les tienes que decir que eso no se hace”, describe.

La visión del voluntariado que da Solano es uno de los espejos del propósito social de CaixaBank: conseguir que cada uno transforme su realidad con algo de ayuda. El banco, desde sus inicios en 1904 como Caja de Pensiones para la Vejez y de Ahorros de Cataluña y Baleares, se creó con el objetivo de que la población pudiera ahorrar, y hoy mantiene actualizado su compromiso social. Entre sus principales acciones están las de adaptarse a las necesidades de las personas en situación de vulnerabilidad (canaliza ayudas a más de 5.000 entidades sociales en todo el país a través de la colaboración con la Fundación “la Caixa”), facilitar a las personas mayores la gestión de su dinero, llegar a aquellas zonas rurales más aisladas o ayudar en el impulso a los emprendedores que lo necesitan. Como la propia entidad afirma, sus productos financieros se conciben para ofrecer oportunidades, favorecer la integración y fortalecer el bienestar colectivo.

Los ejes de CaixaBank que modelan una banca más humana Accesibilidad, también en zonas rurales Sus 4.200 oficinas dan cobertura en más de 3.700 municipios de toda España, con una presencia en el 99% de localidades con más de 5.000 habitantes, según datos de CaixaBank. La entidad también está presente en las zonas rurales: Es el único banco en 460 pueblos, y sus oficinas móviles llevan servicios financieros a más de 1.420 localidades sin sucursal bancaria o con acceso limitado en las que residen más de 630.000 personas.



Fotos: CaixaBank Acompañamiento personalizado a personas mayores CaixaBank ha desarrollado un protocolo de atención especial para las personas mayores, que incluye la formación de más de 30.000 empleados en atención preferente, más de 11.000 cajeros de uso fácil, horario de caja sin restricciones, adelanto del pago de pensiones al día 24 y asistencia personal por teléfono y WhatsApp con más de 600 agentes. La oferta la completa su programa Generación+, con servicios como la planificación del ahorro, el acompañamiento para la jubilación o la gestión de la prestación de dependencia. Inclusión social para grupos vulnerables La entidad financiera ofrece servicios personalizados para colectivos en situación de vulnerabilidad. Unos 400.00 clientes tienen cuentas de pago básicas y la entidad tiene oficinas, cajeros y plataformas digitales accesibles y fomenta el lenguaje económico claro. Para las personas con discapacidad auditiva, ha desplegado en toda su red el servicio de videointerpretación en lengua de signos SVisual, que permite a este colectivo acceder a la información bancaria de manera autónoma. Un sostén para los emprendedores El banco social del Grupo CaixaBank, MicroBank, cerró 2025 con cerca de 280.000 operaciones por más de 2.400 millones de euros. Sus funciones han favorecido el emprendimiento, la creación de empleo y la igualdad de oportunidades. Esta propuesta se suma a otras iniciativas, como los Premios EmprendeXXI para startups de alto potencial; la imaginPlanet Challenge de imagin para jóvenes con proyectos de sostenibilidad; o el programa Tierra de Oportunidades, que fija población y crea empleo en el entorno rural para hacer frente al reto demográfico.

Esta idea tan amplia de inclusión real se traduce directamente a pie de calle en medidas concretas, como que la mayor parte de las oficinas de CaixaBank estén diseñadas para ser accesibles físicamente, con rampas, puertas automáticas y mostradores adaptados para personas con movilidad reducida. Sus cajeros también están adaptados a personas con discapacidad, con opciones como un teclado en braille y navegación guiada por voz para personas como problemas visuales, menús fáciles de entender y pantallas con alto contraste. Con estas medidas, CaixaBank trata de establecer un equilibrio entre el negocio y diferenciarse con la dimensión social.

Su consejero delegado, Gonzalo Gortázar, sostiene que “CaixaBank es una entidad con valores profundos, capaz de tener éxito en el negocio y, al mismo tiempo, aportar una dimensión social fundamental”. Y añade: “Tenemos una manera de hacer banca diferente, centrada en la inclusión financiera, tanto por nuestra presencia territorial, con una red extendida por toda España, como por nuestro compromiso en no dejar a nadie atrás”, explica el CEO del banco.

Una nueva visión de las personas sénior

A veces, son las oficinas las que llegan a los usuarios, y no al revés. El servicio de las 32 oficinas móviles de CaixaBank permite realizar las operaciones bancarias más habituales (sean o no clientes de la entidad) a casi 630.000 personas que viven en más de 1.420 pequeñas poblaciones sin oficina bancaria o con restricciones que limitan el acceso a los servicios financieros. Casi 270 de estas localidades tienen menos de 100 habitantes. Estas oficinas sobre ruedas suponen un importante impulso a la inclusión financiera, recorriendo cada mes más de 75.000 kilómetros en 17 provincias de siete comunidades autónomas.

Hay un colectivo que se ve más beneficiado con el servicio de oficinas móviles: el 70% de usuarios de oficinas móviles son personas de más de 65 años. Cuatro de cada 10 clientes de este segmento en España confían en CaixaBank, según datos de la entidad. Y es probable que la cifra aumente, si se tiene en cuenta que dentro de 50 años el 30,9% de las personas residentes en España tendrán 65 años o más, según el Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE).

Para adaptarse a esta evolución demográfica, CaixaBank ha rediseñado su propuesta de valor. La entidad trata de fortalecer a este grupo de edad que, más o menos activo, no solo necesita que se le pongan las cosas fáciles ―por ejemplo, a través del protocolo de atención especial―, sino también productos adaptados a la mayor longevidad.

A través de programas como Generación+, CaixaBank proporciona asesoramiento patrimonial, apoyo en la dependencia y soluciones financieras adaptadas a las necesidades de cada etapa vital. Ramiro Elena

A través de programas como Generación+, CaixaBank ofrece asesoramiento integral del patrimonio, ayuda en la tramitación de la dependencia, rentas vitalicias para complementar la pensión sin renunciar a la herencia o se encargan de elaborar testamentos y garantizar que se respeten las voluntades. Su enfoque se basa en la diversificación y en moldear las soluciones al ciclo vital de cada cliente, de manera que la planificación financiera evolucione con sus necesidades (y con sus circunstancias). El objetivo, señalan desde la compañía, es combinar eficiencia fiscal, liquidez, rentabilidad y protección.

La apuesta por considerar a este grupo demográfico como personas activas también se respalda en el emprendimiento sénior, y los microcréditos pueden servir de incentivo. Durante 2025, MicroBank, el banco social de CaixaBank (como ellos lo denominan), financió 2.303 proyectos de emprendimiento liderados por personas de 55 años o más, por un valor total de 36,5 millones de euros. Su importe medio se ha situado en cerca de 15.900 euros: la mayoría (el 77%) solicitó financiación para ampliar su negocio, mientras que el 23% lo ha hizo para abrir nuevas iniciativas empresariales.

Emprendedores rurales, al frente

Esos microcréditos del banco social llegan, además, a otras generaciones, y el año pasado destinaron financiación principalmente a cinco sectores: restauración, transporte por carretera, belleza, albañilería y reformas y talleres mecánicos. La estrella fue el primero, la restauración, que implicó más de la mitad de los 4.477 nuevos negocios que se alcanzaron gracias a la entidad en España en ese periodo de tiempo.

Enfocada en emprendedores rurales con proyectos activos, la entidad bancaria impulsa además el programa Tierra de Oportunidades, que busca fijar población y empleo en la España rural, a través de ayuda económica, formación y acompañamiento. Una de las iniciativas beneficiadas en la última edición fue la empresa Gurevet, en Mezkiritz (Navarra), que presta atención de servicios veterinarios de animales de compañía a domicilio en toda la Comunidad Foral. Al principio, en 2021, Teresa Etxarri (32 años, Mezkiritz, Navarra) empezó sola en su furgoneta adaptada (cuenta un quirófano para hacer cirugías urgentes o sencillas). Con el tiempo, se incorporó su hermana como auxiliar y gerente y, desde hace un año, cuentan también con otra veterinaria porque abrieron una clínica.

Mi hermana y yo somos de un pueblo muy pequeño, del Pirineo navarro. Los servicios llegan en furgoneta: el panadero, el carnicero, el pescadero... y dijimos: ¿por qué no también la veterinaria? Es una forma de poder ayudar a diferentes zonas. Teresa Etxarri, veterinaria y empresaria de Gurevet (Mezkiritz, Navarra)

Pero la cualidad de sus servicios reside en que Etxarri se desplaza hasta los hogares para vacunar, realizar consultas o chequeos o aplicar cuidados paliativos, entre otras cosas, sobre todo a perros y gatos. “Hay cosas que empiezan siendo algo leve que, si no tuviésemos este servicio, se quedarían sin atender y acabarían siendo cosas graves; la gente es más consciente de tener las vacunas al día o de esterilizar a sus animales”, detalla. La relación con el cliente es más cercana, se basa en la confianza, y ellos responden. “Queremos dar a las zonas rurales el mismo servicio que tendrían en una ciudad”, incide.

Gracias a la aportación de CaixaBank, la emprendedora consiguió un apoyo no solo económico, sino también visibilidad: “Por ejemplo, nos ayudaron a hacer vídeo en condiciones para redes sociales. La verdad, es que nos han ayudado a coger confianza con determinados clientes”. En definitiva, Tierra de Oportunidades les sirvió de “acompañamiento y de difusión”.

La veterinaria Teresa Etxarri (derecha), atiende a un perro dentro de su furgoneta. Cedida por CaixaBank

La “inquietud de ayudar”

La vocación de ayudar es una especie de “inquietud” que se lleva dentro siempre, califica Pepi Solano. “Sabes que quieres hacer algo, pero no sabes cómo ni dónde”, describe. Esta andaluza ha podido desplegar esa energía de la mano de Voluntariado CaixaBank. “Por mediación de su voluntariado, ellos enseguida te localizan y te dicen: ‘Pepi, mira, nos están pidiendo ayuda en tal sitio’. Y yo respondo: ‘Ahí estamos”.

Mi marido, que trabajaba en CaixaBank, sabía que yo tenía la inquietud de probar un voluntariado y me enseñó las oportunidades que daba el banco. Nos metimos juntos a ayudar y, desde hace más de 10 años, colaboro con distintas entidades sociales. Pepi Solano, colaboradora en proyectos de Voluntariado CaixaBank en Cádiz

Desde hace más de una década ha participado en talleres de cocina online para jóvenes migrantes, actividades para niños con discapacidad, visitas a las residencias de mayores o apoyo escolar a chicos de un barrio vulnerable de Cádiz. “Algunos de los que ayudé de pequeños ya son mayores de edad y seguimos en contacto. A veces, vamos a tomar un café o me llaman, me van contando su vida”, describe, con cariño. La han acompañado (se han contagiado de su entusiasmo) su marido, sus dos hijas y algunos amigos. Todos han tenido la misma sensación: “Siempre sales de allí feliz y piensas: esto hay que repetirlo”.

Como ellos, un total de 24.000 personas participaron en actividades de voluntariado en 2025, más de 19.000 eran empleados ―el 45% de la plantilla―. Además, entre mayo y junio de este año se ha celebrado la cuarta edición del Mes Social que, gracias a la colaboración de unas 1.400 entidades sociales locales, ha beneficiado a más de 155.000 personas en situación de vulnerabilidad y ha permitido impulsar más de 4.600 actividades solidarias en todas las comunidades autónomas. Solano afirma que las personas a las que ayuda responden con rotundidad: “Siempre te dan mucho más de lo que tú das”, asegura.

World.title: Calpe, renovarse a la sombra del Peñón
World.content:
Además de por su paquidérmica y famosa formación rocosa, la ciudad alicantina merece una visita por las Salinas, el conjunto arqueológico Baños de la Reina y una gastronomía en la que destaca la gamba blanca

Siempre que vuelvo a Calpe (cosa que pasa menos veces de las que querría) me sorprende y me exalta la colosalidad irredenta del peñón de Ifach. Esta paquidérmica protuberancia, ocasionalmente envuelta de nubes como la aureola de un santo, parece siempre a punto de saltar sobre el mar, que le es refugio y no abismo. Y, en efecto, ese tosco poliedro es una prolongación de la cordillera Bética, que se sumerge audazmente bajo las olas para dirigirse a Mallorca. Un tótem prodigioso, una ofrenda desmesurada y, quizás, en su priapismo cósmico, un tabú.

El parecido de esta gran roca con la de Gibraltar ha propiciado teorías diversas, normalmente descabelladas pero siempre amenas. Que Gibraltar e Ifach estuvieron unidos físicamente antes de abrirse el Estrecho es una de esas leyendas. Sí que es cierto que, en la antigüedad, el nombre Calpe designaba al peñón de Gibraltar. En un tiempo tan dado a las supercherías y otros golpes en el pecho de la ignorancia suprema me extraña que nadie haya propuesto que este titánico pedrusco pueda ser una ofrenda a algún dios. O quizás un monumento obra de los extraterrestres, como algunos partidarios desaforados del delirium tremens dicen que son las pirámides de El Cairo. Ajeno a todas nuestras elucubraciones, el Peñón sigue aquí, como el dinosaurio de Monterroso: una erección ciclópea, una insurgencia calcárea insolente y retadora, un desorbitado capricho morfológico.

Con este atractivo paisajístico, la ciudad alicantina necesita poco más para atraer visitantes. Y, sin embargo, las calidades de su oferta no dejan de aumentar. Ya se sabe que desde hace décadas recibe un elevado número de turistas extranjeros (muchos, hoy, residentes permanentes), principalmente procedentes del Reino Unido, Alemania, Bélgica y los Países Bajos. Este carácter cosmopolita no le ha hecho perder personalidad. Su casco antiguo con restos de los muros medievales resulta muy evocador, con sus calles estrechas, sus plazas tradicionales y edificios históricos como la iglesia Antigua (del siglo XV) y el Torreó de la Peça (baluarte defensivo de la antigua muralla). A esto une una variada oferta de restauración y comercio, amén de las actividades náuticas de su puerto deportivo o el senderismo que puede practicarse en el Peñón.

Torreó de la Peça, baluarte defensivo de la antigua muralla, en Calpe. TONO BALAGUER (GETTY IMAGES )

Entre sus atractivos naturales están las Salinas y el conjunto arqueológico Baños de la Reina. Las Salinas son parte de una antigua bahía cerrada por una barrera de dunas que unía el Peñón con el continente. La explotación de sal se cerró en 1988, así que, clausurada la industria, ha florecido la biodiversidad: allí viven 173 especies diferentes de aves. En cuanto a Baños de la Reina, es un yacimiento arqueológico, anexo a las Salinas, donde debió vivir un noble romano. Además de su lujosa villa, incluye una piscifactoría (donde se llevaba a cabo la salazón del pescado), unas termas, una noria y cuatro aljibes.

Esta antigua actividad pesquera ha llegado hasta la actualidad. A diferencia de otros destinos muy orientados exclusivamente al turismo, Calpe ha mantenido una flota de arrastre significativa. Su puerto alberga una de las lonjas más importantes de la zona, donde se realiza la ancestral e imprescindible subasta del pescado y el marisco locales.

Vista de Las Salinas, parte de una antigua bahía cerrada por una barrera de dunas que unía el Peñón con el continente. Jacek Krysciak ( GETTY IMAGES )

Su gran tesoro marino es la gamba blanca. Aunque la gamba roja de su vecina Dénia tiene una fama más consolidada, las propiedades de la blanca (su dulzura natural, su carne firme y sedosa, el suave aroma a yodo acabada de pescar) no son precisamente despreciables. Desde 2025, este fruto del mar goza de marca de calidad propia. Según el Portal Agrari de la Generalitat, ese año se capturaron y comercializaron más de 1.600 toneladas de gamba blanca en la Comunidad Valenciana (casi toda en la costa de Alicante). Es la tercera especie local en número de capturas (después del boquerón y de la sardina): genera 13,5 millones de euros, superando a la gamba roja y al boquerón, que hace años lideraban el ránking marino. Y ahora ese tesoro, que era cuantitativo, ha empezado a volverse cualitativo.

Parte de los Baños de la Reina, un yacimiento arqueológico anexo a Las Salinas. Teo Moreno ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Es precisamente en la gastronomía donde Calpe ha afinado más su renovación en los últimos tiempos. La versatilidad culinaria de ese prodigioso crustáceo ha llamado la atención de los chefs más reputados de la zona. Dos ejemplos: los restaurantes Onami y Beat.

Marisco fresco expuesto en el puerto pesquero de Calpe, Alicante. Manoli Perez ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Onami abrió este pasado mes de junio en el hotel AR Diamante Beach. Este imponente establecimiento ya disponía de otros dos locales de restauración, el Audrey’s (el primer local con estrella Michelin de Calpe) y el Amas. Onami comparte chef con Amas: Diego Laso. La diferencia entre los dos —inspirados ambos en la cocina japonesa— es que en Onami no hay carta y se come en la barra. El servicio está concebido como un menú degustación al estilo kaiseki-ryori: la forma más refinada y tradicional de la alta gastronomía japonesa. Onami es un juego de palabras entre ona (ola, en valenciano/catalán) y nami (mismo significado en japonés). Esto da la medida de su filosofía: ofrecer un diálogo entre la cocina valenciana y la nipona. De aquí la receta de gamba blanca en Amas (curada con sake y servida con crema inglesa y algas de Galicia), o el nigiri de este mismo crustáceo en Onami, simplemente pelado y servido sobre arroz.

Segundo ejemplo: el restaurante Beat (una estrella Michelin), ubicado en The Cookbook. Este hotel acaba de renovarse en profundidad. En Beat reina desde hace diez años José Manuel Miguel, el único cocinero valenciano que ha obtenido estrellas Michelin en Francia y en España. Si en Onami dialogaban la cocina local con la nipona, aquí la fusión está protagonizada por lo valenciano y lo francés. El gran referente de José Manuel Miguel es Paul Bocuse, emblema de la nouvelle cuisine gala. El bogavante lo cocina a la manera de la Salade de homard à la française de Bocuse, pero la gamba blanca no requiere mayor transformación: su hechizo radica en la ausencia de cocción.

Con todo esto ya se puede volver a visitar Calpe y saborear algo más que la siempre imponente vista de su Peñón. Tradición y modernidad, lo llaman.

World.title: National water shortage officially over but troubles continue
World.content:
The Netherlands is officially out of a water shortage, but the drought that left houseboats stranded and cargo barges part-loaded throughout the summer will be felt for months to come, the infrastructure ministry has said.

Weeks of rain and falling demand have allowed the ministry to move the country from level two to level one on its three-stage scale of water shortages – from an actual shortage back to an impending one. Crops are being harvested, farmers are irrigating less and cooler weather means less water is evaporating.

The government team that met weekly through the summer to tackle the shortage will now disband, though the national water distribution committee, which warned of serious water shortages in July, will keep meeting, and the weekly drought monitor continues.

Recovery will take months

The downgrade does not mean the drought is over. The Rhine is still carrying only about half its normal volume for early September and river levels could stay low until the end of the year. Groundwater will also take even longer to get back to normal levels.

For the houseboat owners stranded on stretches of the Rhine that dried up months ago, there will be little immediate relief. Their homes will not refloat until levels rise. Shipping also faces reduced services and delays at locks.

Water abstraction restrictions still apply across the higher sandy soils of the east and south, and salinisation of the IJsselmeer remains a concern for drinking water suppliers, though some water boards have begun rolling back restrictions. Drinking water supplies remain secure.

World.title: Inspectors allow only Dutch online abortion service to continue
World.content:
The Dutch’ healthcare inspectorate has found that the country’s only online abortion service fell short on its duties for care, but will let it keep operating after the site agreed to change its practices.

Thuisabortus.nl, which launched in March, was the first service in the Netherlands to let women get the abortion pill prescribed without an in-person visit to a GP or clinic.

The inspectorate, the IGJ, said the main problem was that women who ordered the pill through the website usually had no personal contact with a doctor before it was prescribed but it also found no serious risk to patients and so no reason to shut it down.

As a remedial measure, the site has since telephoned every woman who applies, discussing the stage of the pregnancy, possible complications, aftercare through her own GP and alternatives to abortion.

Concerns raised at launch

When the site was launched, the family doctors organisation KNMG and the GP organisation LHV questioned whether issuing the pill without a consultation met the legal duty of care.

Health minister Sophie Hermans told MPs on Wednesday that the government regretted the shortcomings, and described the conversation between a woman and her doctor as an “essential part” of careful abortion care.

The site’s founder, GP Peter Leusink, said he would comply but disagreed, arguing that a phone consultation is not needed for safe care and pointing to home use of the pill in the US, the UK and Sweden. “We have to comply with that outdated law,” he told NRC.

Doctors remain divided

The abortion doctors’ association NGvA said the report confirmed its concern that the platform had started in a hurry and overlooked parts of proper care, and that it was now exploring a digital service of its own. The GPs’ professional body NHG has backed online abortion care as a useful addition and called for GPs and the site to work together.

The LHV said it still had concerns about who handles complications at night and at weekends. The orthodox Protestant SGP and the ChristenUnie went further, with SGP MP Diederik van Dijk saying the service should have been taken offline.

GPs have been able to prescribe the abortion pill since the start of 2025, after completing extra training. Thuisabortus.nl says it has prescribed around 1,680 pills since April, about a quarter of all abortion pills issued in the Netherlands. The inspectorate has given the site until mid-November to complete the remaining changes.

World.title: Illegal casinos hijack thousands of Dutch websites
World.content:
At least 1,000 legitimate Dutch and European websites, many belonging to companies, charities and freelancers, have been quietly turned into shopfronts for illegal online casinos, an investigation by radio station BNR has found. The real figure might be over 8,000.

The sites have nothing to do with gambling, and their owners are usually unaware. Criminals either hack poorly secured websites and add casino pages, or buy up an organisation’s expired domain name and fill it with gambling content.

Because search engines already trust those addresses, the casino pages rank highly. Someone searching for an online casino may land on a seemingly reputable site before being redirected to an illegal operator.

BNR found gambling pages on an old domain once used by broadcaster and writer Wilfried de Jong, on sites formerly run by the liberal VVD party in Zeeland and Brabant, and on the website of a business lawyer, where at least 50 casino pages had been added.

The national gambling authority called it “a very big problem” and is working with SIDN, the body that manages Dutch internet domains, to shut down redirect pages, but the process is slow because there is no legal power to block the sites, which SIDN says it wants.

It can also do little about .com or .eu addresses, which fall outside SIDN’s remit, so it is hoping Google will step in. The search engine removes adverts for illegal casinos but leaves the sites and redirect pages in place.

The cabinet said in June it was drawing up new tools with the authority to tackle illegal gambling, including the power to block websites. Regulators have struggled to keep up, with more now being spent on illegal sites in the Netherlands than on legal ones.

World.title: Minister given permission to axe far-right TV broadcaster
World.content:
The Netherlands’ media minister, Rianne Letschert, has obtained the legal authority to strip the far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland (ON) of its licence, meaning it could be taken off air from public broadcasting and lose its public funding.

The Dutch media authority set out a case in a letter to Letschert, weeks after ON presenters spoke of their approval and agreements with certain Adolf Hitler remarks in a July broadcast.

It called the show a turning point and said it no longer trusted ON to run its operations properly.

Letschert has said a licence can only be withdrawn once two formal sanctions are in place, both of which have now been fulfilled. The first was a fine imposed last September for conflict-of-interest breaches and for ignoring editorial rules, and a separate penalty order for withholding records of how it spent public money.

ON director Peter Vlemmix told the ANP news agency the broadcaster would continue its “fight for survival” and accused the authority of overlooking improvements made over the past year.

Letschert has promised to tell MPs her decision on ON’s future before a parliamentary debate on September 24.

World.content:

A court in The Hague ruled on Thursday that the public prosecution service (OM) must hand over the names the 14 prominent doctors who signed a letter urging an investigation into the case of Milou, a 17-year-old died by euthanasia in 2023.

Her parents, who were subjected to death threats after the letter was leaked, sued to obtain the names of the medical professionals who penned the later.

The OM had refused to provide the names, six of which are already known, citing privacy concerns.

Judges in The Hague said that it was “unreasonable to refuse to provide the letter containing names to the parents” who have a “compelling interest” in the information.

The parents could choose to pursue disciplinary or civil legal action against the doctors.

Milou had suffered from mental health problems from the age of 11 following sexual abuse. She was again sexually abused in an institution by another patient.

After years of treatment and various suicide attempts, she chose euthanasia at the age of 17 on the grounds of unbearable mental suffering.

The psychiatrist who approved her decision acted in accordance with the guidelines, the regional euthanasia review committee RTE found.

The committee reviews all euthanasia procedures to make sure the correct procedures have been followed and reports back to the OM, which now has five days to hand over the names.

World.title: Student room shortage stays above 20,000 despite new builds
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

More students in the Netherlands are staying in their parents’ home or giving up the search for a place of their own, as the shortage of student housing remains high despite thousands of new rooms being built each year.

The country is short of more than 20,200 student rooms, barely down from 21,000 a year earlier, according to the annual student housing monitor from knowledge centre Kences, published this week.

Social housing providers have built nearly 5,000 units a year since 2022, meeting the targets they were set.

Kences had expected the shortage to climb, because private landlords have been selling up in response to new rent rules and higher taxes. Some 32,300 fewer students have rented from private landlords since 2024.

That did not translate into a sharp rise, largely because student numbers have also dropped, including among international students. The share of students living away from home has fallen from 50% to 43% over eight years.

Fewer rooms, riskier ads

The rooms still on the private market are increasingly hard to rent safely. Many are advertised above the legal limit.

Scammers, meanwhile, have flooded TikTok with fake listings that pocket deposits for rooms that do not exist.

Internationals are especially exposed to housing fraud, as they rarely have a family home to fall back on and often do not know their rights.

Kences wants the profit tax paid by housing associations scrapped, which it says would fund 15,000 to 25,000 more student homes over ten years. “Every euro we hand to the tax office, we would rather put into housing,” director Reijnder Jan Spits told broadcaster NOS.

Even if every current building plan goes ahead, the centre warned, the shortage could still stand at between 10,000 and 35,000 rooms in eight years.

World.title: Cybercrime and online fraud hit 2.5 million people in 2025
World.content:
An estimated 2.5 million people in the Netherlands fell victim to cybercrime or an online form of fraud, deception or intimidation last year, according to a new report by prosecutors and police that warns the threat is becoming harder to contain.

The Cybercrimebeeld Nederland, published every two years by the public prosecution department (OM) and the Dutch police, says offenders are increasingly working across borders and paying for whatever expertise they lack.

Technical skill is now widely for sale, the report says: ready-made tools, stolen data and services allow novice hackers to create complex attacks.

“Criminals combine data from earlier hacks with newly stolen data,” said Christa de Pagter, the national public prosecutor for cybercrime. Offenders use it to make more targetted attacks on victims, she said, often posing as a bank or crypto platform to pressure them into acting.

State actors blur the line

The report also revealed the growing role of state actors, which it says are increasingly entangled with criminal groups through hybrid warfare, eroding the line between cybercrime and national security. States can use criminals as proxies, directing them or supplying money and infrastructure.

In May, Dutch investigators arrested two men over servers used for Russian-linked cyberattacks; the report also cites two 17-year-olds detained last year for mapping wifi networks around government buildings in The Hague.

Lured through online games

Prosecutors and police also describe a new generation of young, Western cybercriminals, driven by money and status rather than ideology, who meet in loose online networks and specialise in data and cryptocurrency theft. They range in age from 11 to 25, police cybercrime lead Stan Duijf told broadcaster NOS.

Children are often lured in through online games such as Roblox, Fortnite and Minecraft, where they can be groomed in chat rooms. “It’s just like the schoolyard: they start with mischief,” Duijf said – but some go on to become cybercriminals.

The report highlights this year’s hack on Odido, which police believe a Dutch gang using the name ShinyHunters carried out, exposing the data of 6.2 million customers and prompting a €1 million ransom demand the firm refused.

AI is described as a “catalyst”: the report says it does not fundamentally change cybercrime but increases its speed and scale, and makes scam emails harder to spot.

World.title: Rabbit farms face prosecution over abuse footage
World.content:
Sixteen Dutch rabbit farms could face criminal prosecution after undercover footage showed bunnies being lifted by the ears and thrown into crates, and sick animals beaten to death, junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens has said.

The images, filmed by campaign group Animal Rights, were shot at 16 companies that export live rabbits to slaughterhouses in Belgium. They show the animals being picked up by the ears, fur, legs or head and thrown in large numbers into transport crates and shopping trolleys, where they can be crushed.

“What can be seen in the footage is terrible,” Erkens said in answer to parliamentary questions from D66 and the animal rights party PvdD, calling the treatment unacceptable. Some people, he added, appeared to feel free to handle animals this way when no inspector was nearby.

The food safety board NVWA has received a large amount of recent footage and is checking it for authenticity. If abuse is found companies are prosecuted. In 2024 a slaughterhouse was fined for cruelty after activists released undercover video.

Footage seen so far points to structural and serious failings in how the animals are handled, Erkens said. He has also set up new checks on how rabbits are caught and loaded – a stage of animal transport that inspections had largely overlooked, and will update parliament by the end of the year.
