Indiaâs solar energy expansion is entering a new phase, with floating photovoltaic projects emerging as a potential answer to two of the countryâs biggest renewable energy challenges: limited land availability and the need for more reliable power generation.The Union governmentâs approval of the Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY) on July 31, 2026, marks a major push in that direction. According to the Press Information Bureau (PIB), the scheme will support 5,000 MW of floating solar photovoltaic capacity on reservoirs and other suitable inland water bodies, backed by energy storage systems with a minimum two-hour storage capacity.With an overall financial outlay of â¹5,070 crore, the scheme will be implemented from financial year 2026-27 to 2030-31. The government says the programme could help reduce pressure on land resources, improve grid reliability and open another avenue for India to expand its renewable energy capacity.Indiaâs solar sector has undergone a dramatic transformation over the past decade. According to government data, installed solar capacity has risen from approximately 3 GW in 2014 to 162.15 GW as of June 30, 2026, representing more than a fiftyfold increase.The expansion has been supported by large-scale solar parks, rooftop installations, solar-powered agricultural pumps, competitive bidding and policies designed to strengthen domestic manufacturing.The government said India added 44.61 GW of solar capacity in FY 2025-26, almost twice the 23.83 GW added in the previous financial year. During the same period, total non-fossil fuel capacity reached 283.46 GW, including 274.68 GW from renewable energy sources.The latest policy push towards floating solar builds on this broader expansion, while attempting to use a resource that conventional solar projects do not require: water surfaces.The PM-SSY is designed to support 5,000 MW of Floating Solar Photovoltaic projects with co-located Energy Storage Systems, according to the PIB.The storage component will have a minimum capacity of 10,000 MWh, equivalent to two hours of storage for the planned 5,000 MW floating solar capacity. This is intended to help states manage periods of peak electricity demand and address one of the central challenges associated with solar power, its variability.Floating solar panels are mounted on buoyant structures and deployed on reservoirs, lakes, ponds and other suitable water bodies. Instead of competing with agriculture, settlements, forests or other land uses, the technology allows electricity generation from water surfaces.The government estimates that India currently has around 700 MW of floating solar capacity. The PM-SSY would therefore represent a substantial increase in the country's floating solar footprint.The scheme is based on an assessment by the National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE), which estimates that India has around 102.18 GWp of floating solar potential across reservoirs and suitable inland water bodies.The attraction of floating solar goes beyond saving land. Floating photovoltaic systems can benefit from the cooling effect of water, which can improve the operating efficiency of solar panels compared with installations exposed to higher temperatures on land. Research cited in the supplied material indicates that floating systems can generate between 0.6% and 4.4% more energy than comparable land-mounted installations, although actual performance varies according to site and technology.The panels can also shade portions of water bodies, reducing exposure to sunlight and potentially lowering evaporation. This could be particularly relevant in water-stressed regions where reservoirs are used for irrigation, drinking water or hydropower.The scale of the potential benefit depends on factors such as climate, the percentage of the water surface covered and the characteristics of individual reservoirs.Floating solar can also be paired with existing hydropower infrastructure. Solar generation can use existing transmission connections, while hydropower or pumped-storage facilities can provide a means of balancing variable solar output.This combination could become increasingly important as India adds more renewable capacity to its electricity grid.India is not starting from scratch. Some of the country's largest floating solar installations are already operating or under development. The Omkareshwar floating solar project in Madhya Pradesh, located on the Narmada River reservoir, is designed for a capacity of 600 MW and is among the country's most prominent floating solar developments.Other major installations include NTPC's 100 MW floating solar project at Ramagundam in Telangana, built on an ash pond near its thermal power station, and a 92 MW project at Kayamkulam in Kerala.These projects demonstrate how floating solar can be deployed on different types of water bodies, including reservoirs and water surfaces associated with existing industrial infrastructure.The experience is particularly relevant as the government seeks to expand floating solar beyond individual projects and create a larger national programme.Floating photovoltaics are no longer a niche technology. The first floating solar installation was developed in Japan in 2007, while larger projects began appearing during the following decade. Global installed capacity expanded rapidly, rising from around 1 GW in 2018 to 13 GW in 2022, according to figures cited in the supplied material.Asia has been at the forefront of this expansion, with China developing some of the world's largest floating solar installations.In 2022, China added a 320 MW floating photovoltaic facility in Dezhou, Shandong, developed by Huaneng Power International. Earlier large projects included installations at reservoirs and former mining sites.The technology has also expanded beyond inland water bodies. Offshore floating solar remains comparatively young, but pilot projects have been developed in marine environments, including installations in the Maldives and the North Sea.The economics of floating solar have also improved. While floating projects once carried a substantial cost premium over conventional solar, costs had moved closer to land-based systems by 2020. However, the supplied research indicates that installation costs remained around 10-25% higher in 2023, largely because of additional anchoring and mooring requirements.Land availability is becoming an increasingly important consideration as India expands renewable generation.Large solar parks require substantial tracts of land, and acquiring suitable land can involve competing demands from agriculture, settlements, conservation and other economic activities.Floating solar offers an alternative by allowing electricity generation on existing reservoirs, industrial ponds, irrigation basins and other artificial water bodies.Indiaâs conventional solar expansion has already demonstrated the scale required to meet national targets. Large projects account for 118.79 GW of installed solar capacity, while grid-connected rooftop systems contribute another 27.88 GW, according to the government.Floating solar can add another layer to this mix without necessarily requiring comparable amounts of terrestrial land.The potential is especially significant around existing hydropower reservoirs, where solar generation can potentially share transmission infrastructure and complement hydropower generation.The PM-SSY's storage component is particularly significant because India's solar expansion is moving into a phase where generation capacity alone will not be enough.Solar power is produced primarily during daylight hours, while electricity demand can remain high after sunset. Energy storage can help shift some of that generation to periods when it is needed most.Under PM-SSY, every supported floating solar project is expected to be associated with energy storage of at least two hours. The government expects this to help states manage peak demand while improving the reliability of renewable power.The combination of floating solar, existing reservoirs and energy storage could therefore create a model that goes beyond simply adding more generation capacity.In locations with hydropower or pumped-storage infrastructure, the relationship could become even more valuable. Water reservoirs can potentially function as part of an integrated renewable energy system, allowing solar generation to be balanced through stored water or battery systems.Floating solar's environmental advantages need to be considered alongside its potential risks.Partial coverage of water surfaces can reduce evaporation and sunlight penetration, potentially helping to conserve water and limit some forms of algal growth. However, extensive shading can also alter aquatic ecosystems.The environmental impact depends heavily on the type of water body, the percentage of its surface covered, the depth and movement of the water, and the design of the floating system.Marine floating solar presents additional challenges. Anchoring, mooring and installation activity can disturb sediments and potentially affect benthic ecosystems. Large installations can also alter the amount of sunlight reaching seagrass or coral habitats.This means floating solar cannot simply be treated as a zero-impact alternative to land-based solar.For India, where reservoirs can serve multiple purposes including irrigation, drinking water, fisheries and hydropower, careful site selection and long-term ecological monitoring will be important as deployment expands.The government's floating solar push comes against the backdrop of a broader policy architecture that has driven India's solar growth.The National Solar Mission, launched in 2010, helped establish long-term targets, while the Solar Parks Scheme and Green Energy Corridor programme addressed infrastructure and transmission challenges.The Solar Parks Scheme has supported 54 parks with a combined sanctioned capacity of 39,188 MW, according to government data as of February 2026.The Green Energy Corridor, meanwhile, is intended to move renewable electricity from generation-rich regions to major demand centres. The programme had enabled evacuation of 24,567.8 MW of renewable energy through strengthened transmission networks as of February 2026.Competitive bidding has also transformed the economics of solar power. The government says solar tariffs fell from around â¹18 per unit in 2010 to â¹2.44 per unit at the Bhadla Solar Park auction in 2017.The expansion is now increasingly being supported by domestic manufacturing. Solar module manufacturing capacity grew from 2.3 GW in 2014 to around 172 GW as of March 31, 2026, according to the PIB.India's solar transition is also becoming increasingly distributed. The PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana, launched in February 2024 with an outlay of â¹75,021 crore, is aimed at expanding rooftop solar among households. More than 43 lakh households had been solarised by June 2026, according to the government.In agriculture, PM-KUSUM supports solar pumps, decentralised solar generation and feeder solarisation. Nearly 11.49 lakh off-grid solar pumps had been installed, while more than 15.89 lakh agricultural pumps were covered through feeder-level solarisation, according to government figures cited in the supplied material.Together, rooftop solar and PM-KUSUM contributed substantially to distributed solar capacity additions during FY 2025-26.Floating solar now offers another form of distributed geography, not necessarily through small installations, but by making productive use of water bodies that already exist.India's solar story has moved from building capacity to integrating that capacity into a more complex electricity system.The country's Panchamrit commitments include achieving 500 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030, alongside the longer-term goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2070.Floating solar is unlikely to replace conventional ground-mounted or rooftop solar. Instead, its significance lies in expanding the range of locations where solar generation can be developed.The government's estimate of 102.18 GWp of floating solar potential suggests that water bodies could become an important part of that expansion. PM-SSY's 5,000 MW target is only a fraction of the assessed potential, but it could provide a large-scale test of the technology.The scheme is also expected to create 16,000-17,000 full-time equivalent jobs and support domestic manufacturing of floating structures, photovoltaic cells and modules and energy storage systems, according to the PIB.If the technology can deliver reliable generation while limiting ecological disruption and managing its higher installation costs, floating solar could become an important component of India's renewable energy mix.For a country attempting to add hundreds of gigawatts of clean capacity while balancing land, water, transmission and reliability constraints, the next solar frontier may not necessarily be another field of panels on land.It could be the reservoirs already sitting at the heart of India's power and water infrastructure.

World.title: Kin of custodial death victim try to block CM’s Vijay’s convoy outside Secretariat
World.content:
Relatives of a man who allegedly died in police custody attempted to approach Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay’s convoy and submit a petition outside the Secretariat on Thursday.

The incident occurred when the convoy was proceeding from his Neelankarai residence to the Secretariat. Over 100 people had gathered near the entrance of Fort St. George to meet the Chief Minister.

Among them were Rajesh Kannan, 50, his wife Anandhi, 43, relatives of Akash Delison, who allegedly died in police custody at the Manamadurai police station in March. The family alleged that though a case had been registered against six police personnel, no action had been taken and sought a CB-CID probe.

As the group crossed the barricades and entered the road, security personnel intervened. A constable fell and suffered a minor injury while trying to stop them. The police said Kannan breached the barricade and ran towards the convoy. When constable Ramkumar of the Tondiarpet police station tried to stop him, Kannan allegedly punched him in the chest. Mr. Ramkumar later complained of chest pain and was taken to a government hospital.

The convoy reached the Secretariat portico at 10.02 a.m. Police detained eight persons, including Kannan and Anandhi, for questioning in connection with the security breach. They are expected to be released after the Assembly proceedings on Thursday.

World.title: ‘I’m Game’ movie review: Dulquer Salmaan-starrer squanders a winning idea
World.content:
Grabbing an audience by the collar and taking them along the way is no easy task. In I’m Game, Nahas Hidhayath had an idea that could do just that, though Hollywood has dabbled with similar themes before. But unfortunately, the filmmaker holds on to his fascinating concept for only a while before loosening his grip and veering off into familiar narrative patterns.

Dan John (Dulquer Salmaan), a spoilt child of a rich family, runs a company just as his father wished, but his heart lies in gambling like there is no tomorrow. Despite his wealthy background, his gambling habit leaves him neck-deep in debt. But something bizarre happens to him, changing his life’s trajectory, as well as that of quite a few others.

Film: I’m Game (Malayalam) Direction: Nahas Hidayath Starring: Dulquer Salmaan, Kayadu Lohar, Mysskin, Samyuktha Viswanathan, Vinay Forrt, Anthony ‘Pepe’ Varghese, Kathir Storyline: The life of a gambler, neck-deep in debts, changes after a bizarre event. Runtime: 174 minutes

For Dulquer Salmaan, making his appearance in Malayalam cinema after a while, this was a perfect comeback opportunity, with his character having immense scope for humour and action. The film does offer them for a while before getting derailed.

Nahas Hidayath debuted with RDX, a film with a bare-minimum story that gave the audience the emotional need to root for the three protagonists during the lengthy action sequences. However, in I’m Game, despite the multiple story threads and ideas, everything happens at a distance, with the audience remaining untouched by what happens to any of the characters. This also makes the slickly edited and shot action sequences feel a bit stretched after a point.

ALSO READ: ‘Bethlehem Kudumba Unit’ movie review: Girish AD works his magic yet again in Nivin Pauly-Mamitha Baiju starrer

One of the strangest writing decisions screenwriters Sajeer Baba, Ismail Aboobacker and Bilal Moidu make is the lengthy flashback story revolving around betting in a major cricket league. What could have been told in a few cleverly shot scenes is presented as a full-blown narrative. With an over-melodramatic romance also thrown in the mix, the core supernatural story takes a backseat, and Dulquer’s character disappears from the screen for quite a long time. The film never really recovers from the dip it suffers during this phase, where we are made to wait till the flashback meanders to a predictable end.

The hope that things would change for the better after the extended flashback goes in vain as the writers let go of the interesting core concept and focus on a run-of-the-mill revenge story. In the end, the only real creative spark was in the supernatural idea, with a lot of generic elements woven around it. Human greed, the behavioural change of a spoilt rich kid, and the corrosive influence of money on sports are left unexplored after they are briefly addressed.

In I’m Game, Nahas Hidayath loses the bird in his hand, chasing two in the bushes.

I’m Game is currently running in cinemas.

World.title: Direct Uttarakhand CM to register FIR against those behind ‘purification’ of Haldwani rally site, Kharge writes to Nadda
World.content:
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Thursday (September 3, 2026) said the shuddhikaran (purification) of the Ramlila ground in Uttarakhand’s Haldwani, where he had addressed a political rally, amounted to practising “untouchability”, and said his party would approach Rajya Sabha Chairman C.P. Radhakrishnan over the issue.

On September 2, Mr. Kharge, who is the Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha, wrote to Union Minister and Leader of the Rajya Sabha J.P. Nadda, urging him to direct Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami to ensure that a First Information Report (FIR) was registered against those responsible for the alleged purification ritual.

In his letter, Mr. Kharge recalled that he had raised the matter in the Rajya Sabha on August 13 and that Mr. Nadda had assured the House that the incident would be investigated and strict action taken against those found guilty. The Rajya Sabha Chairman had also expressed his grief over the incident, he said.

“Even after 24 days of this incident, not even an FIR has been filed against the organisations and individuals involved in this heinous act,” Mr. Kharge said.

Mr. Kharge linked the incident to the history of caste discrimination, recalling that during the Mahad Satyagraha, when B.R. Ambedkar drank water from a public tank, caste Hindus had subsequently performed a purification ritual using gomutra and gobar. Such practices, he said, could not be sanctified merely by chanting mantras or performing a havan.

“This issue transcends my personal self or the office of the Indian National Congress president; it is deeply connected to the sentiments of crores of people who confront this harsh reality on a daily basis,” he said in his letter.

The Congress president said the ritual at the Ramlila Maidan, following his August 8 rally, was contrary to the spirit of the Constitution and human values. “This is an incident of untouchability; it is not just about purification,” he told reporters at his official residence in New Delhi.

Mr. Kharge also questioned the silence of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah on the issue. “Whenever something wrong happens, they remain silent,” he said, citing the alleged theft of donations to the Ram Temple, and atrocities against Dalits as other instances.

He also defended the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, who had criticised the purification ritual and demanded an FIR under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. An FIR was subsequently registered against Mr. Gandhi in Uttarakhand over his remarks.

Congress General Secretary (organisation) K.C. Venugopal said Mr. Gandhi will not be intimidated by cases against him. “These people [BJP] is a problem for Rahul Gandhi. He will be scared like Mr. Modi. It’s not like that. He is the most courageous leader today,” Mr. Venugopal said.

World.title: City hospital performs ABO-incompatible kidney transplant
World.content:
Apollo Speciality Hospitals in Madurai has performed an ABO-incompatible living-donor kidney transplantation using advanced antigen-specific immunoadsorption therapy.

According to a press release, the procedure enabled a 40-year-old man with blood group O positive to receive a kidney from his wife, who had blood group A positive.

Consultant Nephrologist P. Arun Prasath said ABO-incompatible transplantation requires meticulous immunological preparation, particularly when the recipient has a high antibody titre. ABO-incompatible recipients have naturally occurring antibodies against the donor’s blood-group antigens, which, if present at high levels, can attack the transplanted kidney and lead to antibody-mediated rejection and compromised graft function.

Therefore, desensitisation to reduce these antibodies to an acceptable level is a critical part of transplantation across an ABO barrier. In this case, antigen-specific immunoadsorption provided a targeted approach by selectively removing anti-A antibodies while returning the treated plasma to the patient. The patient’s anti-A antibody titre was successfully reduced from 1:256 to 1:8, enabling us to proceed safely with transplantation, he said.

The successful outcome demonstrates the importance of personalised desensitisation strategies, careful monitoring of antibody titres, and close assessment of the patient’s overall clinical condition, particularly in a case where conventional plasma exchange presented challenges. Immunoadsorption can offer a targeted method of antibody removal in appropriately selected patients undergoing ABO-incompatible transplantation, he said.

World.title: TVK Ranipet MLA wants non-existent factory shutdown, draws criticism on social media
World.content:
A company that did not exist in the region came under fire in the Tamil Nadu Assembly on Thursday, with Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) Ranipet MLA I. Thahira demanding its closure, alleging that it was causing severe pollution in her constituency. She mentioned that JK Tyres had been polluting the region. “In our regime, we should shut down that company,” she said. She also said that people in the area had staged protests, but no action had been taken.

The issue took an interesting turn when Environment and Climate Change Minister V.K. Rajeev immediately responded in the House, asking the Ranipet MLA to share the details and assuring her that he would ask officials to inspect the matter immediately.

JK Tyre has only one manufacturing plant in Tamil Nadu, located in Sriperumbudur.

Tamil Nadu’s Former Industries Minister T.R.B Rajaa immediately took to social media and posted a comment on X saying: “And now this TVK MLA wants to Shut down @JKTyreCorporate. WHAT is wrong with these people ! If there is pollution issues then take action and rectify it! Calling for an outright shutdown is madness and sends out a very poor signal to #Industry circles!” “Am absolutely distraught at the way our #TamilNadu’s professional stature is being sullied and squandered by such immatured senseless statements,” he added.

And now this TVK MLA wants to Shut down @JKTyreCorporate 🤦🏾🤦🏾🤦🏾

Am absolutely… https://t.co/q1cyL5NzqP — Dr. T R B Rajaa (@TRBRajaa) September 3, 2026

Mr. Rajaa in a second post mentioned: “I did a small search on the JkTyre company that the TVK MLA asked to be shutdown. I know there is one factory in Kanchipuram District but did not know there was one in Ranipet District. So we did a search for major subsidiaries which could be manufacturing for @JKTyreCorporate but still couldn’t find anything big and polluting. Then I found out why I did not know about the “JKTyre company” near Ranipet. Because...the TVK MLA is said to have called a tyre retreading outlet as “JKTyre Company” Now, one thing is clear one should not take anything said by the TVK MLAs as hard facts just like their reels. But, Wonder why their own govt acknowledged it and even defended it.” “For them a retail retreading shop seems to be a polluting industry worthy of a question raised in the assembly, instead of asking the local authorities to take action. Is this the kind of “industry” they are going after!” he added.

So we did a search for major subsidiaries which could be manufacturing for @JKTyreCorporate… pic.twitter.com/9DSdp2vcM5 — Dr. T R B Rajaa (@TRBRajaa) September 3, 2026

Later in the evening, Tamil Nadu’s Industries Minister S. Keerthana took to X and posted: A reference was made in the Assembly today to a JK Tyre unit in Ranipet. On verification, JK Tyre does not have a manufacturing facility in Ranipet. The environmental issue raised by the Hon’ble Member will, however, be looked into to identify the concerned non-JK tyre unit and appropriate action will be taken wherever required.” “My response in the House was on a larger and important principle, Tamil Nadu needs industries and jobs, but growth cannot come at the cost of environmental compliance. Both have to go together. JK Tyre has also clarified that its operations are in compliance with all applicable statutory environmental clearances and regulatory requirements. It is also important to place on record that JK Tyre recently reaffirmed its confidence in Tamil Nadu by signing an MoU with Guidance Tamil Nadu at the VETTRI Tamil Nadu Investment Conclave for an investment of ₹5,143 crore, with the potential to create 3,510 employment opportunities,” she had mentioned in her post.
