A team of experts has already gone to the penitentiary to speak with Khachatryan and monitor respect for his rights.

The ombudsman’s office has also asked the relevant authorities for explanations to establish all the circumstances. After it completes the investigation and reviews its findings, the Human Rights Defender will present its position.

Comments

Human rights defender Zaruhi Hovhannisyan believes that the published photograph of the defendant on a stretcher in the courtroom is “not simply a sad scene”. In her view, the situation raises questions about the state’s attitude towards human rights:

“The photograph shows a 71-year-old man with serious health problems lying on a stretcher, completely covered, in the middle of a courtroom. People involved in the proceedings, tables, microphones and documents surround him. On one side stands the entire institutional machinery of criminal justice, organised by the state. On the other stands a person whom the system completely ignores.

The issue is not to make people feel sorry for the man lying on that stretcher, or to discuss why he ended up in court, what case he faces or how many charges he faces. The issue is that this is an extremely dangerous picture. When the state becomes accustomed to subordinating human dignity to a judicial process, it puts not only one person’s rights at risk but also the boundary that should prevent the state from gaining unlimited power over an individual. Human dignity and the prohibition of torture limit the state’s power over a person.”

Former head of Armenia’s State Revenue Committee in court on a stretcher

The NGO Disability Rights Agenda also issued a statement about the videos that Gagik Khachatryan’s lawyers circulated:

“According to the defence, doctors diagnosed Gagik Khachatryan with spinal stenosis in 2015 and implanted special devices in his cervical spine. The footage also shows him in a semi-conscious state while people were moving him.”

The organisation’s experts believe the authorities should structure the court proceedings in a way that prevents harm to a person’s health or humiliating conditions. Appropriate specialists should accompany people with limited mobility at all times. Medical professionals should supervise their movement and authorities should provide the necessary technical equipment.

“Regardless of the nature of the charges or his former position, humanitarian principles and safeguards for physical integrity must remain unchanged,” the statement says.

The organisation called on law enforcement agencies to take the following steps during further procedural actions:

rely only on impartial professional assessments,

provide the necessary medical care,

prevent any actions that cause a person unnecessary physical pain.

Former Armenian revenue chief in court on stretcher

World.title: Amnesty International: Georgia must not deport Denis Kulanin to Russia
World.content:
Denis Kulanin’s case

Amnesty International is calling on the Georgian authorities to prevent the deportation of Russian citizen Denis Kulanin to Russia, where the organisation says he faces a real risk of imprisonment and torture.

The organisation says Georgia should protect Kulanin from being forcibly returned to Russia because he has publicly opposed Russia’s war in Ukraine and expressed support for opposition leader Alexei Navalny. According to Amnesty International, both positions could lead to criminal prosecution in Russia.

“Denis Kulanin has publicly opposed Russia’s war in Ukraine and expressed support for Alexei Navalny — both actions constitute criminal offences in Russia and can lead to imprisonment. The Georgian authorities must ensure that he is not deported to Russia. Amid the harsh repression of people who oppose the war, he faces a real risk of arbitrary criminal prosecution, imprisonment, torture or other ill-treatment,” said Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s deputy director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia.

He said Georgia must uphold the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning a person to a country where they face a real risk of serious human rights violations.

“The Georgian authorities must also ensure that Denis Kulanin has an effective opportunity to seek international protection, including by allowing him to leave voluntarily for a safe third country,” Krivosheev added.

Who is Denis Kulanin?

Denis Kulanin is a Russian citizen who lived in Georgia and took part in pro-European protests. Police arrested him on 28 March 2025 during a demonstration outside parliament. The authorities accused him of smashing a police car window and sentenced him to two years in prison.

On the Orthodox Christian feast of the Dormition of the Mother of God, President Mikheil Kavelashvili pardoned Kulanin. However, because Kulanin is not a Georgian citizen, the authorities did not release him. Instead, they transferred him to the migration department.

According to his lawyer, deporting Kulanin to Russia would be both unacceptable and dangerous. While in detention, Kulanin sent a letter in which he wished Ukraine glory and peace. His lawyer says that in Russia, authorities can interpret almost any statement about the war in a way that could lead to criminal charges.

Denis Kulanin. Photo: Publica

On 30 August 2026, the Tbilisi City Court ordered Denis Kulanin to be held at the temporary detention centre run by the Georgian Interior Ministry’s Migration Department. He will remain at the centre until the grounds for his detention cease to apply or the authorities enforce the decision to deport him from Georgia, but for no longer than three months.

On 31 August, Kulanin’s lawyer was told that he would not be allowed to leave Georgia voluntarily until the Tbilisi City Court considers his deportation case.

On 1 September, Kulanin’s lawyer said the Migration Department had asked the Tbilisi City Court to deport him to his country of citizenship, the Russian Federation.

World.title: Opinion: ‘An attempt to make Abkhazia’s residents feel part of single political space with Russia’
World.content:
Abkhazia is actively preparing for Russia’s State Duma elections, which will take place on 20 September 2026. Most Abkhazia residents hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, which gives them the right to vote in the elections.

Russia will open 319 polling stations in 152 countries for citizens voting abroad. 35 of them — more than 10% — will open in Abkhazia.

Many people think this is excessive for a small republic with a population of 250,000.

One of those who objects is Akhra Bzhania, a prominent Abkhaz blogger and public figure. He believes that the “excessive” number of polling stations and the active election campaign aim to create a sense among Abkhazia’s residents that they somehow “belong” to Russia.

Akhra Bzhania: “There is a standard procedure for people with dual citizenship who vote abroad.

Usually, two or three polling stations open, plus a polling station at the consulate or embassy. That’s it.

Abkhazia cannot use its budget to cover the costs of holding a constitutional event of a foreign state. That makes no sense.

If someone argues that the Russian side is paying for the campaign, that is even worse!

Let me explain why. Fifty or 60,000 votes from Abkhazia will have no impact on the overall balance of parties in the State Duma.

This means the election campaign here must serve a different, ideological purpose — to create a sense among Abkhazia’s citizens that they share a single political and administrative space with Russia. And from there, a common state is not far away.”

I have no doubt that some Abkhaz citizens with dual citizenship care deeply about the differences between the programmes of Russian political parties. For them, State Duma elections are therefore not only a civic but also a political act.

But in that case, they can plan ahead and vote in Sochi, Krasnodar or Moscow, as Russians living in Armenia, Kyrgyzstan and elsewhere do.

Yet our entire republic is covered with banners urging people to vote for a government body of another country! We plan to open 35 polling stations, just as we do for our own presidential elections!

It seems strange to me — and not only to me — and out of line with the status of our state and the level of Abkhaz-Russian relations.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Abkhazia prepares for Russia’s State Duma elections

World.title: Karabakh Revival Fund partners the first Lachin International Film Festival (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. The Karabakh Revival Fund (KRF) served as an official partner of the first Lachin International Film Festival, held in Lachin from 24 to 27 August.

The festival formed part of the ceremonial programme marking Lachin City Day and represents a further step in the cultural revival of Karabakh and East Zangezur.

Held under the banner “Where Film Meets LIFE”, it was organised by the Hoçazfilm studio with the support of the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Azerbaijan, the Special Representative Office of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the Lachin district, the Karabakh Revival Fund, the Film Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan and Bakı Abadlıq Xidməti.

As the first international film festival ever held in Karabakh and East Zangezur, it showed once again that the reconstruction of the liberated territories is not a matter of infrastructure alone: restoring the cultural and civic life of these lands is no less of a priority.

The festival will be remembered as more than a programme of screenings — it was a cultural event that embodied the idea of revival itself. Its significance works on several levels at once: it brings new creative voices to light, introduces Lachin’s cultural revival to an international audience, and establishes the city as a new creative venue on the map of world cinema.

Among those attending were government officials, prominent figures from culture and the arts, guests from abroad, and residents and visitors of Lachin.

Speaking at the ceremony, Rahman Hajiyev, Chairman of the Executive Board of the Karabakh Revival Fund, said that alongside the large-scale reconstruction under way across the liberated territories, bringing cultural life back to the region remains a particular priority.

The festival, he said, gives filmmakers from Azerbaijan and abroad a rare chance to see Karabakh as it is today. He expressed confidence that the initiative will inspire the international film community with the story of the region — its past and its present revival — and encourage filmmakers to take up Karabakh as a subject in future work.

Close to 300 films from 47 countries were submitted to the festival, of which 20 titles representing 15 countries were selected for screening. Among them was a special Karabakh premiere of the Uzbek film Amir Temur, directed by Jacob Schwartz.

The closing and awards ceremony was held as part of a special event for Lachin City Day, attended by hundreds of residents and visitors. Official Selection certificates were presented to 39 participants, and 17 awards were made in total. The festival’s official prize, the Golden Oak Branch, went to five Azerbaijani and two international directors.

World.title: TURKPA Secretary General meets with OSCE PA President (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. The Secretary General of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Turkic States, Ramil Hasan, held a meeting with the OSCE PA delegation, headed by the President of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, Pere Joan Pons Sampietro, who is on an official visit to Azerbaijan, at the TURKPA International Secretariat.

The meeting addressed issues of mutual interest, including the effective and active cooperation of TURKPA with the OSCE PA since 2010. The parties also exchanged views on the steps taken to obtain observer status for TURKPA in the OSCE PA, the voting process on this issue at the OSCE PA annual session held in The Hague in July, and the next stage.

The meeting also covered the parliamentary elections held in Kazakhstan, TURKPA's large-scale and productive engagement in recent times, as well as effective cooperation between the OSCE PA and TURKPA in promoting dialogue, peace, stability and mutual understanding. Both the OSCE PA President and the TURKPA Secretary General underscored that more active participation of their respective delegations in future activities would serve the common interests.

Meanwhile, the OSCE PA President thanked for the warm welcome, expressed his satisfaction with the cooperation with TURKPA, and expressed his willingness to provide all possible support to TURKPA’s further activities in the processes related to the development of parliamentary diplomacy, where democratic values ​​serving mutual dialogue are prioritized.

The Secretary General emphasized the importance of joint participation in mutual activities and projects, noting that this is one of the main factors serving common interests.

The meeting was attended by the OSCE PA Vice President and Special Representative for the South Caucasus, Luís Graça, and the Deputy Secretaries General of the TURKPA International Secretariat, Talgat Aduov and Muhammet Alper Hayali, as well as the Secretary of the Commission, Aynura Abutalibova.

World.title: Azerbaijani MPs discuss peace process and regional economic opportunities in S. Caucasus with OSCE PA President
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. Members of the Azerbaijani Parliament Delegation to the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly (PA) have discussed the peace process and regional economic opportunities in the South Caucasus with the President of the OSCE PA, Pere Joan Pons Sampietro.



This was reported by the Press and Public Service of the Milli Majlis (Parliament) of Azerbaijan following the meeting between the delegation members and Sampietro, who is on an official visit to the country.

According to the report, one of the members, MP Gaya Mammadov, spoke about the peace process in the South Caucasus, regional economic opportunities, and the importance of international dialogue. He emphasized that the establishment of peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan is a historic achievement.

Participating in the meeting, the delegation members shared their views on the new geopolitical realities emerging in the South Caucasus and regional transport and logistics projects.

Sanpietro highly appreciated the regional peace-building process and noted the importance of the organization's adaptation to new geopolitical realities and support for sustainable peace in the region.

The meeting also exchanged views on other issues of mutual interest.

World.title: OSCE PA, Azerbaijan need to enhance cooperation - Sampietro (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. OSCE Parliamentary Assembly and Azerbaijan need to enhance cooperation, the OSCE PA President Pere Joan Pons Sampietro said in an exclusive interview with Trend, as he visited today Baku.

Sampietro noted that is important to enhance cooperation between the OSCE PA and Azerbaijan, including with the Azerbaijani Delegation to the OSCE PA, particularly around humanitarian mine action and other matters of urgent concern.

“International institutions are important platforms for addressing disagreements through dialogue. We seek to listen to Azerbaijani concerns and explore possibilities for parliamentary engagement,” the OSCE PA president added.

He noted that the Azerbaijani Delegation to the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly has always been quite active and engaged.

“The OSCE PA remains one of the few parliamentary platforms where Azerbaijan and parliamentarians from across Europe and North America continue to engage directly, and in this respect, we have a responsibility to continue providing a platform for open dialogue. This is a responsibility that we embrace. We welcome all constructive initiatives to enhance dialogue and cooperation,” Sampietro said.

World.title: OSCE PA President calls for stronger int’l backing for Azerbaijan’s demining (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. Azerbaijan should be able to draw more on international expertise, technology and donor support in demining, President of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly Pere Joan Pons Sampietro said in an exclusive interview with Trend, as he visited today Baku.

The OSCE PA president noted that landmines are a tragic, long-term consequence of conflict that require immediate and sustained international attention.

“The scale of mine and explosive-remnant contamination remains a serious humanitarian and development challenge for Azerbaijan. The ANAMA conference this week has demonstrated clearly that demining is not simply a technical issue: it is about civilian safety, return, reconstruction and livelihoods, all of which, of course, are essential for economic development,” he said.

Sampietro believes that international cooperation is indispensable.

“Azerbaijan should be able to draw more on international expertise, technology and donor support as clearance and reconstruction continue. Our Assembly is an important platform to sustain the attention towards these issues on the international agenda and create opportunities for further cooperation between our countries,” he added.

World.title: MEDIA slams disinformation campaign against Azerbaijan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 3. Media Development Agency of Azerbaijan (MEDIA) has condemned the disinformation campaign against Azerbaijan.

This is reflected in a statement of MEDIA following a biased information release by the Nexta channel, headquartered in Poland, regarding the fire incident near Nizami village of Azerbaijan's Goranboy district on September 2, 2026.

The agency said that the information, based on subjective considerations, attempts to present the issue in the context of interstate political relations and aims to confuse public opinion.

According to the statement, analyzes show that what is happening is part of a hybrid information campaign to be managed from a single center. The Western media, which constantly accuses forces outside its information environment of hybrid war, is conducting an organized disinformation campaign against Azerbaijan.

This fact once again shows that the normalization of relations between the neighboring states in the region, strengthening of stability and prosperity, doesn't meet the interests of certain circles, so classic cases of disinformation aimed at polluting the information space of Azerbaijan and creating artificial public anxiety have intensified.

Monitoring and analysis of the general information environment shows that in recent times, a campaign of spreading false information against Azerbaijan has been launched in a number of Western media resources. In particular, the obvious one-sided approach and unfounded considerations in the materials published in the UK's The Independent, The Guardian newspapers, and the BBC television and radio and broadcasting company, the U.S. CNN TV channel, the French Le Monde newspaper, the Polish TVP TV channel, and other resources are part of the information attack targeting the international image of Azerbaijan.

The spread of such assumptions and claims should be regarded as a clear manifestation of information manipulation.

The Media and Broadcasting Council of Azerbaijan will continue necessary measures to investigate such cases and prevent disinformation attempts aimed at overshadowing the country's sovereignty, domestic and foreign policy, as well as its international reputation.

World.title: States fume over private health changes 'robbing Peter to pay Paul'
World.content:
The states and territories have set the stage for a showdown with the Commonwealth over its proposed private health insurance rebate changes, with some demanding the federal government ditch the plan amid new warnings it will worsen the strain on public hospitals.

Health ministers will head into a meeting this morning in Sydney armed with a list of concerns, including the Commonwealth's proposed changes to the private health insurance rebate for older Australians and the rapidly growing number of stranded aged care patients in public hospitals across the nation.

Currently, those aged 65 or over receive a larger rebate on premiums than someone aged under 65 on the same income.

However, earlier this year, the federal government announced it would seek to establish greater equity between generations by ditching the Howard-era policy, meaning more than 3 million older Australians would have to pay hundreds of dollars more for their private health insurance each year from next April.

People over 65 to pay more for private health The federal government argues the move will help re-establish fairness across the generations.

The federal government's modelling has indicated that about 44,000 Australians would dump their private health insurance as a result.

Those figures have been backed by independent modelling from health economists at the University of Melbourne, who said the impact on hospitals would likely be small.

However, NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said his health department's modelling showed the proposed changes would have a much more significant impact on the public health system.

The upper end of the modelling estimates that in NSW alone, 80,000 residents aged 65 and over may either cancel or downgrade their private health insurance as a result.

It also estimates that it could result in public hospitals in NSW picking up more than 23,000 additional surgeries a year.

"The Commonwealth's proposed changes to private health insurance rebates will place additional pressure onto NSW's public hospitals at a time when health services are already experiencing significant demand," Mr Park said.

Ryan Park says his department's modelling shows the proposed changes would place a much greater burden on public health systems. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

New South Wales is among states and territories like South Australia, Victoria and the Northern Territory which have raised concerns over the proposal.

"Any change that would leave older Victorians worse off and put additional pressure on Victoria's public hospitals is unacceptable," Victorian Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said.

However, the Queensland LNP and Tasmanian Liberal governments have gone further, demanding the plan be ditched.

"This is, I think, robbing Peter to pay Paul — and Paul hasn't been paid yet," Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls told the ABC.

Tim Nicholls says the Commonwealth plan should be ditched. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

"We think that the Commonwealth has not yet got a full understanding of the impact … if we see more people dropping out of private health insurance, then we'll see more people turning up in our public health institutions, including our public hospitals."

The issue has become increasingly political, with Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston vowing the Coalition would block the legislation in the Senate because it was "nothing more than a cost shift onto older Australians to the public hospital system."

Aged care crisis worsens nationwide The number of aged care patients stuck in hospitals has jumped by 35 per cent in less than a year, fuelling fresh demands for the federal government to stem the crisis.

That means the federal government will need the support of the Greens to get the legislation through parliament, with the party yet to land on a formal position.

Despite the backlash, the federal government is vowing to push ahead with the plan, arguing the decision will save the government $3 billion over four years, with savings spent elsewhere in the aged care system.

"While some people may choose to leave private health insurance because of this change, we project this would be around 0.4 per cent," a government spokesperson said.

3,700 aged care patients stranded in public hospitals

The health ministers have also mobilised to launch another coordinated attack against the Commonwealth over the number of stranded aged care patients.

New figures collated by the states and territories have revealed there are now more than 3,700 aged care patients languishing in public hospitals across the country.

That is compared to about 2,500 last September, an increase of about 50 per cent in 12 months.

Those patients have been medically cleared for discharge but remain in hospital because there is nowhere suitable for them to go.

"I think it is the singular biggest issue that the South Australian health system faces today," South Australian Health Minister Blair Boyer told the ABC.

Blair Boyer says SA's biggest issue is aged care patients being stranded in public hospitals. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

"They are beds that we don't have available to us today for people who might be presenting at an emergency department or arriving by ambulance, in some cases for elective surgery that is planned."

While states run public hospitals, the Commonwealth is responsible for funding and regulating aged care services.

Tensions flared in the lead-up to the latest public hospital funding agreement cinched in January, with state governments of different political stripes abandoning party allegiances to unite on the issue.

The Commonwealth is responsible for funding and regulating aged care services. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

As well as occupying beds and placing increased pressure on hospitals, long stays in hospitals also strip elderly patients of independence and put them at a greater risk of illness and infection.

Tim Nicholls this week revealed a patient had been stranded in a Queensland public hospital for more than 1,000 days, with more than a dozen other patients stranded for more than 700 days.

He said long-stay patients accounted for more than 11 per cent of the state's acute hospital capacity.

"This is an enormous issue for all states," he said.

Government lands last-ditch hospital funding deal Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has bowed to mounting pressure from the states, promising an extra $25 billion for public hospitals.

"Every bed that is taken up by someone who could be out of a hospital means that we can't move people out of our emergency departments and that means we can't transfer people from the back of an ambulance into an emergency department to receive treatment."

WA Health Minister Meredith Hammat said the issue had reached "worrying new heights".

"It is having an impact on people's ability to be able to access care in our hospitals where they've got acute care needs," she told the ABC.

The Commonwealth has pledged an additional 5,000 aged care beds a year by 2029. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

The Commonwealth has pledged an additional 5,000 aged care beds a year by 2029 as part of a $3.7 billion package, alongside funding for specialist dementia care units and a joint taskforce examining long-stay hospital patients.

"Under the historic national hospital funding deal secured by the Albanese Labor Government in January, the Commonwealth is delivering an additional $24.4 billion in funding to the states and territories over 5 years to help them manage their hospital systems," a federal government spokesperson said.

"The Commonwealth expects that record $219.6 billion investment would flow into states and territories' hospital systems to help cut waiting lists, reduce waiting times in emergency rooms, and get older long-stay patients out of hospitals, and manage ramping."

World.title: We can't stop listening to these 10 albums from August
World.content:
Whenever we bring you the best 10 albums of the month, we wish we could write another article for the records we didn't have space for.

Below, you won't find mention of Rapsody, Rowena Wise, Overmono, Alabama Shakes, Ravyn Lenae, Weezer, Jem Cassar-Daley, Floating Points, Dinosaur Jr. or Don Walker. You should still seek out their new albums, all of which are excellent.

But our critics found the following 10 releases impossible to go past, and reckon you'll like them too.

Phoebe Bridgers — Lost Weekend

The poster child for 'sad girl music' stretches her sound into an immersive, emotive album experience. (Supplied: Dead Oceans)

Spotify | YouTube | Apple Music

Since her 2020 breakout album Punisher, Phoebe Bridgers has graduated to music's big leagues. Selling out tours, topping charts, collabs with Taylor Swift and becoming 2023's most decorated Grammys winner as part of 'sad girl' supergroup Boygenius.

Success, however, hasn't inoculated her from personal difficulties. Arriving to feverish anticipation, Lost Weekend pens another set of poignant, gut-punching songs inked with love and loss.

Specifically, the death of Bridgers's father, Tony, with whom she had a conflicted relationship. Plus, the demise of her high-profile relationship with actor Paul Mescal (chiefly on the starlit The Governor's Waltz) and the beginning of a new one with musical comic Bo Burnham.

Or Bobby, as he's affectionately called on a song rendering the giddy rush of new-found romance in walls of guitar and howling fanfare.

Designed as a front-to-back experience, Lost Weekend is an adventurous, capital A album. Made alongside an all-star production team (featuring Jack Antonoff, Alex G, and Tony Berg), it eschews conventional structure for music that eddies and morphs, mirroring emotional fluctuations.

Icy vocoder conveys the dissociation of sudden fame and a funeral on The Outside; hushed synths detonate into a rush of fragmented textures on the title track. And Bon Iver is a clear influence, particularly on the dynamic, pedal-steel kissed I Can't Wait, featuring Geese frontman Cameron Winter (credited as Son-John Johnson).

For all its experimentation, Lost Weekend remains anchored in Bridgers's speciality: quietly devastating lyricism that's funny, eloquent, and surgically sharp.

Observe the cutting couplets of the bluegrass Haunted ("been daydreaming about sleeping/But by the evening, I'm wide awake") or the shocking allusion to domestic abuse in Still Standing. ("I found her bleeding over the sink/But when you said sorry, you were looking at me.")

Scaling her melancholy and fragile optimism to the arenas that will now be her habitat, Bridgers delivers the most immersive, experimental yet lush album of her career.

For fans of: Boygenius, Conor Oberst, Bon Iver

Al Newstead

Erykah Badu & The Alchemist — Before The World Blows

Fans expected Erykah Badu and The Alchemist to release their first collaborative album 12 months ago. It's finally here. (Supplied: Control FREAQ Records)

Spotify | Apple Music | YouTube

When this album didn't arrive as promised 12 months ago, fans feared the worst. In the 16 years since her last album, Erykah Badu has promised lots of new music and delivered little.

Not only does the first collaboration from the R&B icon and legendary producer The Alchemist now exist, it's also exactly what we wanted.

The production — shared between both artists — respects both their pasts. Alchemist's signature moody, dusty vibe works hand-in-glove with Badu's rich and familiar voice in its smoothest moments. Elsewhere, they pack their soulful psychedelic hip hop with sonic jump scares, adding layers of intrigue, not just sound.

Steve Lacy, Thundercat, DRAM, and Kamasi Washington rise to the occasion, but the most striking collab comes with No ID, its terrifying production a perfect match for Westside Gunn's menace.

Badu's rich, lowkey croon stands on its own, and her unique point of view keeps us gripped. She references John Lennon and Odd Future in its opening minutes, gets waxed at the end of Love Me Not, ties Ozempic, DMT and lean together in Black Box. You never know what she'll say, but you know it'll be worth hearing.

Many of Badu's lyrics are about freedom: from slavery, from labels, from expectations, from bad relationships … yes, we waited 16 years, but maybe to get the best out of Badu, we need to respect her freedom to operate as she wants.

For fans of: Parliament-Funkadelic, Ms. Lauryn Hill, Thundercat

Dan Condon

Miss Kaninna — BLACKPRINT

Miss Kaninna's debut mixtape is a fierce display of her strength and power. (Supplied: Soul Has No Tempo)

Spotify | Apple Music | YouTube

In 2001, Jay-Z dropped The Blueprint. In 2014, Nicki Minaj tipped her hat with her third studio album, The Pinkprint. Now, in 2026, Miss Kaninna has entered the canon with her fierce mixtape BLACKPRINT.

The title's play on hip hop history serves as a north star for Kaninna. She's rapping and singing to the standard of the titans who came before her, while keeping her perspective as an Aboriginal woman front and centre. In doing so she provides a blueprint of her own, one shaped by the world's oldest living culture.

In a time where white nationalism — fuelled by online algorithms and bad faith actors — is on the rise, a voice like Kaninna's cuts through the noise. There's a punk ethos to both the production on BLACKPRINT, and Kaninna's writing throughout. It's stacked with anti-colonial bangers and witty, razor sharp bars.

For fans of: KNEECAP, Amyl and the Sniffers, Vince Staples

James Brennan

King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard — Alien Metal

The 28th (!!!) album from the Naarm/Melbourne journeymen introduces a new member: a modular synth named Nathan.

Bandcamp | YouTube | Apple Music

King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard, benders of sounds and minds, have finally dived right into a pool they've been dipping a toe into for a while: the rave cave.

Joined by their somewhat-official seventh member 'Nathan', a multi-player Eurorack modular synthesiser, the Melbourne collective warp and chop notes until they're nearly unrecognisable.

Alien transmissions beamed down into a bunch of music-obsessed gremlins dialled into their harebrained contraption.

It's not the first time we've heard King Gizzard lean into this glitchy side, their 2023 album The Silver Cord melded hooky, looping lyrics with a club-considered beat and wandering synths. But this is the first time they've amped up the BPM and focused on the hypnotic instrumentals.

Born from experimenting and mucking around with Nathan's various dials, knobs and cables, King Gizzard spent years refining, reshaping and completely re-doing what became Alien Metal.

The 28th studio release for the prolific jammers comes after a 14-month pause, which could be considered an age in Gizz terms — this is a band who released five projects in a year. Twice.

While Alien Metal enters somewhat uncharted territory for the band, it's still remarkably King Gizzard. It's weird, expansive, intricate and exactly what you'd expect these wizards to drop in a dungeon club in a dark corner of the Gizzverse.

For fans of: Charlotte de Witte, Four Tet, Floating Points

Courtney Fry

Grace Cummings — Bloodhorse!

Botox, The Beatles, bro-country AI slop!? It can only be Grace Cummings. (Supplied: Sugar Mountain Records)

Spotify | YouTube | Apple Music

Australia's Grace Cummings has one of the most beguiling and powerful voices going 'round, and the grand, wildly original ideas to match.

Bloodhorse! is a natural successor to 2024's riveting Ramona, reuniting Cummings with producer Jonathan Wilson (Father John Misty, Angel Olsen) who again facilitates her with the orchestral grandeur and classic rock backings her forceful singing always deserved.

Inspired by a bad botox experience, the title track sounds like a vengeful show-tune, with its galloping rhythm, sinister strings and vaudevillian chorus. It's backed up by a seemingly AI-generated country-pop sung by a horny cowboy that'll have you checking your music player hasn't malfunctioned.

A Burt Bacharach arrangement powers John Lennon: a sincere ode to the Beatle lamenting how "the war still isn't over/Even though we want it gone."

Things even get a bit Sgt. Pepper's in an extended coda of organ, bells, choir and caterwauling saxophone on 'WITCH! WITCH! WITCH!', which contrasts sweet, sweeping melodies with the night terrors that have plagued the 32-year-old Cummings since childhood.

Regularly evoking twists on the classics, like Annie Lennox and the Bad Seeds or the spy movie strings of FAKE being swallowed up by ominous, droning synth, Bloodhorse! features plenty of inscrutable moments.

But there's a surreal, Lynchian logic to theatrical songs where the beautiful and unsettling mingle, the way a dream can subtly shift into a nightmare, or vice versa.

You might not understand, or even appreciate, every one of Grace Cummings's choices. But you can be sure they're bold, artistic and distinctively hers.

For fans of: Liz Stringer, Nick Cave, Nina Simone

Al Newstead

Margaret Glaspy — I Am Both

Margaret Glaspy will not remain silent on personal and universal matters on her new album I Am Both. (Supplied: ATO Records)

Spotify | Apple Music | YouTube

It opens with grievances surrounding a break up: in the first minutes of American singer-songwriter Margaret Glaspy's new album, it's clear she's going to tell it how it is.

Not everyone wants to step into their power. But the world can be awful, and the consequences of silence — for oneself and for society — are often worse than the discomfort frankness can bring. Hiding in plain sight might be heaven, but it also feels like hell, as Glaspy sings in Reminder.

To sit with I Am Both feels like sitting with Glaspy herself as we unwind the woes of the world — both personal and universal. It's a glass of wine with a close friend, some of her revelations surprising but most of them relatable.

Some lyrics may come across inelegant, but that ultimately adds to the frankness and immediacy of her emotional content. Rather than reaching for the best word, Glaspy goes for what's there. Simply telling it how it is helps with the closeness.

Deeply intimate, emotive and objectively beautiful: I Am Both is understated, but lean in for a moment and you'll be gripped.

For fans of: Adrienne Lenker, Laura Marling, Joni Mitchell

Dan Condon

Tiny Habits — Keepers

The second album from the Boston-bred trio brings their sublime singing to sunnier music. (Supplied: Mom + Pop Records)

Spotify | YouTube | Apple Music

Tiny Habits' 2024 debut album had a folksy slant, all soothing melodies and easy listening that purged not-so-easy emotions. It made admirers out of old guard like James Taylor and David Crosby, but also Gen Z idols Gracie Abrams and Phoebe Bridgers.

Their second album is a slicker, peppier affair. Hitting play greets you with the tongue-in-cheek Love Ruins Everything with its effusive groove and Earth, Wind & Fire trumpets.

It's immediately clear that Maya Rae, Cinya Khan and Judah Mayowa have graduated from singing seamless three-part vocal harmonies on the Berklee College of Music stairwell toward more audacious territory.

They successfully expand their pitch-perfect voices to shiny pop (Someone You Love), sensual R&B (Belt Loop), ABBA-scented soft rock (Right In Front Of Me) and down-tempo tropical rhythm (Towel).

Beneath the glossy exteriors, the trio's sobering sincerity remains, unpicking hard lessons learned from turbulent break-ups and make-ups.

Anything He Was channels the heartbreaking realisation you're struggling to fill the shoes of a former flame, with help from The 1975's Matty Healy. Meanwhile, the graceful Survivors Guilt conveys exactly what you'd expect.

Making heart-wrenching revelations sound achingly beautiful, or even joyful, might seem counterintuitive. But the command Tiny Habits have over their lush, confessional songwriting elevates them above so many twenty-somethings similarly setting their heartbreak to music.

For fans of: Parcels, Haim, Bruce Hornsby

Al Newstead

Mastodon — Marrow Deep

Marrow Deep is loosely inspired by the Three Fates of Greek mythology, symbolised on the album artwork. (Supplied: Loma Vista Recordings)

Spotify | YouTube | Apple Music

Atlanta's Mastodon has long split the difference between Metallica's visceral shredding and the prog-rock leanings of Rush and Iron Maiden to chart-topping success, with one accomplished concept album after another.

But Marrow Deep, their ninth album, might be their biggest make-or-break release yet.

It's the first without co-founding singer-guitarist Brent Hinds, who was fired from the band last year only to die in a motorcycle crash a few months later.

Your Ghost Again is a tribute exorcising "crushing feelings of regret" over cathartic riffage. Stand-out Snakes For Dinner threads grief with blistering riffs, a towering chorus, and ominous vocals from Queens of the Stone Age's Josh Homme.

This isn't the group's first mournful metal opus. The demise of close ones animated 2009's Crack The Skye and their last full-length, 2021's Hushed & Grim, was a double album grieving the death of their manager.

The bitter irony is Marrow Deep has the blood and thunder of Mastodon's early material, which Hinds lamented they'd lost. His guttural vocals and fireworks fretwork is sorely missed, but Mastodon recruit an extensive cast to compensate.

Black Sabbath's Geezer Butler and Gojira frontman Joe Duplantier augment The Vanishing across a psychedelic six-ish minutes. João Nogueira's cosmic synths are a star attraction, providing spacey flourishes on the ballad Moth And Bone and roaming keys on closing epic, The Three Fates.

Even without their formative, fallen comrade, Mastodon thrash past tragedy once more and ever forward. They've proven, 26 years into their career, to remain vital.

For fans of: Gojira, Opeth, Baroness

Al Newstead

The Womack Sisters — The Womack Sisters

The Womack Sisters come from an incredible family. Once you hear their debut album, you'll realise that's the least interesting thing about them. (Supplied: Daptone Records)

Spotify | Apple Music | YouTube

Kucha, Zeimani, and BG Womack are the granddaughters of Sam Cooke, daughters and former backing singers of Womack & Womack, and nieces of Bobby Womack.

But listen to 10 seconds of their debut album and nepotism will be far from your mind: these women deserve all the acclaim they will surely soon earn.

It's easier than ever to make soul music with style but no substance, but their inspired arrangements and charming hooks are the antidote to machine generated vibes: the talent and passion in these performances stroke your soul.

Their rich voices and natural familial harmonies cut through the warm, comforting production — provided by Daptone Records boss Bosco Mann — in the same way those Womack voices have for decades.

From the smooth, intimate, understated R&B of Didn't Mean Much To Me to the grandiose You Went Away Too Long and the playful exotica on If I Let You, the sisters inhabit these songs in just the right way.

They've spent their lives in show business, and while music industry bullshit meant their debut album is a couple of decades overdue, it is more than worth the wait.

For fans of: Sharon Jones & The Dap Kings, The Supremes, Baby Rose

Dan Condon

Kayps — Bunuba Baby

At just 20 years of age, Kayps is one of Australia's most exciting new rappers. (Supplied: Bad Apples Music)

Spotify | Apple Music | YouTube

In a stacked year for Australian rap, you won't find a more focused body of work than Kayps's Bunuba Baby. The debut from the Walmatjarri and Bunuba artist feels like the culmination of an adolescence processed through writing. A compelling mission statement from someone who has something to say and who's here for good.

Kayps is still only 20 years old, but there's a maturity to his pen that feels wise beyond his years. He told Perth's RTRFM that he and co-producer Calvin Bennett started work on the project in the wake of 2023's 'No' vote to the Indigenous Voice to Parliament.

The result is a record that's deeply personal, triumphant and distinct. Bookmarked with community radio mic breaks voiced by his aunt, there's a broad mix of genres and culture at play here. Whether it's over G-Funk synth lines or Kamasi Washington-style jazz runs, Kayps honours his home, family and culture while delivering world class raps over equally impressive production.

For fans of: Kendrick Lamar, A.B. Original, E40

James Brennan

For more of the great new music you'll love, make sure you're tuned into Double J.
