World.title: Sydney scientist behind ‘moon landing’ cancer vaccine wins top science prize
World.content:
NationalCancer Sydney scientist behind ‘moon landing’ cancer vaccine wins top science prize Angus Dalton September 3, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The scientist who transformed advanced melanoma into a treatable cancer and led a recent large-scale trial into a world-first personalised mRNA cancer vaccine has won the research prize at Australia’s premier science awards. Professor Georgina Long was cautious to discuss the melanoma vaccine trial given that full results won’t be released until October, but described it as an “absolute landmark, fork-in-the-road for cancer” ahead of being awarded the Eureka Prize for Scientific Research at the Australian Museum on Thursday night. Professor Georgina Long has won the Eureka Prize for Scientific Research. Tim Bauer “It represents a huge body of work and team effort, and it’s an honour, really, to represent all the people that I lead,” the former Australian of the Year said of the award. “We’re a small but mighty country. We’ve got to keep the investments in Australia. We’ve got to take greater risks.”



Long is on a sabbatical in Lisbon, Portugal, away from her duties as medical director of the Melanoma Institute Australia at the University of Sydney to think and plan the next stages of her research. The new vaccine, developed by Moderna and Merck, aims to prevent recurrence of melanoma after a tumour is removed. Long was the principal investigator of the phase 3 trial and said it provided “the first real data that demonstrates mRNA technology can absolutely change the face of cancer”. Without yet providing details, the companies said on August 20 that the late-stage trial produced clinically and statistically significant improvements in high-risk melanoma patients. Moderna’s market value leapt by $62 billion in a day. “We are not even a speck of dust in this universe. And there’s only one point: to make a difference as much as you can, and do it well.” Professor Georgina Long For the trial, 1137 high-risk melanoma patients were given the cancer drug Keytruda. Half also received the experimental vaccine.



Researchers sequenced patients’ tumours after surgery and identified mutations, unique to each person’s cancer, that code for abnormal proteins on the surface of cancer cells called neoantigens. A custom mRNA vaccine was crafted for each patient based on the specific neoantigens in their tumour, teaching the immune system exactly what to look for. Normal cells have proteins which stop the immune system attacking healthy tissue. Melanomas hijack these cellular signals, masquerading as normal cells and growing unchecked. Keytruda stops this from happening, ripping off melanoma’s invisibility cloak. Results presented from a much smaller phase 2 trial in June showed combining Keytruda and the vaccine led to a 49 per cent reduction in the risk of recurrence or death, compared to just the cancer drug.



As the president of Merck put it, the mRNA vaccine, called intismeran autogene, gives the immune system the scent of the enemy. Then Keytruda releases “the dogs of war”. “It is a moon-landing moment,” Long said. Others are investigating whether the same approach could work in lung and pancreatic cancer. Britain’s King Charles is briefed by co-medical director Georgina Long as he visits the Melanoma Institute of Australia in Sydney in 2024. AFP The award on Thursday was in recognition of more than a decade of research. When Long started working in melanoma, faces in her waiting room would change within six to nine months. “It was the orphan cancer up until about 15 years ago. You think of the worst cancers now, and I can name them – pancreatic cancer [and] glioblastoma – melanoma was worse than those two. Nothing worked ... chemotherapy did nothing.



“The waiting room would be completely different because people died, and the majority of people died within 12 months.” Long and her collaborators have turned that story around. A trial Long led in 2018 found combining two immunotherapy drugs – nivolumab and ipilimumab – had a 46 per cent response rate in patients with melanoma that had metastasised to the brain, compared with 20 per cent when just one drug was used. The finding changed clinical practice “overnight”. Seven-year follow-up data reported in The Lancet Oncology last year found 51 per cent of patients given the combination immunotherapy as a first-line treatment had survived, compared with 29 per cent on the single drug. That’s just some of Long’s work, which is credited with ushering the survival rate of advanced melanoma from 5 to 50 per cent. She and colleague Professor Richard Scolyer were named Australians of the Year in 2024 for their research on cancer.



Crucially, tactics pioneered in melanoma treatment have gone on to have a “massive impact” in cancers of the lung, kidney, head, neck and bladder and some lymphomas, Long said. Professor Georgina Long and Professor Richard Scolyer at a ceremony in Canberra where they were named joint Australians of the Year in 2024. Alex Ellinghausen “Every single drug developed in melanoma first … has gone on to impact an extraordinary number of patients with other cancers,” Long said. Long’s focus is on the patients resistant to treatment: the difficult territory between what we know and don’t know where “courageous medicine happens”, such as the testing of drugs never trialled in people. She calls it the “third space”. “We’ve cured 50 per cent, [but] we’ve still got 50 per cent who die, and they die quickly like the old days. They are our third space,” she said.



“We’re all on this planet for a tiny, tiny, tiny time. We are not even a speck of dust in this universe. And there’s only one point: to make a difference as much as you can, and do it well.” Examine, a free newsletter covering science, is sent every Tuesday.

World.title: Feminist activist and writer Gloria Steinem dead at 92
World.content:
CultureCelebrityVale Feminist activist and writer Gloria Steinem dead at 92 James Costa Updated September 4, 2026 — 3:54am ,first published 8:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

American journalist and second-wave feminism leader Gloria Steinem died at age 92 on Wednesday, according to a post on her official Instagram account. “Yesterday, Gloria Steinem passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her,” the post read. Gloria Steinem speaks onstage during Visionary Women in November 2019. Getty Images for Visionary Women Steinem was a leading activist for the second-wave feminism movement in the late 1960s and 70s, which focused on sexuality, reproductive rights, and critiquing patriarchal social structures and institutions, among other issues. Former US President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013 for her work in the women’s liberation movement.



“Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” the post said. Steinem also wrote and contributed to publications, including New York Magazine, Esquire, The New York Times, and Cosmopolitan, and co-founded the feminist magazine, Ms. “She spent her recent years doing the two things she loved most: being in community with others and writing,” the post read. “Gloria loved the tradition of lighting signal fires on hills to light the way to the other side of the mountain. Lighting your own candle for Gloria makes you part of this global and celestial community circle.”



Gloria Steinem at a New York City gala in November 2022. Getty Images Among the tributes, former US secretary of state and former first lady Hillary Clinton said Steinem had “pushed open doors not just for herself, but for literally millions of women behind her”. “Gloria Steinem was, at heart, an optimist. Her activism was rooted in optimism, and that’s a moral choice she made every day. Even though we’ve faced setbacks to women’s full participation and equality in America and around the world, I want Gloria’s voice to remain in our heads,” Clinton said in a post on social media. Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, celebrated the life and legacy of Steinem, her “friend and mentor”. “Publicly, we did interviews together, called young voters to encourage them to have their voices heard, attended award ceremonies, and brainstormed how to help this beautiful yet complicated world to become more equitable,” the tribute read.



“Privately, she was even better than you would imagine – spending Thanksgiving with our family, introducing me to one of my best friends (forever the champion of female friendship), loving our children with her whole heart, counselling me during hard times, and giving extraordinary advice and perspective with a cup of tea and an unrivalled cheekiness and wit.” Oprah Winfrey said Steinem had left “with more freedom than she inherited and with the responsibility to keep widening that freedom for the women and girls who come next”. Steinem was born in Toledo, Ohio in 1934. Steinem’s forthcoming book, titled An Unexpected Life, is a memoir of her early life and her journey to activism. It is due to be released in late September.



Editor's pick Literature ‘Thanks Miss Dolly’: Parton’s gift of books a legacy for children around Australia The Instagram post announcing her passing shared a quote from the book: “I have now lived for more than fifty years in this brownstone, in rooms that have witnessed lives before mine, and will know others after I am gone.” “This book, along with her commitment to her home becoming a centre for social justice movements, are among the many gifts Gloria has given the world with the hope they have ripple effects for generations to come,” the post said. “In lieu of flowers, Gloria has asked that those wishing to honour her with a gift, may make a donation to Gloria’s Foundation.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Three resources have dominated Karratha’s economy, but a fourth is on the rise
World.content:
NationalWAThe Pilbara Three resources have dominated Karratha’s economy, but a fourth is on the rise Michael Philipps September 4, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Since 1972, the Pilbara town of Karratha has held an annual fête known to locals as the FeNaclNG Festival. Originally started as a fundraiser for the Karratha Lion’s Club to support local community projects, the family friendly carnival-like event has grown over the years to celebrate its 54th anniversary in 2026. Karratha, in WA’s north-west, is a regional city built on the back of the state’s resources industry. Bloomberg While locals love the Pilbara’s answer to a classic agricultural show, one of the first things newcomers or out-of-towners notice about the festival is its unusual name. “FeNaClNG” – mind the capitalisation – is drawn from three of the natural resources that helped build the mining town into the modern-day city it officially became in 2014.



Fe is the chemical name for the iron that made the Pilbara famous, NaCl the compound of the salt that was also mined in the region during its early days, while NG stands for natural gas, from the rich, albeit controversial, North West Shelf. While the three resources that combined to form the festival’s name continue to provide for the city, there are arguments to be made that a fourth should be added into the mix. In March next year, fertiliser company Perdaman’s Ceres urea project is set to come online, with full production scheduled to begin in June – just before next year’s 55th anniversary of the FeNaClNG Festival at the end of July. Backed by the Commonwealth, the operation is set to provide around 2.3 million tonnes of urea each year once at capacity. Company chairman Vikas Rambal said the nation’s reliance on imported fertiliser was laid bare when the US war in the Middle East led to blockages in the Strait of Hormuz.



While the majority of Australia’s attention was focused on the impact the war had on the price of fuel, the nation’s farmers had more pressing concerns, with more than 90 per cent of urea imported from overseas. The Ceres project aims to ease concerns that a similar situation in the future will be avoided. Perdaman Group boss Vikas Rambal at the company’s Project Ceres in the Burrup Strategic Industrial area. Colin Murty “Farmers love me,” Rambal said to journalists during a visit to the site this week. “If we don’t have fertiliser in this country, farmers are helpless. It’s a must-have in any country.”





Friends of Australian Rock Art and the Australian Conservation Foundation currently have a legal challenge before the Federal Court over the federal environment minister’s decision to approve the expansion of Woodside’s North West Shelf operations until 2070. Following in fertile footsteps Ceres is not the first project in the region, however, with Yara Pilbara Fertilisers first commissioned in 2006 and is now producing liquid ammonia from natural gas. Around half of the 850,000 tonnes per year the Yara site produces is exported for use as a foundational ingredient in fertiliser. The Yara plant accounts for around 5 per cent of worldwide traded ammonia and is Australia’s largest NH3 production facility.



Since 2016, Yara has also operated a co-located Technical Ammonium Nitrate facility, which takes some of the ammonia produced onsite to manufacture technical ammonium nitrate, providing more than 40 per cent of the key ingredient used in explosives at the Pilbara’s iron ore mines. Yara Pilbara chief operating officer Laurent Trost said the site also included Project Yuri, a renewable-hydrogen demonstration project which will substitute renewable hydrogen for a small proportion of the hydrogen conventionally produced from natural gas. The Yara ammonia plant on the Burrup Peninsula. Yara However, he adds that decarbonisation needs to be viable and commercially driven. “There is no green transition with red numbers,” he tells journalists at the company’s site near Karratha.



“Australia has a choice. It can become a country that congratulates itself as emissions fall because industry leaves, or a nation that proves a highly regulated and resource-rich democracy can both sustain and drive decarbonisation.” Related Article Mining Stokes-backed BCI bankrolls $1b salt project without full green approval Yara is already on the radar for Perdaman, with Rambal suggesting he would be willing to snatch up the operation if it ever came on the market. Can one of the world’s biggest salt operations help its fertiliser friends? Just 80 kilometres from Karratha sits BCI Minerals and its Mardie project, considered the third-largest solar salt operation in the world, and the biggest in Australia.



While salt – the “NaCl” in “FeNaClNG” – is the major product, once it is crystallised, what is left behind holds the ingredients for sulphate of potash (SOP), a premium, chloride-free fertiliser used on high-value crops such as fruit, vegetables and nuts, both in Australia and internationally. While Australia currently imports almost all its SOP supply, BCI is preparing a pilot plant to test whether the fertiliser ingredient can be produced at Mardie, an important next step in maximising the value of the resource. CI Minerals Managing Director David Boshoff in the company’s Perth office. Trevor Collens Commissioning is targeted for the start of the second half of next year, with piloting expected to run for approximately 12 months. BCI Minerals managing director David Boschoff said when Mardie was fully operational, it would support about 140 permanent roles, and over its 60-year life the operation is forecast to contribute $4.8 billion to the Australian economy.



“What we have built at Mardie is not one business. It is three valuable opportunities drawn from a single resource,” he said. “Salt is the foundation, SOP is the upside, and the port is the gateway to our customers for both.” Perhaps one of the trickiest parts of the growth of fertiliser among the major industries supporting Karratha, is how to include it in the FeNaCling Festival’s name. The writer travelled to the Pilbara as a guest of the WA Chamber of Minerals and Energy.

World.title: Trolley trouble: Perth councils want supermarkets to pay up for abandoned carts
World.content:
NationalWALocal government Trolley trouble: Perth councils want supermarkets to pay up for abandoned carts Indigo Lemay-Conway September 4, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An abandoned trolley on a suburban footpath used to be a minor nuisance. Today, it is the centre of a jurisdictional war testing the limits of local government power across Western Australia. Shopping trolleys have continued to be abandoned across Perth. At least three local governments have cracked down on the issue. Louie Douvis As thousands of carts spill out of shopping precincts each year, three major Perth councils have launched separate crackdowns – ranging from three-hour collection windows to state-level lobbying – to decide who ultimately holds the bill. In 2024, the City of Swan implemented their updated shopping trolley local law after a trial run of a trolley collection system resulted in an average of 77 trolleys being collected every week.



“Abandoned shopping trolleys can reduce the visual appeal of public places, obstruct roads and footpaths, and even end up in local waterways. Like many local governments across WA, they are a frequent source of frustration for the Swan community,” the city’s website reads. Related Article Property market The Perth suburbs where home values are starting to drop “The City has decided to act on this issue. Ultimately, it is hoped this approach will lead to retailers taking more responsibility for their property and being more proactive about keeping their shopping trolleys at the shops.” Under its law, the city can impound abandoned shopping trolleys, while also charging a fee to retailers for their collection and disposal if they are not collected. “Simply put, it allows the City to remove abandoned shopping trolleys from public places, while minimising the cost of that service to ratepayers.”



Retailers can be stung with a $100 fine for breaching the law and an additional $20 for each day or part of a day during which the offence has continued. A repeat shopping trolley ditcher was also slapped with a $5000 fine in February after on three occasions, they were found pushing shopping trolleys loaded with various materials and abandoning both the items and trolleys on a verge. The person was charged with several offences including littering and the abandonment of shopping trolleys in South Guildford. After failing to appear in court, the individual was handed the fine as well as being ordered to cover the City’s legal costs of $1646.30, and clean-up costs of $2617.96, bringing the total amount imposed by the Court to $9264.26. Swan’s local law was passed through official channels without any issues, but the City of Stirling’s recently amended law is not having the same luck.



In March, the city’s Shopping Trolley Local Law was passed by the local council but ran into a hurdle when in June, before it could be enforced, the state’s Joint Standing Committee on Delegated Legislation made a motion to disallow it. Related Article Waste Trash to power: Councils to send rubbish to Kwinana as leachate takes over Tamala Park Stirling Mayor Mark Irwin said there were 343 abandoned shopping trolleys reported within the city of in the 2026 calendar year, 57 per cent by residents and 43 per cent identified by the community safety team. A total of 127 trolleys have been referred to retailers for recovery with no enforcement action taken as a result of the disallowance motion. Their new law would have seen retailers required to collect their abandoned shopping trolleys within three hours of them being reported or run the risk of receiving a fine.



“We did seek some particular reform around having powers on private property, the three-hour time limit in getting shopping centres to actually pick up their shopping trolleys, and the significant uplift in the fines that they would receive if they weren’t contained,” Irwin told 9News Perth. “Under the proposed local law [a fine could be] up to about $2,000. In reality, that will be disallowed, and that won’t be the case.” Currently, retailers are only at risk of a $200 fine. Irwin said he believes the Joint Standing Committee wants to disallow the law because there were elements that were “probably a bit contentious”. “We received feedback already from the delegated powers to look at that and to take some undertakings. We’ve declined to do that,” he said.



“We believe it weakens the local law we are proposing. We’d rather seek other legislative powers to be able to contain them.” Stirling IGA owner Richard Maio. 9News Perth Stirling IGA owner Richard Maio said he understood why the city wanted to ramp up its enforcement around abandoned trolleys, but it would hit smaller businesses the hardest. “At the end of the day, they’re pushing the responsibility on us owners,” Maio said. “That’s fine in that they’ve got a three-hour collection that you’ve got to go pick them up in the park or wherever they are, but to put three hours on us is very hard.”



He said they bought 40 to 50 new trolleys each year because they got stolen, which costs $200 per trolley, so the possibility of a $2000 fine for not picking one up when the business could be running short-staffed would be difficult to swallow. Meanwhile, the City of Canning has leaned on the Western Australian Local Government Association to advocate the state government for legislative reforms around abandoned shopping trolleys. Canning amended its shopping trolley local law in 2025 to ensure that whether inside or outside a shopping precinct, trolleys are the responsibility of the retailers they belong to. Retailers have 12 to 24 hours of being notified to retrieve an abandoned trolley, depending on the location and failing to collect them could cost their owner $250, with court-imposed penalties reaching up to $5000 and $500 per day for continuing breaches In June, the city put forward a motion at the WALGA South East Metropolitan Zone Meeting to request the organisation to escalate their advocacy for state government legislative reform.



The reforms would give councils greater capacity to regulate and manage the problem of abandoned shopping trolleys by requiring retailers to install and maintain approved containment systems such as wheel-lock technology and introduce modified penalties. Related Article Fremantle Dockers Your guide to the AFL finals in Fremantle as the Port City turns purple The resolution was considered by WALGA State Council at a meeting in July, where it agreed to refer it to the relevant portfolio for consideration and action. Irwin, who is also the WALGA president, said once shopping trolleys were removed from retail premises the expectation typically shifts to local governments to manage them. “WALGA’s position remains that the state government consults with the sector and prioritises legislative changes requiring retailers to contain shopping trolleys within shopping centre property boundaries,” he said.



“This should include enforcement measures and modified penalty mechanisms that create a realistic economic imperative for retailers to comply with containment requirements.” A state government spokesperson said Local Government Minister Hannah Beazley was aware of the concerns raised in relation to abandoned shopping trolleys in local streets and will “request the Department of Local Government, Industry Regulation and Safety look into the matter.” The motion to disallow the City of Stirling’s law is expected to be dealt with by parliament in October.

World.title: ‘You have to hope for a time like this’: The full story behind Will Day’s tears
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘You have to hope for a time like this’: The full story behind Will Day’s tears Peter Ryan September 4, 2026 — 1:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Perth: Will Day’s emotions were not the same as his teammates after the Hawks claimed the first sport in this year’s preliminary finals with their brilliant win over Fremantle. He was in tears in a post-match interview, and then hugged his mum, Monique, and dad, Julian, in the Optus Stadium rooms with as much vigour as any of the 57 fierce tackles the Hawks had laid during the pressure-packed win, 5.10 (40) to 10.12 (72). After missing the past two finals series through injury, he had finally made it to the line for his first final. Will Day is arguably the Hawks’ most important player. AFL Photos Sam Mitchell knew how big a moment it was for the 25-year-old, saying post-game he could only imagine how he must have felt when he woke up on Thursday morning with the match just hours away.



Day decided there was only one way for him to attack what was ahead of him. “I just stripped back all the pressure, [and] took off all the expectation,” Day said. “I knew just by being out there I was going to help the team, so I did not want to try to do too much.” View post on X As he spoke, the emotion welled in his eyes again as familiar faces in the rooms loomed in his vision. “I just keep locking eyes with a lot of people that have helped me so much ... they are happy tears,” he said.



Happy tears were everywhere for Hawks fans who have ridden Day’s journey, ruing his absence through injury in their past two finals series when they seemed a midfielder short. After missing out on securing Essendon skipper Zach Merrett through the trade period, they then had their summer ruined by the sight of Day leaving the track with a shoulder injury in early January. James Sicily, who was brilliant in the qualifying final, celebrates the win with co-captain Jai Newcombe. AFL Photos The optimism most Hawks fans carry as though it’s a birth right suddenly slipped. To make matters worse, Day, himself, was quite reasonably wondering how his shoulder had become as pear-shaped as his career.



“[I was] pretty defeated. The last two finals series, especially last year losing the preliminary final, you feel so helpless, you just want to be out there and help,” Day said. Related Article AFL 2026 Dockers v Hawks player ratings: From a skipper’s career night, to the gun forwards who disappeared “It was tough early [this year], but you just have to switch to a positive outlook. It was very tough and very much easier said than done, but you just have to hope for a time like this, and it has been so worth it.” Against the Dockers, he was more than just out there helping. With James Sicily putting on a masterclass down back with a best-on-ground performance alongside his defensive allies Josh Battle, Blake Hardwick and Tom Barrass (who all dominated their opponents), the scene was set for Day to break open the game.



When the Dockers threatened to charge with minutes remaining in the third quarter, Day won two critical possessions that helped Nick Watson to deliver the settler. Editor's pick Exclusive

AFL 2026 Sydney Swan Nick Blakey tells associates he wants to be traded Watson, Dylan Moore and Jack Ginnivan rattled the Dockers’ defence with their pressure from the start, while the Hawks surprised the Dockers by pushing Jack Gunston high and leaving Mabior Chol deep. There was nothing Hollywood about the Hawks this time around. Instead, they produced a low-budget, no frills classic. Day finished the match with 24 disposals and eight centre clearances to show why he was so missed in September.



Mitchell hugged him post-match. He knew what his midfield star had overcome to be there with his mates, one match away from being in a grand final. View post on X “He showed it a lot more than I did, but I felt exactly how he looked after the game,” Mitchell said. The contrast with Justin Longmuir could not have been more stark as the Dockers coach attempted to rally his demoralised team after their first loss at home for the season. Day (centre) sings the Hawks’ famous song alongside Nick Watson, Mabior Chol, coach Sam Mitchell, and Dylan Moore. AFL Photos



“It’s not the way we wanted it to go [tonight], but we are not dead and buried,” he said. The Dockers could do worse than look to the way Day responded to his January jolt for inspiration. Because, to adapt a line from Mike Brady’s One Day in September, the resilient Hawks midfielder is finally seeing “the joy that hard work brings”. World.title: Dockers v Hawks player ratings: From a skipper’s career night, to the gun forwards who disappeared
World.content:
Loading

It loomed as a good, old-fashioned “danger game” for the Dockers, who finished clear on top of the ladder, but no one could have predicted just how thoroughly they’d be outplayed by Sam Mitchell’s men in their qualifying final at Optus Stadium. Our experts, AFLW star Libby Birch (Dockers) and Scott Spits (Hawks) rate every player’s performance from a stunning night out west. Justin Longmuir’s Dockers were thoroughly outplayed from the outset. AFL Photos



Fremantle (3) Caleb Serong: He worked his way into the contest after a quiet start, but never exerted his usual influence around stoppage. Didn’t help the midfield play to the conditions. 4/10 (5) Heath Chapman: Provided important drive from an under-siege defence, although he was beaten in the air in some costly moments. 6/10 (6) Jordan Clark: Fremantle’s standout, defending desperately and repeatedly driving them forward with bold run and excellent ball use in his milestone match. Fremantle’s best player for the night. 8/10 Two-time All-Australian Jordan Clark could hold his head high for the Dockers. AFL Photos



(8) Andrew Brayshaw: He started slowly and his early possessions lacked impact, but lifted after half-time to inject urgency and kick a much-needed goal. 6/10 (9) Luke Jackson: Kicked the opener, competed strongly around the ground and was Fremantle’s second most influential player through the first half. 7/10 (10) Shai Bolton: He was barely sighted early on a night that should have suited him, before providing flashes of energy through give-and-go football after half-time. 4/10 (13) Luke Ryan: Valiant and unrelenting under sustained pressure, he read the play well and producing several important spoils. 7/10 (16) Murphy Reid: The youngest player on the field looked composed around stoppage and was clean when opportunities came, but he struggled to impact in the second half. 5/10



(18) Mason Cox: Struggled to impact early as Jackson’s ruck support, but improved as the game wore on and took important defensive marks. 4/10 (20) Patrick Voss: Could not win enough contests ahead of the ball and was repeatedly worked underneath it by James Sicily. 2/10 Patrick “Prancing Pony” Voss had a night to forget. AFL Photos (21) Oscar McDonald: Conceded an early high free kick to Jack Gunston and lost another crucial contest in the goal square on a difficult night. 4/10 (23) Karl Worner: Produced a huge chase-down tackle and a goal-saving smother, but an errant kick that gifted Hawthorn a goal proved costly. He gave it a crack. 6/10



(24) Jye Amiss: He was frustrated and largely unsighted in the first half, but gave Fremantle an immediate lift with the opening goal after the half-time break. 3/10 (25) Alex Pearce: Battled hard against Mitch Lewis and offered a strong presence in a defence that was repeatedly placed under pressure. 7/10 Alex Pearce (second from left) will set his men to bounce back and go again next week. AFL Photos (26) Hayden Young: His early ball use was uncharacteristically poor and he struggled to generate his usual damage through the midfield. 4/10 (28) Neil Erasmus: One of Fremantle’s better early contributors, using the ball with purpose and looking through the corridor when others played safe. 6/10



(30) Nathan O’Driscoll: Needed to be stronger aerially early, but lifted his intensity and produced a fierce third-quarter tackle on Newcombe. 3/10 (31) Brandon Walker: A surprise inclusion for just his second game of the year, he competed bravely on Watson before an ankle roll contributed to another Hawks goal and his night done. 5/10 (32) Michael Frederick: Was unable to find space or use his speed, remaining largely unsighted. 2/10 Josh Treacy and his teammates had a horror night against a rampaging Hawks side. AFL Photos (35) Josh Treacy: He fought a difficult battle against Hawthorn’s organised defence but had little impact and went without a single kick deep into the third term. 2/10



(39) Sam Switkowski: He had a brilliant third quarter and kicked a huge goal to give Fremantle a (slight) sniff – the first finals major of his career. 6/10 (43) Isaiah Dudley: Missed an early opportunity but grew into the contest, improving his defensive pressure and contributing to Fremantle’s second-half ball movement. 4/10 (44) Matthew Johnson: One of Fremantle’s better midfielders in the first half, competing strongly and providing some composure amid Hawthorn’s pressure. 5/10 Sam Mitchell embraces Nick Watson after a finals win for the ages. AFL Photos



Hawthorn (1) Harry Morrison: Showed a few flashy moments midway through the third term. He can point to kicking the first goal of the final term, giving Hawthorn a match-high 38-point lead, for his golden moment. 5.5/10 (2) Mitch Lewis: A player of influence. He overcame a shoulder injury scare just before half-time. Look back to the early minutes of the game, when the action was hot, and Lewis pulled off a great run-down tackle and earned a free kick. 7/10 (3) Jai Newcombe: Not Hawthorn’s most important or valuable player, but that was a good sign for the brown and gold. Led Hawthorn’s tackle count at the main break, however. 6/10 (4) Jarman Impey: Reliable deep in defence in his All-Australian season. It was hard to find fault with his game as Hawthorn’s defence shone brightly all the way. 6/10



View post on X (5) Nick Watson: A top game. Lively and dangerous from start to finish, he kicked a goal out of nowhere – Hawthorn’s first – after just six minutes. It was emblematic of Hawthorn’s smash and grab approach. For Hawthorn’s most “Hollywood” player, it was instead a blue-collar night. 8/10 Related Article AFL 2026 ‘You have to hope for a time like this’: The full story behind Will Day’s tears (6) James Sicily: A sterling game and one easily worthy of best on ground honours. A pillar in Hawthorn’s brutal defensive unit all match, he completely nullified Voss’ danger and influence, especially in the first half when the win was set up. Composed and reliable, this was a true leader’s match. 9/10 (8) Dylan Moore: He kicked Hawthorn’s second goal – again when the match was up for grabs – but it was his work-rate that stood out. “That workrate is as good as it gets,” reflected Kane Cornes on Seven, noting Moore’s ability to run hard back at goal. “Their tackling in the forward half has been unbelievable.” 6.5/10



(9) Connor Macdonald: Got better and better as the match wore on, and had some influence in the third term when Hawthorn had to keep the threatening Fremantle at bay. 6/10 (10) Karl Amon: Another solid contributor. By early in the final quarter he only had kicks – not handballs – on the tally board, showing just how much the Hawks rely on his foot skills. 5.5/10 (12) Will Day: One of Hawthorn’s best, who effectively became “the Clearance King”. Like others, Day got better and better as the game wore on and never stopped running. He went one-on-one with Brayshaw at stages and won the battle. 7.5/10 View post on X (15) Blake Hardwick: Went to the dangerous Reid early on. Hawthorn basically didn’t have a passenger in their 23, and Hardwick deserves recognition too. 5.5/10



(16) Massimo D’Ambrosio: Had a fantastic game and was influential (especially in the first quarter) when the game was being won. While he missed two shots at goal in the opening stanza, he dragged in nine touches as he regularly found space with his hard-running. 8/10 (17) Lloyd Meek: Probably won’t get enough plaudits for an impressive game. Won the opening tap-out against Luke Jackson but, yes, was done for holding the ball moments later. Got some eye-catching clearances, a trait normally reserved for his immediate foe Jackson. 7.5/10 Editor's pick Opinion

AFL 2026 In an AFL world of corporate-style spin, we shouldn’t slam North’s leaders for speaking their ‘Clarko’ truth Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age (18) Mabior Chol: Did his bit and with style. As Hawthorn ran with Jack Gunston a bit further from goal than normal, Chol became the focal point in the forward line. Importantly, he got physical in countless marking contests, bringing the ball to ground at the very least. 7/10 (19) Jack Gunston: He gave Freo’s Oscar McDonald a bath. He regularly beat his man in the first half as Hawthorn stamped their authority on the game. By early in the second term, the veteran already had his two goals. He only touched the ball five times, but that didn’t matter. 7.5/10



(23) Josh Weddle: Another player vying to be Hawthorn’s best (behind Sicily) on a memorable night for the brown and gold. He was especially influential in the second quarter as Hawthorn looked to consolidate their great start. 8/10 Josh Weddle and the Hawks were all over Sam Switkowski and the Dockers. AFL Photos (24) Josh Battle: He played an outstanding game and was a crucial member of Hawthorn’s brilliant defensive unit. He went to Treacy and won that battle in a horrid game for Freo’s forwards. Dragged in 16 disposals in a top game. 8/10 (25) Josh Ward: Another top contributor, he worked hard across the game. In one first-quarter moment, he pulled off an excellent pass to D’Ambrosio up forward, but his teammate was off-line with the kick. Raised his arms in celebration after a defensive spoil by a teammate at one point. 6/10 (28) Cam Mackenzie: Another player who had a growing influence across the game. Had 11 touches by half-time and finished with 20. 6.5/10



(33) Jack Ginnivan: Had an unsung, low-key role early for the Hawks after returning to the team, but the 2023 Collingwood premiership player had a huge moment in the second half by taking a composed mark, and going back and kicking a goal that, again, kept Freo at bay. 6.5/10 Tom Barrass and the Hawks didn’t give the Dockers an inch of space all night. Getty Images (37) Tom Barrass: He played a brilliant defensive game. He manned Jye Amiss for most of the game and, like others in the brown and gold, won his night. Look back at the moment when Barrass applied an excellent punch deep in defence just before half-time. That was telling. Then in the third term he took a few key intercept marks. 8/10 (40) Max Beattie: An inexperienced player who looked comfortable out there in what could have been a tough environment. He did have one bad turnover in the second term when he really shouldn’t have been run down. Only had about 60 per cent game time. 4.5/10 (42) Bailey Macdonald: Also had limited game time and picked up eight touches. There were no Hawthorn passengers, remember. 5/10

World.title: Sydney scientist behind ‘moon landing’ cancer vaccine wins top science prize
World.content:
NationalCancer Sydney scientist behind ‘moon landing’ cancer vaccine wins top science prize Angus Dalton September 3, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The scientist who transformed advanced melanoma into a treatable cancer and led a recent large-scale trial into a world-first personalised mRNA cancer vaccine has won the research prize at Australia’s premier science awards. Professor Georgina Long was cautious to discuss the melanoma vaccine trial given that full results won’t be released until October, but described it as an “absolute landmark, fork-in-the-road for cancer” ahead of being awarded the Eureka Prize for Scientific Research at the Australian Museum on Thursday night. Professor Georgina Long has won the Eureka Prize for Scientific Research. Tim Bauer “It represents a huge body of work and team effort, and it’s an honour, really, to represent all the people that I lead,” the former Australian of the Year said of the award. “We’re a small but mighty country. We’ve got to keep the investments in Australia. We’ve got to take greater risks.”



Long is on a sabbatical in Lisbon, Portugal, away from her duties as medical director of the Melanoma Institute Australia at the University of Sydney to think and plan the next stages of her research. The new vaccine, developed by Moderna and Merck, aims to prevent recurrence of melanoma after a tumour is removed. Long was the principal investigator of the phase 3 trial and said it provided “the first real data that demonstrates mRNA technology can absolutely change the face of cancer”. Without yet providing details, the companies said on August 20 that the late-stage trial produced clinically and statistically significant improvements in high-risk melanoma patients. Moderna’s market value leapt by $62 billion in a day. “We are not even a speck of dust in this universe. And there’s only one point: to make a difference as much as you can, and do it well.” Professor Georgina Long For the trial, 1137 high-risk melanoma patients were given the cancer drug Keytruda. Half also received the experimental vaccine.



Researchers sequenced patients’ tumours after surgery and identified mutations, unique to each person’s cancer, that code for abnormal proteins on the surface of cancer cells called neoantigens. A custom mRNA vaccine was crafted for each patient based on the specific neoantigens in their tumour, teaching the immune system exactly what to look for. Normal cells have proteins which stop the immune system attacking healthy tissue. Melanomas hijack these cellular signals, masquerading as normal cells and growing unchecked. Keytruda stops this from happening, ripping off melanoma’s invisibility cloak. Results presented from a much smaller phase 2 trial in June showed combining Keytruda and the vaccine led to a 49 per cent reduction in the risk of recurrence or death, compared to just the cancer drug.



As the president of Merck put it, the mRNA vaccine, called intismeran autogene, gives the immune system the scent of the enemy. Then Keytruda releases “the dogs of war”. “It is a moon-landing moment,” Long said. Others are investigating whether the same approach could work in lung and pancreatic cancer. Britain’s King Charles is briefed by co-medical director Georgina Long as he visits the Melanoma Institute of Australia in Sydney in 2024. AFP The award on Thursday was in recognition of more than a decade of research. When Long started working in melanoma, faces in her waiting room would change within six to nine months. “It was the orphan cancer up until about 15 years ago. You think of the worst cancers now, and I can name them – pancreatic cancer [and] glioblastoma – melanoma was worse than those two. Nothing worked ... chemotherapy did nothing.



“The waiting room would be completely different because people died, and the majority of people died within 12 months.” Long and her collaborators have turned that story around. A trial Long led in 2018 found combining two immunotherapy drugs – nivolumab and ipilimumab – had a 46 per cent response rate in patients with melanoma that had metastasised to the brain, compared with 20 per cent when just one drug was used. The finding changed clinical practice “overnight”. Seven-year follow-up data reported in The Lancet Oncology last year found 51 per cent of patients given the combination immunotherapy as a first-line treatment had survived, compared with 29 per cent on the single drug. That’s just some of Long’s work, which is credited with ushering the survival rate of advanced melanoma from 5 to 50 per cent. She and colleague Professor Richard Scolyer were named Australians of the Year in 2024 for their research on cancer.



Crucially, tactics pioneered in melanoma treatment have gone on to have a “massive impact” in cancers of the lung, kidney, head, neck and bladder and some lymphomas, Long said. Professor Georgina Long and Professor Richard Scolyer at a ceremony in Canberra where they were named joint Australians of the Year in 2024. Alex Ellinghausen “Every single drug developed in melanoma first … has gone on to impact an extraordinary number of patients with other cancers,” Long said. Long’s focus is on the patients resistant to treatment: the difficult territory between what we know and don’t know where “courageous medicine happens”, such as the testing of drugs never trialled in people. She calls it the “third space”. “We’ve cured 50 per cent, [but] we’ve still got 50 per cent who die, and they die quickly like the old days. They are our third space,” she said.



“We’re all on this planet for a tiny, tiny, tiny time. We are not even a speck of dust in this universe. And there’s only one point: to make a difference as much as you can, and do it well.” Examine, a free newsletter covering science, is sent every Tuesday.

World.title: 'It's physically and mentally exhausting': Doctors challenge politicians on health reforms
World.content:
Doctors disheartened and exhausted at state of health system Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Doctors say they're disheartened and exhausted by the current health system, as they challenge politicians to work together on long-term reforms.

The Association of Salaried Medical Specialists (ASMS) held their annual conference at Wellington's Te Papa museum on Thursday. The theme was "Hitting the target, missing the point".

ASMS vice-president Sylvia Boys, who works in Middlemore Hospital's emergency department, said working there resembled "scenes from overseas during the Covid era and during armed conflict".

"It's physically and mentally exhausting," she said.

There weren't enough beds - especially as the demand grew with an ageing population - and the three-year political cycle was ill-suited to long-term planning and reform, she said.

"My challenge to our politicians and especially going into this next election is to work together.

"As leaders of the country, we need people who are prepared to put the country's interests first and to make a long-term plan."

She said there also needed to be more focus on prevention, to ease pressure on the health system.

"Part of the difficulty is we know that 80 to 90 percent of health is determined by those social determinants rather than the health system.

"And you cannot fix 10 to 15 years of rough sleeping presenting with a chest infection with a course of antibiotics."

One doctor says working in Middlemore Hospital's emergency department resembles "scenes from overseas during the Covid era and during armed conflict". LDR

She explained that social factors such as secure income, employment, housing, exposure to stress and healthy foods played a fundamental role in a person's health.

Author and journalist Rebecca Macfie gave the keynote speech at the conference, which included her research on the intersection of poverty and health outcomes.

Her findings revealed that many children in high-equity index schools had difficulties with their hearing and sight.

She said that almost a third of the 18,000 children screened by NGO Painga Project needed to see an optometrist.

"If your household is crowded because that is your whānaus rational economic response to unaffordable rents and low incomes, the before-school check is very much less likely to screen you or see you.

"So those are some of the reasons why a child can end up at the age of 10 or 11 with some of their most fundamental health needs unmet - unable to see or hear properly," she said.

ASMS member Tanya Wilton, who works as an emergency physician at Hutt Hospital, said she felt "ashamed" of the care provided to the elderly.

"It's really disheartening to be in the position where you can't provide what you would consider basic."

She said she'd recently cared for a patient with a broken pelvis in their late nineties, whom she knew personally and admired.

"But that person spent 48 hours in a corridor on a trolley."

ASMS President Katie Ben, who works as a consultant anaesthetist at Nelson Marlborough, said it was "very disheartening" to work in healthcare right now.

Dr Katie Ben Matt Shand ASMS

"We don't have enough staff, we don't have enough beds, we don't have enough nurses, we don't have enough equipment, we don't have enough protected infrastructure.

"We don't have enough basic attention to the simple things that would make life work - an integrated IT system so that one hospital can talk to another."

She revealed that she was receiving messages the morning of the conference to help organise cover.

"We carry on 'til we can't. We get fed up with being told we have to cancel our long-standing family commitments. We get fed up because we have to work yet another shift."

She called for a long-term workforce strategy that would allow patients to access the same quality of care regardless of their income and location.

Health minister 'isn't fit to hold the health portfolio'

Ben was critical of Health Minister Simeon Brown for not attending the conference.

"Yes, he was probably subject to some expressions of extreme disappointment from the audience but I respected that he showed up and fronted up to us," Ben said.

"And for him not to even do that this year just makes me think this person actually isn't fit to hold the health portfolio."

The minister responded by saying the government had delivered a record investment in health, part of which included hiring hundreds more full-time doctors.

Simeon Brown said health targets were working and pointed to shortened wait times across the country.

Health Minister Simeon Brown did not attend the conference in Wellington. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"There is more to do, and I welcome the call for cross-party collaboration. That's why I am calling on all parties to commit to keeping these targets, so we can build on this progress and keep driving waiting lists down."

He said he met with doctors regularly: "I value the chance to hear from them directly and I will keep doing so."

A Health NZ spokesperson said it recognised the significant pressure clinicians faced and that it was committed to ensuring "the right workforce capacity and skill mix to deliver safe, high-quality patient care".

The spokesperson said Health NZ was actively recruiting and developing domestic training pathways.

"Patient safety remains our priority, and we continue to use workforce planning, safe staffing and service management processes to maintain safe, high-quality care while addressing workforce challenges across the health system.

World.title: Weather: Wind warning in place for Wellington, heavy rain for the South Island
World.content:
A strong wind warning is in place for the capital on Friday, while parts of the central and northern South Island are being drenched with heavy rain.

MetService said a front impacting parts of the South Island and the Tararua Range had hit on Friday and strong northwesterlies could reach a severe gale in eastern areas from Canterbury all the way up to Hawke's Bay.

A strong wind warning had been issued for Wellington and Wairarapa, excluding the Tararua District, from 4am on Friday through to 12pm.

Severe gales gusting up to 120 kph in exposed places were possible, the forecaster said. This could bring damage to trees, powerlines and unsecured structures and make driving difficult for high-sided vehicles and motorcycles.

Heavy rain warnings were also in place for the Headwaters of the Canterbury Lakes and rivers until 8am on Friday, and the Tararua Range until 1pm.

A road snowfall warning was also in place for Milford Rd (SH94) until 6pm on Friday, with the possibility of 2 to 5cm of snow accumulating by the tunnel.

The weekend was looking more settled, according to MetService, with some rain. The North Island would see a few showers in the west on Saturday, but be mainly fine while the South Island could expect rain or showers in the west and south with possible heavy falls.

World.title: How much did Immigration NZ's ill-fated IT project really cost?
World.content:
The government is staying tight-lipped about how much it might have to pay a company working on Immigration NZ (INZ)'s ill-fated IT project.

And 18 months into its new $336 million IT project, Our Future Services (OFS), officials have admitted they overstated its cost savings.

The government says it's awaiting the results of an inquiry into the Biometric Capability Update before commenting on a $12 million potential liability.

In briefing papers from 2024 officials also told minister Erica Stanford the key vendor NEC could claim at least $4 million in sunk losses. A quality assurance report also cited NEC's intention to charge INZ up to $750,000 a month for going past a 2025 deadline.

INZ and Stanford both refused to comment. "MBIE is cooperating fully with the inquiry and will take any appropriate actions once this process is complete," said a ministry spokesperson.

A $90 million deficit is predicted this year in INZ's visa accounts, including spending on the agency's new eight-year automation project, OFS.

It's one of the factors that has led the government to review its visa fees again - two years on from a large hike aimed at balancing the books.

Eighteen months after starting OFS, officials have admitted they overstated its cost savings.

In post-budget responses to MPs, Stanford said she had since found out mistakes had been made in OFS' business case forecast benefits. It had included staff cost reductions of 118 full-time equivalents and also overhead costs associated with those reduced staffing numbers, covering ICT, property, corporate services, and stewardship.

"I have subsequently been advised that during the development of the initial business case that errors were made in the assumptions about reductions in the Ministry's overheads.

"These allocation costs are largely fixed and do not reduce proportionately to workforce reductions. While the Ministry will continue to identify savings opportunities, the total monetised benefits from FTE reduction is expected to be lower than initially projected."

Predicted productivity increases of 30 percent were also overly optimistic, with student visa productivity 7-20 percent higher than the average for the preceding six months.

"Work is underway to understand drivers for productivity across visa processing to support the productivity uplift reaching the level anticipated in the business case.

"The forecasting and realisation of benefits is an area that I have specifically requested is looked at in the upcoming independent review."

The complexity of some of the changes only became clear once the project started, leading to delays. It also missed its customer satisfaction target.

The Treasury Investment assessed the project's own risk profile as 'high', based on its complexity, the need to migrate multiple products onto one platform and decommissioning old systems.

The option Cabinet chose, although the most expensive out of four presented, was assessed as offering the most value for money.

INZ's visas memorandum account, which reconciles department costs and user-pays fees, reached $134.6m in 2020 and a series of write-offs cost the taxpayer about half a billion dollars.

It now forecasts it will be $90m in the red in the current financial year, two years after visa fees were last hiked.

Stanford said the last fee and levy review forecast higher levels of work visas and overstated revenue from visas that are not fee-waived.

The OFS programme has increased expenditure, though it was due to pay for itself over time. A separate briefing from the date that the BCU was axed said that the change in identity management programme would also affect the financial benefits forecast for OFS.

"Returning the account to surplus will require a combination of expenditure management and revenue recovery measures. This includes maintaining tight control of expenditure by limiting growth in the Immigration budget baseline, identifying savings opportunities across the Immigration system, and delivering productivity improvements through the Our Future Services programme to reduce the ongoing cost of service delivery."

Another review of visa charges would start late this year, "to ensure future charges better reflect the cost of delivering immigration services, improve cost recovery, and help manage the accumulated deficit".

National campaigned on making the visa processing system largely user-pays in order to recoup what it called a heavy taxpayer subsidy. In October 2024, fees for the skilled residence category rose from $4290 to $6450, partnership residence increased from $2750 to $5360, and student visas doubled from $375 to $750.

World.title: 'Appalling': Gloriavale school should've been shut down decades ago, barrister says
World.content:
A barrister representing Gloriavale leavers says the Christian community's school should've been shutdown decades ago.

The Ministry of Education wants to cancel the school's registration, effectively closing it, after a special report by the Education Review Office (ERO) found it was not providing a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

It's the Ministry of Education's second move to cancel the school's registration in less than a year.

The school remains open after an attempt in December was challenged at the High Court by the school's board.

On Thursday the ministry applied to the court to lift the orders preventing the school's closure, which has a roll of about 80 students.

Barrister Brian Henry, who has fought for Gloriavale leavers to be recognised as employees, backed the move, but simultaneously criticised the ministry for what he described as decades of inaction.

He said the ERO report revealed nothing new and that the school should have been closed 20 years ago.

"They have, as a historic department, not done their job. Finally someone's done it and I applaud them for that."

However, Henry said the fact that it had taken two attempts to cancel the registration was "appalling".

He said the ministry should have been ready to follow through with it in December but wasn't, meaning the school's closure got "bunged up" in litigation.

The ministry rejected Henry's criticism and said closing a registered school was a significant statutory decision that had to follow a robust process.

The Gloriavale compound on the West Coast. Jean Edwards

After Gloriavale filed court proceedings, the ministry and the school agreed to defer the decision until the legal process had finished, it said.

Henry wouldn't speculate on when the school would shut its doors, but said the students would need to be educated elsewhere.

"They just need to put on a school bus and shift them - like all country kids are shifted - to a public school."

Education services deputy secretary Geoff Short said the ministry would work with the school community to determine the most practical timing for the school's closure.

In a statement, the Gloriavale Christian School board said it was considering its options.

"The school strongly disagrees with the ministry's decision and is currently considering its options to challenge it. Given that the matter is ongoing, we will not be making any further comment at this time," the board said.

The ERO special review report said the school had failed to meet one of eight criteria - to provide a physically and emotionally safe place for students.

While the school met the other criteria, such as providing suitable premises, provision of tuition, and suitable staffing, and that there had been "some improvement", it said the improvement was "partial and, in key areas, not yet sustained".

World.title: Why renting retirees might be better to save nothing if they don't have $200,000
World.content:
Is there any point in KiwiSaver if I'm on a total remuneration package? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

New Zealand's current settings mean renting retirees who do not have at least $200,000 saved may be better off to have nothing.

The accommodation supplement is available to help with housing costs for people on lower incomes, but it requires that single people only have assets of $8100.

Couples or sole parents can have $16,200. This asset limit has not changed in the time the supplement has been in place.

The amount available as a weekly payment depends on the area that a person lives in and whether they have children.

A couple without children can access up to $235 in the highest payment area.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub calculated that a renter would need to have about $200,000 saved to generate sufficient money to replace that, assuming the money was drawn down over 25 years.

"The effective tax rate for the first couple of hundred thousand of savings is 100 percent."

At the end of last year, there were 48,789 people receiving NZ Super and an accommodation supplement, up from 47,223 in December 2023 and 34,279 in December 2019.

Eaqub said the system needed to be redesigned to make it fit for purpose in the future.

"That argues for a better design for eligibility rather than a cliff at one cutoff point."

He said it could be that there was a small free zone and then a gradual taper so that saving a bit more did not leave people worse off.

"The Australian method, the deemed rate of return, is an easy way to convert income and assets into one income test for AS. That makes it all nice and tidy in my view. But it would increase the cost of AS because more people would be able to access it."

People who decided not to save would be relying on the continued availability of the accommodation supplement, which is not guaranteed. Eaqub said it was likely that fewer people would be eligible for it in future.

Teresa White, general manager at ACBC Financial Mentors, said the cash asset limit did stop some people accessing the supplement but there needed to be fairness in the system.

"Perhaps it is the cash asset limit needs more regular review, especially now as we are seeing more people enter retirement without owning their own home and having to rent.

"The tension between savings and the cash asset limit is likely greater on low to mid-income workers with limited savings or those who have been on a benefit leading up to retirement age with KiwiSaver that they can now access, which could put them over the cash asset threshold. But is still not enough to compensate fully for not getting the accommodation supplement and maintain a decent level of savings. Essentially then the KiwiSaver then steps in as the supplement until it reaches the cash asset limit."

She said it was generally better to have savings, even if people ended up having to use it to fund their basic costs.

Ministry of Social Development group general manager of client service delivery Graham Allpress said he would encourage people to speak to Work and Income to understand exactly what they may or may not be entitled to before making significant decisions.

"How people approach paying for accommodation in retirement will depend on their personal circumstances, and ultimately is their choice.

"There are likely to be a number of factors that feed into these decisions, and so we wouldn't be able to say either way if there is a 'better' option to pay for rental accommodation in retirement.

"However, having smaller financial assets may limit people's options in other areas of their lives, and this is something we would encourage people to take into account."

World.title: Pacific Islands Forum winds up by condemning China nuclear test
World.content:
Leaders in the Pacific have registered their concern over a nuclear-capable missile test conducted by China in July, calling on all states to provide advance warning ahead of any testing.

Nauru - one of the 18 Pacific Island Forum (PIF) members - noted its dissent from the statement.

Partners to the forum will also be split into two tiers in future, and member states agreed to a declaration for urgent and inclusive climate action to keep 1.5 degrees of warming within reach.

The Pacifc Islands' Forum in Palau has concluded, with leaders taking part in a daylong meeting on Thursday to discuss various issues, releasing a joint statement outlining their conclusions.

The Pacific Islands Forum has been winding up discussions in Palau. Ohanna Rabo Galo/TMC Palau

Specifically, the forum noted an intercontinental ballistic missile test that had "overflew" a number of members "without adequate notice".

The members called on all states undertaking testing of intercontinental ballistic missiles to provide transparency and reassurance, including advance notification of at least 24 hours.

Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr who read the statement concluded by saying: "I might note that the Republic of Nauru has dissented."

The forum has been overshadowed with the tensions between China and Taiwan.

One local told RNZ all he'd been hearing about was "China, Taiwan, and how the outside world, outside countries are ... making certain nations either afraid to talk or not standing up boldly."

"All I hear is about just drama, and that defeats the whole purpose."

He said he wanted to hear more about what other countries were going through, whether that matched up with the problems facing Palau - like outmigration, cost of living, and drugs - and see what could be done by working together.

New Zealand Prime Minister Chirstopher Luxon said on Thursday that China-Taiwan hadn't been a focus inside the PIF.

"It's a piece of a conversation, but it's not the dominant conversation."

But another geopolitical issue was the lingering desire by many in the forum to reach consensus on condemning the intercontinental ballistic missile test by China.

It's understood Nauru and Kiribati, both closely aligned with China, stood in the way of full consensus on a statement earlier in August.

Even as the meeting on Thursday was taking place, China's foreign ministry made accusations toward Palau, after the host of the forum urged the group to condemn China's launch.

"Palau has repeatedly raised this issue in an ill-intentioned attempt to hijack the position of other member states of the Pacific Islands Forum. It will not have its way," the ministry said.

Prime Minister Chistopher Luxon says it;s important to push back over nuclear missile tests that are not signalled in advance. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Luxon himself felt strongly about the matter, telling reporters later it was important to push back so the behaviour wasn't normalised.

"Given all the history in our part of the world with nuclear testing … that's just not something we want to see."

Luxon described Nauru as being "in the room", and wanting to be "disassociated with the statement".

"We said, look, that's great, but we're not going to not make a statement as a Pacific Island Forum because of the objection of one country, and you'd have to ask them as to what their rationale for that was.

"Suffice to say, everyone else was fully on board."

When pressed on whether Kiribati was also on board, Luxon said Kiribati had no representation in the room.

Even stranger was the delayed recognition during the closing ceremony of Kiribati's representative to the forum, David Teaboo, well after all the other leaders had received applause.

The forum also confirmed it would run a tiered system next year, splitting around 30 partners into two streams: one for strategic partners, and one for sector partners.

"Everyone's a partner, but we just need to make sure that we can manage it well going forward," said Luxon.

"We have to acknowledge that as we go forward, we can't treat them all the same or give the same sort of effort."

Foreign Minister Winston Peters at the forum. Supplied / screenshot

Taiwan remains a development partner, and while its foreign minister, Lin Chia-lung, was attending the forum this year after being invited by Palau, New Zealand's Foreign Minister indicated on Thursday that wouldn't be the case next year.

New Zealand adheres to the One China policy, which means it doesn't have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan.

That would prevent the foreign minister being invited - instead representation at a lower level would be likely at next year's forum.

Despite the geostrategic tensions at play throughout the forum, Luxon said PIF was at its "strongest."

Before setting off to Palau, Luxon denied PIF was being weakened as a mechanism for resolving region-wide difficulties.

"No, I think it's about strengthening it, though," Luxon said.

After his hours' long meeting on Thursday, he said he wanted to see PIF "continue to evolve and strengthen and move - it's the arc of progress that we're focused on".

World.title: How long is unlimited? Driver v Tesla over charging promise
World.content:
On 4 August 2019, Tesla announced on its X account: "BREAKING: All new Model S and Model X orders now come with free unlimited Supercharging".

It was that marketing campaign which convinced Mrs Chew to buy her Tesla Model S.

"Because when I bought it, they say in the future, there's more superchargers, free unlimited supercharging for my vehicle," the Aucklander told RNZ.

RNZ has agreed not to use Mrs Chew's first name as she has concerns over her reputation in her community.

Since 2019, Tesla has expanded its supercharging sites from 12 to 31 and that was the message Mrs Chew got from the marketing campaign.

But for Mrs Chew, there's only 11 that she can use, unless she forks out $483.79 to upgrade her vehicle.

That's because Tesla has upgraded most of its supercharging stalls from Type 2 ports, to a system called CCS or Combined Charging System.

Mrs Chew's car has a Type 2 port and is not compatible with the newer CCS system.

She spoke with Tesla in New Zealand, who told her she could still access some Type 2 superchargers.

A Tesla Model S. Supplied

In a statement to RNZ, Tesla said it had 11 sites with 50 chargers that were compatible with Type 2 charging.

Living in Auckland - a city with five supercharger sites, Mrs Chew is only 2.6 kilometres away from a supercharging station, but none of the chargers there are compatible with her car.

To charge her car, it's a 22-kilometre drive.

Alternatively, a Tesla agent told Mrs Chew she could pay $483.79 to retrofit her car to make it compatible with the new chargers; a cost Mrs Chew said was unfair.

"I need to pay more money to enjoy the benefit, that's not right. This is why I think what they give it to me for the Tesla free unlimited supercharging. In the real world, I can't use it."

In correspondence seen by RNZ, an agent explained to Mrs Chew that her vehicle still retained lifetime free supercharging, and enabling CCS access would only broaden her supercharging access to the full network.

Mrs Chew said the inconvenience was not just the cost.

Without the retrofit, she said she could not use most commercial superchargers even if she's happy to pay for the charging, and that's a concern for longer drives.

To fully charge her car, it takes less than an hour at a supercharger, but over 35 hours at a household charger like the one Mrs Chew owns at home.

She feels, as one of the earlier adopters to Tesla, she's at a loss.

University of Auckland commercial law professor Alex Sims said the situation is potentially covered under the Fair Trading Act.

The act specifies: "No person shall, in trade, in connection with the supply or possible supply of goods or services or with the promotion by any means of the supply or use of goods or services, make a false or misleading representation that goods or services have any sponsorship, approval, endorsement, performance characteristics, accessories, uses, or benefits."

University of Auckland commercial law professor Alex Sims. Supplied

Sims said the "free unlimited supercharging" could be seen as a promotion of a benefit.

"It looks like Tesla was using that free unlimited charging as a selling point, trying to get people to buy the cars. To my understanding, it only offers it at certain periods. So, it's seen as a definite benefit.

"And at the time and even now, the electric charging was being built out so that people knew it was relatively limited, but there'd be more and more coming online. And now, the ones that are coming online cannot be used by the purchaser of this car."

But could Tesla argue that by still being able to access 11 charging sites, Mrs Chew hadn't lost much from the 12 charging sites she could access back when she bought the car in 2019?

Sims said that was debatable.

"Well, they could try. This is the thing is, that no one knows until it goes to court. So, this is just speculating. But you've got to also think at the time, Tesla and other entities were saying that they would build more (charging stations). So, people would have had the expectation that more was coming online."

Consumer advocacy group Consumer NZ also thought Mrs Chew may have a case.

In a statement, a spokesperson said the consumer could take Tesla to the Disputes Tribunal.

"Given Tesla advertised "free unlimited supercharging" but subsequently changed the charging technology, we think it would be reasonable for the customer to request Tesla covers the cost of retrofitting the new charger. If Tesla refuses to cover the cost, the consumer could take Tesla to the Disputes Tribunal. Alternatively, they could pay for the cost themselves and attempt to recover the cost at the Disputes Tribunal."

RNZ asked Tesla questions on access to chargers, and any rationale for asking customers to pay for the retrofit.

In its statement, Tesla did not respond to why it asked customers to pay for the retrofit, and said customers were still able to access free supercharging at Type 2 compatible sites.

The company provided a list.

World.title: North Shore residents show support for nurses at public meeting
World.content:
North Shore residents have been showing their support for nurses having a "nightmare" winter at their hospital.

About 200 people - residents, nurses and politicians turned out to a public meeting in Northcote on Thursday night.

North Shore's hospital emergency department nurses spoke out last month about having to leave patients in soiled beds and treat them in corridors and waiting rooms.

There had been little respite, with flu data showing hospitalisations were still climbing nationwide.

The union, the Nurses's Organisation, encouraged residents to come to the meeting and voice their concern about the emergency department.

But there was also a clear political theme, with people there urged to think about health when they cast their vote.

The crowd at a public meeting about North Shore Hospital and the health system, run by the Nurses Organisation in Northcote on 3 September 2026. RNZ / Rowan Quinn

Resident Chris was one of many worried about the state of the hospital.

"Like a lot of people, I'm pretty angry about it and particularly now with the way hospitals are - understaff and clearly, clearly overidden with winter ailments," he said.

Another resident, David Lloyd, said he spent a lot of time in the hospital last year when his wife's mother was dying and said the nurses were wonderful despite their challenges.

"You could see the stress that they were under. And they need more support, more staff, more love put towards the staff," he said.

Another attendee, Caroline, said the hospital was a topic of discussion among those she knows.

"They're appalled and they talk about delays and waits and compare the current period with past periods and how good the hospital system seemed to have been in the past," she said.

ED nurse Jean Moore said she was very grateful to have the support of residents.

This week was another difficult one in the department, she said.

"You could not walk through the waiting room because of the number of people who were in there. I went home and told my son about my shift and cried," she said.

Nurses from several other parts of the health system spoke to the meeting.

One had worked through a shift with pain she later found out was appendicitis because she did not want to let her patients down, another was frustrated that district nurse patients were not been seen and could end up in an emergency department themselves.

The Nurses Organisation said it invited all the major political parties to the meeting

Labour's Shanan Halbert, New Zealand First's Daryl Harbraken, the Green's Hūhana Lyndon and Opportunity's Daniel Eb all attended, with each asked to talk for two minutes about health.

World.title: Hawks complete stunning upset over Freo to clinch prelim berth
World.content:
James Sicily (right) had a huge night in the Hawks' backline as his team took care of the Dockers in the west (Getty Images)

The Hawks kicked six goals to one in a dominant first half in Thursday night's clash to set up the 10.12 (72) to 5.10 (40) win and secure a home preliminary final.

Fremantle, who had been a perfect 12-0 at Perth Stadium this season, will now confront either Carlton or Geelong in a cut-throat semi-final in Perth next week.

The Dockers were a dominant force during the home-and-away season, stringing together a 14-game winning streak at one stage on the way to a league-best 19-4 record.

But the minor premiers looked overawed in the finals cauldron on Thursday night in front of 59,446 fans — Fremantle's largest ever home crowd.

Fremantle's first-half return of 1.4 (10) was their lowest such score in a final, even worse than the 1.6 (12) they kicked across the opening two quarters of their 2013 grand final loss to the Hawks.

The Dockers will now have to win their semi-final and then an away preliminary final in order to make their first grand final since 2013.

Sicily, Tom Barrass and Josh Battle were rocks in defence, keeping Jye Amiss, Josh Treacy and Patrick Voss to two goals and 19 disposals between the three of them.

Treacy's first kick of the game — a set-shot goal — only arrived with five minutes remaining in the match.

Hawks veteran Jack Gunston kicked two clutch goals in the first-half onslaught, while Dylan Moore chipped in with two majors.

Watson was a human highlights reel at times on the way to two goals from 19 disposals.

"The belief in the group's outstanding," Watson told Fox Sports after the match.

"We knew it was going to be hot. It was hot early, but the boys stood up well."

Fremantle ruckman Luke Jackson kicked the opening goal of the match, but the rest of the first half belonged to Hawthorn as their slick ball movement and fierce tackling left the Dockers looking second-rate at times.

Watson's soccered goal from nearly 20m out sparked a run of four consecutive goals as the Hawks took a surprise 28-9 lead into quarter-time.

Hawthorn's pressure continued to be off the charts in the second term.
