Live Photo comments are now available globally, while photo carousel comments are rolling out globally over the next month.

Tech.title: GPT-6 Astra Is Here—and OpenAI Thinks It May Kick Off the AGI Era
Tech.content:
OpenAI announced Thursday the launch of its next generation AI model, GPT-6 Astra, which the company claims is state of the art at navigating computers and web browsers, writing software, and solving difficult math problems.

It plans to make GPT-6 Astra available to paid customers in the coming days, starting with enterprise clients in its Daybreak early access program, followed by ChatGPT Plus, Pro, and Business plan subscribers. OpenAI did not say whether GPT-6 Astra will be available to free users of ChatGPT.

In a press briefing with reporters, OpenAI executives made it clear that they feel very confident about the company’s latest AI model. President and cofounder Greg Brockman says he personally believes the world is now in the era of artificial general intelligence, or AI systems that are generally smarter than humans.

“It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” Brockman told reporters. “I think that if we fast forward a couple of years, when we look back and say, ‘When was it really that AGI was created?’ I think it's going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model."

OpenAI is releasing GPT-6 Astra at a critical moment for the company. The ChatGPT maker is trying to rapidly advance its technology and boost sales ahead of a planned initial offering while simultaneously avoiding compromising on safety and security. OpenAI is also facing stiff competition from Anthropic, its most important rival, which is also working on an upcoming IPO.

In a blog post, OpenAI calls GPT-6 Astra the “world’s best computer use model,” claiming it can navigate computers and web browsers on behalf of humans far better than its predecessors. AI companies have historically struggled to make models that can reliably browse websites, fill out forms, and manipulate software tools quickly and accurately enough to replace humans. In tests, OpenAI says GPT-6 Astra was able to book DMV appointments, search for job listings, and apartment hunt faster than the average person could.

The company also claims GPT-6 Astra is also the most safe and aligned AI model OpenAI has ever released. Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, told reporters that the company is monitoring GPT-6 Astra’s chain-of-thought—the model’s internal scratchpad it uses to work through problems—to ensure it is deployed safely. However, Pachocki said that making sure advanced AI models don’t cause unintended harm is increasingly a challenge, and may present a bottleneck to further AI progress.

“We kind of take this visibility for granted, and we are seeing that as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging,” said Pachocki. “We think confidence in monitoring may constrain further development, because we would not accept degradation in our ability to monitor model alignment beyond a certain level. We would withhold scaling until we can regain enough confidence.”

Tech.title: OpenAI Cut Off a Billion-Dollar Customer to Avoid Elon Musk
Tech.content:
In a late-night blog post last Friday, OpenAI said it would wind down its partnership with Cursor, the startup behind one of the most popular AI coding tools on the market. The reason OpenAI gave for the decision is effectively that it can’t trust Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX recently acquired Cursor in a $60 billion deal.

In doing so, OpenAI walked away from one of its most important customers. Cursor has long paid OpenAI fees to offer the ChatGPT-maker’s models to developers using its AI coding editor. At the start of 2026, Cursor was one of OpenAI’s top five customers in terms of revenue, people familiar with the matter tell WIRED. By the spring of this year, OpenAI estimated Cursor would bring in more than $1 billion in annualized revenue for the ChatGPT maker, based on the partnership’s performance at that time, the people said.

The figures, which have not been previously reported, indicate the financial loss OpenAI is willing to take on to avoid doing business with Musk. OpenAI declined to comment. Representatives for SpaceX and Cursor did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment.

“We are making this choice because we cannot be confident that SpaceX will use our technology within our terms of service, based on our experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts,” said OpenAI in the blog post.

As OpenAI prepares to go public next year, it’s trying to show investors a more stable business—ideally one that doesn’t rely so heavily on the goodwill of Musk. OpenAI reportedly now generates more than $40 billion in annualized revenue, drawing on several different lines of business, including subscriptions, ads in ChatGPT, and selling access to its AI coding tool, Codex.

Losing a major customer like Cursor may not hurt OpenAI financially as much as it once would have, but it was certainly a difficult decision. The company acknowledged in its blog post that ending the partnership may damage its standing with developers—a community it has spent years carefully working to win over—by cutting off a major channel they use to access OpenAI’s models.

Michael Truell, Cursor’s founder and CEO, who is now leading teams at SpaceX, responded publicly to OpenAI’s announcement hours later on Friday in a post on X, claiming that the ChatGPT-maker’s models only “serve about 5% of Cursor user traffic.” The comment seemed designed to imply that OpenAI’s models weren’t very popular with developers using Cursor, and wouldn’t meaningfully affect its business.

OpenAI’s head of core products, Thibault Sottiaux, was quick to point out that token usage is “not a proxy for revenue nor value created,” and asked Truell to “share the math” behind the 5 percent number.

WIRED previously reported that Cursor leaders hoped to remain a platform for third-party AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic, even after the SpaceX acquisition. Some AI insiders considered that wishful thinking, assuming that Cursor and OpenAI’s breakup has long been a foregone conclusion. As OpenAI builds Codex into a large AI coding business, it increasingly finds itself competing with Cursor for customers. Nevertheless, the companies have operated relatively peacefully, as partners and competitors, for well over a year.

Evidently, that arrangement was no longer possible with Musk in control of Cursor. OpenAI may have determined that its Cursor partnership was not worth the risk that SpaceX might distill its best AI models. The company noted in its blog post that, earlier this year, Musk seemingly said that xAI—now a part of SpaceX—used OpenAI’s models to train its own. The apparent admission came during Musk’s deposition in his lawsuit against OpenAI, in which he claimed that Sam Altman and Greg Brockman had stolen a charity they created together roughly a decade ago. A federal jury dismissed the suit earlier this year.

Tech.title: Lenovo’s Project AeroBlade Fanless Laptop Takes Thin and Light to the Extreme
Tech.content:
Lenovo is well-known for its creative, if wacky, concept laptops, usually involving some sort of display trickery. But at the IFA Berlin 2026 consumer electronics trade show, the company showed a proof of concept that actually looks production-ready.

The Project AeroBlade Concept laptop is built around a new active cooling technology from Frore Systems that uses air pressure—instead of fans, heatsinks, and large vents—to expel heat from the CPU. That means thinner laptop designs and quieter operation, and the space savings allow for larger batteries. According to Lenovo, it could reimagine how future high-performance laptops are designed.

Under Pressure

Photograph: Les Shu Photograph: Les Shu

Lenovo is the first computer manufacturer to unveil a laptop that uses Frore’s AirJet Mini fanless air-cooling technology. Frore is known for its liquid-cooling tech that’s used in data centers, but the AirJet is designed for consumer computers.

Dubbed the Lenovo Active Flow Thermal Solution, the AirJet module pulls ambient air that’s inside the laptop to create 2,000 Pascals of back pressure (around 124 miles per hour). This high-speed air is then spread onto a copper base layer through tiny jets in the AirJet module, which Frore claims will disrupt the boundary layer that causes heat buildup and throttling. Without a boundary layer, the processor’s heat is dissipated out the back. Lenovo had a motherboard sample from the AeroBlade concept laptop that showed four embedded AirJet modules, located along the top of the laptop.

Frore says each AirJet module can create 10 times the back pressure of a regular laptop fan and can pull and expel air without needing many vents. Lenovo claims the Active Flow Thermal Solution uses the same power as a traditional fan, but it’s debris- and water-resistant.

While Lenovo may be the first to demo a laptop using AirJet, it’s not an exclusive partnership, so we could see other laptop makers employ it.

So Light, It’s Dreamy

The circuit board is surrounded by AirJet Mini modules.

With its typical, unassuming laptop design, nothing about the AeroBlade Concept screams that it’s a concept. But at 10 mm thin and weighing 1.8 pounds, you can’t help but think there’s something special. With a magnesium-aluminum body, it’s so lightweight that it makes some of the current lightest laptops, like the Asus Zenbook A14 or MacBook Air, feel downright heavy. I spent longer than I should have just lifting it up and down, and marveling at its portability.

Tech.title: I Got a Brief Look at ‘Guild Wars 3,’ and I’m Excited
Tech.content:
Hardly a year goes by without me whistling the Guild Wars 2 loading theme, rewatching clips of the original to soak up that Pre-Searing Ascalon nostalgia, or subjecting my wife to yet another Grawl impression. (Gui-la-la!)

That's how monumental ArenaNet's MMORPG has been in my life. So you can understand my excitement when the game developer announced Guild Wars 3 earlier this summer, with a beta set to launch in late 2027.

I spent countless hours playing Guild Wars in middle school and high school, and an ungodly amount of time playing Guild Wars 2 with my roommates in college. Guild Wars always felt like the dark horse in the MMORPG world, never reaching the scale and attention of World of Warcraft or Final Fantasy XI, yet maintaining a massive user base with a cult-like following. (It uniquely did not require a monthly subscription.) You wouldn't hear anyone talking about it in the school cafeteria like you would the other two titles (I was not a Cool Kid). Still, it always had a grand scale of wonder, adventure, and lore that drew me in—props to my older brother for discovering the game and its many discs, and building a PC to run it.

Guild Wars 3's setting predates the events of Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2, which means you don't really need to know anything about the series to dive in. It marks the first time the franchise is heading to console with a PlayStation 5 release alongside PC. And while developers typically wind down support for predecessor titles ahead of a sequel, ArenaNet plans to maintain both the original Guild Wars and Guild Wars 2 for years to come. (It recently released the original game as Guild Wars Reforged with system enhancements and a mobile port.)

Details on the game—built on Unreal Engine 5 and in development for 4 years—are limited, but ArenaNet gave me a brief glimpse of early alpha footage showcasing gameplay components that have me excited to jump back into the world of Tyria.

Joy of Movement

Photograph: Courtesy of ArenaNet

Gliding is already a movement mechanic in Guild Wars 2, but when you stop and start running, the transitions are awkward and slow. All of that is becoming more fluid in Guild Wars 3, alongside some new range of movements. In some ways, it brings the game closer to an action RPG.

Tech.title: Nvidia RTX Spark ‘Superchip’: The First AI PCs Are Here
Tech.content:
Three months ago, Nvidia took the wraps off its RTX Spark “superchip” and a handful of future laptops that would use it. It felt like a consequential moment in the history of the PC, despite all the questions that remained.

And now, as announced at the IFA 2026 tech show in Berlin, we’ve had our first hands-on look at one of these laptops, as well as some announcements around RTX Spark-powered mini desktop PCs. Demand for running agentic AI workflows like OpenClaw locally on your computer keeps rising, and these new PCs look like they are designed specifically to feed it.

Nvidia Alternatives to the MacBook Pro

Photograph: Les Shu Photograph: Les Shu

The laptop in question is the Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1, a 16-inch laptop with a 360-degree hinge. As I assumed it would, this thing looks incredibly premium, aiming to be a MacBook Pro competitor in every aspect. The OLED touch display has a sharp 2880 x 1800 resolution and a 120-Hz refresh rate. The whole chassis is surrounded by rounded metallic edges and some very thin display bezels. Other high-end features we don’t typically see include a six-speaker sound system and a 9.2-megapixel webcam.

But here’s the important bit: It’s 0.69 inches thick, just 0.03 inches shy of the 16-inch MacBook Pro. That’s possible thanks to Nvidia’s Arm-based chip under the hood, which combines a Grace CPU with “up to 20 cores” and a Blackwell RTX GPU with “up to 6,144 cores.” The CPU, GPU, and memory are packaged together into a single system-on-a-chip (SoC), sharing more in common with Apple silicon than a conventional Windows laptop. Based purely on core count alone, that would theoretically put the integrated GPU capability of this chip somewhere between an RTX 5070 Ti and an RTX 5080 as found on laptops available today. Those specs also indicate that lower-powered configurations will be sold, though we don’t know how broad the performance range will be. There was no mention of battery-life claims, though presumably one benefit of using an Arm-based SoC (rather than a discrete GPU) is greater efficiency and, thus, better battery life.

Tech.title: Nvidia’s Hugging Face Acquisition Is a $12.9 Billion Bet on Open-Source AI
Tech.content:
Nvidia has agreed to acquire Hugging Face, which makes online developer tools and maintains a massive library of open-source data sets, for nearly $13 billion. While the deal had been rumored for weeks, the companies made it official Thursday morning.

The deal signals Nvidia’s seriousness about being steeped in the software side of generative AI development as well as in infrastructure. Nvidia already offers customers a suite of free, customizable open-weights AI models, known as Nemotron. As part of its announcement, Nvidia committed to maintaining Hugging Face’s current open standards, suggesting that the chipmaker is positioning itself as an even greater resource for developers looking to access cutting-edge, nonproprietary tools.

The move also underscores Nvidia’s position that open-weights models are better for the tech industry than closed, proprietary AI models like those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic. Earlier this month, Nvidia rallied more than 80 companies to sign an open letter asking the US government to defend open-weight AI models. Nvidia also launched an initiative called SAFE, or Shared AI Findings Exchange, that encouraged tech companies to “confidentially collect and analyze AI incidents and near misses, identify recurring control failures and publish evidence-based operating recommendations that reduce systemic risk.”

“Open models let startups, businesses, universities and public institutions build on advanced capabilities without training every model from scratch,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in the press release announcing the deal. “AI advances faster when people can build together.”

Nvidia’s embrace of open-source software and open-weights AI might seem like an abrupt turn, especially given that CUDA, the software layer for its highly coveted GPUs, is itself proprietary. But as frontier AI labs and some of the large hyperscalers, including Amazon and Meta, seek to build their own custom chips, Nvidia has begun to position itself as a maker of not just GPUs but also high-performance CPUs, and has widened its software offerings in order to keep developers building on Nvidia’s platforms.

Business Insider previously reported that the two companies were in talks, and The Information later reported that a deal had been reached.

Hugging Face was founded a decade ago by three French entrepreneurs in New York City, who wanted to launch an AI “companion” app. That didn’t catch on, but the team’s efforts to build their own natural language processing (NLP) tools inspired their next move: making complex tech tools more accessible to developers. Hugging Face eventually became a platform for developers to freely share source code, data sets, and, in the generative AI era, large language models.

“Open-source AI is at an inflection point,” wrote Hugging Face cofounder and CEO Clément Delangue in a post on X announcing the acquisition. “Thanks to the community, we’ve shown that it can be a complement, and even an alternative, to closed-source APIs. But for it to happen at larger scale, it needs more compute, more support, more collaboration and more visibility.”

According to PitchBook data, Hugging Face had raised nearly $400 million in venture capital funding as of December 2025. Some of its backers include Betaworks, Lux Capital, Sequoia Ventures, Coatue, and Addition. Notable individual investors include Greg Brockman, Richard Socher, and the NBA player Kevin Durant.

Hugging Face has more recently been front and center after its platform was hacked by AI agents from OpenAI. The incident sparked a broader conversation across the tech industry about the safety, security, and manageability of the autonomous agents being touted by top AI companies.

In a 2023 interview with CNBC Delangue predicted that the number of developers working with AI models would soar, and estimated that within five years, “you’re going to have like 100 million AI builders. And if all of them use Hugging Face all day, every day, we’ll obviously be in a good position.”

Obviously, Nvidia seems to agree.

Tech.title: Scientists Have Found the Most Convincing Evidence Yet of a Dark Matter Particle
Tech.content:
More than a kilometer underground, in what used to be a gold mine, inside a tank filled with tons of liquid xenon, “something” struck the nucleus of an atom. The tiny collision left an unusual energy signature that researchers are still unable to explain, but the scientists behind the experiment believe this could be the most convincing physical evidence of dark matter to date.

Dark matter is one of the most important and elusive substances in astrophysics. Though it makes up about 85 percent of the matter in the universe, we can’t observe it directly because it doesn’t interact with light or much else. Most of the evidence for its existence comes from its gravitational effects, the mass of dark matter having tugged on the atoms of the early universe to form stars, galaxies, and the vast web of intergalactic structures visible today.

But the enigma of dark matter is complex. Scientists don’t even know what it is made of, whether it’s a single type of particle or an entire set of particles that interact with one another in ways we do not yet understand. The most fantastical explanations even suggest that it consists of black holes. One of the most widely studied theories on dark matter has dubbed its components WIMPs, short for Weakly Interacting Massive Particles, meaning the particles have a mass and thus a gravitational pull but otherwise interact weakly with conventional matter.

If WIMPs exist and are part of the dark matter of our galaxy, enormous quantities of them could be passing through the Earth continuously without leaving a trace. However, it is possible that, very occasionally, one might interact with an atomic nucleus and transfer some of its energy to it, which is why an inexplicable collision is exciting in the world of particle physics.

In the strange disturbance recorded at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in South Dakota, the detector monitoring the tank recorded that a xenon nucleus received energy and recoiled. Though researchers have not yet been able to satisfactorily explain the cause, some models suggest a WIMP could produce such a reaction.

The scientists stated that this single event is statistically too small to be considered the discovery of a new particle. In 220 days of observations conducted between 2023 and 2024, only one such anomaly occurred. “With only one event, we don’t want to get ahead of ourselves. We are not claiming to have seen dark matter. But we have seen something interesting that we want to share with the scientific community for their input,” Rick Gaitskell, a professor at Brown University and a member of the team leading the project, said in a press release.

The team behind the experiment has published their study as a preprint, meaning it has not yet been peer reviewed. They have, however, presented the results to the scientific community at the 2026 TeV Particle Astrophysics Conference in Japan.

Discoveries made around dark matter tend to elicit this kind of restrained excitement. When in November 2025 a team of Japanese astronomers announced that they had seen signs of dark matter in the Milky Way, they too advised the research community not to count their chickens.

But even if cautious, there are reasons for enthusiasm. If the impact was caused by dark matter, there is enough evidence for researchers to begin characterizing the responsible particle. For example, the team has already calculated that, under the WIMP models they analyzed, the particle is about 200 times more massive than a proton. The impact could help us understand how this type of matter interacts with conventional matter.

Tech.title: Ugly AI Food Photos Are Only the Beginning
Tech.content:
I can’t stop staring at the AI-slop images of Mexican food I see during my morning walk to work. On the menu posted outside, the taco truck displays lunch options that appear uncanny and unappetizing, as if an alien who’s never eaten human food before drew a taco from memory. This food truck is not alone in putting AI-generated images on its menu. It’s everywhere.

AI menu slop is now going viral for being disgusting, and these posters seem to be an evolution of the “ChatGPT flyer pandemic.” Whether it’s a maggot-infested burrito or a plasticky pasta, consumers are expressing online how gross these fabricated images look. The aesthetic is distinctively off-putting, sometimes with random holes throughout a dish or otherworldly cuts of meat served as an entree.

The images are immediately noticeable but only scratch the surface of how generative AI tools have already overhauled restaurant menus. Sellers aren’t just generating AI images of burgers, they’re also relying on AI to decide what goes in between those two buns.

Digital Demands

The birth of the online menu set us on the path toward these monstrosities. More consumers started deciding what to eat based on online menus and by ordering delivery from their phones to their doorstep. Faced with growing pressure, restaurant owners digitized their menus and created additional visuals.

Stores wanted to capitalize on delivery sales and leaned into generative AI images, vying for a visibility boost on third-party apps like DoorDash without paying for a photoshoot. While the most powerful models currently on the market can output photorealistic images of food, many of these images appear to be generated by tools with worse capabilities, like the default setting of a free chatbot.

“I went to order pizza one night on Uber Eats,” says Brendan Sweeney, CEO and cofounder of Popmenu, a digital marketing software company for restaurants. “There were five different pizza places that were using the same AI-generated image.” He says if the food image appears “completely inauthentic” and “obviously AI,” then the restaurant is making a worse decision than foregoing photography altogether.

What was originally generated to satisfy digital demand is now creeping its way into the physical world. AI menu slop expanded from its online origins into posters in coffee shops and signs displayed as deli menus. Restaurant owners sometimes seem oblivious to how off-putting low-quality image generations look.

TasteGPT

Noticeably AI-generated images stand out on modern menus for all the wrong reasons. But AI tools are influencing what appears on your local coffee shop’s menu, beyond just images.

Tastewise, one of the largest data insights companies in the food and beverage industry, partners with companies like Nestlé, PepsiCo, and Kraft Heinz. It’s currently all-in on “agentic” automations for every step of the food creation process.

Tastewise’s library of automations is meant to help companies decide what foods to sell and how to sell them. There’s an agent to help you track how product launches are going, an agent to test new concepts (banana creatine smoothies, anyone?), and an agent to find opportunity gaps in current menus.

“I think the bigger question for them is how do they guide and train the AI on what should be in that burger and what should be on the menu,” says Michael Bortinger, Tastewise’s director of marketing and partnerships. “We have billions of data points understanding what consumers are doing with food, what’s actually happening on menus and in the retail landscape.”

Tech.title: OpenAI’s Astra Is Here: What to Know About GPT-6
Tech.content:
The next flagship generation of ChatGPT is here. OpenAI announced on Thursday that it is beginning to roll out GPT-6-Astra, which president Greg Brockman called a “generational leap in capability” that brings the frontier fully into the “AGI era.”

According to evaluations released by OpenAI, Astra performed better than its previous family of models, GPT-5.6, and its flagship model Sol. On computer-use tasks, it touted higher performance in less time. Like every model release, OpenAI says the new one (Astra) is better than the previous ones on a number of topics, including coding, alignment and safety.

Astra is also built to run more and better AI agents, or bots that can handle autonomous tasks. That’s a key piece for workplaces adopting AI, as well as for Astra’s improved ability to create documents, spreadsheets and presentations based on specific information on your laptop (not just random internet garbage).

To create Astra, OpenAI did “by far our largest scale training run,” Aidan Clark, vice president of research, told reporters. The company pre-trained the model on more than 100,000 GPUs, meaning it used a very significant amount of compute. Astra was also OpenAI’s first model that involved previous AI models very heavily in the training process, with the older generations helping train the new one.

“This is really only achievable because everything from the data center networking to inference kernels to the shape of Astra itself is all designed from the ground up to enable this level of training scale,” Clark told reporters on Thursday. “It’s this scale of pre-training which gives Astra a deeper and more robust understanding of the world.”

But Astra may be one of the last big flagship models from OpenAI, at least for the immediate future. In August, the company said it was going to pause its work training new models due to cybersecurity concerns. OpenAI, along with Anthropic and Meta, had some of its AI agents breach its training environments and hack websites this summer, reigniting concerns about AI’s impact on cybersecurity.

OpenAI said Astra has been extensively tested for cybersecurity-related vulnerabilities, and it will be staggering its rollout. GPT-6-Astra will be available to approved cybersecurity defenders in OpenAI’s Daybreak program starting on Thursday, with plans to bring the new model to paying ChatGPT subscribers and its API over the next several days.

OpenAI said the new model was approved by the White House after it went through the Trump administration’s voluntary review framework. The specifics of that process — what is evaluated and how — are still not public.

Jakub Pachocki, the company’s chief scientist, said international shared safety standards are necessary for the industry as AI models (and their capabilities) develop.

“As AI takes on more of its own development, we need to keep people meaningfully involved,” Pachocki said. “People must remain able to decide the direction of further progress and the future that it creates.”

Tech.title: Dyson’s New Robot Vacuums Aim at Shark With UV Stain Detection and Powerful Scrubbing
Tech.content:
Dyson makes some fantastic cordless vacuums, and many of its models have earned top spots in our lab-tested picks. Our lab testing history for Dyson’s robot vacuums is a bit of a mixed bag, with the older models we’ve tested not always offering the cleaning performance of top competitors like Shark, Roborock, Dreame and iRobot.

Dyson’s new Nurovi robot vacuum range, consisting of three new models, may be set to change that by incorporating stain detection and stain-cleaning features we’ve seen on models like the Shark UV Reveal, with improved AI recognition.

“Now we have shifted from purely mechanical devices to intelligent machines that can see, think and respond,” said Jake Dyson, chief engineer at Dyson in a press statement. “We’re using artificial intelligence, vision systems and machine learning to allow the machines to understand the environment they are operating in. The approach is the same, whether it’s operating in your mouth, on your hair or around your home.”

The R3 Nurovi uses UV light, AI and more advanced stain detection to clean stains. Tara Brown/CNET

I was able to see all three units in action prior to IFA Berlin 2026 in Dyson’s demo areas, which showcased their ability to clean in tight spaces and avoid obstacles. While the demos were limited in scope, the design changes and improvements were promising.

The $1,199 R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV is the top-end model in Dyson’s Nurovi lineup that will be available on Sept. 15. It uses a mix of UV light, AI vision and the green LED illumination we’ve seen on Dyson’s cordless vacuum models to identify 200 different types of household substances and spills. Once it detects spills, Dyson says it uses a 12-point hydration system to apply 158-degree Fahrenheit water to the self-cleaning roller mop to scrub stains. The roller itself is microfiber and extends 1.6 inches to the edges. It also features a 30,000-pascal motor, a self-emptying cyclonic bagless dustbin, and a self-cleaning dock, as we’ve seen with the other Spot+Scrub models.

I’ve certainly seen more companies try to tackle the problem of cleaning older, tough and dried stains, with differing degrees of success, so I’ll be interested in seeing how the Nurovi lineup fares in our lab testing.

The R1 Nurovi is only for dry cleaning for hard floors and carpet. Tara Brown/CNET

The $699 R2 Nurovi Wash+Dry comes in at the middle of the pack in price. The big feature here is the completely redesigned Reuleaux triangle mopping pads, rather than traditional circular spinning pads or a roller like the R3. It’s certainly the most distinctive mopping pad design I’ve ever seen, and a Dyson representative justified it by pointing out that the triangles have a constant width and movement that allow them to wash directly into square corners, unlike circular mopping pads that miss spots.

The R2 also uses 167-degree Fahrenheit heated water to remove more stubborn stains. It has a twin-capture system that can mechanically sweep up larger debris like a broom, while the suction power is reserved for finer dust particles. It also comes with an acoustic piezo sensor that adjusts suction based on the floor type and dust levels. It’ll be available Sept. 3 exclusively at Costco.



The $549 R1 Nurovi Dry is Dyson’s most basic vacuum model. As the name suggests, it’s only for dry cleaning of hard floors and carpet. However, it features the same twin-capture system as the R2 with a side-sweeper that has a web connector to brush or guide debris into the airflow path and reduce hair tangles.

Dyson

Finally, while it’s not a robot vacuum, Dyson has also updated and improved its PencilWash mop with the new W1 PencilWash+Dok. The new cleaner is slimmer and lighter than the older model, includes a more absorbent roller, a hygienic waste system, and self-cleaning features built into the dock. It will cost $349 and will be available in the fall.

I’m expecting to lab test all of the new models in this lineup, and we should have results in the coming months.

Editors’ note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: I Was Disappointed by Miele’s Last Vacuums, but the New Lineup Changed My Mind
Tech.content:
Miele is known as one of the most reputable brands for home appliances and cleaning, but when we lab tested the Miele HX2 cordless vacuum last year, we were a little let down by it — it performed poorly in sand tests for low and midpile carpet, and the design was a little finicky to use compared to lightweight competition from Dyson and Shark. It also cost $1,100 at full price, making it a hard sell.

With this in mind, when Miele showed me its new HX3 and HX3 Plus Aqua, I was skeptical it would be more than an incremental jump, but after spending some time using it at the Miele Experience Center in Manhattan, I came away impressed by several of the changes.

Ajay Kumar/CNET

To start with, while there hasn’t been a complete redesign, one of the big changes is rebalancing the weight distribution so that more of it is at the bottom, reducing the strain up top when you’re vacuuming. You can also change out where the motor and waste bin are, depending on how you attach the nozzles, so it’s up to you how you want the weight to fall, though this was also a feature on the HX2.

A Miele representative showed me an example of how you might want it more top-heavy when you’re using it to clean the corners of ceilings and higher-up spots. You can also convert it fairly easily back into the self-standing vacuum mode, a traditional stick vac or a handheld.

There are also other quality-of-life tweaks, like push-button controls, easier dustbin emptying, finer particle capture, automatic flooring-type detection and the ability to stand upright. It offers 70 minutes of running time, which Miele says should be good enough to clean 1,700 square feet in a single charge, and some models have an extended battery included for even more juice. All key things that I value when vacuuming.

Ajay Kumar/CNET

The big improvements come in performance. The HX3 has notably better pickup on both carpet and hard flooring. The Miele representatives even helpfully provided me with some condiments to imitate sand and pet hair to try to suction up from the carpet. While it wasn’t quite the same as CNET’s rigorous lab testing, the outcome of my vacuuming session offered solid results. The HX3 was able to remove most or all of the pet hair with a single back-and-forth motion, while the imitation sand was no challenge at all on hardwood (though that’s true of most vacuums and robot vacuums we test).

Overall, the HX3 seemed to do a great job of picking up dirt and debris from different floor types. There’s also a powerful Boost mode that can give you extra suction beyond even the highest setting, but it drains the battery the fastest, so it’s limited to just 10 seconds.

The HX3 Plus Aqua is basically the same as the regular HX3; it just comes with Miele’s first mopping attachment, the Aqua Twister Floorhead. It consists of dual spinning mop pads that are machine washable, a 300-milliliter water tank and a 360-degree light. I also took the mopping attachment for a spin, trying out its different modes on hard flooring to clean stains and dirt. Again, the results were impressive, with the amount of water being dispensed fully adjustable, allowing you to tackle bigger messes and spills. When the mopping head is attached, Boost mode also dispenses more water for 30 seconds, so it’s good to see the feature has been integrated into both cleaning heads.

Ajay Kumar/CNET

While there are two distinct models, the HX3 and HX3 Plus Aqua, there’s a somewhat more consumer-friendly price spread: The base HX3 starts at $849, while the top-tier HX3 Aqua Plus, with all the accessories, including the mopping head, runs $1,249. Tech.title: Motorola Spiffs Up the Razr With Swarovski Meteorite Finish, Adds Watch Ultra and Edge 70 Plus
Tech.content:
I’ve long admired Motorola’s commitment to making fun phones, and especially fun foldable phones. It’s in the company’s DNA, which is why it’s not a surprise — but still a delight — to see it zhuzh up the already fun and flirty Motorola Razr 2026 (or Razr 70, as it’s known in Europe) with Swarovski crystals and a Pantone meteorite (that’s black, to you and me) color variant.

The phone, which Motorola unveiled at IFA in Berlin, has a quilted back studded with 35 hand-positioned crystals and an additional 32-facet crystal on the hinge for that extra razzle-dazzle. We scored the original version an 8/10 in our review, praising its great cover screen and fast charging capability. This base model retails for $800, but the limited edition Swarovski version is listed for a price of 1,000 euros ($1,159).

Two further phones round out Motorola’s handset offering at IFA: the Motorola Edge 70 Plus and Edge 70 Plus Neo. They’re part of the same line of phones as the Edge 70, announced last November, which stood out for being ultra thin at 5.99mm and having a 4,800-mAh battery.

The Edge 70 Plus and Neo aren’t quite as thin, measuring 8.49mm each, but they have even bigger batteries — a whopping 6,500-mAh and 7,000-mAh, respectively. These phones should easily last you all day and then some.

As well as a slight difference in battery size, the two models are set apart by their cameras. Both have a 2-megapixel macro camera and 32-megapixel front camera, but the Edge 70 Plus has a 200-megapixel main camera, whereas the Edge 70 Plus Neo packs a 50-megapixel Sony LYTIA 710 sensor.

Motorola’s phones are all based on Pantone colors. Motorola/CNET

The Neo might boast fewer megapixels, but that Sony sensor marks it out as superior, promising greater dynamic range with less image noise, especially in low-light situations. Keep in mind that more megapixels doesn’t mean a better image — if you’re looking for the phone with the better camera, the Neo is the one for you.

Both phones feature a 6.78-inch Extreme AMOLED screen and should offer strong performance for mid-range devices thanks to a Snapdragon 7s Gen 3 processor. They’ll be available in a range of Pantone shades, including mountain view (green), gray lilac (mauve), milky blue (blue) and sage (a different shade of green).

Moto Watch Ultra

Motorola also unveiled the Moto Watch Ultra at IFA, which is an LTE version of the Moto Watch — a device we reviewed earlier this year. This new watch packs a bigger screen — a 1.5-inch OLED display, compared to the earlier watch’s 1.43 inches, but it’s also a hair thinner at 46mm rather than 47mm.

The new Moto Watch comes with LTE. Motorola/CNET

In our review we praised the watch for its display, its solid battery performance and the partnership with Polar, which continues to lend its science-backed expertise on sleep and activity tracking to Motorola for the Watch Ultra.

We were less impressed with the watch’s running tracking, which overcounted steps. Let’s hope Motorola has fixed this in the Watch Ultra, which also offers a running coach. In Europe, the Watch Ultra’s price is listed as 429 euros ($497) — significantly more than the Moto Watch, which retails for $150.

Motorola’s IFA portfolio is rounded out by the Moto Snap Wireless Charger, which provides up to 25-watt fast wireless charging to Qi-compatible products, and up to 30 watts for supported Motorola devices, thanks to the company’s own charging protocol.

Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs for the IFA conference were covered in part by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Tech.title: Lenovo Showcases Silent Ultraportable and Latest Rollable Laptop Concepts at IFA 2026
Tech.content:
When it comes time for a big computing show, you can always count on Lenovo to exhibit some wacky proof-of-concept machines.

At CES 2026, for instance, the Chinese company debuted an AI-powered tracking webcam and a horizontal rollable gaming laptop display. Just this year, my personal favorite gaming handheld prototype debuted at Mobile World Congress, alongside a detachable dual-screen ThinkBook concept. Now, Lenovo’s coming out swinging again with its IFA 2026 exhibition – the company debuted two new concepts this time around in Berlin.

Project Swan is a 14-inch consumer laptop that can easily be toted around from place to place, before its horizontally rolling screen extends to 17 inches for work or entertainment. Project AeroBlade introduces a completely new ventless cooling system that minimizes noise pollution and supposedly doesn’t require any major compromises in compute performance.

If theoretical and fantastical concepts aren’t what you’re looking for, you’re boring and probably lack whimsy. But fret not, because Lenovo debuted plenty of products that it’ll be bringing to market over the course of the next 12 months, including a new type of OLED monitor, beefy (and expensive) desktop PCs and a handful of new consumer laptops.

The 14-inch design of Project Swan makes it ultraportable, but the screen extends to 17 inches when you need it for work sessions or entertainment. Josh Goldman/CNET

The Project Swan concept takes Lenovo’s rollable laptop screens in a new direction

Lenovo has never shied away from funky device displays. The company released or has shown off concepts for computers with vertical motorized rolling screens, laptop displays that wrap around the top lid to show off widgets while closed and screens that turn to keep you centered in the built-in webcam. At this year’s Mobile World Congress, Lenovo even showcased a prototype handheld gaming console with a folding screen that works in horizontal and vertical configurations.

The company is keeping the ball rolling at IFA with Project Swan, its first horizontally expanding, rollable work laptop. The 14-inch device can extend into a 17-inch display at the touch of a button. It’s a very large screen packed into one of the most portable clamshell designs possible.

The Legion Pro Rollable, shown off at CES 2026, uses much the same technology — but that was a gaming-centric laptop, tailored toward first-person shooters and other games that benefit from a wide field of view. I’m not sure how folks will respond to the deluge of laptops with rollable displays, but by my estimation, the Project Swan concept is one of the most practical Lenovo has shown off yet.

This seems like the starting point for a solid workhorse laptop: I can imagine using it for work and packing it away for trips, then unfurling the screen to use the computer for periods of high-productivity multitasking – or as a portable entertainment center for movies and shows. If this concept ever comes to fruition, it might be the most family-oriented rollable in Lenovo’s stable.

Lenovo’s experimental new ventless cooling system, AirJet, rests on Project AeroBlade’s chassis. Josh Goldman/CNET

The Project AeroBlade concept might save your legs from getting toasted

I don’t know about you, but I’m tired of singeing my legs when I push my laptop a little too hard and the vents dump all that excess heat right into my lap. I also hate when I’m bundled up under a blanket and the blocked fans start whirring concerningly loud.

Lenovo’s Project AeroBlade feels like the type of concept device that would tangibly improve just about any laptop user’s experience. This 14-inch ultraportable laptop has a new fanless design that Lenovo says won’t compromise performance. Instead, there’s a single vent running along the hinge, which allows outside air to pass through the internal thermals. And moving air through the laptop aren’t fans but tiny modules that use ultrasonic vibrations. Lenovo calls this vibrating cooling tech AirJet.

At a press event in New York, a member of Lenovo’s design team explained that the new cooling design is more akin to “a bike pump than a leaf blower.” Whereas the average laptop dumps heat in a single direction, Project AeroBlade pulls in cool air from its surroundings and circulates it through the inside of the laptop.

Whether or not this iteration of Project AeroBlade comes to fruition, it’ll be interesting to see if Lenovo’s new cooling solution ever makes it to the market. A cooler, quieter and higher-performance system feels like more than a marketing gimmick – if it works as advertised, this could seriously sway consumers toward a better type of laptop design.

Lenovo’s ThinkVision P27UL-40 monitor is the company’s first commercially available IJP OLED display. Lenovo/CNET

The ThinkVision P27UL-40 monitor is Lenovo’s first InkJet printing OLED display

If you’re looking for a best-in-class monitor, odds are good you’re looking for a display with an OLED panel – the quicker response time gives the tech an edge over IPS LCDs. But while OLED monitors have become significantly more affordable over the past decade, they’re still a bit too pricey for some folks.

Those prices may start to come down an appreciable amount again in the near future, thanks to new inkjet-printing OLED tech. These displays literally use a printer to deposit organic material on a glass layer thousands of times per second.

The result is a display that doesn’t compromise color contrast or picture quality, though it hasn’t achieved anywhere close to the same level of brightness as traditional OLEDs. Some analysts believe the IJP OLEDs might cut production costs by up to 20%, and some of those savings will be passed on to the consumer.

Lenovo isn’t the first to create a consumer IJP OLED screen, but the ThinkVision P27UL-40 is the first inkjet-printed monitor the company is bringing to the market. This 27-inch monitor has a 3,840×2,160-pixel resolution panel and an up to 120Hz refresh rate.

The ThinkVision P27UL-40 will be released in March 2027, starting at $1,300, which is still a significant chunk of change. But if industry analysts are right, this might be the start of a trend leading to more competitively priced OLED monitors.

Other ThinkVision monitors also debuted at IFA 2026, but none of those models use the same IJP OLED technology as the ThinkVision P27UL-40. Instead, they’re rather standard LCD monitors.

The ThinkVision T32WD-4v is a 32-inch IPS monitor with 3,840×2,160-pixel resolution and an up to 120Hz refresh rate. It’ll start shipping in February next year and start at $900.

The ThinkVision T34WD-4v is the larger addition to the ThinkVision T series lineup: It’s a 34-inch VA monitor with 3,440×1,440-pixel resolution and an up-to-120Hz refresh rate. That monitor will start shipping in January with a starting price of $1,000.

Lenovo’s ThinkCentre X Ultra desktop has high compute performance with a price to match, but it’s packaged into the tiny form you see above. Lenovo/CNET

The ThinkCentre X Ultra desktop is a rather robust AI-first workhorse

If you’ve got enough pocket change to ignore the surging hardware costs spurred by the RAMageddon, maybe Lenovo’s new ThinkCentre X Ultra desktop PC is for you. This veritable powerhouse is an “AI-first” juggernaut, with a design crafted to optimize compute power (though a computer like this could realistically handle most tasks you throw at it).

This 4.4-pound computer is powered by AMD silicon, housing an up-to-Ryzen AI Max Plus Pro 495 processor. It features integrated graphics, up to 128GB of RAM and 8TB of system storage. There are two expansion slots for additional SSDs, assuming you have the cash for upgrades after buying this desktop. The ThinkCentre X Ultra will be released in November at a starting price of $3,700.

Alongside the ThinkCentre X Ultra, Lenovo is debuting two other desktop PCs. The 2.6-pound ThinkCentre M75q Gen 6 is even more compact than the Ultra, but still retains some beefy AMD processing power. This desktop is powered by up to Ryzen AI 7 Pro 450GE silicon, has integrated Radeon 860M graphics, up to 64GB of RAM and 4TB of storage space. The M75q Gen 6 will be available later this month at a starting price of $1,380.

The ThinkCentre M75s Gen 6, on the other hand, is the largest desktop PC in the new lineup. Weighing in at 10.6 pounds, this computer is powered by an up-to-Ryzen AI 7 Pro 450G processor, 64GB of RAM and 4TB of storage. Different configurations come with integrated Radeon 860M and Radeon RX 6400 8GB graphics. The M75s Gen 6 will be available next month at a starting price of $1,490.

I put my hands on the ThinkBook 14x Gen 2 at a press event in New York – it was an appreciably slim ultraportable clamshell design to refresh the lineup. Josh Goldman/CNET

Two new sleek and slim 14-inch ThinkBooks

Lenovo may not have debuted any wacky new ThinkBook concepts at IFA, but the company showed off two new 14-inch iterations of its popular work laptop lineup that will begin shipping soon.

The ThinkBook 14 Gen 9 is a balanced 2.8-pound laptop, packaging a decent 14-inch, 1,920×1,200-pixel resolution display and solid internal specs into a single clamshell. It’s powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus processor and a Qualcomm Adreno GPU, and has up to 32GB of LPDDR5x RAM and a 1TB SSD (with the option to slot in a second SSD). The ThinkBook 14 Gen 9 will be released next month with a starting price of $1,300.

The ThinkBook 14x Gen 2 is the sleek ultraportable offering, weighing just under 2.2 pounds. Lenovo packed some decent hardware into this clamshell despite its diminutive size, and the optional 2.8K OLED screen will provide snappy color contrast that’ll satisfy most folks.

The ThinkBook 14x Gen 2 is powered by Intel Core 7 Series 3 silicon, integrated graphics, up to 32GB of LPDDR5x memory and 2TB of storage space. It will be released in early 2027 and start at $1,000.

Tech.title: Nvidia PAIR Speeds Up AI Agents by Annexing PCs on Your Network
Tech.content:
Nvidia

Nvidia PAIR, which stands for Personal AI Router, is a clever solution to a problem a lot of us don’t have — at least not yet. It’s a new system for people who frequently need to run complex or GPU-intensive AI agents at home. If your agents’ tasks can be broken into multiple subagents that can work in parallel (so they don’t depend on each other), PAIR helps speed up the agent or free up the main system by offloading that work to other computers on the network.

In other words, I could, in theory, run PAIR on my desktop PC but let my MacBook Pros handle the onerous job of classifying and analyzing my tens of thousands of photos, or for you to manage your smart devices (I have a dumb home), while we individually play games on our PCs. It all stays local.

PAIR is open-source; it entered beta today and is available on Github. It’s also built on standards, including mDNS (for device discovery on the local network) and MTLS for security.

How it works

PAIR can work with Windows, Mac and Linux systems, though I think the primary system has to be running an RTX-class GPU. Nvidia doesn’t mention system requirements for Windows or Linux, but it does need a relatively recent Mac with an M4-generation processor or later. Because the agents run on the remote systems, the systems have to be equipped with and able to use the necessary AI models, and at the moment, it’s only compatible with the Ollama and LM Studio engines. (It’s not clear whether that includes the new LM Bionic.)

Once you’ve installed the software on each system and connected them, you run your agent, like Hermes Desktop or OpenClaw, on the primary system. The agent orchestrates the process, such as deciding and codifying what subagents need to be assigned, and sends the subagents to PAIR as if it were the engine (as a proxy). PAIR, in turn, assigns the subagents to the other computers and receives their results to feed back to the agent. The agent decides what needs to be run, and PAIR handles where to run it and manages communication between the agent and the subagents.

What it’s not

PAIR allocates subagents based on multiple criteria: whether a system is accepting assignments, if the requisite inference engine and model are installed on it, what a system’s current workload is and how much free GPU bandwidth it has. Nvidia says it’s working on expanding and refining those criteria. It has a dashboard view displaying real-time status.

The software doesn’t compensate for a less tractable problem: insufficient resources on the given systems. It doesn’t pool GPU processing or memory, so you can’t use it to run larger models if the systems can’t normally accommodate them. But if the various subagents run on separate systems, at least the parallel tasks won’t crowd a single memory pool. Nor does it break down subagents to work across systems. Each one gets assigned to a single system.

For it to work optimally, you presumably have to leave a lot of systems powered on that you might not otherwise want to. And it’s not clear what happens if someone decides to, say, stream video or play a game while a system is already in the middle of running a subagent.

Tech.title: Nvidia RTX Spark Systems Approach the Starting Line
Tech.content:
Launched on June 1 at Computex 2026 with a handful of big-name laptop partners, Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X designed-for-AI chips are still lacking any notable details beyond the basics. Only that there are two versions: a 20-CPU-core and 6,144-GPU-core version for laptops and desktops — which supports up to 128GB unified memory — and one with 18 CPU cores and 5,120 GPU cores — which supports only up to 32GB memory — that’s designated for laptops. But we do now have more precise availability information than “fall”: It’s expected next month, in October.

It strikes me as a bit odd that the 18-core version maxes out at only 32GB RAM, especially since it’s shared between the CPU and GPU. It seems like an awfully powerful chip that could potentially become bottlenecked by memory. On the other hand, that could be a power or space constraint, since it’s intended for light, thin laptop designs. But these are intended to be power systems — mainstream workstations, really — for AI and gaming.

As with all hardware announcements these days, there’s no pricing info available yet. Component cost volatility is driven by shortages caused by large-scale demand for AI silicon from data centers, which compete for chip and memory manufacturing and packaging resources. Nvidia is partly responsible, since it’s one of the biggest companies driving these installations.

So it’s anyone’s guess, even as close to shipping as we are, what the prices of these premium models will be. My fellow hardware sheriff Josh Goldman summarized the conundrum succinctly: “Workstation performance in a smaller, thinner, lighter package that no one can buy ’cause the costs are too high. Nvidia has dug itself an affordability hole it can’t get out of.”

Hardware’s coming

While I don’t expect it to lag behind existing competitors, take its performance claims with a grain of salt. In this case, Nvidia blithely says the Spark has a “1 petaflop GPU.” But that’s for its NVFP4 data type. FP4 is a low-precision type optimized for efficiency, meaning it prioritizes speed and low memory overhead over accuracy compared with higher-precision formats such as FP16 or FP32, which are also more common as a basis for comparison –especially since, as far as I can tell, no prosumer integrated GPUs support FP4 natively. The disadvantage of FP4 is that it’s more likely to experience rounding errors than the higher precision formats. In practice, that can mean, for example, lower detail or less variety during local image generation. (Procyon has a great visual example of what speed versus accuracy tradeoffs can mean for image generation.)

A rendering of Acer’s upcoming compact desktop, based on the RTX Spark N1X. Acer/CNET

Lenovo was one of the announced partners at launch, with its Yoga Pro 9n and Yoga 9n two-in-one, but at IFA, there were more concrete details and models to show. Unlike the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, which has a MiniLED backlit IPS display, the Lenovo models incorporate the reference design recommendation of Tandem OLED screens.

Tech.title: Dyson’s Huge Pipe-like Air Purifier Moves Like a Dune Sandworm and Blows Air Across the Room
Tech.content:
Dyson’s HushJet air purifiers have been some of the versatile air purifiers on the market, able to cool, purify and heat the air, so you get climate control capabilities in addition to purification. The new HushJet purifier range, announced at the IFA 2026 trade show in Berlin, incorporates all of these capabilities with a complete redesign and I was able to see all three models in person prior to the show.



The new HushJet models look like large curved pipes, a design Dyson calls the “HushJet Nozzle.” It incorporates the directed-fan capabilities of the HushJet MiniCool Fan that we loved for portable summer cooling, with the aerospace turbine design of the HushJet Compact, for more consistent performance and reduced noise and turbulence.



The largest and most impressive of the units is the $1,099 Dyson HushJet Big+Quiet Cool Pure+Formaldehyde. The name is a mouthful, but it’s the company’s largest air purifier, with the most powerful compressor, designed to handle multiroom air purification and mixing. It even has wheels so it can be moved from room to room (it’s not self-propelled, unfortunately), and controls that let the nozzle-like head move and rotate in a way that’s vaguely reminiscent of a Dune sandworm. The head can tilt up and down, letting you angle the airflow for direct cooling or broader room circulation.

Dyson

Impressively, despite the unit’s sheer size, I didn’t really hear the airflow except at the highest settings. Meanwhile, the sheer amount of air it emitted through the large, open demo area was impressive. I could really feel the air circulating and starting to clear up without it feeling like I was being blown directly by a fan. The unit can capture 99.99% of pollutants down to 0.01 microns and destroy formaldehyde, a chemical byproduct that can be present in many homes.

The medium-sized $599 HushJet Pure Cool+Formaldehyde is the unit I expect most people to get because it’s on the more reasonable side while still delivering powerful purification and cooling. Dyson says it can deliver three times the purification of predecessors and still clean large spaces while acting as a fan to provide personal cooling.

The $599 HushJet Hot Cool Pure+ is similar, but it adds heating capabilities in addition to the purification and cooling. Dyson describes it as a three-in-one unit that can also be useful as a space heater in the winter, not just a fan in the summer.



All three Dyson HushJet models are expected to launch in fall 2026, and we look forward to testing them at CNET Labs.
